paragraphs.text: OF OUR HOLY FATHER AND CONFESSOR THEODORE, ABBOT OF THE STUDIUM: FIRST BOOK. A SELECTION FROM HIS VARIOUS LETTERS, FROM THE FIRST AND SECOND EXILE.

1. To Plato, his spiritual father. What shall we say to you, O our sweetest Father, we who for God's sake have been orphaned of your holy heart? What gentle or joyful word shall we speak? We will not speak words of mourning and grief, complaining of this so-called exile. You taught us not to recognize any exile, since we are sojourners in all the earth, except one: falling away from God and being cast far from him by transgressing any one of his commandments. So we rejoice and are glad that, though we are unworthy of heaven and earth, we have nevertheless been [?counted worthy], together with you our holy one, to suffer these things for his commandment and to be deprived of your bodily company. In every other way you are always with us, Father, seen and spoken with. How else could we live, each of us set apart on his own, unless the shelter of your holy prayers guarded us unharmed by the evil one? Yet we have been guarded and preserved [?], and we are all gathered together. And though we suffered some hardship on the road, and some of us also fell ill, still he who said, "Look at the birds of the air and the lilies of the field," and who never lies in his promises, has [?] us beyond all our hopes and set us down here.

He has also moved the hearts of the men here to compassion for our hardship, especially the archbishop's. Now we have one care left, one unbroken meditation, with earnest though unworthy prayer: that you be made strong, our much-longed-for Father, and remain unbending and unmoved in what has been resolved in the confession on behalf of God's truth. May you never be frightened or waver at the attempts of those who set out to overturn the struggles for piety that you have built up by God's grace. For the word has resounded everywhere. It has put almost every soul to shame, raised up a horn of salvation among Christians, and taken away the reproach from the monks. And I know that every right-thinking person would say that Christ lives in us and reigns, and is obeyed rather than the men he fashioned, who were made not to disobey him but to glorify him. You know all things; you know what is needed; you have no need of our reminders. But you commanded us beforehand to write in this way. So do not fear man, Father, and do not be crushed by a mere mortal. You know that the saints, counting these things a dream and a shadow, were made wonderful in heaven and on earth. Let us toil a little, I beg you; let us endure a little longer, and our good race is finished. The crown is woven, the eternal reward is being prepared, and you will be called a friend of the heavenly King, a companion of the saints, and a confessor before men. Yes, yes, I beg and implore my fatherly heart: be our fortress, our endurance, our steadfastness. For if you stand firm, Father, we your useless children are strengthened, and we shall bear nobly whatever befalls us, by God's power and your prayers. It is God who has permitted this, surely because he is pleased to order our affairs this way, and he himself gives the power. Do not be dismayed, Father, by the clever arguments of those trying to bend you away from the truth. The matter is simple. Holy Epiphanius says somewhere in his discourse on Easter: "Whoever a man may be, if he gives counsel contrary to what is laid down in divine Scripture, he speaks from his own heart and recounts the commandments of men." And concerning such people he cites the Apostle's words: "Even if it is an angel from heaven, let him be anathema." And where shall we put the saying, "My priests set aside my law and profaned my holy things"? That is a prophetic saying, and the Theologian took it up in his great Apologetic and added: "They made no distinction between profane and holy, but everything was common to them." And how many other passages there are, if one wished to [?]! Let those who pervert God's truth with lying words stop, then, and look to themselves. The commandment is perfectly clear, and it threatens eternal fire to those who transgress it. So we will not bow to human fears or toils. No, by the struggles for virtue! If blood must be shed, we will shed it with joy, with God giving us strength through your holy prayers.

Be brave yourself, then, brother, lord [?]. You have fought a good fight. Let us not fall away from one another, my light and my heart. Let us not lose the blessed life for a little passing comfort. Do not take delight in present pleasures, brother, and do not give way before hardships. Do not turn your back. Christ rejoiced to see you beaten for his sake. Do not grieve him, my beloved, nor the angels who rejoiced, nor our lord Father, nor our venerable Mother, who also travailed with us in the Holy Spirit, nor all your brothers, and least of all me, whom you say you love as a gift [?]. We are three brothers according to the flesh; let us be three according to the spirit too. Let us not dishonor that precious number, the number of the Godhead. Let us give ourselves to suffer for God's commandment, so that we may live for ever. Yet we have great grief too, Father, over our other sweetest brothers, wondering how the Lord has disposed of them. Sinners though we are, we pray that he himself will care for them, govern and guide them, and direct their affairs as he knows, commands and wills. For truly we shed bitter tears for them. Their faces are always before our eyes, and we need their prayers to help us in our slackness. But pray, Father, for all of us, that we may gain endurance, good fortune, shelter from God and help against the devil's temptations. And concerning seeing you, or our brothers, in the flesh, may whatever pleases God come to pass, may it come to pass. We ask you, and we make bold to send our greetings to our sweet brother, if he is with you, or to any other brother of ours, whoever he may be, if you are able to let him know. With me, your holy soul is greeted by the lord deacon, our Father; by my good brother; by your son the steward; and by the other honored and much-loved brothers. Pray for us, Father, fervently and without ceasing, as you command. What else is there to say?

This is now my second letter [cod. Regius: second reply] to my lord and Father. I do not know whether you received the first. In it we said whatever the occasion required and was within our power, unworthily but said all the same. And now we shall address to you whatever is fitting and whatever God grants for the benefit of my lowly soul, and also, I dare say, for the comfort of your great soul, O Father. And I say this now, as I have often said it before, by way of excuse: if I have any skill with words or any small aptitude for writing, it has been given not for my own sake, wretched servant of yours that I am,

but for your sake, who have abundant grace welling up in your heart. That is why you gladly and joyfully make it your work to teach and instruct not only us, whom some mistakenly took for your nephews, but also all whom you have begotten in the Spirit as your sons and children. And events have shown you in truth to be the true shepherd who has laid down his life for his own sheep, as long as we do not turn aside somewhere from the truth, we who have perhaps chosen readily to pour out even our own blood. This, then, is the oversight of a true shepherd: it exposes the falsely named ones and is shown truly worthy of God the Father and of the chief shepherd. So I offer you, in some small measure, what has been granted to me through you. It is as though I were gathering fruits from the seeds you sowed in me with great care and abundance, like a good farmer, though I do not know how to describe these fruits except as meagre. What more, then, shall I say that is fitting and acceptable to your good soul, my sweetest Father? Who has parted me from your face that I ever long for? From your sweet-voiced company? From your saving guidance? You are my light, the ever-shining lamp for the dark thoughts of the soul, the staff that props up my weak heart. You turn my despondency around and anoint me with eagerness. You are my good news, my joy, my feast, my glory. Without you even the sun is night to me. I had no wish to look at the sky unless I could also look upon your features. Nothing on earth was sweet to me without your company. For what is more longed for than a true Father, especially one received for God's sake? A child who loves his father knows this, one who is truly his own. What need of many words to tell [?] what I used to experience? Often, even when I had not meant to go to your holy cell, I would somehow find myself before your face without noticing, as if someone were drawing me there. And when you asked, as you often did, "What do you want?", I did not know how to answer, so completely did my salvation hang on you. And who does not run toward the light? But I thank God that through you I was snatched from the hands of those who trampled on his law and of those who began [?] the like. May the Lord my God not count this sin against them; may they come to recognize their audacity, so that they too may be found guiltless in this matter. They shut you up, as we have learned, in a little hut; but they have shown you to be a dweller of heaven. They kept you under guard, but did not realize that they were guarding a treasure: the confession of God. And from this, if they would only look, they might learn that they have made you known as precious to men, a means of salvation to the world, and a sight that many long to see. You accepted dishonor and insults with Christ. You were persecuted, as one blessed. They scattered your sheep, because, as with Christ, they struck you, the shepherd. And though it is bold to say, his voice too [?] ... patrician and [?] of the Scholae [?] ... Plato into the city, and shut him up in [?] in the church of the Archangel in the [?]

"They persecuted me, and they will persecute you too"; and [?] all the things that bring his followers a share in the same sufferings. "If indeed we suffer with him," as the great Paul says, "so that we may also be glorified with him." So much for that. As for me, prodigal and unworthy though I am, the merciful Lord has granted me comfort through your holy prayers, righteous Father, and has let me be with you in spirit. I am always as if I were seeing you and talking with you, receiving your prayer and your shelter, giving and receiving words to strengthen the confession you have made. And I seem to hear your voice in my ear saying: "Child [?] Theodore, truly we suffer only a little, since God holds out a good hope." These words are my comfort, these my refreshment. Do not be afraid, Father, for me, your servant, utterly cast off as I am. For I am the defilement of heaven and earth, more chilled [?] than any man. Yet unworthy as I am, I dare to say that I am hopeful. I look upward, strengthened by your intercession. I am not displeased at what I have suffered. Rather I blame myself for not bearing it bravely and as I should, and because what I suffered is small and worth nothing when I look at the life-giving sufferings of the saints. I happened to read many accounts of martyrs written out in twelve volumes, and my heart was so struck that I do not even dare to say that I have suffered anything for Christ. And what is sweeter, Father (I remind you as your servant), than to suffer for him? Look up, Father. See the Lord. Behold the ranks of angels. Fix your eyes on the choirs of saints. See the Judge of the world on a throne high and lifted up, who will proclaim you a faithful servant, a keeper of his commandments and, greater still, a confessor. Then where will he send you? Not into the eternal fire that receives those who disobey his law, but into a place of life, an immortal rest, a gladness of endless exultation [ms. Reg.: divine gladness]. "Enter," he says, "into the joy of your Lord." The eyes of all of us are on you. We are all great-hearted as long as you stand firm. May God's help be with you more and more, fortifying you, empowering you, strengthening you, making you brave. You who fear God, do not fear what man has done to you, or may yet do. You trust in the Lord; you are Mount Zion; you will not be shaken for ever. For dwelling within you is the architect and maker of the Jerusalem above. There are those who creep up on you like serpents and want to drag you away from the life-giving tree of truth. Flee their venomous and deceitful voices, and [?], once and for all strengthened in the truth and bound fast into complete immovability by the many testimonies of holy Scripture, and sometimes of pious men too. Then you will win the praise of that saying: "Whoever does these things shall never be shaken." All the brothers are well: the lord deacon, my Father; my sweet brother, now more worthily longed for than ever; and the rest of my dear and honored ones, your children. Pray for them all together with me, Father. They are all faring

well. All they long for is your health in the Lord, and whatever they suffer is bearable to them. Of course we are also grieved and distressed and vexed and slack, and troubled by evil thoughts. It is impossible to pass through this life without afflictions. But because of our hope and your prayer we [?hold out]. Pray for me, Father, because I am learning holy Isaiah by heart. And tell me whether, besides writing, you want me to read.

3. To the same. My tears pour out before my words. My heart is shaken, my hand trembles as I write, I am pulled every way, and I cannot bear the pain. Oh, how shall I bear your Christ-like sufferings, Father, Father? How shall I endure your lofty and holy humility? How shall I answer you fittingly in writing? Where shall I turn, and where shall I begin my letter? Do you write such things to me, Father? To me, the worm, the mire, the prodigal, does the Father speak words fit for a child? You take on the posture of a suppliant, you who ought to be supplicated. What then shall I, wretch that I am, say? How shall I humble myself before my righteous Father? Still, I received your holy letter, Father, in unworthy hands, as though it were tablets written by God. I heard your written voice as one would hear the voice of an angel or an apostle. It broke my heart and drew forth tears, and I wept and lamented. It was not a lament like Jeremiah's over sufferings that came about as God's hateful punishment, but a lament of my own, born of love for my father and truly a thanksgiving to God. For what you have sent, Father, comes from true understanding [?], and is worthy of being copied, since it makes known your wholehearted purpose toward God. So you have established our minds, Father, and braced our hearts. Your courage is beyond our hopes, your boldness beyond our expectation. You have appeared to us as someone other than we knew, wholly changed in God. Glory to him who strengthened you! Fear of the emperor did not shake you. Bewitching flattery did not weaken you. You did not choose to enjoy a passing pleasure, but chose to face danger for God's truth. You are the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep, and who is now a prisoner under guard, like an apostle of Christ. Oh, that room in which you are kept and move about, a precious and useful vessel for the Lord God! Would that I could embrace the floor where the feet of my lord and Father walk! Would that I could venerate the keys and bolts locked against you, as guardians of a treasure of piety! Better still, I long to kiss that precious mouth that confessed the word of truth, and the holy hands raised in holy and acceptable prayers. Where has my sweet face flown away to? Where has the saving voice been silenced? See, I am an orphan, pitiable and utterly forsaken, without

the physician and nurse of my lowly soul, with no protector, no defender against those who make war on me unseen. I have become like a raven in a ruin [?], like a sparrow on a housetop. Day after day I keep looking out, glancing here and there and all around, and nowhere do I see the face I long for. And even so I could not lament my suffering as it deserves. Yet I give thanks, and more than thanks, that I have been counted worthy of these things for the sake of God's law, and that I have been called the child of such a Father. Perhaps I may think that I am reigning today through you, holy Father, if your prayer keeps me safe. For I fear my sin and my prodigal ways. But know that I am strengthened and set firm by your holy prayers, though I am very easily overcome. And not I alone: all of us are one, of one mind and one soul with you, choosing to suffer with you even to death. So do not be afraid on our account at all. Well done, Father, well done! Well done, excellent helmsman, zealot for piety, imitator of the saints! You have truly fought magnificently; [?] you have contended beyond measure. I know that your spirit is with the martyrs. That is how matters stand, though I have not yet said it as my desire and your worth require. But since you bid me tell you everything in order, from the day we underwent that painful separation, about the journey and what happened to us on it, I am not equal to the task; yet I will do as I am told most readily. On the very day, then, when you, Father, by your own choice set out on the road to death, we started on our [?] journey into exile, mounted on whatever animals were at hand. Since at first we had no experience of such a drama, we were rather downcast. We passed through some villages, made a spectacle before people of every appearance and age, and both our ears rang with uproar and shouting, both when we set out and when we stopped while our escorts were getting provisions. But as we went on and grew used to it, we bore the hardships more easily. What grieved us more was the illness of our Father, the lord deacon. And so we finished the journey, weighed down and overwhelmed. These were our stopping places: from Kathara to Libiana; then to Leukai; then to Phyraion. There something painful happened to us, worth telling. Nine of the leading brothers somehow appeared unexpectedly, like scattered sheep, and stood around us weeping and breaking our hearts. Our escort would not even let us speak to them. But we saw them and were seen, a pitiful sight, and called out a few words to one another, and at last we parted in tears. Then we were brought down to Pylai, where we found your much-honored sister with lord Sabbas. We met in secret and spent the whole night together, saying what was fitting,

and we embraced one another as men about to die, and parted groaning and lamenting. There one could see hearts torn and convulsed, as nature was overcome in a way that befits God. From there we rested at Loupadion, where our host treated us kindly and with sympathy. We also took a bath for our sores, for the journey had left some of us with wounds that were hard to heal. Then we were brought down to Tilis [?]. There Abba Zacharias and Pionius caught up with us. They wept, out of their warm devotion, and chose to travel with us, though they were not allowed to. From there we went to Alkeriza; from there to Anagegrammenoi; then to Perperina; and from there to Parion. The bishops there received us into communion, though we humbly reminded them that they had sworn [?]. Then to Horkos, and from there to Lampsacus, where we found men from Heraclea and rested with them three days, since we could not sail. Then we put out and sailed down to Abydos, where the governor of the place showed us mercy out of piety. We stayed there eight days, until the Sabbath, and then sailed off to Eleous. We stayed there a week, since sailing was impossible, and when a favorable wind blew we flew across to Lemnos in nine hours. Here the piety of the bishop of that place makes me pause in my story. He, more than anyone, welcomed us, comforted us and supplied us for the road. Sailing from there in fear because of the hostile nation nearby, we crossed with a whistling north wind behind us in twelve hours, though the sea there is a hundred and fifty miles wide, and anchored at Kanastron in the territory of Thessalonica. Then we went on to Pallene, along the shore of the gulf, and then to the Embolon. From there we mounted animals again, and on Saturday, the day of the feast of the Annunciation, at the third hour, we were brought into the city. And what an entrance it was! I must not pass over this either. One of the eparch's notables had been sent ahead with soldiers and was waiting at the eastern gate. When we arrived, they met us standing in silence. After we had entered, they shut the gates and led us through the marketplace, parading us before the eyes of those who had come running for the purpose. Then they took us away and brought us in to the governor. Credit to the man: he showed us a kindly face and, after we had bowed down before him, spoke kind words to us. He sent us on to the archbishop, after we had first prayed in Hagia Sophia. When we had prayed in his chapel, the most holy man received and embraced us, spoke to us as was fitting, kept us with him at once, and refreshed us with a bath and food. Early on Monday they took us away, and at our request let us pray at Saint Demetrius. Then they separated us all from one another, after we had prayed together and embraced one another. The two of us brothers they brought up to the place where I am now, and parted us as we kissed each other in tears, so that even some of the onlook- (5) "On the day of the feast of the Annunciation": The fe- [?]

[?] to be troubled by sympathy. This is how things stand with us, Father. And now here I am, the lowly one, dragging out a painful life full of groaning. We received the blessings from your holy hand as having the power of the Holy Trinity. We keep them as an amulet, and we press them to our eyes as if we were kissing your right hand. Tears again; again my insides are wrung. I want to bring my words to an end. O Father, why have you forsaken me? But you have not forsaken me. How have you gone far from me? But you are within me. Where shall I still see you? How shall I behold you? Where shall I hear your sweetest and saving voice? When shall I share your table? Where shall I enjoy your company? When shall I ever read aloud in your hearing, or sing before your face, or be corrected, or rebuked, or reminded, while making a habit of what is dear to you in feasting, food, drink, conversation, standing, sitting and reclining? What has befallen me? I call men as witnesses, and I call the heavenly powers too as my advocates: it is the law of God that has separated you from me, one eternal commandment. Let all under heaven hear it. For this reason I rejoice and raise a voice of praise to God. I have everything, and more than enough. I exult. I shall no longer be orphaned, I shall not grieve, and I shall not utter anything ignoble. Accept what I said above as well, Father, as pure, for those words are tokens of my longing for you. Even so, I shall still weep, but such tears are acceptable. But you, thrice-blessed Father, rejoice and be glad. The prizes have been woven for you, and the place of rest has been prepared. Your zeal according to the [?]

When the lord deacon gave us the answer, my true and much-longed-for nephew, we wished to write to you at once. But since it was the winter season and the return voyage was restricted, we thought it good not to reply quickly. But since you asked for a letter along with your question, why should one still hesitate and not [?] what lies at hand?

First I will say this, and please accept it from me, most honored one. As you yourself know, I have presented my own life to many as an example of great wickedness. There is hardly an error one could name in which I have not shared myself and into which I have not led others. But I learn of God's love for mankind: that he rescues even one carried down to the depths of wickedness, and stretches out a hand toward repentance. So I fled despair and seemed to prop myself up a little toward what is right. For this reason, as God who knows hidden things is aware, I cut myself off from the company of my relatives, from familiarity with my friends according to the flesh, and from anything else whatever. In all this the power of God alone came to the aid of my weakness. And now, as for what you sought to learn from me, an unlearned man: it is as the lord deacon told you. We did not declare or undertake this without discernment. We were confirmed and strengthened in it by searching and examining the divinely inspired Scripture, and also by consulting those whom one ought to consult. Indeed, the truth is so, since the divine law clearly forbids it. It does so not only through the divine Basil but also through other theologian Fathers, who clarify this very point, make it plain, and join in declaring the apostolic command. How then can I be irrationally indifferent? Should I not rather set myself apart and withdraw from what harms my wretched soul? And think what danger there would be, since the chief of the Fathers cries out that whatever is contrary to the commandment, or damages the commandment, must in no way be tolerated, even if it holds out a promise of life, even if it threatens death. I pass over the many other citations that exist besides, which do not allow us to be drawn even the smallest step outside the commandment. Above all, we again have the instruction of Basil the Great that we must keep, without omitting anything, all that the Lord handed down through the Gospel and the apostles. I have made bold to make this plain to you as to a father and a beloved one. As God who knows hearts is witness, we neither preach (for we are not men of eminence) nor [?]. On the contrary, we hold the emperor and most pious sovereign enshrined in our hearts with love, and all my relatives too, since I am fond of my own, as you know. We commemorate him in the divine liturgy and pray for him privately and publicly. And we are in communion with the Church; may it never happen that we are split from it. Forgive me, a solitary sinner: I chose to lament my sins

[Note: "most pious emperor" [?]]

in this corner, and not to mingle with those in the world. What crime is that? Grant me this, most beloved nephew. For I know that you [?] are able both to keep quiet here and to stand apart from perhaps everyone. With your well-tuned shrewdness, make the crooked things straight and level the rough places. Be the umpire of our peace and the defender of our quiet, so that, if there is anything here that serves us, you may arbitrate justly and reasonably.

5. To Stephen the a secretis

Yesterday, since we had the privilege of your glorious presence, after some other conversation (in which the reason for your coming here also came up), we somehow got onto scriptural questions. Caught up in much uncertainty, we parted from one another without either side being convinced. We, master, being unlearned, will by no means match the wisdom you have shown. But we must not bring judgment on ourselves by keeping silent about what ought to be said (for it says, "You shall surely rebuke your neighbor, and you shall not incur sin because of him"), and we will be loved the more for rebuking a wise man. So we thought it necessary to set before you what is fitting. To put it briefly, my lord, and to pass over the many questions and objections: you said that if the presiding chief shepherd does something forbidden, whether in ignorance or willingly, in matters other than faith that concern the Lord's other commandments, he ought not to be reminded of it by anyone. We said that he certainly should be [?], but by those who surpass the others in knowledge and understanding. From what sources can we not show you the absurdity of your argument? First, from the Old Testament. What do you think of the case of Daniel? He was not yet of the lawful age to speak and speak boldly in the assembly. Yet when the elders acted lawlessly in condemning the divine Susanna, was he not praised, not only for reminding them but also for condemning them? Yes, surely. Then do you not accept Joab in the numbering of the people? Since that act provoked God, he entreated and implored the divine David and tried to persuade him not to do it. You know the story. I am put to shame by Jethro as well. He reminded the great Moses and advised him not to govern the people that way, as if teaching him the basics, and he reshaped his practice according to his own counsel. And who was he? A foreigner, though a father-in-law. And to whom was he speaking? To one who did everything by revelation from God. So much for these, briefly, so that we do not go on too long. We must pass on to the New Testament. Let us respect, if you please, most renowned one, the precept of the clarion herald of the world: "If a revelation comes to the last, let the first be silent." This was not, as your friendship objects, said about faith alone. And there is something that almost escaped me: the great herald of truth, John, rebukes Herod. I ask you, answer me.

But I know that laughter at my expense is close at the door, on the grounds that I am putting myself on the same level as the prophet. But it is not so, my excellent friend. For it says, "These things were written for our admonition." And again Paul says, "Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ." And how can one who does not act rightly [?] be orthodox, when the divine James insists that faith is shown by works, and that those who fail in the one do not have the other either? With so many and such great witnesses, I do not think your nobility will contradict me. If you do, then write back to our [?]. Give reasoned solutions to the points that have been put forward, and clearer counter-arguments to whatever you assemble against them. If any are forthcoming, we at least will fall silent and ask pardon for our objection, though it was made out of zeal. For merely to censure is easiest, and anyone who wishes can do it, as you read. But to set one's own opinion against it with the testimony of divinely inspired Scripture is the mark of a truly sound and sensible man. So as not to stretch the letter beyond measure, we have ended our argument here, appending some citations of Basil the Great as fuller proof. May you then be preserved for us with all your household, our beloved master, in good health in both respects. For we long to keep the good of your love, whether we write or not.

From the twentieth discourse [?] of the Ascetica of Saint Basil [?].

That the superior should be reminded by those of eminence in the brotherhood if he ever errs. From the thirty-fourth. Whoever does not accept what has been approved by the superior must contradict him, openly or privately, if he has some strong argument in keeping with the meaning of the Scriptures. Otherwise he must keep silent and do what he has been ordered. And if he himself is ashamed to do so, let him use some others as intermediaries. From the Morals, [?] Rule seventy [?].

That those hearers who are instructed in the Scriptures must test what is said by their teachers. That the one who presides over the word must do and say everything with much circumspection and testing, aiming to please God, since he must also be tested by those entrusted to him.

6. To Theoctista, his own mother

If tears could be carried in letters, I would have filled this letter of mine with them and sent it to you in these days, my honored, sweet and God-loving mother. For truly I cannot bear to hear the news about you; I do not say of burial, but of illnesses that could be deadly. Why, my mother, have you chosen to leave us, having come to love [?] departing from us and being at home

with the Lord? But surely you have come to love the things of that world. Your heart moved there by a greater longing, you desired instead to rejoin my good and holy sister and my sweet lord Euthymius, or rather the choir of the saints. O mother, how shall I get through this letter without tears? Is this what lies in store for my wretched life: that I should [?] your death too? That I should sing a lament over you? That I should see your tomb and inscribe elegies on it? That you should be laid beneath the earth in body (for in spirit, I know, you will dwell in the heavens), while I remain above the earth, still dragging out my painful and very sinful life? How is that bearable? May it not happen to me! Yet everything must be yielded to the counsel and will of our supremely good God. He knows what benefits each one and understands what is needful. He fits together what is fitting. He is a loving Father. He arranges all things well: aptly, wisely, with perfect wisdom and perfect beauty, leaving nothing undone. And "O the depth of his wisdom and judgments! For his ways are unsearchable and untraceable." He took to himself first the sister, and second the brother; now he seeks the third. Who might this be? If it is you, great is your praise. For you are winning the prize of a share in the Trinity. You have exchanged your life well. You have left everything and given everything to God: your head, your limbs, yourself. You have worn down your honored body in asceticism and come through a life of many afflictions, or rather, you have walked the narrow and hard way of the Lord. And now, in a good old age, you are seeking your departure. For now, then, I pray against this. Yet what is dear to God is best, and who will plan our affairs more fittingly than he [?]? Farewell to me, mother, whether you live or fall asleep. For you will not die, because you are alive. By your own choice you have died to the world. You have fought the good fight. You were deprived of earthly things so as to inherit the heavenly. You took part in the contests of martyrdom without bloodshed, cutting us, your own limbs, away from yourself for love of the Lord. You depart free of care and without a will. For you have nothing to bequeath except your garment of hair and whatever other makeshift belonged to your unfurnished life. From here you now stand naked before God, bearing a soul cleansed of the filth of material things. But you do have something to leave us: your mighty prayer. You sent it down on us almost from our infancy, signing us and sealing us in the hours of the night and offering supplications to the Lord for us at all times. You will leave us too your tirelessness in the divine liturgies, your love of purity, your earnestness, and the apostolic boast of toil. For truly much labor has gone out from your holy hands. It has covered and warmed not only us but the whole brotherhood, who have you as a spiritual mother and cherish you, and who, like us, grieve for you and call upon you. We have written these things in the letter as though they were not happening, to console ourselves and to show you what is in our heart, which you know also from your own

heart. As you know, my holy mother, even if I wanted to come in, I had no way to do it, because of the charge laid on me, unworthy as I am, for what reason I do not know. For it says, "How remarkable that Saul too is among the prophets!" And so too Theodore is among the abbots. This has confined me; this has bound me. If I were held fast by iron chains, I would burst them and stand before your face. But now, instead of myself, I have sent you the priest for a little consolation, since he too is dear to you and honored by you. He is to be with you in your weakness in everything, visiting you and seeing to what is needed. If you stay where you are, he will stay; and if you go out, he will go out with you, together with the steward. For the rest, my honored mother, carry on as God grants success and as your illness allows, and do not strain beyond your strength in wanting to go out. Send us word quickly of how you are faring in your sickness, so that we may take a little heart. All the brothers at once performed a canon for you, and they pray continually for your health. Grant us your holy prayer; bless us with a mother's gifts; embrace us through your letter. Give us the peace that you have through the grace of Christ, and will have to the ages of ages.

7. To Irene the Empress

"A voice was heard in Ramah," says Jeremiah, the greatest seer of God, "lamentation and great mourning": Rachel then weeping for her children. But the present events, how remarkable and how great they are! Where did they come from yesterday, our all-good sovereign lady, those messengers from your sacred palace who appeared and made us hear all the praises of the deeds you have just accomplished? Both our ears truly rang. What, then? You have raised a signal of such great piety to the ends of the earth, and behold, from every side countless prayers come to you like flying clouds, glorifying God for your auspicious achievements. Tell us, sovereign lady, who raised your most pure mind to the heights of the thoughts of truth, so that you looked down, as from some lofty, elevated watchtower, on such things pleasing to God and [?]? Teach us where such a love of piety was implanted in you, so that you are nobly insatiable for what pleases God and go beyond all sparing in your greatly beneficial provision for Christians in soul and body. Or was it that, being much given to divine things and longing for them like a mother, you did not think it enough merely to redeem your people with help from above, as from a kind of Egyptian bondage (I mean the impious faith)? Did you therefore add the present grace as a kind of crowning of the virtues, on top of the earlier good deeds that shone forth from you in many ways like stars? Holy, holy, holy! "Let the heavens rejoice

[Note 11: "to enter, I had no way." This letter [?]]

above," we shall cry out with Isaiah, the most loud-voiced of prophets, bold though it may be, because God has had mercy on his people through you. Your whole empire has been filled with joy and exultation, because the lawless yoke that lay upon it has been removed, and the rod on the neck of such domination. Who has heard of such things? Come, men, tell us! And who has seen such and so great an achievement in any other reign? Praise her, all you peoples; magnify her with us, rulers and ruled, priests and monks, and the whole Christian race. It is not only marvelous that so many talents of gold have been remitted, though that in itself is unsurpassed. It is also marvelous that a manifold channel of injustice has been cut off along with it. A most holy deed! The stranglehold of violent and soul-destroying exactions has been removed from our midst. It had gripped all who reigned before you, even some who reigned piously. This was reserved for you. The forced oaths have ceased, the oaths without number, or rather the perjury, on the part both of those who exacted and of those from whom it was exacted. Both were thereby lost, as it happened, since the one tried to hide whatever he could and the other laid siege to squeeze out whatever more he could. The oppression of the [?] has ceased, and the anxieties of the poor. They did not seek some remedy against poverty, for then the grief would have been less. They sought only a way to pay the collectors that unheard-of levy, which had somehow crept in from above as the offspring of sin. No longer are tolls charged on the roads, whether by land or by sea. These things answer what was said by the great and holy Chrysostom. No longer are the people of the mainland unjustly fleeced in the narrows by those stationed there like some wild demon or untamed beast, who would always take their taste from the poor traveler's load. Nor do the needy stay at home any longer for fear of such shameful takings, unable to reach either the city or the coastal places, since the rocks of injustice stood in the way everywhere. No longer are sailors setting out and putting in from east and west and [?] choked, as though paying the toll from their throats at the narrow straits. Those who pursue the craft of hunting have been released and carry it on with a light burden. O Irene of holy soul! The fisherman who has perhaps hauled up three fish, and only after toiling hard the whole day, does not hand one of them over. The archer or fowler, with the perhaps few birds he has caught, from which he gets his necessary food, remains unassessed and lives well. Soldiers' wives, who have their own grief at the loss of their husbands, will no longer bitterly lament the pitiable and inhuman exaction levied on account of the dead man. I pass over the swineherds, the sheep-dealers and the wine-sellers. I leave aside the butchers, the weavers, the coppersmiths, the shoemakers, the dyers, the perfumers and the master builders. In short, I leave aside every craft practiced in gold, in wood, or in any other material, so as not to stretch my speech out at length with such minute detail. O all-good sovereign lady, [it] has applauded

…with their hands, all of them, and they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy, having spoken those words: “I will bless you, Lord, for you have had mercy on me and have become my salvation. Therefore I will trust in your God-given rule.” All these things (15) are full of praise and hymnody, Irene, beloved of Christ, you who are Peace, sweet both as a thing and as a name. These things will be spread not only throughout the dominion of your empire but to the ends of the inhabited world, and foreign nations will hear of us, and marvel, and be struck with awe at the success of your wise measures. For “even enemies,” says the herald of the theologians, “respect the virtue of men.” Thus your empire is kept unbroken; thus your subjects gladly yield to you and obey you. In this way you serve the Divine; in this way you gladden God’s elect angels, and also those who live holy and righteous lives, Irene, who bear a divine name. In these things your piety shines out. In these things every mouth and every tongue is opened in your praise. This is truly the glory of the Church; this is the seal of the ancestral and God-inspired orthodoxy of Christians which you have secured, avenger of God and champion of the truth. So great are your advances in virtue, so great and praiseworthy your rewards, so abundant and surpassing your recompense from the God of all. For it is a great thing even to save one person. How could it not be? Since, as the divine Scripture says, “He who brings forth the worthy from the unworthy shall be as my mouth.” But to save so many souls, the whole people, how is that not great and venerable, and truly worthy of the munificence from above? You, then, who are truly the great and real name, have entered the palace with every good thing; and may you leave the remnants of righteousness to endure forever.

8. — To Symeon, abbot.

Your fatherly holiness, supposing our affairs to be above what we are, spoke to us in its two autograph [variant reading: “sacred”] letters of strange and astonishing things. As for the letter-carriers, God was pleased, once the abbot had yielded, that they should be received back into their own monastery; and your piety did well in this, bringing them back by its instructive word into the fatherly and spiritual bosom. But as for our brother who deserted, and was banished, as from paradise, from the cenobitic life, I do not know what to say. We too had seen the man formerly as truly a vine planted by God, wholly true, wholly fruitful. And how is it that now the boar out of the wood has ravaged it, and the wild beast has fed upon it, so that it has turned, so to speak, into

[?]nes, second [?]: In the month of March of the ninth indiction, the pious Irene remitted the civic taxes for the people of Byzantium, and lightened the so-called kommerkia [customs duties] of Abydos and Hieron; and so she was greatly thanked for these and many other benefactions…

deadly bitterness? For is it not so, that, having been handed over to the savage beasts of the passions—love of the flesh, I mean, and love of rule—he can now be seen, in the mind’s contemplation, being devoured by them and torn to pieces as from the mouth of lions? For the divine Basil, as you know, judges the fall of one who withdraws without reason and separates himself from his father to be equal to that of one who casts away the divine profession itself. For this reason they are also under the same sentence of excommunication and the other penalties. But as for him, we sinners pray that he may look once more toward the former light, out of his dim-sighted and darkened mind, and come home again to his sweet Father and his dearest community. And we exhort the brothers themselves to stand nobly in the cenobitic contest and not to be shaken [?] by the fall of the impious man; rather, from this, to lay hold more and more of a more genuine faith and an unbroken union, even to the point of blood, as the God-bearing Fathers declare; so that by the perfection of their life of obedience they may bind on the crown of martyrdom on the day of judgment, dancing with Dositheus, Acacius and Dometian, those all-holy men who completed their course in perfect obedience. For today, as the rest of your holiness’s words say, there is utter lack of discernment and insubordination, since nearly everyone, one might say, relies on human customs and on the practices of their predecessors [?], which run contrary to the commandments of God, and they prefer to keep [?] the way of life of this or that abbot rather than that of our divinely inspired Fathers. Hence we shepherds, of whom I am the first, have become foolish; we do not seek out the Lord, nor follow the track of a blameless and unshaken way of life, but act as though the divine law had grown old, the Gospel had become void, and the spiritual ordinances had lost their force—and, to say something still more blasphemous, as though the unchangeable God had changed. For that is what it amounts to when people speak of and blame the times and days and generations, saying that those were one way and these are another. But I answer that this has not come about through any difference in the times. For the heaven has not changed its form or its motion, nor is the maker of the day, the great luminary, of a different brightness, nor is the universe borne along and governed otherwise than in its former order. [?] For he established them, as the Scriptures say, forever and to the age of ages; he set [?] a decree, and it shall not pass away. Rather, this has happened, most holy one, through the alteration of free choice, which has grown negligent of divine love and has given over its desire to material things, and does not wish or choose to grasp the glorious examples, nor to copy from the archetypal, ancestral and godlike image, but from deformed, strange and monstrous ones. That is why we bear images in our souls that have partly a human part, partly a dog’s, partly perhaps a leopard’s, partly a fish’s, or [?] that of some other of the creeping

things—your holiness will take these words figuratively. Therefore those who babble such things out of deceit should either tear up, bareheaded, the Gospels and the testimonies and the ordinances of the Lord, and every book handed down by the saints; or, if they will not do that, let them lay aside their childish and unreasoning mind, as those who are truly attaining to mature manhood, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, according to the [?] handed-down words; and let them walk accordingly and instruct others; or, if they do neither of the things mentioned, let them at least accuse their own unwillingness and dissipation. For perhaps there will yet be a time for them to come to their senses. But alas for me, most honored Father, that, guilty as I am of everything mentioned and a servant of every perversity and crookedness, I have begun, as it were, to trample on others and lay down laws. Let even the senseless stones weep and lament over me, who am in danger every hour and who tear apart the flock of Christ unworthily entrusted to me. So much I was led to say in answer to you at your command, O God-honored one. But as for you, stayed upon the power of the Spirit and holding fast to the lawful and ancestral commandments, may you remain immovable, unshaken and undaunted by the petty speeches thrust upon you in many ways by certain people, like winds or towering waves, walking on the royal road of an untainted way of life and passing by the vain talk of men on either side, and praying unceasingly for the best for our lowliness.

9. — To Gelasius, disciple.

O my child, [?] Gelasius, how did Satan, the author of evil, ever banish you from the paradise of the common life, as he once banished Adam from Eden, when you were persuaded by the counsel of the serpent-minded Ammoun? And now you lodge in places the Lord does not watch over, bearing thorns and working in the sweat of your face the passions of dishonor. For what good have you done or [?] since you left? What, rather, have you done that is not evil and abominable? The spiritual light of guidance has failed in you; the spark of spiritual friendship has been quenched. Your friends and neighbors—I mean not only your beloved brothers but also the angels of God—have stood far off from you, and the demons have drawn near, seeking to destroy your former ascetic labors. Where now is your pure prayer? Where your unshaken [?]? Your light-giving confession? Your place in the angelic choir? Your God-imitating obedience? Your Christ-bearing humility? That good and pleasant thing of which David the psalmist sings, your dwelling together with the brothers? Since you have been deprived of all these, my child, you have their opposites brought in instead: darkness of mind, insensibility of soul, hardness of heart, distrust, hopelessness, negligence, fear of death, dread of the reckoning. And why list them one by one, when you surely go through life groaning and trembling like Cain? And I do not yet speak of the swarm of fleshly [Patrologia Graeca XCIX]

passions fanning the flame within you and setting sin ablaze. Therefore, my child, now that you have recognized the truth through my humble letter, look up to the light; be pricked to compunction by God and struck as by a friend; take full account [?] and recognize from where you have fallen, in what terrible straits you are, and where you are sojourning—with the tents of Kedar, so to speak. Come to your senses, spring up, rise, be renewed, be warmed again; and do not wait an hour, a day, a week, but quickly bid farewell to everything and come resolutely and without hesitation to me, your wretched Father, and to your good brotherhood, and to the great Father, mine and yours. For this purpose, when I learned that you had been driven off there, I wished [?] to send a brother with the letter to rescue you. But since the letter-carrier, a presbyter, assured me that you would certainly come on the strength of the letter alone, I was content with the letter. And indeed, my child, as has been said, not only I, the wretch, and my Father, but also our masters, the Forerunner and the Theologian, command you to set out as quickly as possible, before an unexpected death overtakes you and brings your end. But if—which I do not suppose—you harden yourself and act stubbornly, know that you are excommunicated by all the saints and by us sinners until you see our face. But if you set out as we have commanded, you are already released the moment you start coming, both as regards the divine gifts and as regards other food.

10. — To Nicholas, disciple.

Since by God’s good pleasure you have been advanced, my spiritual child Nicholas, to the dignity of abbot, you must observe all that is enjoined on you in the present letter. You shall not change, without necessity, the pattern and rule you received from your spiritual monastery, in anything at all. You shall not acquire anything of this world, nor store up anything privately for yourself, not even a single silver coin. You shall not divide your soul and heart in attachment and concern beyond those entrusted to you by God and spiritually begotten by you as sons and brothers—not toward those who were once your own according to the flesh, whether relatives, friends or companions. You shall not use the goods of your own monastery, either in life or after death, as alms or inheritance, for any of those mentioned above

[?] you are reckoned as master and teacher. You shall not keep an animal of the female sex for service, you who have renounced the female altogether, either in the monastery or on the estates; just as none of our holy and saintly Fathers [?], nor does nature itself permit it. You shall not ride on horses and mules without necessity, but shall go on foot in imitation of Christ. If not, let your mount be a colt. You shall by all means take care that everything in the brotherhood is common and undivided, and that nothing belongs to any individual as his own, not even a needle. And let your own body and soul, to say nothing of anything else, be shared out in equal love among all your spiritual children and brothers. You shall not exercise authority over your two brothers, who are my children, to do anything regarding office or ordination apart from your father’s instruction. You shall not enter into adoptive brotherhood or co-godparenthood with laypeople, you who have fled from the world and from marriage. For this is not found among the Fathers; and if it is found, it is rare, and that does not make it a law. You shall not eat together with women, except your mother according to the flesh and your sister, unless perhaps there is some compulsion and necessity, as the holy Fathers enjoin. You shall not be given to frequent outings and roaming about, leaving your own flock without necessity; for even when you stay at home the rational sheep, so changeable and so prone to wander, can scarcely be kept safe. You shall by all means take care to give the catechesis three times a week, in the evening; for this has been handed down from the Fathers and is saving. You shall not give the so-called small habit and then, after some years, another as the great habit. For the habit is one, just as baptism is, as the holy Fathers practised. You shall not neglect the laws and canons of the Fathers, above all those of our holy Father Basil; but whatever you do or say, do it as one who has testimony from the Scriptures or from the custom of your father, without transgressing God’s commandment. You shall not leave your flock and move to another, or hasten to a higher dignity, without your father’s judgment. You shall not form a friendship with a nun, nor visit a women’s convent, nor converse alone with a nun or a laywoman, unless necessity compels you somewhere; and then with two persons present on each side. For one alone, as the saying goes, is easily open to slander. You shall not open the door of the fold for any woman whatsoever to enter, without great necessity; but if you are able to receive her without being seen [?], not even this is ruled out. You shall not make for yourself or your spiritual children a lodging in a lay household where there are women, frequenting it often; but you shall choose to see to your passing and necessary needs in the homes of pious men. You shall not, out of attachment, take a youth as a disciple in your cell; but have your service done by someone above suspicion and by various brothers. You shall not acquire unusual and costly clothing, except when you serve as priest; but you shall dress and shoe yourself in humble things, in imitation of your father. You shall not live luxuriously, either in your own expenses or in

the entertainment of guests; for this belongs to the lot of those who enjoy the pleasures of the present life. You shall not store up gold in your monastery; but whatever is surplus, of every kind, you shall share with the poor, opening your gate, as the holy Fathers also did. You shall not keep a strongroom and the care of the household management for yourself; but let all your care be for souls. The gold and the necessities you shall entrust to the steward, to the cellarer, and as is fitting in each office; while you plainly hold authority over all, transfer each office as you wish to whatever person, and receive an account of each administration as you command. You shall not do or carry out anything on your own judgment in any matter—neither in going out, nor in selling and buying, nor in receiving or dismissing a brother, nor in changing an office, nor in any other bodily matter, nor even in the faults of souls—without the counsel of those preeminent in knowledge and piety, one or two, or three, or more, according to the matter in hand, as the Fathers have enjoined. All these things, and whatever else you have received, may you keep and guard, that it may be well with you and you may prosper in the Lord all the days of your life. As for the contrary, far be it from me even to say or think it.

11. — To Anastasius, bishop of Knossos.

What has come over you, most sacred Father, and why, after one refusal and a second, do you still press so hard to receive a word of benefit from me, ignorant and passion-ridden as I am? It is I rather who need to be enlightened by you—I who am second in rank and darkened in my life—not about the duties of a bishop (alas for my folly!) but about the monastic, or rather the abbatial, state: how by governing rightly the flock unworthily entrusted to me I might find God merciful on the day of my dread accounting. But you have surely done this out of extreme modesty. For it is not right for me to suspect that your high-priestly dignity is testing my lack of education. I, then, fear the duties of my own rank, O sacred head, and grow dizzy over the guidance of souls [?], wondering how I might bring this tiny rational vessel entrusted to me safely through the turbulent, ever-surging spiritual sea to the harbor of salvation; for this requires both an untainted way of life and the attainment of sufficient knowledge, so that, steering as with two rudders, I may vigilantly and skillfully keep myself and those who follow me from being swamped by the waters of sin. This, then, is my defense, wretch that I am. But since it is by no means without danger to disregard your holiness’s command altogether, even if it is beyond my strength and I seem disobedient, and especially since I have received an order to submit from my own Father, trusting in obedience to both of you I will say this to you, most divine Father, by way of reminder: the ship of your perfection is far greater and surpasses my little boat—I mean the episcopal

eminence compared with the abbatial dignity—and by as much as you have been deemed worthy to rule over more people, and these perhaps neither willing nor of one mind, nor of the same nature and rank, but men and women, monks and laypeople, rulers and ruled, married and unmarried, slaves and free, orphans and widows, rich and poor, powerful and oppressed, debtors and creditors, those living in luxury and those dying of hunger, the wealthy and the homeless, those dressed in soft clothing and those clad in rags. These and more besides do not appear in our life; but yours is full of them. Nor is all your people governed by a single care; nor do you know the faces and names of all, nor discern the way of life of each; but they differ widely, one from another. Some, perhaps, farm, others sail, others tend flocks, others are idle, others are agents and collectors; and great is the account to be rendered for the work seen in each. And on top of all this, how great and how vast is the labor—incalculable, as I reckon it: how much sweat, struggle, running, exertion, care, anxiety, wasting of the flesh, pain of soul, exhaustion of mind! Just as the one who steers a ship in a great storm and a [?] sea is wholly alert and unswerving, keeping his eye unsleeping—for even a slight lapse into inexperience and negligence brings no small danger—so much the more must the helmsman of souls understand the work of leadership with greater effort and precision, lest he be sunk in the depths of perdition. That is why, I think, most holy one, the great Apostle cried out: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?” And again: “To the Jews I became as a Jew, to those under the law as one under the law, to those without the law as one without the law—not being without law, but under the law of Christ. I have become all things to all, that I might win all.” See, such are the canons and definitions of the episcopate according to him, as our divinely inspired Fathers themselves also declare. Since, then, you have read and studied the writings of the saints and have in hand the God-given oracles, why do you seek anything of this kind from me, a wretch? I take the bishop to be an overseer, accountable for the conduct in all matters of those he governs: an angel never silent, proclaiming the ordinances of God; an unsleeping eye watching over the ways of each of those led by him; an image of Christ, by looking to whom his followers shape their own lives according to the Gospel; an ever-shining luminary, made known to those benighted by ignorance and sin; one who dispenses the word of teaching to those who thirst for salvation; a supreme steward, who is to give account of each one’s life at the time of recompense. There is therefore nothing greater than nearness to God and love for him, nor again [?]…

…more richly rewarded than such a great charge, as Christ himself says to the chief of the apostles: "Peter, if you love me more than these, feed my sheep." Nor is anything more dangerous and ruinous for those who take it up unworthily. But you, best of fathers, I know well, have always laid down your life for your sheep like the good shepherd. You put yourself in danger for each one of them. You are not frightened by human threats, and you do not hold back the word of truth before those who oppose it, for you serve the will of the only King. Besides this, you rebuke with boldness and reprove with compassion. You make peace and reconcile those who are at odds. With sound judgment you separate the profane from the holy and the healthy from the diseased, so that the sick may not pass their sickness on to their neighbour. You turn back the straying, strengthen the weak and bind up the broken. How great your work truly is! You oversee abbots, examine those who live in cells, ordain priests and deacons, and keep watch over the lives of all of them. You protect widows, help orphans, avenge the oppressed and defend the wronged, and you also keep up proper deference to those in authority. For when nothing harms or hinders godliness, it is fitting for us too to submit to every rule and authority, and, if possible, to be on friendly terms with everyone at all times through generous and kindly welcome and readiness to give. Far be it from me to say about your blessedness what belongs to the opposite party, the bad shepherds. They shepherd the flock for shameful gain. They regard such a dignity as a means of livelihood, as rest for the flesh and enjoyment of desire, as a way to hold on to wealth that flows away and to acquire so many acres of land, a herd of slaves and a multitude of cattle. So they leap at the height of leadership in a human and not a divine way, in order to raise their brows against those beneath them and to preside haughtily over those more worthy of honour. I pass over those who fight like lawyers over perishable affairs but do not stand up for the doctrines of true religion. I pass over, too, what is far worse: those who filch and bruise the property of their subjects and in this way amass power and wealth. To the poor, to whom they ought rather to stretch out a hand, they do not shrink from squeezing them little by little. To whom will such men be likened? To Peter and John and their followers, who, as Scripture says, had no silver and gold but only the grace of the divine Spirit? Or to Simon Magus, Judas the traitor, Gehazi the lover of money and the other rich men of this age? I mean those who look only to how things may go well for them in the present. They pamper the flesh and set their heart on gold. Perhaps they also lend it at interest or deal it out to the needy for profit. They hold on to it for their own wishes and lavish it with partiality on the un-

worthy or on their own kin. Perhaps they give all their care to sowing much and reaping, to planting so much and harvesting, to adding to and multiplying their herds and flocks. Like farmers who watch for their chance and trade on shortages, buying and selling this and that, they conduct themselves like dealers and merchants and not like bishops and priests. A bishop's only aim should be to give the soul wings, snatch it from the world and give it to God, and save the whole flock from the death of sin; only then, as a secondary matter, should he provide the necessities of this present life through stewards and managers. But woe is me, for I have listed these things against myself, drawing from my own passions faults that are not found in others. But you, most venerable Father, are pure of such things. May you drive the spiritual wolves away from your Christ-sealed fold by your holy prayers. I know well that you lead your sheep and guide them into the pastures of the virtues, feeding and fattening them on the grass of your well-tuned teaching and the water of your pure faith. I know that every time you offer to God acceptable sacrifices in your spiritual and purified worship. But anticipate me with your supplications and shepherd me too, most wretched and greatly sinful as I am, I beg and implore you. And forgive me if I have made myself ridiculous to you by my ignorance. I did not do this willingly; I was compelled by your holy and spiritual love, or rather your command, to lower myself to it. I did not speak in order to benefit you in any way, but, as I said, to show my unfeigned obedience to you. Farewell in the Lord, and pray for us, the only sinners, Father most holy in all things.

[?] To Thomas the former consul (15). [27]

What greeting, what word of consolation could we lowly ones find for your lordship in the sorrows that beset you, my master? You have been made a stranger to the city that bore and raised you. You have been robbed of your great household and stripped of your splendid rank, and, I will add, of your property too. You have been parted from your friends, your companions and your dearest children. You have been banished here and there. And how many hardships exile brings to your unaccustomed body: lack of food, drink and baths, no one to talk with, and plenty of people to trample on you and strike you. For those who were once well disposed are now perhaps ill disposed. Your friends and acquaintances, whether near or far, may have turned their faces away from recognizing you and loving you and [?]

On top of this there is your anxiety for the servants and slaves still left to you, and above all for your most excellent (15) [?] To Thomas the former consul. [?] [Theophanes?] under the year 5[?] [?] Leo [?] and chamberlains; and these too, and other devout men, venerating the holy and [?] icons; [?] a certain Thomas, a patrician who had been a former consul, who

children. And you have no power to help them. With all this you sit outside the city, as Israel once sat by the rivers of Babylon when it was carried off to the Assyrians: "There," it says, "we sat down and wept when we remembered Zion." So your lot is groaning, dejection and tears. But you have the gift of knowledge and the grace of prudence, so we do not believe that you are at all overcome by these things. You know that "the life of man is a trial," in the words of the celebrated Job, and your long experience knows what he suffered. You also know the unstable course of this present life, which changes from one state to another almost every day and every hour. For it is like a stream that flows on and away, like flowers and dreams and all the other likenesses that the divine words of the saints offer. Let your honourable soul consider how much has happened in the time since you were deported: some have fallen and others have been raised up; some have died, others have prospered, and still others have met misfortune. There is no standing still in the unstable and swift race of our life. This too is true: all of us human beings are in exile. As Scripture says, through the first-formed man we were banished from paradise to dwell in this deadly place, until we sing, "Bring my soul out of prison, that I may give thanks to your name," and pass from sojourning to freedom. Strictly speaking, then, human beings cannot even exile their fellows, since they themselves are exiles. For we are all marked out as sojourners and strangers. If there is any medicine of comfort like this, any solace of consolation, we ask and implore you to bear what has befallen you with patience and your sorrows with thanksgiving. We are persuaded that you already do so. For where else could we find the remedy? Then there is this: from these very things we shall gain great rewards. Through inactivity we gain a greater good action, through poverty a wealth that cannot be lost, through disgrace an untarnished glory. And perhaps our pious reigning emperors will at last be moved to bring you back home and restore what is due to you. For we know their love of mankind and their readiness to change their minds, which they show to a great degree in such cases. As long as you remain there, may the Lord God comfort you with a consolation full of patience and thanksgiving. May he also persuade the rulers to do for you what we have said, and to restore you, so greatly missed, to those who love you.

[?] On the ministry to the unprovided-for. [29]

Since man was created in the image and likeness of God, human nature must, as far as it can, bear within itself imitations of its archetype, as an image does. Since, then, the Divine extends the providence of its own goodness to all things, it would be right for humankind to imitate, as far as possible, the provident governance of the ineffable wisdom. Hence

we, lowly and least of all, have looked reverently to the divine [?] and taken up a loving disposition toward our own kind. We have committed ourselves to this pious association, as set out below, to make provision for the bodies left unprovided for: that is, the dead who, through poverty or because they are foreigners, have no means to be carried out and buried in this queen of cities. Relying on this divine pattern, each year we make a contribution from the gifts that come to us from God, each according to his means, for buying grave-clothes and the other things needed for burial. And we lay down the following in the Lord. When any of those gathered in the brotherhood, in the course of his rounds, is told of or sees a dead person, that person is to be carried out in proper grave-clothes and laid in the holy tombs assigned to us. Moreover, during the year, at the beginning of the indiction and at the [?] of Pentecost, we are to celebrate in common the memorials of all who have been buried. On the same occasion we are to hold, from the contribution, a love-feast for bodily refreshment. This is not, however, to go beyond the established limits of sufficiency, so that we do not make a riot of the memorials with much wine or much eating. Rather, after we have reverently offered a doxology to God, who has counted us worthy to perform this holy rite, we may then go to the table for our needs, while the book is read aloud, so that even at our meal we may pursue what pleases the Lord. Whatever is left over is to be given to the poor. No idle words are to have any place at the feast, no jesting, still less games, since Scripture does not allow even an ordinary Christian to indulge in them. If there is need to speak, let it be of things fitting for Christians: that we should guard ourselves against oaths; have love for one another; bring forth truth from our mouths; flee from deceit and envy; hold fast to doing good as far as we can; visit those in prison and those who are sick; attend to the readings and to the gatherings in church; outdo one another in showing honour, especially to priests of God and monks; pursue hospitality; abstain completely from fornication and drunkenness; hold the orthodox faith; and avoid communion with heretics. For talk about such things, and reflection on them, would bring us many blessings. Consenting to these divine covenants and following them, we have given ourselves to this association as to the Lord. For he says: "Whoever has done it to one of the least of these my brothers has done it to me." We are to set aside nothing that has been laid down and neglect nothing. So if any of the brothers is ever found either overlooking a dead body lying unburied and failing to report it to the one who holds first place in the brotherhood, or saying at the meals what is not permitted and doing what is unholy, and so provoking God, he is to be given a penance by the president: three days' abstinence from wine and a payment of money [?]. After that he is to ask for amendment in future.

Besides this, you are also to observe the following: when the death common to all comes to one of your brothers, all are to gather together and carry out his funeral and burial, so that in this too your good association may be praised, to the glory and praise of our bountiful God. In faith and fear, then, we have enrolled ourselves in this document and signed our names below with the amount we give. We await the reward for this least of our intentions in the age to come from the giver of rewards, the just judge of all, Jesus Christ our Lord and God.

14. To Ignatius, abbot.

Before anything else I pay the debt of a greeting to your fatherly holiness, for I owed it. Then I shall explain the reason for this letter. One of our rational sheep, brother so-and-so, was lured by the many-wiled cunning of the soul-destroying wolf and driven out of our humble flock. As we have learned, he has been received in your holiness's monastery. Suppose you had received him and at once admonished him to return, showing him the deception and ruin he had suffered, and then, having improved him, had sent him back to our lowliness. There would have been nothing unseemly in that; it would have been fitting for you, as the saints have commanded us. But so much time has gone by and there is no sign of his return anywhere. So I want to ask on what grounds your [?] keeps my disciple, as if unaware of the matter. You should have recognized the situation and sent away one whom you did not tonsure, since you know how harmful this is. For you know what the divine and great Basil lays down: that one who runs away from union with his own brothers is not to be received in any brotherhood. How could the coenobitic houses hold together if this chief rule were not observed before all others? Even among the schoolmasters of this world, it is not permitted to take into one's lessons a boy entrusted to another school. Anyone who does so is fined by all of them together. How much more must this hold for us, most holy Father, who have charge of the Churches of God and guide souls in imitation of our first teacher and shepherd, Jesus Christ? I know, then, that you are full of wisdom and knowledge. But I beg you to recognize the impropriety being committed, especially since you yourself are ahead of others and carry weight in a holy brotherhood. Do you not know, most holy one, that it harms your own flock too to join to it a sheep belonging to another master? Since the wrong is so great and so plainly admitted, we beg you, when you receive our humble letter, to hand him over to our brothers who have been sent for this very purpose, so that they may lead him back to his own flock, together with the Church property he has taken for himself. If the brother is disobedient, may you be pleased to drive him out of your holy flock at once. But if, which we do not expect, you wish to go on keeping him after learning this, let it be known that he is bound

by us, not without reason but on very careful judgment. Or rather he is bound by the Holy Trinity and by all priestly legislation to be excluded from communion in the divine gifts, just as he is also excluded from sharing in outward food, until he returns and is settled again in his own fold. It is in no way lawful for anyone to loose a disciple of your own whom your holiness has bound, for that is an act of lawlessness and, by the common vote of the whole Church [Reg. ms.: "common"], incurs the same condemnation. In the same way your holiness must certainly not lay hands on our authority, which the Lord has given us, unworthy as we are, not for tearing down souls but for building them up. For the judgment is fearful. Therefore, since we ask this of you, your holiness will surely hand over our spiritual child to the brothers, and pray for us sinners without ceasing.

15. To Theodulus the Stylite. [32]

For a long time, up to the present, my most holy Father, I have wanted to come and receive your holy prayers. But no way has opened for me, surely because of my sins, and this is still the case now. So I have been compelled to send our brother Kalogeros to make up for the absence of my lowliness. We too will come to venerate your precious footsteps, if God grants us a good journey. Forgive me, Father, for what I am about to say. I say it in simplicity, out of sincere love and from my desire that your way of life should be blameless. Some people have hinted that your holiness is acting improperly. They know that I am your true and like-minded friend and child, and they are especially close friends themselves. I was annoyed at this, objected and spoke of the great achievements of your lofty life, and on that point they agreed with me. But they found fault with certain words and deeds. To mention just one thing, they said that you have painted angels on the windows, crucified in the same way as Christ, and that you have painted Christ himself and the angels as old men. I questioned them at length about this, but I could not answer them. For they said that you had done something strange and foreign to the tradition of the Church, and that the thing was certainly not from God but from the adversary, since in all these years, among so many God-bearing and holy Fathers, no example of this peculiar practice is to be found. Whatever is now newly introduced, even if it comes from an angel, the Apostle warns us not to accept, when he says: "Even if we ourselves or an angel should preach" (I will add, "or hand down") "anything contrary to what we preached to you, let him be accursed." So, my holy Father, I do not know what to say to this. In my perplexity I was compelled to write to you, so that we may clear ourselves of all harm in the eyes of those who accuse us in words, as though the charge came from the whole Church. For God's sake, accept me as your child and adviser. I labour on your behalf and count your glory as my own, and I do not wish to hear anyone find fault with you in [?]

[Reg. ms.: "Theodore."] [?] Gal. 1:8.

16. To the Emperor Nicephorus (16).

Our good God, in his care for his Church, was to set your piety over the present generation to reign over Christians.
