He did this so that not only the worldly government, which was in a bad state, might be put in good order, but also the leadership of the Church might be set right where anything was lacking, and there might be a kind of new dough in both. By his grace your Christ-loving reign has achieved this in one part, and may it achieve still more, strengthened by divine help from above. What remains now is for the other part to enjoy equal forethought and care. You would grant this, after God and with God, through the lawful choice, pleasing to him, of the one who is to be high priest. You have also sought to learn from us, sinful and unworthy as we are, what we think, as before the Lord who is to call us to account, and of which we shall have to speak on the day of judgment. This is our view. We do not know or recognize anyone in particular. This is not because there is any lack of men shining in life and word; they exist, and they are evident to God and to men, though not in equal measure, and above all to your luminous soul. But reason and the desire of your majesty seek a man of a certain kind. He must be able to seek out the ordinances of God with a perfect heart. He must have been advanced little by little, by degree and rank, to the higher place. He must have been tested in every way, so that from what he himself has suffered he can help those who are tempted. But why say much to you, who know this well and from your own position and [?] picture such a man? He ought to outshine the many as the sun outshines the stars. Since, then, we do not see such a man, we do not dare to [?]. We put the following before you as a reminder, with reserve and modesty, though it is certainly not hidden from your experienced and divine magnanimity. Take a selection from the bishops, the abbots, the stylites and the recluses, and then from the clergy. From those put forward, choose the ones who surpass the others in understanding, prudence and life. Let the stylites come down and the recluses come out, since what is being sought is for the common good. Then judge, and together with them appoint the worthier man. Blessed are you, or rather thrice-blessed, our Christ-imitating masters, if you carry this whole matter through. And by this your [?] will be strengthened still more…

…kingdom”; your name will be magnified from generation to generation, and the years of your rule will be lengthened. For God has given Christians these two gifts, the priesthood and the kingship. Through them earthly things are cared for and set in order as they are in heaven. If either of the two is in unworthy hands, the whole must share the danger. So if you wish to secure the greatest blessings for your reign, and through your reign for all Christians, let the Church also receive its own president, one who matches, as far as possible, the virtue you show in your reign. Then the things of heaven will rejoice and the things of earth will sing. May the hand of God, in which your heart also lies, guide you and reveal what is better. And in return for the labours, cares and worries you spend on this work, you will receive from that hand the kingdom that has no successor.

[?] — To John the spatharios. [34]

We have heard of a godly act performed by your lordship, and we have marvelled at your truly great faith, man of God. The person who told us says that you used the holy icon of the great martyr Demetrius in place of a godparent, and in this way completed the baptism of your God-protected child. What confidence! “Not even in Israel have I found such faith”: I think Christ said this not only to the centurion back then, but now also to you, who rival him in faith. He obtained what he asked for, and you too have received what you trusted in. There the divine command took the place of bodily presence; here the material image took the place of the original. There the great Word was present with the word, invisibly working the wonder of the healing by his divinity; here the great martyr was present in spirit, receiving the infant through his own icon. To profane ears and faithless souls these things are unacceptable, since they do not believe them, and above all to the Iconoclasts. But to your piety the signs and proofs have been made plain. For what can God not grant to those who believe? And how is the one depicted not seen in the icon, sharing its name, and believed to be present there? “For the honour paid to the image,” says Basil the Great, “passes over to the original.” So the martyr was clearly receiving the infant through his own icon, since that is what you believed. And how glorious for your greatness to have gained so great a co-parent, as people call it! Not this man or that, some ruler perhaps or some potentate; one might say not even the man who wears the diadem himself, for the one you have found is greater and higher. He is the mightiest of martyrs, the most renowned of wonderworkers, the true friend of Christ, the fellow citizen of the angels. He has had and still has so much power, and of such a kind, among those under heaven that from one end

of the earth to the other he is proclaimed by the trumpet of his miracles. You are truly blessed, most pious man, to have found such a sponsor, and your child is thrice blessed to have been received by one so great in glory and power. If you come down to us, may we see your son, the namesake of Saint Demetrius. Then we too, sinners as we are, may embrace him as the saint's son and say to him what is fitting, and we may also have the story to pass on to others. For good things must not be kept quiet. They should be set before others as clear examples of pious faith.

18 [?] — To Staurakios the spatharios. [35]

We have already given the reason for our humble absence, and there is no need to apologize further. But how shall we begin, or what strength could be found to share the suffering of your precious souls? A physician called to a disease that is hard to cure is at a loss how to begin his treatment. In the same way we are bewildered over how to offer a word of comfort for your most grievous suffering. O the misfortune! O what has happened! A fine and lovely boy has gone from you. He was the one who ended his mother's first birth pangs, the one through whom you first bore the name of parents. He was the beginning of the family's line, the root of your childbearing, the first shoot of a rational offspring, the first-blooming rose, as it were, of his father's fruitfulness. How could I describe the child's beauty, except to say that the child grew and advanced in stature and understanding, and the grace of God was upon him, as we ourselves came to know a little? Such a child, so precious, has been cut off by the sword of death, cut, one might say, from your very loins. How could this not cause an inconsolable pain in your heart? Who would not lament and grieve along with someone whose limb is being cut off by a sword, as is happening to you? Fathers might well groan to see the loss of so beautiful a child, and mothers might well weep to see so lovely an offspring of the womb torn away. For truly a limb of yours has been cut off. Your own flesh has been cut out. The pain is great, and the healing remedy is hard to find. Gloom has settled on the house, grief on the servants and sorrow on the relatives, and above all on the grandfather, the lord patrician, and the grandmother, the lady protospatharia. On every side are dreadful and painful things. But come now, good man, you who are rich in understanding and wise in judgment, who have gathered much knowledge over many years: treat yourself, heal yourself. I urge you to turn the eye of your mind to the contemplation of creation. Look at the ancient generations, starting from our forefather Adam himself, and see and learn who has

remained in this world after coming into the light. Has anyone not sprung up like grass, quickly bloomed and withered away through death? Or is it not as with a flowing river, where some water flows out and other water flows in? The race passes on by succession and never stands still, but runs past day after day. So it was with those who begot our parents, and with those before them. If our account goes back, it will reach the beginning, and if it comes down again, it will arrive at the end of this universe. And, as it is written, “there is no one who will live and not see death.” The present life is an appointed service, a single day's business, followed soon by a return home. I mean the passage from here to there. The patriarchs have passed away; the prophets have departed; fathers and mothers are gone; brothers, friends and relatives have run their course. And what about kings? What about satraps? What about rulers? What about every age and every race of men? Have they not all gone under the earth, and will not all who have sprung from the earth soon do the same? But this is what matters: that we pass through things here well and live by the will of God who made us, so that when we stand before that most fearful tribunal we may be found free of condemnation. And this is what your child has surely and certainly found and attained. For it says, “Blessed is the short-lived among those born of women, whom the Lord has chosen and taken to himself in early youth, untried by the bitter sins of this life.” The lord Soterichos has gone out and departed in salvation, as his name foretold. He has been found worthy of the sound of those who keep festival, of joy beyond words, of a place among the holy infants who rest in Abraham's bosom. He is no longer a slave to corruption and the flesh but dwells in eternity. This is where we want you to find reasons for consolation and encouragement. Become a maker of gladness and a healer, not only of yourself but also of the lady spatharia, who most needs healing and comfort because she feels things somewhat more deeply, and then of the others who are dear to you. In this way you will show that you are taught in divine things and ruled by God's law. You know where the one who departs goes, and above all your sweetest child: not to death or to nonexistence, but to eternal life and to God who made all things. And to fathers and to all the acquaintances gathered at the funeral you will be shown as a good example of how to bear the loss of children with thanksgiving and self-control, without resisting the commands of God.

19 [?] — To [?] of the people of Agesarchos.

We have received a letter from your honour about our disciple. Long ago he ran away, and somehow, in ignorance and impiety, he was received among you there. In a cave he has built not a monastery but a robbers' den of the passions. You ask us to grant him release. Our answer is brief.

Marcian, our disciple, will remain bound, condemned and unworthy of communion until he returns to his own monastery, where he made the vows of his renunciation with God as witness. This is in accordance with the God-commanded canons that have been written. The threat hanging over him does not come from us but from the God-inspired Fathers. So if you want him to be saved, urge him to go back home. If he repents and returns, we are ready to receive him with a father's compassion and to forgive him all his sins. A sheep torn from its own fold that strays away cannot escape being caught by wild beasts. In the same way, a monk who lawlessly leaves his monastery by his own will and settles in a place the Lord does not watch over cannot escape being caught by demons. His cell, then, is a lair of demons, a trap for souls, a school for women, a workshop of every kind of lawlessness, whatever words and means he or you may try to use to explain away what we say. If he obeys, and you obey, it will be well for both of you, since you will escape God's wrath and threats. If not, you will see the fruits of your disobedience before your own eyes. The most holy bishop is blessed by the Lord for keeping the laws and driving the unholy man far away. For he is not worthy of ordination at all, even if he comes back here. I know his affairs better than he does himself, since I am his father…

[?] — To my children Pinouphios and Mares. [38]

I did not want to write to you, because your second letter did not agree with the first. The first held out the promise that you would soon change your minds and come to us; the second was a refusal and a reversal. You offer excuses of every kind instead of honestly confessing your fault, lamenting and repenting of what you have done wrong. If, then, you repent, and there is a spark of the fear of God in you, rekindling your hearts toward the professions and vows you made to God and to us at his fearful altar, with the angels and the whole brotherhood as witnesses, well and good. Look neither this way nor that, but quickly break free of your attachment and self-will, the snare of the demon. He has led you astray, thrown you out of the community and led you around to places the Lord does not watch over (for how could he watch over a place where his holy commandments are set aside?). Come to us. Come with a contrite heart and humble words, to take up a new life better than the former one. The former life was perverse: little by little your slackness, your boldness and your contradiction led you into the fall of apostasy. Though we are sinners, we will receive you with a father's compassion and

will lay down our own humble soul even to death to bear your weaknesses of soul and body. Since you slipped away we have not been free from worry, just as we were not in the case of the others. Our hearts are melting within us, and we raise to God our pitiful and unworthy voice, asking him to bring you back to your fold by breathing into you a thought of repentance. If you do this, you will once again serve God and us sinners. For he does not desire the death of the sinner so much as that he should turn back and live.

Return, then, return, before destruction suddenly comes upon you, as it came upon Petronius, and you are found repenting in vain and to no purpose, when repentance brings no gain. Where now are your words, Pinouphios, and yours, Mares? You were eager to accept the contests of martyrdom for the sake of our humility, or rather for the salvation that comes through obedience, and you said this often. Yet a little breeze came and blew you away like some [?]. Come to your senses, look to God, and fear his judgments and the deeds you know you have done. For those deeds alone your whole life is not enough for repentance. Why, then, do you heap further sins on top of grievous sins? As for our writing to the people you mentioned, who gladly received you and are giving you hospitality, this we will not do. You did not leave us by a word of obedience, so that we could judge you worthy of being received. On the contrary, we hold it against you and decree as follows. From the day you receive this letter, leave and abandon what you have there. If you persist in disobedience, which God forbid and which I pray will not happen, you are excommunicated, condemned and sentenced by the judgment of truth, dead in soul and deprived of the Spirit, as the great and divine Basil declared. Nor are those who receive you free from condemnation, since they do not keep the divine canons.

[?] — To Symeon the monk. [39 ?]

We have known from past occasions too, Father, what kind of man you have been toward our humility, and how great. In all the afflictions that have befallen us you have smoothed things over and arranged everything for our good. We know that you are grieved now too, because of the brother's report on the present situation. But what are we to do? God's commandment stands before us, and the canons of the Fathers forbid us such communion. So may your swift intervention come to our aid, along with your sincere love toward God and toward us sinners. Then you may turn the trial aside like a great wave and calm the disquiet of our pious

masters. Our refusal of communion is not aimed at them, nor are they the cause of the dispute. Rather, we owe them honour and [?], friendship and intercession, as is their due. It is aimed at the man who unlawfully crowned the adulterer, as the Lord's word calls him; at the man who dared to become the minister and confirmer of so great an evil before the whole world. Christ himself has deposed him, since he has fallen under two canons, and others besides. He falls under the first because a priest is not even permitted to attend the wedding feast of a man marrying a second time. The canon did not even dare to write about an adulterer's wedding; how much less may he crown one? He falls under the second because someone who has fallen into some fault and been excommunicated for it may no longer have his plea heard unless he contends for his [?] within a year. But this man let nine years pass and then leapt back into the Church. If he is blameless, then the adulterer is much more so. But if the adulterer is guilty of sin, who can doubt that the man who joined the couple and blasphemed against the Holy Spirit is more accursed and more profane? These, holy Father, are the things that frighten and [?] our heart. It was for these reasons, because we would not commune with him or with the previous patriarch when he gave communion to the adulterer, that we were confined: I in the place where you live, and the abbot and the others banished to Thessalonica. But God gathered us together again through your prayers. Even then we did not unite ourselves with the patriarch lightly, but only once he admitted that we had acted rightly. When the adultery and the breach of the canons were in force, we did not shrink back, by the power of God. How, then, shall we shrink back now, when the empire is pious, for the sake of one priest, and betray the truth at the peril of our souls? By no means. We would rather bear anything, even death, than share in communion with him and with those who celebrate the liturgy with him, until he ceases from priestly ministry, as was done in the earlier case. Let him be steward; but why does he perform priestly functions unworthily? He has ceased to be a priest. If those who celebrate with him think nothing of it, they will answer for what they do. Let them spare our humility. We have kept quiet and have said nothing until now, but have acted with restraint for these [?] years since he came in, so that we might get through more peacefully. Our good masters are mediators and judges of what is just, and they love those who speak frankly in the truth, as their own honoured lips often declare. Let the priests make their case as priests should: either they will persuade or they will be persuaded. If none of this happens, and even our merest murmur is not tolerated, God watches over all. No one is greater than he; his fear alone is to be feared, and his is the tribunal there before which we shall all stand to give account for everything. But we beg your [?], and as though falling at your honoured feet we urge and entreat you to show mercy to us,

and to bring a common benefit to our pious emperors themselves, to the most holy patriarch and to the whole Church, not only ours but the Church throughout the world. Let that one man step down for the glory of God, so that his Church may not be thrown into turmoil. If not, then at least grant the second option, that we may remain as we have been during these ten years. As for the others, even if there are countless hierarchs, priests and abbots who are in communion with him, that is no wonder, since they too went along with the adulterer and none of them said a word. God says these things through us, if it is not too bold to say so: he both entreats and calls out to you. And do as you see fit.

22. — To the same. [40]

Once again we have thought it good to beg your fatherly holiness to devote itself to what is for the common good and most profitable. As we wrote before, our refusal of communion is not aimed at our pious masters, nor are they the cause of the dispute. Rather, we owe them honour and obeisance, submission and intercession, as is their due. It is aimed at the man who unlawfully crowned the adulterer, as the Lord's word calls him; at the man who dared to become the minister and confirmer of so great an evil before the whole world. To make our meaning clearer, not to teach you but to remind you, we will, if you permit, set out the holy prayer itself that is said at the crowning of a marriage. From it let us see how this man, who presents himself as blameless, spoke against Christ himself and fought against him, if it is not too bold to say so, through his accursed deed. Christ called the man who puts away a wife lawfully joined to him an adulterer. And adultery, as you know, is a grievous sin, as serious as murder, sodomy, bestiality, sorcery and idolatry, according to the canon of the divine Basil. Yet this man stood that adulterer before the altar and, in the hearing of all the people, dared to utter those profane words. Let us consider, Father, I beg you, how fearful and outrageous this is. The prayer runs as follows: “Master, send forth your hand from your holy dwelling place and join your handmaid to your servant. Yoke them together in harmony of mind. Unite them into one flesh, those whom you have been pleased to join to one another. Make their marriage honourable, keep their bed undefiled, and be pleased that their life together may remain spotless.” Is it not terrible to hear and to think about? How great must we suppose the Holy Spirit's anger to have been at such blasphemy, and the holy angels' anger at such slanders? Why did the earth not open at once and swallow him, as it swallowed Dathan and Abiram, this teacher of falsehood, who displayed darkness as light and set Christ against [?]…

[?] …into contradiction. For assuredly, whatever the priest signifies, God also promises to ratify, according to the great Dionysius. But God in his long-suffering bore with him, opening a door of repentance to the one guilty of the sin. Yet instead of weeping and mourning until death, and being abhorred and shunned as an example of divine zeal to later generations, such a man has entered the Church again and is again openly a priest. So he has come in as though he had done something good; and Christ has been defeated, as he absurdly declares by his conduct. And through his public celebration of the liturgy this must be spread [?] to our whole Church, and everyone must consent to such a deed. For what else will come of it but this? May it not be! Perhaps from now on such things must be done in emulation of him: let adulterers be crowned, and those who crown them, as if they had achieved something great and were able to benefit the many and lead them to the same way of life. Let them be embraced by the many! But may it not be! For neither is he a priest, nor are those who imitate him. Let no one be deceived on the ground that the adulterer was an emperor. For the laws of God rule over all, as it is written. And yet, having done this most grievous thing, he still strives to have lawlessness recognised as righteousness, and, as the saying goes, to prove himself wiser [?] than the Forerunner and Baptist. For while John rebuked Herod's adultery and died for the truth, this man crowned the second Herod, truly shown to be such by an adultery of the same kind, and embraced him until death, proclaiming, not in words but by his very deeds, that John the Forerunner was mistaken, rebuking out of season and unlawfully, and dying for it. But may it not be! For the one was the defender of the law and the reprover of the defilement; the other a trampler on the divine mysteries, and the joiner and sealer of the lawless union. The one, even in death, cries out: 'It is not lawful for you to have the wife of your brother Philip.' And in the person of Herod he cries out to the whole world that such a thing must never again be dared. But the other to this day cries out [?] by his very deeds to the second Herod: 'It is lawful for you to have Theodote the harlot as your wife'; and in his own person he expressly commands men to commit adultery forever, and those who [?] such people to be priests. O daring heart! O contempt for the judgments of God! Why then does not each one rather denounce the affair and keep apart from such a man, even in eating or meeting with him, unless he confesses his sin, after first being entirely barred from every priestly function? For this reason we beseech your piety, and your life befitting the holy habit, to sound such words in the ears of our pious [?] lords. We believe that if they restrain him with the approval of our supreme

patriarch, the angels will applaud, all the saints will acclaim, and the whole Church will rejoice; and great increase of divine help from above will be added to their power, both in the subduing of enemies and foes and in a peaceful and long life for them. And where, holy Father, shall we set aside the sacred canons that bar him from exercising the priesthood? The first does not allow a presbyter to be entertained even at the wedding of a man marrying a second time, although that is permitted by God. But since he feasted for thirty whole days at the wedding of the outlawed adulterer, and not only this, but also placed the crowns of victory over virginity on the adulterous and unclean, of what would he be worthy [?]? Is deposition perhaps a small thing? If this goes unpunished, divine things are a game and the canons are stale. Again, according to the second canon, one who has fallen into some fault and been excommunicated for it, if he does not contend for his own vindication within a year, may no longer have his plea received. But he, after nine years had passed, burst [?] into the Church. And if he should say that he received permission from the previous patriarch and that the matter is blameless, why then did the one who gave permission not do the crowning himself? For it is certainly patriarchs who crown emperors, not some priest; that has never happened. But clearly, since the danger of deposition from the high priesthood itself hung over him, and he found this man so eager (for he lodged in the palace), he shifted the danger onto that man's person—if it is even true that he gave permission. For we do not believe it, and we have fully assured you and many others of this. And if again he should say that he had not been excommunicated by the previous patriarch, why then did he not celebrate the liturgy during the nine years? Why has he now, as he says, been released [?] by a synod? Clearly it is the one who is bound who is loosed, not the one who is unbound. So here too he trips himself up and is barred, since he did not show himself innocent within the year, as the canon requires, and obtained his release openly—if indeed there could be any release for one wholly bound, even if he brings forward countless false witnesses. These, holy Father, are the things that frighten and oppress our heart. It was for these reasons, so as not to communicate with him and with the previous patriarch when he gave communion to the adulterer, that we were shut away: I in the place where you now reside, and the abbot and the rest, together with the archbishop, banished to Thessalonica. But God gathered us together again through your prayers. And so, as it happened, we were united with the patriarch, once he had acknowledged that we had acted rightly. If, then, even when the adultery and the transgression of the canons were in force we did not give way, by the power of God, how now, when the empire is pious, shall we give way for the sake of one deposed presbyter and betray the truth, putting our soul

[?] …entered, so that we may proceed more peaceably. Our good lords are mediators and judges of justice, lovers of those who speak freely in truth, as their own honoured mouth often declares. Let the priests put the case in a priestly manner; either they will persuade or they will be persuaded. But if nothing of the kind is allowed, and even our merely muttering is intolerable, God is watching, than whom no one is greater, whose fear alone is to be feared, and the tribunal there, before which we shall all stand, called to account for everything. But we beseech your goodness, and as though rolling at your honoured feet we urge and implore you to show mercy to us, and common benefit to our pious emperors themselves, to the most holy patriarch, and to the whole Church—not ours alone, but that throughout the whole world: that the one man may cease, for the glory of God, and his Church not be troubled; or if not, then at least the second course, that we remain in the same state as during these ten years. For that the rest, even if they be countless hierarchs, priests and abbots, communicate with him is no wonder, since they also went along with the adulterer, and none of them said anything. These things God, through us—if it is not too bold to say—both urges and declares, and as it were commands. (19). 23. — To the same. [?]

[?] Of all that you have now made known to us, holy Father, nothing is so grievous as that our pious lords do not wish us to come as usual, to be granted the honour of venerating them, and, like everyone else, to offer words of farewell and prayer at their departure. But surely their gentle, forgiving and Christ-imitating heart would not do this wholly to our humiliation; for it knows how to be reconciled even with enemies, let alone with us, who with a true heart

love and revere them. Your holiness did excellently in laying our humble replies before their sacred ears; and that they assented is due to their magnanimous, God-given understanding, for they know how to judge divine matters rightly, being filled with wisdom and full of the knowledge of God. They command us to be asked why we gave ourselves up to the episcopate when the fault was known. To this we answer with respect that, as far as it depended on us, we did not wish it, partly because of the danger of the office, and partly because of the very matter of the steward. But when the Thessalonians came, supplicating as if on behalf of the whole city, and our good lords joined in endorsing the decree, we were afraid to disobey and to set ourselves against God and our pious lords. We reckoned that, since the ordination was being performed by his own bishops, it was possible to escape the danger mentioned. As for what would follow: on the one hand, he would be living far from those here; on the other, even when visiting it is possible to guard oneself in many ways. Then too, deaths occur, and the stumbling block is removed from the midst; just as happened with us lowly ones residing here, who have been preserved until now by using economy. For one must, as far as possible, withdraw from temptations, especially those who do not hold the rank of bishop. For these reasons, as with God for witness, we gave ourselves up, thinking—to say this too—that it was certainly not unknown to our pious lords, who know things far and distant through their supreme sagacity; nor indeed to the most holy patriarch himself, since we had written to him about the matter at the time: namely, that it was for this reason, so as not to communicate with the one who crowned the adulterer and with the previous patriarch only when he gave him communion, that we underwent exile in various places; and besides, their honoured mouth itself often examined and recognised that these things were so. This is our defence; and, as you command, refer it to their gracious power. That your supreme eminence takes pains over our affairs out of surpassing love for God was shown by the words conveyed through the most reverent abbot, and has now been made plain by the messages and replies conveyed through our brother in answer to what was sent. And for so good a disposition of yours towards the common benefit, the rewards

God, who determines all things by measure and weight, will surely reckon to you, even if we do not say so. But what economy, master, must be made on our part beyond what we have made? Until now we have held ourselves back and kept silence, I and the archbishop, since there is a time to speak and a time to be silent, contriving in every way that the matter should not come out into the open. But the one who searches has searched, and the one who said it did not lie: 'There is nothing hidden that will not be made manifest.' So, even without our choosing it, since things are so by nature, it could not for long appear [?] otherwise. Even now, using economy, we say these two things: either the deposed man ceases from priestly functions, and at once we communicate with this holy patriarch—which is to the common advantage; or, if that is intolerable, we remain in the same withdrawal as before, leaving to the Lord the vindication of such a matter. Anything beyond this is no longer—forgive me—a form of economy, but the guilt of lawlessness and of transgressing the divine canons. For the definition of economy, as you know, is not to set aside anything of what is established altogether, but where possible to relax a little according to circumstance and reason, so as thereby to obtain exactly what is sought, rather than being driven more violently by events and losing the more perfect things. And this we have been taught: among the apostles by Paul, who purified himself and circumcised Timothy; among the Fathers by the great Basil, who accepted Valens's gift and for a time kept silent about plainly calling the Spirit God. But Paul did not go on purifying himself, nor did Basil continue to accept Valens's gift and to refrain from proclaiming the Spirit to be God; on the contrary, both are seen to have chosen death for these things. So the one who exercises economy from the outset [?] does not fall short of the good, for he soon recovered what he had briefly given up—as with a helmsman who slackens the rudder a little because of a contrary squall. But one who is carried off course otherwise misses the mark, accomplishing transgression instead of economy. The examples are many, but it is superfluous to write them out because of their length. As for your lordship's saying, concerning the apostolic canon on those who ordain and are ordained for money, that Chrysostom made some relaxation in the case of the six bishops whom he deposed: there is no deviation there, even if it seems so, since, while estranging them from all priesthood, he allowed them only communion at the altar. But let us grant that it was a deviation and a relaxation. Let those who wish imitate it, and no one will prevent them; for he too is a mouth of God and a fellow tent-dweller with the apostles, whose many deeds are remembered to this day, and no one has disagreed about this. But here it is not so. For the man who crowned the adulterer is officiating again as though he had done nothing wrong; and he is not coming in somewhere out of the way, [?]

but in the catholic Church itself, set before the priests as a fine example. And what is the bigamy of Valentinian to us, [?] and who, having crowned him on that occasion, is proclaimed a saint and not a lawbreaker—if indeed he was crowned at all? And which of the inspired Fathers of that time handed down in writing that Valentinian acted piously in taking two wives, and that this should be done from then on? Many others too, since their own will is law to them—not divine law but human and condemned—have done such things and will perhaps do them until the end of the age. But the Church of God has remained unharmed, though struck by many arrows, and the gates of Hades have not been able to prevail against it; nor does it tolerate doing or saying anything contrary to the established definitions and laws, even though many shepherds in many ways have acted foolishly. For they have even convened great and very numerous synods, and called themselves the Church of God, and seemed to be concerned for the canons while in truth they were acting against the canons. What wonder, then, if now perhaps fifteen bishops gathered and acquitted the man deposed by the canons on two grounds, releasing him to officiate? A synod, master, is not simply a gathering of hierarchs and priests, however many they may be—for 'better,' it says, 'is one who does the will of the Lord than ten thousand who transgress'—but a gathering in the name of the Lord, in peace and in the keeping of the canons; and it binds and looses not at random, but as seems right to the truth, to the canon, and to the rule of exactness. Either let those who assembled show that they have done this, and we are with them; or, if they do not show it, let them expel the unworthy man, so that this may not be handed down as a charge against them and against later generations. For the word of God is by nature not to be bound; and in no case has authority been given to hierarchs over any transgression of a canon, but only to keep to what has been decreed and to follow those who went before. I do not know, unless something is uncanonical and has been overlooked. On this point there is a canon of St Basil concerning a priest who had sworn in truth to be content with his own church alone and to offer the gift nowhere else. And again, one of the council in Carthage, concerning those who ordain men who run away from monasteries: that such men must not officiate in any church other than the bishopric each one holds, and that those so ordained are deposed. If, then, in these slight matters, which to many do not even seem sinful at all, the judgments and ordinances of God do not go unavenged, how much more in the present case! It is not permitted, then, it is not permitted, master, either for our Church or any other, to do anything contrary to the established laws and

canons. For if this were allowed, the Gospel would be empty and the canons in vain; and each man, during the term of his own high priesthood, since he would be free to act as he pleases with those around him, might as well be a new evangelist, another apostle, another lawgiver. But by no means! For we have a command from the apostle himself: if anyone teaches or commands us to do anything contrary to what we have received, contrary to the canons of the ecumenical and local synods held from time to time, we are to hold him unacceptable and not count him in the lot of the saints; and the harsh word that the apostle himself said we refrain from repeating. For us, then, who are outside the world, nothing else is required than to seek and to do such things, from which come our being lifted up together and our zeal [?]. If life is to be had in these, well and good. If not, it is better to go about under heaven homeless and without a hearth, in every affliction and distress. Let your God-loving soul, then, help as far as it can, and, being zealous for the

25. — To Patriarch Nikephoros. [49.] Using our poor little letter as a kind of screen, out of reverence for the angel of your blessedness, we lowly ones present ourselves before your most sacred head, as necessity requires. For just now John, our fellow servant and disciple, reported to us that, having been granted to venerate your august person, he heard from you certain strange and abominable things: 'You are schismatics,' you said, 'from the Church.' At such words, most blessed one, how could our soul not reasonably be grievously affected? And how could we not speak out in defence to your holiness, rather than confirm the accusation by our silence? But before the defence I respectfully submit this: one must not open one's ears indiscriminately to anyone who wishes to say something against someone, nor pronounce judgment without trial against the person accused. 'Does our law,' it says, 'judge a man without first hearing from him and learning what he does?' So when your blessedness heard this grievous and pitiable charge about our lowliness—for what greater evil is there than separation from the Church, and than the chief shepherd losing a sheep, or rather a fellow shepherd? For even we sinners, though unworthily, have from God the anointing and name of shepherd—you ought, I dare say, to have borne with us, examined us, admonished us, now privately, now publicly, according to the teaching laid down by the Lord: 'between you and him alone,' or 'with two'; and only then, if he persists, as he says, 'let him be to you as the Gentile and the tax collector.' But until now we have received nothing of the kind from your holy soul, either through a messenger or in person; we have neither been heard nor admonished—and yet a sentence has been pronounced. Let your perfection consider whether this has not rightly been grievous to your children.

[Let us come] to the defence itself, addressing our words to God who oversees all and to your high priesthood. We are not schismatics from the Church of God, O holy head; may we never suffer such a thing! Though in other respects we are in many sins, we are nonetheless orthodox and nurslings of the catholic Church, rejecting every heresy and accepting every approved ecumenical and local synod, and indeed also the canonical decrees they pronounced. For one who thinks he holds the faith rightly but is not guided by the divine canons is not perfectly orthodox, but only by half. And we accepted your blessedness when you were promoted, as we declared in our defence in your hearing. From then until now we commemorate you in the sacred liturgy, as is fitting; and, as God is witness, had you sought on that very day for us to communicate with you, we would have communicated with you without any hesitation, since you have been dear to us from the beginning. What is being talked about arises because of the steward, whom the truth itself has deposed, since he has fallen under many canons. For even before the open adultery, while the former emperor was committing adultery with various persons, he not only celebrated the liturgy, gave him communion and dined with him, but also placed his portion together with him; and from this he became eager for the open licentiousness, despising God and the divine judgments. And to make what is being said clearer—not by way of teaching, far from it, but only as a reminder—let your holiness, if you will, take up the sacred rite of the marriage crowning itself, and see how much one may perceive there the provocation of the Holy Spirit in such contradictions. For assuredly, whatever the priest signifies, God also promises to ratify, according to the great Dionysius. For this reason we beseech your perfection to stop from priestly functions the man deposed by the canons and barred by your holiness's predecessor for nine whole years, who unreasonably [entered] [?]

For it was only just now that we opened our lowly mouth, when we were accused. When that small gathering took place—I do not know what to call it—I had just come out of prison. And since I saw assembled those who had earlier also accepted the adultery and were embracing the one who yoked the adulterers, I remembered that prophetic word: 'The prudent will keep silent at that time, for it is an evil time.' But since the same prophet says, 'I have kept silent; shall I always keep silent?', I therefore, when slandered, brought forward the facts at a suitable time. For, as far as it lay with me, I took care in every way during these two years that the matter should not come out into the open, saying to myself: since I do not hold the rank of bishop, which would enable me to reprove, it is enough for me to guard myself and not to share in his communion or in that of those who knowingly concelebrate with him, until the

…stumbling-block. This, then, is what we beg and entreat: that your holy soul be moved to suspend the man. Then your irreproachable holiness will not be blamed, the divine altar will not be defiled by the liturgy of a deposed man, and there will be no reasonable grounds for schisms. For let your blessedness know truly and sincerely that, unless this is done with the assent both of your God-loving soul and of our most pious and gloriously victorious emperors (for they are zealous), then God knows what will become of us who stand firm for the commandment. But a great schism will arise in our Church, with God and his elect angels as witnesses. Have mercy, then, good shepherd; help, skilled physician, your flock, your sheep, your churches, by the ways of your wisdom, the words of your understanding, the remedies of your healing. Bar the one sheep from the sacred ministry alone, and gain the whole. Do not let the Church be ruined by the mange of one, the Church which our Lord and God purchased with his own…

26. To Symeon, abbot. [45.]
Your honored paternity has written us a letter worthy of your sanctified and God-bearing soul. It shows at once your loving disposition toward us sinners and your agreement with us about the divine commandments, equal in weight and one in mind. More than that, it teaches what is better and urges us to stand unshaken in the present contests, and never to be overturned by the empty chatter of the heterodox and idle talkers. Your honored letter has truly been to us an infusion of courage and a rampart of strength, so that we glorified our good Lord. He has not utterly abandoned our lowly generation but has given life-giving sparks to those willing to be rekindled for the good work of piety. So much for that. And we pray, sinners though we are, that your life of holiness may endure as a model of salvation for us and for any others who wish it. For those who twist the canons and trip up the rules do not see any uprightness at all in those who rightly divide the word of truth; instead they stir up laughter and heap on reproaches. And what comes of this, except that we are all the more strengthened, learning how rotten and unstable such people are? That your lofty mind is not caught by them is admirable, and something we have often prayed for. You ask to learn whether anything new has happened in the present affair. We have nothing to tell, because the rulers are now away on campaign. For what is there even to say about the high priest, who has neither sent a word nor is willing to grant a hearing, but reserves everything for Caesar? As for the lord Symeon, he is double-tongued, changing now this way, now that. We did, however, exchange words with him again, and we did not give up the truth. And for a little while he softens,

but he remains the same, thinking and seeking whatever is pleasing to the rulers. When our pious sovereign was setting out, we wrote again, since he himself had asked for this. Even so, he did not wish us to come into his presence. But we sinners remain as we were, if our prayer stays wakeful. We are unwilling to betray the truth or to share in their communion, whether exile awaits, or [?] is whetted, or fire [?]. Yet we could not do this, since we are unworthy even of the bare name of monks, unless the Lord heeds your holy prayers and strengthens our weakness and rottenness. Therefore keep watch for this very thing, holy Fathers, and count it as your own, since it is indeed a matter of common concern. When, at God's bidding, our most reverend brother, the steward of your holy monastery, sets out, may he bring your holiness copies of the letters sent to each of the persons concerned. Then you may learn our affairs more clearly from them, and help us partly by letters and partly by supplications. We have also entrusted another message to the brother. He will surely report and deliver it, if he manages to see your honored face. The archbishop, the Kalogeros [?], Abba Leontius and the rest of our brotherhood join us in greeting you. Please greet your holy community for us.
27. To Nicetas the patrician. [46.]
Others, perhaps, are usually raised to the height of high office by human favor. But you, our most pious and much-longed-for lord, were raised to the greatness of your rank truly by virtue and not by any favor. Nor was it for one period and in one office only; virtue has done so at every [?] and in many offices, handling you like gold and fitting you to every kind of ornament for our pious empire. The facts are plain, even if we do not speak of them. So now too our Christ-imitating emperors have fittingly appointed you in these days as the representative of their own nobility in this imperial city. This, then, is our reply, sent now by the letter-carrier, to the greeting your piety sent us. May the Lord our God keep you unharmed in soul and body from now on, as you govern and exercise authority, so that [?] the very deeds may bear witness that authority has been given to you. Your piety, out of consideration for our lowliness (so we believe, and not otherwise), spoke with the brother about the matter of the hair, saying that we had done this and that; that one must look to the right moment, act canonically and stay within our own bounds; and that a patriarch presides here as well. To this we offer the true defense. First, we thank your piety for taking pains and caring about our affairs. And rightly so. For this very thing is a mark

and a testimony of the great [virtues] that we proclaim in you: once you have heard something, you hasten to carry it out, for even a short delay brings no small danger. So too, and much more, for us who have been allotted the priesthood, the danger is greater and more ruinous if we fail to carry out all that God, the King of all, commands through the divine canons and the inspired Fathers. That it is a divine command is shown first by the Apostle; then by the Constitutions; then by Chrysostom, who establishes that for men to wear long hair is an acknowledged sin; and finally by the canon of the holy Sixth Council, which even prescribes excommunication for those who disobey. I have sent you this canon so that, hearing it for yourself, you may know that we sinners do nothing uncanonically. We did not begin enforcing this canon just now, but long ago, and it was known to the previous patriarch too. He discussed it with us in fitting terms, not accusing but approving; for how could he do otherwise, when a canon is in force? He said that he too had been reminded about this, even though we were not heeded. But we did not scrutinize his policy of accommodation. For our part, we have continued in this way up to now, not proclaiming it publicly, since we are not bishops, but keeping it in our own church, because we serve as priests. It is not possible to give the Body and Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ to those admittedly held by sin, whoever it may be, I do not know [how], unless he promises amendment. For to many we have made allowance, and still do, up to a first and a second reminder, or even a third. Beyond that, it is indifference and contempt for the canons, or rather for God, by whom they were given. This is our defense, master, to your surpassing eminence. We ask you, wherever such talk may spread, to put forward what is needed, as one who will be examined and repaid by God. As for the claim that we laid hands on someone here, it is laughable for anyone of sound mind to believe it. Not at all! On our side it was done with every encouragement, and on the side of those who accepted it, with full consent. And even then it was only a trimming of those whose hair was excessively long, reaching almost

to the belt, and who had grown soft. We did this so that we might not seem to fall short of the canon even a little, and perhaps so that from this some return to the better might come about. Pray, then, master, that we may live lawfully and peacefully. Contribute your own part as well, so that your honored soul may share in the good.
28. To Basil the monk. [47.]
We received the letters of your brotherly love, and we were amazed at its sudden change. The earlier ones (to say nothing of the rest, which are not needed at present) contained an accusation against Joseph the steward, that he had entered the Church wrongly. The later ones, on the contrary, show him entirely acquitted. And your godliness ought to know what one of the saints says about a man who now praises and now blames the same person for the same thing. But let this count for nothing, though it is a charge of self-contradiction. Why, though, were you carried away so rashly, before any testing or informed inquiry, as to pronounce that our lowliness had separated from our Church, and on that account to pronounce an anathema? 'Attend to yourself,' says the word; and, 'Do not find fault before you examine'; and, 'Understand first, and then rebuke.' But you observed none of this. Nor did you consider that we too are surely capable of speaking and acting reasonably. Instead you rebuked us as if we were uneducated, irrational, barely acquainted with the monastic life and still among the novices. And not only that, you also reproached us. Would it had stopped there! But you even consigned us to anathema. Alas for human affairs! How is it that you do not keep the bounds of friendship unmoved for long? If that friendship were pure in your honor, you would not have mocked our lowliness so heedlessly. However, we deserve such things, and it is no wonder if we are insulted even by your friendship. What we are is plain to God. But it is right to make it plain to your understanding as well, since it stumbles and takes offense. We are not schismatics from the Church of God, admirable man; may that never happen to us! Even if in other respects we are caught in many sins, still, as members of her body and her nurslings, we long to keep her canons and ordinances along with the divine dogmas. She truly has no spot or wrinkle, either in the word of faith or in the rule of the canons, from the beginning of the age until now. To disturb her and split away from her belongs to those whose faith is perverted and whose life is uncanonical and lawless. One of these is Joseph, who crowned the adulterer. So are those who put up with concelebrating with him as though he were blameless, and indeed those who commend him as officiating innocently. How is it that your reverence writes to us about canons, yet does not know the divine canons, according to which the man is deposed? For if they do not allow a presbyter to feast at the wedding of one marrying a second time,

what of crowning someone married a second time? What of feasting at an adulterous wedding for thirty whole days? And, more ruinous still, what of crowning an adulterer, according to the word of the Lord, when the one who yoked the adulterers said the sacred prayer over the union and godlessly called down divine grace upon the profane? Such a man is abominable before God, according to the divine Dionysius, and unholy. There is no need to write out here the other canons that apply to him. Moreover, he was excommunicated by the previous patriarch for nine years, and if the penalty is not lifted within a year, the canon no longer allows it to be lifted. Where does that leave us? The answer, surely, is that he had been absolved. But if he had been absolved, why does he not officiate? And if he had been absolved, why did he just now seek absolution from a synod? Clearly it is the one who is bound who seeks to be loosed, not the one who is free. So here too the man who wants to move against the truth trips over himself. It is therefore a profanation of the holy things, brother, for this man to officiate, and a complete confusion of the canons not to observe such things. And what does Chrysostom say? That it is not without danger to leave the priest unexamined. He is not speaking about faith when he says this, as you think, but about strictness of life. It is not necessary to seek out and investigate how each person stands, for grace descends even on the unworthy for the sake of those who approach. But it is different with those who are manifestly condemned. Joseph is one of these: he very openly took part in a great lawlessness before the whole world, one the Lord himself declared to be such, and by joining the couple he showed himself more plainly guilty than the adulterer. Not to make the distinction, according to the Theologian, is a clear betrayal of the truth and a dissolution of the canons. Or does your friendship not know that the Godhead itself became its own avenger when the one governing the Church at that time did not rise up, as Samuel once did against foolish Saul, to tear apart the kingdom of the new Herod for his adultery? For that Herod of old suffered the same, being [?] and killed by his own people, when he put away the daughter of King Aretas, his lawful wife, and unlawfully took Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip. If these things ought not to be [?], then John the Forerunner, if it is not too bold to say so, has sinned in the eyes of your love by rebuking Herod and dying for the rebuke. So too has Chrysostom, who showed an athlete's resistance on behalf of the widow's field. 'For perhaps for the good,' says Scripture, 'someone will even dare to die.' And I say nothing of the similar stands taken by the other saints in such matters. Or again, is your honor unaware that Christianity consists of two things, namely faith and works, and that if one is lacking, the other does its possessor no good either? We beg you, then, be zealous for divine things. First, since you are called a child of our common father, be roused along with us to what is needed. Second, since you were a disciple of the blessed

Sabas, embrace strictness not only in the faith but also in the canons. Third, since you are our fellow brother, think as we your brothers do. And, as a reminder, keep to your own cell, lest from there we stumble in the most excellent things. Forgive those who remind you, as a brother, just as we too forgive you. Nor should we be vexed at being reminded. So let your honor not be stung, but rather kindled to love. And write such things as often as you like, for we shall suffer no harm from it, except that we shall live more safely. As for the pope, you say: 'What is it to us whether he acts this way or that?' The one who says this, forgive me, is caught by his own feathers, as the saying goes. For by saying that one need not care at all about the manifest sins of the priest, he has ridiculed and spurned not just some priest but the head of the Church, so much that we were ashamed even to hear it. If it is truly so, alas for the hierarchy! But let us move our tongues sensibly, we beg you, when we speak of those at the head, and not pronounce so vehemently. As for what you wrote, that people are going to open their mouths and say that, having failed to obtain the patriarchate here, we have shifted to another pretext, let your honor not worry. God knows both the first motive and the second; indeed he will also test the third. He will expose it; he will set us before the fearful tribunal; he will repay us according to how we were disposed and how we acted. For it is not for us sinners to say, 'If I were still pleasing men, I would not be a servant of Christ.' We, then, commemorate the most holy patriarch in the liturgy, as is fitting, just as we do our pious emperors. Nor do we refuse to commune with anyone who is blameless. We have also written to the high priest himself, since it has become known to our pious emperors as well that we differ from him in nothing except Joseph alone. As soon as Joseph is suspended from officiating, we will commune with him at once. The man is dear to us, not only because he has become the head of our Church, but also because we have revered him for a long time. And we never cease to extol whatever is good in his life. If it should turn out that he too approves of this zeal (not to mention holy bishops, abbots, monks and a multitude of laypeople), what would your friendship say then? Know, therefore, that this is not a schism in the Church but the triumph of truth and the vindication of the divine laws. The other course, as your honor said earlier, is a rupture of the truth and the dissolution of the canons. These words can rightly be said to you as well: 'The priests set aside my law and profaned my holy things; they made no distinction between the profane and the holy, but everything was common to them.' For to have no spot or wrinkle, to say it once more, should be understood like this: not admitting impious dogmas or uncanonical undertakings, nor indeed complicity with those who do what is forbidden, as the divine Basil says somewhere. With regard to such people, the great Paul does not even permit us to eat with them. For from the time of the

apostles onward, many heresies in many ways have dashed against her, and lawless and uncanonical defilements have spread over her surface, as they do now. Yet in the manner already described she has remained undivided and blameless, and she will remain so until the end of the age, while those who think or act wrongly are removed and cast out of her, like waves that dash against an unshaken rock on the shore.

So let us come to our senses, brother, and step into the light of truth. Let us be seen holding fast to the sacred canons as well as to the dogmas, we monks above all, we above all who seem to be something. For if the light in us is darkness, how great is the darkness! And, 'If the salt has lost its savor, with what will the laity be salted?' We think you are, and pray that you may be, the savior and luminary of those there, a lamp of strictness and piety. That comes not from becoming all things to all people, but from the height of virtue, from a life ruled by the canons, and from conduct befitting sacred things. Bear with your brother's reminder, which is loving, truth-loving and judged by God. My desire draws me to say more, but the excessive length of the letter reins us in and brings us to a stop here. We have received your rich gift. And that you have taken thought for the lowliness of your monastery shows that you spare it and labor for it, and it has cost you considerable toil. But the Lord will repay you with what you need: growth in the virtues and the enjoyment of his eternal goods.
29. To Leo the orphanotrophos. [48.]
We wished to be present ourselves, my most beloved lord, and share in the misfortune that has befallen you in your blessed child, and not merely to lament the suffering by letter and share in your grief. For how is it not pitiable, how is it not stunning, to suffer the loss of one child after another? It is like losing a living treasure: the wealth of the family's succession, the much-prayed-for fruit of the mother's breast, the beautiful eye of the household, the joy of the grandmother, the pride of the whole family. The first fruit came, and it was snatched untimely from the parents' hands. The second grew, and bitter death ravaged it too. The third shoot blossomed as a consolation for the earlier ones, flourishing and lovely, and its life reached three years. The souls of the parents hung upon it. And alas for the misfortune! (Grief cuts off even my speech.) This one too has gone from your sight, and what is more pitiable still, not even in its father's presence. But why should I dwell on the tragedy? Your hearts are cut, the father's, the mother's, the lady patrician's, and a sword has passed through the midst of both. And it will tend the irrational part, not

…a word, not a fable, not from a man, not from an angel, but from God alone, who has set the bounds of our life in this way. For it is he, my lord, who has taken to himself your thrice-longed-for child, just as he took those who went before. Your situation is grievous indeed, and exceedingly so; but it is not so at all for those who have been taken. Since they are pure and unstained by sin because they were newly born, they have passed from things here to the blessed life free of passion. They dance in the bosom of Abraham, they dwell with holy infants, and they sing hymns with the children who bore Christ. So your most beautiful children have not perished. They are saved for you, and they live on. And you will see them a little later, when this life in time comes to its end, rejoicing and exulting, not at a tender age but in the maturity of the fullness of Christ, as it is written. Therefore we urge and entreat you to soothe yourselves with these thoughts, as truth requires, and so to remove the immoderate grief from your soul. For the Lord has given us measures, so that we may show our natural affection and still not overstep the bounds of what is enough. The one moves the Divine to mercy; the other makes us set ourselves against the decrees of Providence. The one gladdens the departed; the other usually grieves the very ones who have attained rest. For everyone wishes to rejoice in his own joy, and does not want those who profess to love him to be grieving. We believe that the lady, the chartoularios's wife, will again be with child and bear a son, no longer short-lived but long-lived, to carry on the family line, if only we moderate our grief and, in deed and word, offer thank-offerings for the child to Christ the Master.

30 [?]. — To Nicephorus the Patriarch. [51.]

It is not necessary to put in writing to the angel of your [holiness?] what was conveyed by word of mouth, [?] if not through both of us lowly ones. But yesterday's meeting of the bishops, held at your command, may have reported something other than what we said there and so troubled your sacred ears. To prevent this, we thought it fitting to set out in summary the whole substance of our defense. We, then, most blessed one, are orthodox in every respect. We reject every heresy and accept every approved council, both ecumenical and local; moreover, we firmly hold to the sacred and canonical ordinances they pronounced. For anyone who thinks he holds the right faith but is not guided by the [sacred?] canons does not rightly and fully divide the word of truth. We also accept the lawful acts of economy that the saints have made at the proper time. Indeed, for us lowly ones now to embrace your holiness despite the [?] of the steward is the act not of those who are strict, but of those who are very accommodating and condescending.

On this same principle we received the most holy patriarch who preceded your holiness in the matter before us, when we returned from exile. The adulterous union had been broken up and the steward debarred from priestly service, [on the understanding] that we should have no share, neither in this age nor in the age to come, in the adulterer's being given communion indiscriminately by his holiness. He had already said, 'I was using economy, even in giving him communion for a time.' Then he also declared, 'My hands would have been cut off before [I took part in] the adulterous crowning. Or did I perform the crowning at all?' On these terms, then, we were in communion with him until his falling asleep. We have likewise accepted your holiness into the dignity of the high priesthood, and we commemorate you every day in the liturgy. In nothing is there any doubt, except because of the steward. The sacred canons have deposed him on many counts. Above all, after the nine-year excommunication he again performs priestly service, and not in some out-of-the-way place. That would be bearable, since we would have no part in the matter. But he does so in the very fountainhead, so to speak, of our priesthood, entering and concelebrating with your pure person continually. What is just and holy, and gives no scandal to the peoples of God and especially to our order, is this: the one who entered unworthily should be expelled from priestly service, while we commemorate your holiness and are in communion with every hierarch and priest who is not manifestly condemned, as the Theologian says. But if, because of our sins, this does not happen at all, and something uncanonical and lawless befalls our lowliness at the hands of your holiness (may nothing of the kind happen! We do not say this from fear, but from pity for the common good), we shall endure it by the power of God, whatever may happen by his permission. But we testify to your holiness before Christ, in the hearing of the holy angels, that you are creating a great schism in our Church. And if we seem to wield authority, we are only men. Rather, it is under the authority of the sacred and divine canons [?] that we are governed and shall obey, even against our will. But we beseech your holiness: incline your ear and hear our voice. As a skilled physician, as a good shepherd, bar the one sheep from priestly service and win the whole flock free from scandal. Do not let our Church, which the Lord our God purchased with his own blood, be infected by the mange of one. As for idle talk, let those who wish babble on, and let the slanderers slander. We are ready to make any defense and to refute any charge brought against us. We are your friends and your praisers, and very much so of our most pious and gloriously victorious sovereigns as well. Since we are such, why this turmoil? For what reason will whatever happens happen, if it is contrary to the commandments of God? Grant us your sacred prayer.

31 [?]. — To the brothers at Sakkoudion. [?]

As long as it was time to use economy and keep hidden the matter of our breaking communion with Joseph the steward, we did so, children and brothers. We were not held back by fear, sinners though we are, but acted out of condescension for economy's sake. In this we were imitating, in some measure, our holy Fathers. They too used economy at the fitting time and so withdrew themselves from trials, partly sparing the weaker and those who were suffering [?], and partly yielding a little, as a helmsman does, so that a little later they might achieve the success they sought. But now our good God has been pleased to let the matter come out openly into plain view, and so now we are writing. It came out through the questioning of the logothete of the Course and the archbishop's reply to him. The logothete said: 'Why have you not been in communion with us and with the patriarch until now, though so many feasts have passed? Tell us the reason openly.' And the archbishop confessed; he did not deny it, but confessed: 'I have nothing against our pious emperors, nor against the patriarch either. My objection is to the steward, who crowned the adulterer and for that reason stands deposed by the sacred canons.' To this the logothete answered: 'Our pious emperors have no need of you, neither in Thessalonica nor anywhere else.' That is where things stand. No counter-reply was given immediately, and no further question has been put, though thirteen days have now passed. The only thing is that we have sent a letter to lord Symeon, which we have enclosed with this one so that you may know the full import of the affair. The matter has resounded before the patriarch and almost the whole city. Many share our distress and voice agreement with us. But they are God-fearers by night, unable to speak out openly in the light. As for us, children and brothers, we trust in God and are made steadfast by the truth. We are also strengthened by the very outcome that justice has brought about and made manifest, as was shown before the world, both upon the adulterer and upon those who collaborated with him. So we will not swerve from the commandment and the canons of the Fathers. We will not yield or betray true religion, nor will we tear down what we built well through our resistance in exile, lest we be shown to be transgressors of the law. Held by the divine law, we hold fast, as we held fast before, enduring all things and bearing all things, if God should permit them, rather than share in communion with that man and those who concelebrate with him, until the deposed man ceases from priestly service. People will babble a great deal. They mock and will laugh at us, and, what is more pitiable, not a few of those who share our habit,

Matt. 10:56 [?].

our rank, and seem to be our friends. But this is nothing strange. It is written: 'And a man's enemies will be those of his own household.' They are the ones who acted as go-betweens and collaborators, who ate and drank together at the adulterous wedding, and who dipped their pens to sign our exile. But the Lord rose up then to avenge his law. He shattered the reign of the adulterer by blinding, put his accomplices to shame like the priests of Baal, and gathered our lowly selves back into our monastery beyond all hope. He is present now as well. For a little while he again permitted the unlawful [union?] [?]. Yet he has again been pleased to have the gloating of the adultery-yokers and the adultery-fostering Nazirites rejected, through the just judgment of our pious emperors. After his death they restored the adulterer to his lawful wife, called the harlot an adulteress, and left the adulterously begotten child without inheritance as illegitimate and utterly lawless, according to the Roman laws, as their honored mouth declared in my hearing. Nevertheless, the lawbreakers are not ashamed. Nor does the man who uttered blasphemies against the Holy Spirit in the sacred prayer for the wedding crowning hide himself away. Instead, having leapt into the Church of God like a cat, he jumps again and begins again to defile the holy things by his priestly service. He strives to make lawlessness pass for righteousness and, as the saying goes, to show himself holier than the Forerunner and Baptist. John rebuked Herod's adultery and died for the truth. This man crowned the second Herod, who had been revealed in adultery, and embraced him until death. By this he declared, not in words but in his very deeds, that John the Forerunner was wrong to rebuke unlawfully and untimely, and to die for it. But why speak of John, the greatest of all the saints? Against Christ himself, bold as it is to say, he spoke out and fought with his unholy mouth. Christ called the man who puts away his lawful wife an adulterer. (Adultery is a grievous sin, equal to that of the murderer, the sodomite, the one who lies with beasts, the sorcerer and the idolater, according to the canon of St Basil.) Yet this man set that very person before the altar in the midst of all the people and dared to burst out with those unholy words against the Holy Spirit. He said this (and consider how fearful and monstrous it is): 'Yourself, O Master, stretch out your hand from your holy dwelling place and join your handmaid to your servant. Yoke them together in concord; unite them into one flesh, these whom you have been pleased to join to one another. Make their marriage honorable; keep their bed undefiled; be pleased that their life together remain spotless, in a pure heart.' [?] How greatly, [do you suppose, as you hear this,] was the Holy Spirit provoked by the blasphemy, and how angry were the holy angels along with it? Or [how is it that] the earth did not open at once, as it did for Dathan and Abiram, and swallow the guide of falsehood, who presents

[darkness?] as light and tries to make Christ contradict himself? For whatever the priest signifies, God also declares that he confirms, according to the great Dionysius. Yet he has done this wicked thing and given an example of evil for his subordinates to imitate, which has indeed happened. Still worse, he has given it to those who hold power and rule far away, and the same thing was done in Lombardy and Gothia and its regions. Not even among the heathen has such a thing been dared. And the wretch is not ashamed. As has been said, the unholy man serves at the altar and hastens to exile those who rightly turn away from him. But the Lord is the helper of those who stand firm for his commandment. He will move the hearts of our pious emperors to avenge his Church, as in the case of the adulterer, and may he be pleased to have this man too expelled from priestly service, for the benefit of the most holy patriarch and of the whole catholic Church. So take courage, children and brothers; do not be afraid or lose heart. It is a time for confession, a time for resistance, a time for struggle, and perhaps for other sufferings too. But it is also a time for crowns and heavenly glory. For he says: 'Those who glorify me I will glorify, and whoever despises me will be dishonored.' And: 'Blessed are those who do not turn aside from his commandments.' Therefore, 'Rejoice and be glad, for your reward,' you who endure, 'is great in heaven.' Hold to your works. Pray for our emperors, for the high priest, for Joseph to be expelled from the altar, and for the peace of the Church. Walk in the blameless way, delighting greatly in his commandments, in all good order and a canonical manner of life, until you hear something further or we ourselves send word. Christ be with you; may the Theotokos shelter you; may the Forerunner and the Theologian guard you, and all the saints, by the prayer of my Father and your Father. I greet you all by name. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all, beloved children. Amen.

[?] — To the chartoularios [?].

We had supposed, our most longed-for lord, that your great piety was somewhat hostile toward our lowliness because of some incidental matter. But at this present time you have truly shown that your honored soul is free of all ill will and, more than that, full of all godliness. You became swift and fervent, for the sake of the peace of the Church of God, and were moved at our very first request to work for our reunion with our most holy patriarch. This is the mark of sincere friendship; this is the trait of a God-bearing man; this is the proof of a manifest zeal for truth. And so may the Lord repay you, even if nothing comes of it,

with the full reward of righteousness. For the Divine [?] awards recompense to those who act, not according to the outcome of affairs, but according to their intention in them, whether praiseworthy or not. In a single moment of time, then, you have gained not gold and silver, but unfailing treasures of heavenly recompense. We further urge and implore you to press on in this matter. Then you yourself will gain a rich treasure, and we humble ones will obtain a meeting with the high priest. More than that, the Church of God, set in order by your mediation, will weave many crowns of praise for you. There is no need to say more. But since you asked us to indicate what our lowliness's position is, we now truthfully make known to your most eminent excellency that [?] we will both concelebrate and be in communion, and receive ordination, making no inquiry about

his concelebration during these three years. [We tolerated it] for economy's sake, not out of fear, but for the common benefit and for salvation. Let the lying tongues that are stirred up against the peace of God fall silent. They say that, once the steward is barred from priestly service, we will seize on pretexts to bring down our high priest for having already concelebrated with the deposed man, and after him the most holy patriarch who preceded him. Deceitful are the lips that say such things. This is the scheme of slanderous and envious men who do not want the debt that has fallen upon the Church to come to healing. By no means; God forbid! We both received and still receive the patriarch who went before, and that is why we remained in communion with him until his death. We both received and still receive the present most holy high priest, and for this reason we commemorate him every day. Let the steward who crowned the adulterer be barred from priestly service. Then, as we have already declared, we will concelebrate with him [the patriarch], if he so orders, in the catholic Church, each of us according to our own rank.
