If this happens, there will be joy in heaven and peace in our Church of God. The schism will withdraw, and concord will shine forth brightly. Our high priest will be crowned with praises, so much that his praise will be handed down from generation to generation. Our most mighty emperors, along with their most precious diadems, will be crowned with the acclaim of angels. The priests will be clothed with righteousness, and still more the holy ones (I mean the monastic order) will rejoice with exultation. As for you, our lord, what need is there to say what kind of prize, and how great, you will receive? What good thing will not rather come about? What delight will not [?]? Let us say this too: the steward himself

will be praised and glorified, and for this he will inherit great mercy, both in this age and in the age to come. And we sinners will fall at your feet, do obeisance and give thanks, and contribute in deed and word whatever is fitting, as is due to a high priest above all men. To confirm what we have said, we are setting down our word in writing at length. If, once he has ceased from priestly service as before, we do not immediately enter and take communion, as written above, let the verdict be yours, whatever you wish, and let us no longer be permitted to speak about the matter. And behold, it is not an angel, not a man, but the Lord himself who draws you through us, urges you on and entreats you.

33 [?]. — To Leo, Pope of Rome. [72.]

To the most holy and most preeminent Father of Fathers, my lord Leo, the apostolic pope, from Theodore, the least of presbyters and abbot of the Studites.

Christ our God gave to the great Peter, along with the keys of the kingdom of heaven, the dignity of chief shepherd as well. It is therefore necessary that any innovation brought into the catholic Church by those who turn away from the truth be referred to Peter, that is, to his successor. We humble and least of men have been taught this by our holy Fathers of old. Since an innovation has now arisen once again in our Church, we have thought it our duty to report it to the angel of your preeminent blessedness. We did so first through the most reverent archimandrite, our brother and fellow servant Epiphanius, and we do so now through our poor letter. There has taken place, O most divine head of all heads, in the words of the prophet Jeremiah, a true synod of transgressors and a council of adulterers. What was said there of idolatrous fornication has been shown here in the ratification of adulterous union. Both have rejected the same Lord, the former by transgressing the Law, the latter by transgressing the Gospel. And they did not stop there. At an earlier assembly they became an illicit gathering, as the divine Basil calls it, by receiving the man who joined the adulterers and concelebrating with him. But then, as if to win for themselves the name of an outright heresy, they held another, public synod. There they anathematized those who did not consent to their lawless false doctrine, or rather the whole catholic Church. Of those who had already been brought before them, they banished some far away and hold others in prison, once again starting a persecution, as is customary here. And their justification is the bolstering of a wicked argument. They lay down as doctrine that the joining of adulterers is economy. They decree that the divine laws do not apply to emperors. Those who stood firm for truth and justice even to the point of blood,

…they forbid us to imitate, as they forbid imitating the Forerunner and Chrysostom, and they declare that each of the hierarchs has authority over the divine canons, contrary to what the canons themselves lay down. For this reason, whenever one of the clergy happens to be convicted, secretly or openly, under canons that require deposition, he remains undeposed if whoever holds authority so wishes. A witness to this is the priest who joined the adulterers in marriage: he stands condemned under various canons, along with others, and yet he celebrates the liturgy with them in public. Those who commit lawless acts as acts of "economy" they call saints, both others and themselves, on that very account; and those who do not accept these acts they anathematize as estranged from God. The persecution is a witness to this as well. What, then, can be said about these things, O blessed one, except that apostolic saying, "Now many antichrists have arisen"? For it seems that we human beings are not all subject to the divine laws and canons. Having now reported these things truthfully in our lowliness, we bring to your Christ-imitating Blessedness the cry that the chief of the apostles, with the other apostles, raised to Christ when the waves of the sea were rising: "Save us, chief shepherd of the Church under heaven; we are perishing!" Imitate Christ your teacher, and stretch out your hand to our Church as he did to Peter. But there is a difference: he reached out to a man who was beginning to sink in the sea, while you would reach out to a Church already sunk in the depths of heresy. Emulate, we beg you, the pope who bore your name. When the Eutychian heresy sprang up in his day, he was roused in spirit like a lion, as all know, by his dogmatic letters. So you too, true to your name, I dare to say, roar in a godly way, or rather thunder as is fitting against the present false doctrine. These men took authority upon themselves and did not fear to convene a heretical synod, though they have no authority to convene even an orthodox one without your knowledge, as the custom that has prevailed from of old shows. How much more reasonable and necessary would it be, then, that your divine primacy should assemble a lawful synod? We say this with fear, only as a reminder. Then the orthodox doctrine of the Church would drive back the heretical one. Your preeminence would no longer be anathematized, together with all the orthodox, by these new babblers, and those so inclined would no longer find the adulterous synod a base for lawlessness and slide easily into sin. We have reported these things as befits our nothingness, as the least members of the Church and as those who submit to the divine chief-pastorate exercised by you. For the rest, we ask your holy soul to count us as its own sheep, and to enlighten and strengthen us from afar by its sacred prayers. If you would also teach us, that would be a mark of your divine condescension. For Christ too sent a letter to Abgar, and many of lower rank were deemed worthy to receive letters from apostles and saints. This [letter?] comes from me alone, the sinner kept in prison, [?]

[?] because my Father and fellow servant, the recluse, and the archbishop of Thessalonica, our brother, are likewise being kept on other islands. Yet they too, through [?], say the same things as I do, and with me they embrace the sacred footsteps of your Blessedness.

To the most blessed and apostolic Father Leo, pope of Rome, from Plato the recluse and Theodore, priest and abbot of the Studites.

It is truly a great thing for us lowly ones, and the fulfillment of our highest prayer, to have been deemed worthy to receive from your apostolic Blessedness a word of greeting, and even a written copy of your sacred, Spirit-moved words, through Epiphanius, our fellow servant and beloved child. And this came to us while we were shut up by the heterodox and could see the letter-bearer only from on high [?]. At this we leapt for joy, we exulted, and we gave thanks to the Lord, who through your divine prayers had wondrously granted us, unworthy as we are, what was beyond our hope. We almost imagined that we were seeing your sacred features through your words. In imitation of Christ, you greeted us humble ones and rekindled our [?]; you [?] our weakness and [?] our feebleness, as if anointing us with the words of comfort and admonition you spoke on our behalf, and you urged us to stand unswervingly in the orthodox faith to the end. May it be so for us by your gracious supplications. We nobodies, for our part, have thought it right to report to you once more what is fitting, as we did before through this same most faithful letter-bearer of ours, and again through Eustathius, who is also our child. A synod has been held among us, most blessed one, a general assembly at which the officials in authority also sat, and the synod was held for the [?] of the Gospel of Christ. You received its keys from him, through the chief of the apostles and those who succeeded one another down to the one who preceded your most sacred head. How could your God-imitating gentleness bear to hear of it? Let us begin from the Law and the Prophets. It says: "You shall not commit adultery; you shall not bear false witness; you shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain." Jeremiah says: "Foolish and ungodly is he who keeps an adulteress." And Malachi: "The lips of a priest shall guard knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, for he is the messenger of the Lord Almighty." Let us pass on to the Gospel: "Whoever divorces his wife and marries another," it says, "commits adultery." And again: "What God has joined together, let no one separate." How great the difference is between law and grace we shall learn from the Lord's own words, when he says:

"And behold, something greater than the temple is here." We shall learn it also from the words of the Apostle, who says: "Anyone who has set aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses. How much worse a punishment, do you think, will be deserved by the one who has trampled on the Son of God, regarded as common the blood of the covenant, and insulted the Spirit of grace?" Since this is so, consider what those who disobey the Lord with lawless tongues have done. They have called a saving economy for the Church of God what is in fact the undoing of both the law and the Gospel. First, there is the adultery of the former ruler, who cast out his lawful wife and brought in the adulteress. Then there is a transgression greater and more grievous than this, the adulterous wedding, for in the sacred rite they bore false witness against God and invoked his name over an unlawful act. Moreover, they gave the adulterers crowns of victory against Christ and let them share in the divine gifts. Those gifts were insulted as something common by the priest who joined the adulterers, and he proved in truth to be a messenger not of God Almighty but of Satan, the ruler of this world. Further, there is the transgression of all those who, by their concurrence and approval, took their part in this sin with the adulterer and with the priest who married him. They call this economy so firm and unalterable that they have synodically subjected to anathema, together with imprisonment and other sufferings, those who did not yield and agree with them, for refusing to accept that this economy was a holy deed. "Hear, O heaven," says Isaiah, "and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken." And we lowly ones now say to you: Hear, O great head of God's Church, and give ear to what Satan has wrought. If this assembly and its decree of anathema accord with God's will and approval, then clearly the law is not God's. Nor are the prophets God's, among them the Forerunner who rebuked adultery. Nor, finally, is the Gospel, against which they have made this economy so dear to them [?]. For if they say the law is his, one of two things follows. Either they will declare Christ a liar, who spoke and gave the law of old through the prophets and now speaks in person in the Gospel. Or, if he speaks the truth, as indeed he is himself the Truth, then they themselves are lying and are proven beyond doubt to be accusers of God. In that case they are liable to the anathema they pronounced against Christ and his saints, since they have affirmed adultery, adulterous marriage, and complicity in adultery as an economy of God and of the saints. It cannot be otherwise. For there is no partiality with God, as the Moechians suggest. They hold that his laws do not apply equally to all, but that in the case of kings, as they put it, the laws give way and may be altered. Where, then, is there a Gospel for kings? Truly they have been exceedingly impious. They do not understand that God shows no partiality to anyone, as the holy Apostle said. Nor do they understand that the same God, through one of the

prophets, laments over them and says: "You have not kept my ways, but you have shown partiality in the law. Did not one God create you? Is there not one Father of you all?" Solomon also writes: "Hear, therefore, O kings, and understand." And further on: "Because, though you were servants of the kingdom of the Most High, you did not judge rightly, nor keep the law, nor walk according to the counsel of God, he will come upon you terribly and swiftly, for a severe judgment falls on those in high places. The Lord of all will not shrink from anyone's person." Know again, O sacred and divine head, that through the transgressions already described they have set aside the whole Gospel, since even one lawless act is enough to overturn the entire law. For the commandments, says Basil the Great, are all bound to one another, so that when one is undone, the rest are necessarily undone with it. He says this not of himself but from Christ who speaks in him, who says: "Whoever breaks one of the least of these commandments shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven"—that is, will perish. And the divine James says: "Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all." So they have undone the Old and the New Testament, O blessed one, by breaking not the least but the greatest of the Lord's commandments. The wretches have set up a law against the law of the Gospel: that the will of kings is to be preferred to God's whenever they so wish. But different kings wish different things, and at different times they wish differently. The result is the overturning of everything, right up to the Antichrist. Hence what they call economy, but which comes from Satan, will fittingly be named a forerunner of the Antichrist. As for their transgression of the canons, what need is there even to speak? Since they have turned their backs on the Gospel, they are hardly likely to care about the canons. The Lord [?] says through the prophet: "I will place the key of the house of David on his shoulder; he shall open, and none shall shut; he shall shut, and none shall open." But they act against God. Where he opened, they have shut, deposing the blameless, who seem guilty to them but not to God. Where he shut, they have opened, promoting those who fall under deposition by God's own judgment. Once and for all, and always, they treat the sacred canons as masters treat servants and slaves, using them for whatever seems good and pleasing to them. These are the lawless and impious undertakings of the Moechian heresy, and these are their results. As the least children of the catholic Church, we have been eager to report them to you, our foremost apostolic head, as necessity required. For the rest, it is for you to think and to do what is pleasing to God, moved by the Holy Spirit in this as in other matters. We also entreat you to deem us worthy to receive letters in your own words and inscribed by God, in imitation of the saints who shared your zeal, just as we have now received your rich gifts and blessings, which are beyond our deserts.

Our brother Epiphanius himself has told us, most divine head, that you have brought a charge against us concerning Barsanuphius, Isaiah and Dorotheus, the heretics, on the grounds that we accept them as orthodox. We were greatly astonished at the idea that we lowly ones, who are suffering for orthodoxy, should be taking the side of heretics [?]. Let every mouth that speaks [?] and slanders against us be stopped. We are orthodox, most blessed one, even if we are sinners in other ways. In this we fall short of the apostolic faith in nothing whatsoever. We embrace every synod, ecumenical and local, that has been approved by the truth, together with the holy canons it set forth, and we loathe and anathematize every heresy and every heretic. Anathema to Barsanuphius, Isaiah, Dorotheus and Dositheus, who were anathematized by Saint Sophronius. And if there is anyone else who bears the same names and is likewise a heretic, whether he holds their heresy or another, whether he is a bishop or an ascetic or anyone at all, let him be anathema. And if anyone does not anathematize every heretic at the proper time, as necessity requires, let him have his portion with them. For by your most sacred prayers, all-holy one, we are pure of every heretical opinion. We also report this. In our letter sent through our brother Eustathius, it was not mentioned that we had written to your holy head through Epiphanius. Yet Epiphanius did not lie, and this is how it happened. We had in fact given him the letter, but then we erased it out of fear of those in power. He, however, knew its contents, and after we had been exiled he wisely brought it to your holy footsteps. For he is the mouth of our lowliness and the word that pours forth from our heart. So let your holy soul take no offense at our fellow servant, who is most faithful in all things. Our brother the archbishop of Thessalonica received your Blessedness's greeting with the open hands of his heart, and through us he reverently embraces your most sacred head.

35. To Basil, abbot. [76.]

We humble ones were longing to receive a letter from your fatherly holiness as a thirsty land longs for its rain. When we did not receive one, we were grieved, as was natural. But we learned the reason from Epiphanius, our most beloved and most faithful [brother?]: that it was out of necessity, and not from any contempt for us, who are lowly but ardent lovers of your godliness. So we exchanged the pain of our heart for joy enough to satisfy us. For he reported that you remain the same in your disposition and love toward us, and that you are even growing in goodness in various ways. And the zeal

for piety that has been roused in your holy soul, how great it is, he described to us, and the news rang in both our ears. Blessed be the Lord of hosts, who has set you in the foremost of cities as a luminary shining with the light of God, holding forth the word of life with an abundance of good deeds; who has given you a tongue that speaks freely the divine teachings of orthodoxy with lofty proclamation. So we also beg you to help our Church, both by your own strength and by your mediation with the most holy apostolic [pope]. For your manly defense of the word of truth is a strengthening for the Church under heaven, and the zeal that comes from you always kindles the whole world to an ardent confession of our faith in the Holy Spirit. So your God-honored self knows [?] how great an account you must give for the power of piety, and how great is the praise from God, with worthy rewards, for guarding and proclaiming it. May you guard it and never cease to proclaim it, our most divine and admirable Fathers. For this reason we have sent again our brother Epiphanius, who venerates your footsteps, so that he may report our affairs to you in turn. By your holy prayers all is well: we sinners rejoice and are glad in persecution and in prison, so that we dare to say, "It has been granted to us not only to believe in Christ but also to suffer for him." We also sent him to urge you to more fervent prayer, both for the courage of us weak ones and for the common good. That is our concern, and our petition to you most holy ones is now being made for the third time. We do not ask to be released from prison, for we do not regard it as a disgrace but as the greatest glory, beyond what we unworthy ones deserve. We ask that what benefits the common good may come about, even though we are among the least. For everywhere, says the Theologian, one must disregard one's own interest for the common good of the many. And this is our aim and longing, for it would be of benefit. Those who sat in council against the Gospel of Christ should be rebuked synodically through the most preeminent apostolic [see], as was done in former times and from the beginning. They anathematized those who hold fast to the Gospel and who did not accept adultery, adulterous marriage, and complicity in adultery as an economy of the saints, as the Moechians decreed. In this they called the saints transgressors, yet the saints not only never crowned adulterers or gave them the divine gifts, but declared that one should not even share roof and fire with them, even if they were kings. These men have also insulted the Divine itself through the rites of crowning, bringing the anathema upon God himself by anathematizing those who keep his law. But if this does not happen, then for the rest we pray for the strength of your prayers, the authority of the bonds of love, and the power of your letters in reply. We beg you by all means to do this, consoling the faint-hearted and strengthening

the feeble, our most holy, [?] and ever-venerable Fathers.

36. To Euprepianus and those with him. [88.]

I have good hope, beloved children, regarding your [?] and God-ordered way of life. So I will turn my words to what is urgent. What is that? When we uncover their evil doctrines and show the reasons for which they anathematized us along with others, they are shown to be not simply heretics of some kind, but apostates from the Gospel of God, anathematizers of the saints, and destroyers of the canons. First, they set themselves against the Old and the New [Testament]. "You shall not commit adultery," says the law; "You shall not take the name of God in vain"; "There shall be one law for the native and for the proselyte." Then the Gospel, that is, Christ, says: "You have heard that it was said to those of old, 'You shall not commit adultery.' But I say to you: do not even look at a woman so as to desire her." And: "Whoever breaks one of the least of these commandments shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven"—that is, he will be thrown into the fire, as the Fathers interpret it. But they—O dreadful thing to hear!—have called all this an economy of God, good and saving for the Church. They call it so: adultery, which law and grace alike proscribe, even down to the desire of a look; the breaking of a commandment that is not the least but, one might say, the first and greatest in the practical life; and besides this, taking the name of God not merely in vain but over so unlawful and wicked a deed, I mean the adulterous wedding; the partaking of the mysteries of Christ; and the crowning, which is warfare against God waged by the devil, the author of adultery, and by his servant. Let us stop our ears, brothers, lest we melt at the blasphemy. And their justification is that, as they say, the laws of the Gospel must be overlooked in the case of kings. Behold another forerunner of the Antichrist! Where, then, is "There shall be one law"? Where is "Severe judgment falls on those in high places"? Where is "God does not show partiality to anyone"? And who is the king's lawgiver? Ruler and ruled go together, so if the laws of the Gospel do not bind the ruler, they do not bind the ruled either. If they bind him, they bind them too, so that, ranked under one law and one lawgiver, they remain obedient and free of faction. But suppose the laws do not bind him whenever he wishes—and perhaps he might wish to keep none of them—while they do bind the subjects. Then one of two things follows: either the king is God, for the Divine alone is not under law, or there is anarchy and faction. For where the law is not the same for all, how can there be peace? The king wants one thing, namely to commit adultery or to embrace heresy, while his subjects, though commanded to side with the adulterer, will not agree, nor join in the heresy, nor in any way swerve from what was handed down by Christ and the apostles. How, then, is it not plain from this that the Antichrist is at the doors? For they will dare

…the Moechians say: "Is it not so? Whatever unlawful thing the emperor does, he both does it and commands the people to submit to it." And see, in their argument the Antichrist has fully entered. For he too will be an emperor, and he will seek only this: that what he wills and orders be done. He will differ in nothing from those before him, except perhaps that they do not will and desire it to the same degree, though they may well come to do so even now. This same authority has been proclaimed in synod by the hierarchs. How could anyone with understanding who is not contentious fail to admit that this is so? What heresy will be worse than this one until the Antichrist himself appears? I do not think there is any yet. Rather, this very heresy, having begun now, will come to its end and completion in that time. All who fall into it would have fallen then too, had they been alive; and all who stand and fight against it by the power of God would also in those days be victorious over the Antichrist, dying with Christ. But oh, human wretchedness! How they have turned their backs from this point on! How do we show what we shall be? This is why those who will stand firm are few. This is why Elijah and Enoch (we do not know whether the Theologian and evangelist as well) will come to help human weakness, as front-line champions and prize-winners in the victory won by confessing Christ. This is why the days of that distress will be cut short, brought to an end by the appearing of Christ. You who understand, stand firm, do not deny Christ from now on; for the present things are the beginning of those that will come then. The second point needs little explanation, since it is evident from the first. They have anathematized those who do not accept the adulterous union, the adultery of the emperor, and the lawlessness of everyone who took part in it and threw in his lot with it, as though it were a holy economy. What else have they done but anathematize the saints, and first of all the Forerunner? And to tell the truth, fearful though it is, they have anathematized the very Master of the saints. For he who forbade these things does not accept them, nor obviously approve them. On the contrary, he threatened an inexorable judgment merely for throwing in one's lot with an adulterer, not this one or that one, but anyone at all: emperor, potentate, small and great. For "there shall be one law," he says, and we have received one Gospel. Whoever disturbs even the least thing in this Gospel, even if it is an angel from heaven, then you have certainty enough. Is an emperor greater than an angel? Is not the world-ruler in the world greater than all the demons and men who hold worldly power, though not in the divine order? And what does the Apostle say? "Let him be anathema." Angels do not dare to disturb it, and if they do, they do not escape anathema, like the devil and his apostate host. How then is any man in the flesh who disturbs and innovates, especially with such innovations, not estranged from God? But the one who does not accept what He forbade (for we must take up the argument again from where it went off into a digression [?]) has already been anathematized by the Moechians, or rather the Antichrists. But if

they have called the Master this, just as the Jews said he cast out demons by Beelzebul, what of his servants and attendants? There are two possibilities. Perhaps they regarded the saints as men who did not obey the Master's laws in their acts of economy. In that case they made adulterous union and adulterous communion equal in weight and glory to those acts, ascribing economy to them, and so anathematized the saints as lawless men who broke the commandments; for this they must certainly be anathematized themselves. Or else they confess the saints to be guardians of the law, and so have anathematized themselves. "But we have not anathematized the saints," they say, wretches who have claimed the name of saints for themselves in what they call their economy of adulterous union. And for this reason they have anathematized the saints once again, as men who are not saints. For in their view the saints are those who have practised and still practise economies with the force of adulterous union and adulterous partnership. Those who do not accept their economy founded on adultery, and do not practise economy in its footsteps, are in their eyes estranged from God, lawless, breakers of the commandments and anathematized. So start wherever you like, and look at whichever of their impious statements you wish. Consider it, you of sharp mind, and marvel as you contemplate and take in depth upon depth of godlessness. For heresies do not display their whole impiety openly. Some are entirely remote from the Gospel. Others clothe themselves in certain sayings of the Gospel and slip in along with them. They do not say that one should not follow the Gospel's precepts. On the contrary, they make a great show of championing them, while raising doubts about the divine words, as to whether they should be understood this way and not that. And because they miss the right understanding, they have been called heresies. Here, however, is a manifest falling away from the faith. These men do not err about the meaning. Instead they say: "Christ did indeed say this, and the law may well hold such and such, but in the case of emperors it is done like this, and the Gospel is overruled." Consider how the end follows the beginning. From the incarnation of Christ the heresies began outside the Gospel. Then the devil, repulsed as grace gradually advanced, crept in secretly from within the Gospel itself. He fathered the heresies down to the Iconoclasts, decking out his bait with Scripture and its texts. And when he perceived that men were obedient to him, and the time of the consummation was pressing on, he began from now on, as at the beginning, to kindle murder against the Gospel itself, so that he might arrive smoothly at the Antichrist, in whom he will dwell and in whom all his bitterness and apostasy will be revealed. Him the Lord will destroy by his appearing, and very soon. What shall we say about the third point? Those who have dared to transgress the Gospel bare-headed, and have anathematized those who chose not to transgress it, what care will they have for canons? And yet these too were sealed by the Holy Spirit, and when they are dissolved,

everything that serves our salvation is dissolved with them. For then there is no priesthood anywhere, no [?] authority, none of the other remedies for the sicknesses of our souls. But why do I speak of canons, and make a distinction? The same can be said of them as of the Gospel of Christ. For He himself gave the keys of the kingdom of heaven to the great Peter, saying: "Whomever you loose and whomever you bind, it shall be so in each case." And again to all the apostles: "Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained." And so he passed the authority on to those after them, provided that they acted in the same way. That is why Basil and the saints of equal standing with him accepted the apostolic canons, in that they followed them without innovating anything, though they also added to them as needed. But these new false apostles declare by their deeds that each of the hierarchs may at times act, not entirely according to the established definitions of the saints, but by his own authority and discretion, contrary to what the saints ordained: loosing where the loosing does not come from them, and binding where the binding is not theirs. And you see these things happening every day. The holy things have been profaned, and the adulterous synod has become a licence for sin, both in secret and openly. The man who cannot be deposed is deposed, and the man who has been slandered [?] is ordained. And the man who falls under canons that require deposition is allowed to celebrate the liturgy without being held to account, by human command and not by a divine and canonical vote, which [?]

And, woe is me for the misery of having to lament everything! Who with a heart that can feel does not grieve and groan? What mind that ponders and weighs these things does not confess that, of all heresies, this is the one that has apostatized from Christ? But how could I say everything I have in mind without going beyond the measure of a letter? What I have said is easy to follow, not ornate, not hard to understand. This is partly because I am not able to speak loftily. I am very small, a man of few words and little knowledge, and I have even these through the prayer of our common Father and of you. It is partly also because some of you are not able to grasp the heresy in more doctrinal terms. And at the same time it is because the word of truth is simple, and the heresy is plain, has no real doctrine, and is easily grasped even by a child. For, as God said, the word is brief. These men do not keep in step, and they even anathematize those who do. May the Lord give you grace in all things, beloved
37. To Joseph, Archbishop of Thessalonica. [?] Through your humility and wisdom, your love for wretched me, and your esteem for me beyond my worth, the letter you have now sent me, sincere

and unmixed, shining with the truth from your luminous soul, my thrice-blessed brother and father, I welcomed, and I gave thanks to Christ, who fulfilled my desire and gives all good things. And how could I not? For you, enriched with knowledge and with fitting zeal, and a true child of our common Father besides, think and feel in harmony with us, the least. Well and good. But what I desire still more is the concord of both of us with [?], through which the ray of truth gleams more brightly, while the crookedness, or rather the night-blindness, of those set against it is weakened and darkened. But when I found in your letter the division of the "necessary," forgive me, I was taken aback. For this is not a division of the necessary but of the contingent, which is divided in three: into what holds for the most part, what holds equally, and what holds for the lesser part. The first of these is divided into the present and the future. The present is further divided into the eternal and the "as long as it is." The "as long as it is" is subdivided into subject and predicate. What is contingent for the most part passes into what actually exists, and that into the necessary. The relation does not convert, however, even though the one descends from the other. For if something is necessary, it is not thereby also contingent. But if something is contingent for the most part, passing through the middle term of what actually exists, it is necessary as long as it is. Take "every man is literate" and "some man is literate." The first is contingent, since it can come about. The second is necessary as long as the activity is present, but when the man dies, the activity that was necessary ceases. This is what "as long as it is" means, that is, "while it is." The other kind, the eternal, is what never changes from what it is, such as eternal things like an angel and a soul. And so we have what we are looking for. A man convicted under a contingent canon will sometimes suffer, because of his other wickedness, the penalties of the canon laid down as necessary. But a man under the necessary canon does not receive the penalties of the contingent one. That is not admissible, since it is already equivalent to the impossible. For everything impossible is, by conversion, also necessary. For example, it is necessary that the sun shine, and so also impossible that it not shine. As for your holiness's remark that it once did not shine, you surely mean at the passion of Christ. For at night, I do not know how [?]. But these are portents, not things according to law or canon. They are either above nature or against nature. The first is shown by the economy of Christ. The second is shown by the present lawlessness, especially since it was not done in secret or as a passing deviation, but openly, and was given the force of law as far as it could be, through the synodal act and through the exile of those who resisted for the truth, as if they were guilty of some transgression of the divine canons. To speak more truly, it is a hardened and wicked heresy. Oh, the audacity of those who did it! The greater the condemnation they incur for their outrage against the divine laws, or rather against the Gospel and nearly all the canons, the greater the danger to us, the humble, if we give up anything of what is fitting. How can there be economy for those who concelebrate with the one who joined the adulterous union, and who presided over the synod that ratified the adultery, as the great Basil said?

For he says that those who went off with the insubordinate are often received back into the same rank when they repent, but not by us, if they ever do repent; rather by the [?], as the divine Dionysius said. I leave the rest to your understanding, which has the sacred power to discern what escapes us. Glory to God for the release of the brothers, if it is true. Glory to God also for your God-given endurance, my brother, amid the stings of the people there, who are hard and uncircumcised in spirit. Do me the favour of reminding me always, to keep me sober, for I am drowsy. And now I am in great need of everyone's holy prayer, and especially that of our Father and of you. I have learned that by the grace of Christ you have composed a work. If you bid me, I would read it for my benefit.

38. To his son Arsenius. [104] How greatly I rejoiced once again when I read your letter, my most beloved child! It was not so much at the door that has been opened for you to meet with the brothers, though that too is something to pray for, as at the grace God has given your tongue, with which you shut the unguarded mouths of the chatterers. May the Lord therefore give you still more a word of knowledge and wisdom, to refute thoroughly those who pose as champions of piety, so that you may well sing with the divine David: "I opened my mouth and drew breath, for I did not forget your commandments." Raging against these commandments, the Moechianizers somehow utter with their very deeds that saying of Scripture: "Depart from me; I do not wish to know your ways." For if they had known them, they would not have transgressed the Lord's commands. And had they not transgressed, they would not have decreed in synod that their transgressions were a saving economy for the Church of Christ, laying under anathema those who do not accept them as such. This impious doctrine is so grave that it not only overturns the holy Gospel, since by nature the whole is overturned through a part, but also abolishes the very economy of Christ, for contraries destroy one another. And it is plain to everyone that the adulterous union, decreed to be a saving economy, is contrary to the divine economy that was carried out to abolish sin. Indeed, the adulterous synod is full of other impieties as well, which brother Euprepianus will show you if you happen to see him again. Farewell, child, and keep the faith, driving off on both sides those who strike invisibly, by the strength of faith and of divine fear and love. For since they are repulsed by orthodox thinking when they attack from outside with the heresies they raise, the crafty ones come from within, scheming to plunder the treasure of the soul. May we be delivered from their snares, lifting our hands to God, with the help of the prayers of our common Father and of all the pious: I and you and all our brothers. The abbot of the

Flute-Player's monastery [?] plays the flute, but his notes are indistinct and not in tune with the Holy Spirit. His claim that he looks to Rome shows a weak argument and is a refuge for false excuses for the present. And what he says about Sabas and Theoctistus, those most reverent monks, this and that, and that in Rome such and such happened, is not true. They objected to bishops returning from the Iconoclast heresy being received back into their own ranks. And they did not object to all of them, only to the eminent ones and the ringleaders of the heresy, in keeping with the saying of St Athanasius. That was not unreasonable. But since the synod at that time decided to receive them all, taking the fourth holy synod as its precedent, they went along with it, for nothing essential was being transgressed. As for the Simoniacs, the matter was left aside at that time, so that the question could be examined after the synod. But when it was examined . . . . . first to a penance of a year or more. Oh, the audacity! Together with certain monks, whose names I will not mention, he set a term for expiating a deposition that was meant to be for ever, so that those deposed by God through Peter, the chief of the Apostles, might again be priests of Christ. And since Sabas and his party did not agree to this, and even quarrelled with him, what does he do? He trades a bad thing for a good one. He denies that he gave a penance, or that he admits those who ordained or were ordained for money. In saying so he is refuted by the lady who was ruling at the time, the very one by whom he had been pressed into giving the lawless penance. The day of Christ's Theophany arrived. On that day the penitents came, having completed their penance, and asked for absolution. He refused, but the empress pressed for them to be received. Again the president trades the good for the bad: he concelebrates with them on that same feast in full view, not unwillingly, of course, but willingly. For although he was able not to concelebrate with deposed men, he concelebrated, however much someone may claim that he could not help it. Hence the disagreement of Sabas and his party with him. Hence the dissolution of the divine canons spread further. But Rome did not accept these things, God forbid! It did not even accept the synod itself as ecumenical, only as local, one that had set right the particular fall of those here. For those who sat in it were not representatives of the other patriarchs; that is false. The Romans had been sent here for another reason, not for a synod. That is why, they say, they were deposed by the one who had sent them when they returned home, though they pleaded that they had been forced. The others were indeed from the East, but they had been urged and drawn in by people here, not sent by the patriarchs, since the patriarchs did not even know of it, or learned of it only later, no doubt because of fear of the [?] nation. The people here did this so that they might more easily persuade the heretical

people to be orthodox, on the grounds that an ecumenical synod had supposedly been assembled. You may ask why we did not resist at the time, and why we received ordination from lord Tarasius after the synod. We answer you and everyone as follows. As to the first, we were then among the subordinates, and did not yet know what we learned later. As to the second, we seized on a reasonable ground: Tarasius said that he had not given a penance, and that if he came to know of any such men, he would not concelebrate with them but would even depose them. Even if this was not the truth, as was evident, we nevertheless longed for concord and were content with what he said. We had decided to lean toward the more humane course of peace in a doubtful matter, as the Theologian says somewhere. At the same time, he had been accepted by the other Churches because of his orthodoxy and the courage and zeal he had shown for it. I have made these things known to you, child, so that you may know what is right. You should also know that Sabas and his party, if they disagreed with him for this reason and not for some other unreasonable ones, had and still have good reason. For just as we joined the president under the cover of his saying that he did not receive such men but even deposed them, so they, with what was done openly as their justification, rightly hold fast to the divine canon. And on this point no one can oppose them, even if people should say that Tarasius received the simoniacs by economy. No, not even if Peter and Paul should appear; for they themselves laid down the canon, and they say: "But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be anathema."

39. To Theophilus the abbot. [106] I wanted to write to your holiness sooner, but I could not manage it, being closely guarded. Now that the good God has been pleased to grant both the means and the messenger, I, the humble one, fulfil my longing, and I address and greet my spiritual father, who is truly much beloved. For the rulers of this age have not dissolved our concord and bond with one another in God just because they have separated us in body. Rather, they have strengthened it. For I am persuaded that your holiness also longs for my unworthy self, and remains unswerving in the orthodox and God-pleasing resistance, as you have shown yourself to God and men both earlier and later. So you share with us, the humble, the persecution for the sake of piety, even if the rulers did not wish it. They spared you so as not to exile and imprison many, and so that they might seem by this means to persuade the world that the dispute with them comes down to us alone, and that there are no others who resist, though there are so many of them in the territory under your holiness's authority. Even if from fear or also

…they hide themselves under “economy,” as one can hear the divine David crying out: “I will count them, and they will be more in number than the sand.” For the impiety is no small or hidden thing; it is very great and plain to anyone with sense. They have overturned the economy of Christ, most holy one, as far as it lay with them. They have decreed that the transgression of the Gospel in the adulterous union and adultery is a saving economy for the Church, and they have laid under anathema those who do not accept it so. They have dissolved the Gospel by breaking one commandment, and declared that breaking to be an economy of God. For it is written: “Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all.” Yet these men say that the fault, or rather the faults, of the adulterer and of the one who joined the adulterous union, of the abettors of adultery, and of all who took the adulterer's side, are not those of guilty men but of stewards of God. (For those who did the deed cannot be separated from those who were carried away with them.) In that case the one who declared such people guilty has lied, and the saints are cut off from the stewards of God, since no saint has transgressed the law of God, and no one who transgresses it can be called a saint. Yet these men have set forth a dogma within the transgression, as inviolable as the law of God, and they anathematize those who do not side with them in it. Plainly the saints in heaven and on earth do not side with adultery. It is evident, then, that by breaking the one commandment of the Gospel they have not only overturned the whole Gospel, by defining that breaking in synod as a saving economy for the Church, [?] laying it down as an inviolable law. As far as it lies with them, whenever any commandment is transgressed, its transgression becomes economy and is called economy as well. More than that, they have anathematized the saints who do not accept it, and on their terms not even God is spared. In short, why say more, when a letter cannot hold it all? A grievous false teaching has been decreed in our Church. This is the Moechian heresy, which along with overturning the Gospel has also dissolved the divine canons by acquitting the man who joined the adulterous union, whom they themselves had deposed. If they have set aside the Gospel, they will hardly have time to care for the sacred canons. I have thought it necessary to remind your paternity of these things along with my greeting. Then, knowing that it is a heresy, you will flee the heresy, that is, the heretics. You will neither communicate with them nor commemorate them in your most holy monastery at the divine liturgy, for the saints have pronounced the gravest threats against those who make concessions to it, even to the point of sharing a meal. Your holiness may ask why we did not tell you this before the plundering, and why we ourselves commemorated those in Byzantium. Let your holiness know this: there was not yet a synod, and the wicked dogma and anathema had not yet been proclaimed. Before these things it was not safe to separate completely from the

lawbreakers. It was safe only to avoid open communion with them, while commemorating them for a time out of a fitting economy. But now that the heretical impiety has come out into the open through a synod, your reverence too must speak boldly with all the Orthodox. You must do so by not communicating with those who hold false doctrine, and by not commemorating anyone who was present at the adulterous synod or is of one mind with it. Indeed, holy Father, it is right that you, who in every way live up to your name Theophilus, should love God in this too. For Chrysostom declared in a great and loud voice that the enemies of God are not only heretics but also those who communicate with such people. And if your [?] plays it safe, who then will be saved? And if one who spoke out boldly by the power of God, like a saint, when the heresy was not yet complete, now shrinks back after the heresy, who else will dare to utter a sound? And if the monastic order does not count everything as rubbish (I mean monasteries and everything belonging to them), how will a layman despise wife, children and everything else? Therefore, as your least brother and child, I urge you: let us not keep silent, or we will become the cry of Sodom. Let us not spare the things below, or we will lose the things above. Let us not put a stumbling block before the Church of God, which according to the saints is constituted even by three Orthodox, or we will be condemned by the sentence of the Lord. I do not say these things for my own sake, wretch that I am. For me, though it is bold to say it, even to die for the truth is gain and joy and life, if only I may be strengthened by your holy prayers. I say them for the sake of the long-standing spiritual love between us and for the common good. If the Son of God, the Lord and Master of all, offered himself to God the Father as a sacrifice for all, what do we owe? How much are we not bound to suffer and endure for him? This is above all true of monks, who have been crucified by their renunciation, that is, those who have renounced truly and not to no purpose. Things cannot be judged by the outward habit alone, for many put on masks and are not what they appear to be. The habit is shown by works. So if there are any monks in these times, let them show it by their works. And the work of a monk is not to tolerate the slightest innovation in the Gospel. Otherwise, by setting before the laity an example of heresy and of communion with heretics, monks will have to give account for the laity's perdition. The extreme humility of your holiness, being so ready to listen, has made me prattle on at length on this subject. But you, Father, pray, and pray earnestly, for one who is rotten and sinful, yet who loves you more than anyone. My fellow prisoner likewise greets you, and [?] your
[Letter] 40 [?]. To Naucratius, his son. [?] Once again another imprisonment for you, beloved child. But once again it is a monument to the shame of the ill-named heretics

and for you an addition of contests and heavenly praises. So for them I groan and weep, but for you I rejoice and give thanks. Have you not become more tested by this change of custody, like gold fired twice in the furnace? Be firmly rooted, then, sacred child, and may you appear before the Master and Lord pure and genuine in all things, a truly useful vessel, equipped for every good work. Bear patiently the strange ways of your second jailer. I would not call him an abbot or a priest, for no minister of God, least of all a monk, would perform military duties, nor would he even communicate with one who performs them. All the same, let me know how he treats you, for I think he is quite different from the first. But whether it is so or otherwise, you, my child, stand firm nobly. Lighten what is painful with the joy of your hopes, and win solitude for yourself, which is where dispassion is found. Do this by looking to God alone, who sees you, and holding fast to him. Treat as refuse and winnow away the chaff-like thoughts that the sower of tares brings in at every turn. You asked me to answer in detail about the heresies and the baptisms. That goes beyond the bounds of a letter. Besides, it would be superfluous to recount what the God-bearing Epiphanius investigated and described as none of the Fathers did. Read his sacred book about them, and there you will learn what you want to know. May the good Euprepianus put it into your hands. About those who are baptized I will answer more briefly. The subject falls into three parts. Those who are baptized are the Marcionites, the Tascodrugites, the Manichaeans, and those ranked with them down to the Melchizedekites, twenty-five heresies in all. Those anointed with the holy chrism are the Quartodecimans, Novatians, Arians, Macedonians and Apollinarians, five together. Those who are neither baptized nor anointed, but only anathematize their own heresy and every other, are the Meletians, Nestorians, Eutychianists and those ranked with them, down to the present heresy. I cannot give their number at present, because the Acephali are split into so many factions and the letter is already overlong. You said that the canon makes no distinction but declares outright that those ordained or baptized by heretics can be neither clergy nor faithful. Consider this: the Apostolic Canon called heretics those who were not baptized, and do not baptize, in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. We are taught this by the divine voice of Basil the Great. He says that heresies are those who have broken away completely and become estranged in the faith itself. Schisms are those who have quarreled with one another over certain ecclesiastical matters and questions that can be remedied. Parasynagogues are the assemblies held

by insubordinate presbyters or bishops and by uninstructed people. Of the first kind he himself gives an example, saying to holy Amphilochius: “What reason is there to approve the baptism of the Pepuzenes, who baptize into the Father and the Son and Montanus or Priscilla? Those who were baptized into what was not handed down to us were not baptized.” These, then, and those like them, the canon and the Fathers named heretics, as divine Basil says. Of the second kind holy Basil again gives an example: “The Cathari too are among those who have split off.” But you may ask: “How, then, are these and all the later groups called heretics too?” This is what we say and understand. The first are heretics in the proper sense, because they have committed impiety against the very heart of our Trinitarian faith. The second are called heretics by an extension of the term, as offshoots of the first. Yet they confess that they believe and baptize into the Trinity, with each hypostasis in its own distinct property, and not with only one of the three [?], even if they held heretical views on other points. Of the third kind, the saint himself again gives an example: someone convicted of a fault is suspended from the ministry, does not submit to the canons, and claims for himself the presidency and the liturgy. Just as the second share the name of the first, so the third share the name of the second. Indeed, the ancients call the Meletians schismatics, because they were carried away with Meletius the schismatic, even though they do not hold false doctrine. For when they anathematize their own schism, as they say, they are received into the catholic Church. Heresy as a whole seems to be a chain woven by demons, one link holding on to the next. All of them hang, as it were, from a single summit of impiety and godlessness, even though they differ in name, time, place, quantity, quality, power and operation. Even one and the same body has not just one member but many, and their operations toward one another, their powers, properties, positions and honors all differ. Now to your other questions. The first concerns a presbyter who is Orthodox yet commemorates the heretical bishop out of fear of persecution [?]. Here again: if he does not concelebrate with a heretic and does not give communion to such people, he may be received for a shared meal, psalmody and the blessing of food. This is by economy, and not for divine communion. While the heresy prevails, one must always ask. Having received his confession, one should be satisfied with it, I think, unless it is plainly false. You may say that we are taught by the Fathers not to ask. That applies to a time when no heresy is raging, and to those who have not been plainly condemned. But nowadays it is rare to find such a presbyter who does not mix and communicate with heretics.

The second: about a Christ-loving person who invites someone to hold an all-night vigil in his chapel, and whether one should celebrate the liturgy in it, and with whom. One should comply, go, and sing along, provided, of course, that the one who invites and the chanters are Orthodox and both keep themselves from communion with the heretics. One may also celebrate the liturgy in the chapel, if its owner declares that it is no longer served by a heretic. As has already been said, because the heresy is raging it is necessary to ask about everything. The third: suppose an Orthodox person receives a church from someone, and it is the custom for the people to gather there once or twice a year and for the heretic to be commemorated at the liturgy. He may be allowed to chant there out of necessity, but not to celebrate the liturgy. If it is possible to put a stop to the custom, he may celebrate the liturgy as well. The fourth: there is a church in which the celebrant commemorates the heretic, and the Orthodox priest has an altar consecrated on a cloth or on boards. Is it proper to set it up in that same church, when the one who commemorates is not present, and for the Orthodox to celebrate on it? It is not proper. Rather, if necessary, it should be done in an ordinary house, a chosen and clean [?]

The fifth: suppose an Orthodox person on a journey is invited by some cleric or layman to a meal, and it is the hour for psalmody. How should he conduct himself? I said it before and I say it again: while heresy prevails and has not been overthrown by an Orthodox synod, it is necessary to ask, both about divine communion and about a shared meal. In these matters there is no room for embarrassment or awkwardness. Simply taking bread from anyone at all does not call for questioning. Nor does being fed by him, perhaps on one's own, and lodging with him, unless he is already known to be in heresy or wickedness. About everything else one must ask. The sixth: if in passing an Orthodox person finds a church near a village or city, should he pray there, or even lodge there, to avoid becoming the guest of laypeople? He should both pray and lodge there, if it is on its own. But in a pressing hour of need it is also a matter of indifference whether he stays in the house of a layman or a cleric, as has been said, and eats there by himself without asking, and takes what he needs. As I said, this holds provided the host is not already known to the guest as impious or lawless. Except in necessity, however, it is not good to accept these things just as they come. One should ask, lodge with the Orthodox, and if need be take provisions from them, for this is what the Lord commands through his saints. You answered the presbyter and abbot well: those now ordained by the one who was found [at the synod] are barred from the liturgy, even though he says that the synod was held wrongly and that we are lost. For if he admits this, why does he not flee perdition and separate himself from the heresy, so that he may remain a bishop in God's sight? Then his ordinations would be acceptable at once. And why, with the heresy

in plain view, did the abbot bring the brothers forward for a heretical ordination? If the one who ordained them had set himself right, they could have officiated at once. But since he remains in the heresy by commemorating the heretic, even if he says he holds sound views, those he ordains cannot truly be ministers of God. If, however, a spirit of zeal for God has been kindled in the abbot, and he is eager to put on the crown of confession, let him not celebrate the liturgy in the church in which that man enthroned him, and let him not commemorate him as bishop. Blessed is such a man, for he becomes an example of salvation to many others as well. But if an altar is set up in that same church, nothing prevents celebrating the liturgy there. I will mention here something I failed to note above. Holy Basil says of those who have taken part in a parasynagogue that often even those in holy orders who went off with the insubordinate are received back into the same rank once they repent. Let your reverence not think that this statement contradicts the Apostolic Canon, which says: “If anyone who is a cleric prays with a deposed person as with a cleric, let him be deposed as well.” Consider rather this. The Fathers distinguished which are heresies and which are schisms. In the same way, by the same line of reasoning, a distinction is clearly made between the case covered by the canon that deposes without exception anyone who prays with a deposed person, and the case of one who took part in a parasynagogue. The one who knows that he is praying with a person who has admittedly been deposed is rightly deposed at once, because he was caught acting with indifference and did not heed the canon. The other did not think that the man with whom he was carried away along with the crowd had been deposed, so, as the saint says, if he repents, he is received into the same rank. The saint's statement also contains the word “often,” so it is possible that even one who repents is not received back into the same rank. That statement allows for exceptions, whereas the Apostolic Canon binds necessarily and without exception. I was not at all surprised that the falsely named Christopher has gone back to his own vomit, since I know how unstable and unsteady he is. But I was utterly amazed that Cledonius bore prison and blows from the impious for the truth for only a single day. So if he still holds firm by the power of God, do not, you and the other brothers, neglect to stretch out a hand to him, if possible. As for the groups mentioned above, I mean those who are baptized, those anointed with holy chrism, and those who anathematize their heresy, I have not listed the heresies as the divine Epiphanius arranged and numbered them. I followed a note I found by one of the older scholars, a diligent man who did his research and made his findings from books belonging to the Church in Byzantium. Brother Gregory sends you his sincere greetings. 41. To Silvanus and Euprepianus, his sons.

…and you yourselves often want to send news about them. So I thought it good, both for brevity and for greater secrecy, to indicate these people by the characters, that is, the twenty-four letters of the alphabet. So I say: α stands for our Father; β for the Archbishop; γ for Kalogeros; δ for Athanasius; ε for Barsanuphius; ζ for Nicholas; η for Sophronius; θ for Euthymius; ι for Ioannikios; κ for Dometian; λ for the Steward; ν for Acacius; ξ for Meletius; ο for Lucian; π for Epiphanius; σ for Basil; τ for Euschemon; υ for Silvanus; φ for Euprepianus; [?] for Eustathius; ω for myself. So whenever a character stands in the heading, it will certainly be known whose the letter is: α, for instance, is our Father's, and likewise each of the others. Again, when I ask, “How is β?”, it is clear that the question is understood to be about the Archbishop. Likewise, when I ask, “How are those with β?”, it is evident that the question is about those who are with him. The same goes for the other characters. Another kind of question: “What do you hear about π [?], or about ρ, or about ψ?” The answer is to be given for each character. Again, I may ask, “Who has come from [?]?” You should answer by the character: η, or ο, or one of the others. Or: η has not come in, or ο, but so many of those with η or ο. Or that such and such has happened to a given character. When [someone dies?] [?], again: “Such and such a character has died,” or “is ill,” or “is grieving,” and so on. If someone among those with a given character has suffered something, give his name as well. For example, in the case of Christopher: that he ran away from ε, which is what in fact happened. When you receive letters sent by us, if the letter is from one of the characters, it will certainly bear that character as its heading. And when you yourselves forward letters from these same characters, put that same character on your own letter. If the senders do not know the system, you are to erase the heading and put in the sender's character. If the sender is not one of the characters, let the heading stand, as when I write. If the recipient is not one of the characters, let the heading stand, naming the person to whom the letter is addressed. Note also that on each of my letters to those designated by characters, the heading will be like this: “ω to α,” and so on. And let the letters sent to me likewise bear α, or ο, or another of the characters. This too should be known

…that, since these three are letters which stand outside the twenty-four letters of the alphabet, namely ϛ, [?] and [?]: the ϛ signifies all those of our brothers who have at any time, whether earlier or later, broken faith; the ι [?] signifies the patriarch; the π [?] signifies the ruler. So whenever there is need either for me to ask, or for you to inform me, about one of the three, the indication will be given by the letter.

42. To Anna, a nun. [123]

I thought my blessed mother had died, but it seems she is still on earth. For what more could she have done than you do, who treat me, the lowly one, with a mother's care? But even if I am a sinner, I still trust that the Lord will repay you for what you have done for our unworthiness with no ordinary grace, and with the attainment of what you long for and ask. But what has been done is enough. I pleaded this in my earlier letters as well. You, on the contrary, have added still more, so as to spend yourself out in giving. And how could we fail to remember your godliness now? With the garments, with the holy offering, with the food and drink, you have astonished us from every side. So put an end to the gifts now, and be of good hope about the divine recompense. For he who said that he would give a reward even for a cup of cold water does not lie.

You say that you are grieved by the care of your child, which keeps you from the attention you owe to your soul. But God is able both to manage the affairs of your good child and to set you free above all to give your time to the things that profit the soul, so that you may stand with a ready heart for your departure from the body. You cannot fast and endure hardship, since your body is sickly. Bear this too without grief, offering the Lord what you can, and making up for what is lacking in ascetic practice by abundance of humility.

You ask to be taught how you ought to pray. The Lord himself taught this too, through the words of the “Our Father”, and by telling us to ask for nothing temporal, but for his kingdom and his eternal righteousness. However, the fathers have laid down this pattern: first, thanksgiving to God; then confession of one's sins to him; and so the request for their forgiveness and for the attainment of the other means of salvation. So whenever you are about to pray, give thanks to the Lord and Master that he brought you from non-being into being; that he redeemed you from all error, having called you and counted you worthy to share in the knowledge of himself, away from pagan error and from heretical error; and then that, after you had enjoyed life in the world, he also prepared you to come within the monastic and angelic life. The thought of these things is enough to soften the soul to compunction and the onset of tears. From these come illumination of the heart, sweetness of spirit, and desire for God. When this desire is present in the heart, all wickedness is cast off. When you have thus offered up [?] thanksgiving to God, confess to him, saying: “You know,

Master, how much I have sinned against you, and how much I sin every hour: this sin, and that offence”, and so reckon up those committed knowingly and in ignorance. But do not recount indiscriminately the things whose vivid recollection does harm to the soul. And from this the grace of humility will dawn for you, with contrition of heart and fear of God's retribution. After this ask, groan, and beseech your Lord for their forgiveness, and for strength in the future to please him, saying: “No longer, my Lord, Lord, will I provoke you; no longer will I love anything besides you, who alone are truly beloved. And if I provoke you again, I fall down before your compassion, that strength may be given me to make pleasing you a settled habit.” And if any other good thing comes to your mind that you wish to see accomplished, ask for it fervently. After this, call upon the holy Theotokos to have mercy on you; upon the holy angels, and upon the angel you have as guardian of your life, that he may guard and shelter you; upon the Forerunner, the apostles, all the saints, those whom you are especially accustomed to invoke, and the saint commemorated that day. This, then, seems to me to contain the substance of prayer, even if each person prays in other words and not in exactly the same ones. Indeed, the one who prays does not always say the same things even himself; but I reckon the same substance necessary for all. May you be kept, then, praying as you ought, improving each time, and presenting your whole self pleasing to the Lord through a life lived with exactness.

43. To Joseph, brother and archbishop. [?]

The first letter of your brotherly and fatherly holiness, though small in the number of its syllables, was nevertheless complete in the breadth of its allegorical meaning. And the second was full of all knowledge and humility, with only one fault: its undeserved praise of wretched me. I, however, did not speak ironically, God forbid, but in truth, when I said that you have shone forth in our generation in the dignity of the high priesthood, after the likeness of the holy Fathers. Nor would I be wrong to call you a pillar and foundation of the Church, my most excellent brother. For everyone who takes a stand and suffers for the truth is its support and bulwark.

It is good that you looked into the quires. For your reminder, or rather your command, gave us the occasion to examine and resolve that proposition, which, together with others put forward, I sent to your holiness at the prompting of our Father in the quires written earlier. In the whole treatise I introduced no idea of my own, since it is not right to be more lawful than the law or straighter than the rule; I only arranged and joined together, however unlearnedly, the teachings and precepts of the divine Fathers on the point to which the proposition of the counterargument calls us. And if he does not decline to read it because of the labour, I know it will profit him. That peace is good is admitted by all, for I love it, even though I am a sinner; and that toward it

…having thrown off [our] burden, as the divine Cyril says. On the one hand, when they first acquitted the adulterous wedder, while I was present there, we kept silent, as we had agreed; but silence is a kind of consent, and our opponents, as you know, seized on it and tried to shut us out of our protest. On the other hand, when his second acquittal was being applauded by those who had trampled on the laws of God, we said: “Let him simply remain, enjoying only the honour of the priestly office, according to the canon of St Basil”, even though he had already concelebrated with the patriarch for two years, which was a fearful thing and beyond the bounds of economy. I will not speak of the false pretexts for avoiding him, or of sharing in the blessings at meals as from a presbyter, or of the commemoration of the patriarch.

Yet although we, for the sake of economy, came down so far, they on the contrary were carried away by harshness together with their sin. God foresaw something better, so that we humble ones might not endure the first exile to no purpose, and so that the adultery dared before the whole world might not be lightly belittled through the excessive [?] of the one who joined it. So now it is time for us, beloved, to say: “How long will you practise economy?” and: “Be eager at last to build.” And, as the divine Basil says, it is time for us to serve the exactness of the canons. For there are some words before a war and others after it. And it is time to pass our days in patience, as you have advised, and to pray for those who have persecuted us.

Your three precious [In ms. Reg. …] sayings are welcome to me, and I am of one mind with them: that the churches should not be divided because of the suspicion attaching to one man; that one should not share in the absolution of such a man; and that one may receive communion from any blameless priest, the meaning being entirely as follows. Forgive me, brother, for I speak not as one teaching, but as one clarifying the argument for our common benefit.

As to the first: we do not separate ourselves, because of one man, from the Church of the north and west and sea, nor indeed from the Church here, except of course from those who ratified the adultery. For these are not the Church of the Lord. If they were the Church, we would be separating from the Church because of one man joined to it, that is, by not admitting the adulterous wedder. But since they are not the Church of God, it is they who truly separate themselves from the Church of God because of one man joined to them, like those recorded in the chronicle; while we are not separated from the Church on account of such a man.

As to the second: we do not share in his absolution, that is, we do not communicate with those who openly absolved him. If we communicated with them, we would be sharing in his absolution. But since, as befits God's servants, we do not communicate with those who absolved him, then surely we do not share in his absolution.

As to the third: we receive communion from any blameless priest. For this reason we do not receive it from Joseph, since he stands publicly accused; and those too would surely stand accused

who concelebrate with him, deposed as he is. If we received communion from such men as blameless, Joseph too would be blameless, since he concelebrates with them. But since he truly stands accused, and we do not receive from him, it is clear that we do not receive from those who concelebrate with him either, since they likewise stand accused. So the reasoning of your holiness holds firm, and we are of one mind. And may our unbroken bond, through true agreement here, continue in the age to come, my dearest brother, so that we humble ones too may be counted worthy to carry away some trace of good achievement worthy of our Fathers.

As for your city, you have kindled there a pillar of piety which no man will put out for ever. You should not grieve, but rather rejoice, as I, wretched man, rejoice at the dispersal of my lowly monastery, because the dispersal is for the Lord's sake. Nor is it a great glory only that so many stood firm without bending; it would be so even if only one had. For one who does the will of the Lord is better than ten thousand who transgress it. And you are not to blame for their dispersal, though some talk nonsense; I am, miserable man that I am. But may we share in both, if you will bear it. And may you have as great a reward for the godly dispersal of the brothers as I may find for leaving Thessalonica in accordance with God's law.

About my guard there is nothing to say, since he is the sort of man he is, and of one mind with Joseph. Do not cease praying earnestly for my lowliness, my good and most holy brother and father. Know that Theosostus stood firm in refusing to take communion from the man who mounted your throne unlawfully, and that he was driven violently out of his monastery. Our brothers with Athanasius are still held confined there.

My guard went out and brought me a greeting from the patriarch, who said: “God will forgive you. We were praying to have you here to help us. You went off and sat down there”; and also: “I envy you.” When I heard this I laughed. For there was no need for me to answer for the present, except only: “If he envies me, let him come out too.” The guard has also relaxed my custody, urging me to rest. He also brought me a greeting from Symeon, who says he wants to speak to the emperor, since you have suffered much in prison. And from Leontius a humble greeting, saying: “I acted under compulsion; may God not forgive me for your word [?].” And I said that I did not need these things from him. They compelled him to go to the steward, and to Arsenius and John, saying that the lord Tarasius had released him, and that “now I have recovered my sight.” And they sent him off to the [?]. The one who is with me greets my shepherd through me with much longing.

44. To Sergius the consul. [?]

You, as I hear, are passing from one office to another

under the emperor here below, and against your own wish, my beloved and most honoured friend. But I, the lowly one, do not cease [praying] that you may be, through piety, an intimate friend of the King above, the King of all. For it is better to be ranked even very low, at the uttermost last place, with the heavenly King than in the very first place with the earthly one. Knowing your concern for salvation, I trust that you suffer no loss to your soul from your office, but rather gain by it, since there are not a few ways to profit. For the poor taxpayer is satisfied not only by relief from taxes, but also by a kindly look from the one who collects the imperial revenues, a gentle voice, a word of greeting; and I do not yet speak of loosing the bonds of injustice, and all the other things a ruler can easily do for those he rules. So do not neglect [?] to do good to yourself through kindness to others, my lord. Rather, as one who is wise and knows that in a little while we shall depart from this life taking nothing with us but our deeds, let us devote ourselves to such deeds and store them up, those, that is, which will be our provision for eternal life and for the enjoyment of ineffable good things.

Yes, I beseech you, my own blood, my dear one, the shoot of a truly good root, of that Anna who was revered and most dearly beloved by me above all, and praised by all who knew her for her dignity, who was truly my blessed mother in both respects.

45. To his son Naucratius.

46. To Anna, abbess.

47. To his son Naucratius.

48. To his son Athanasius. [212]
