I read your letter patiently, beloved brother, and was greatly astonished at your sudden change. I will pass over the earlier matter: that when you met me face to face you agreed that the Moechian false doctrine is a heresy, pleading ignorance and the influence of others. But afterwards, having read the Pentalogue, you declared it to be a five-fold light. Now, it seems, you take the opposite view, and your whole discourse breathes the same spirit as your former ignorance, or rather is even more hostile to what my lowliness has said. If these were my own words, it would be no wonder, since I am obscure. But since it has been shown by the voice of the Lord, of the apostles and prophets, and besides by the God-bearing Fathers, that it is a most grievous heresy, let your understanding, and that of anyone else who agrees with you, consider where you are about to stumble. For your premises for its not being a heresy, forgive me, come not from the voice of the Lord, nor from the mouth of the saints, but, to speak in the prophet's words, from those who speak from the earth and from alien laws, and from a multitude that allows itself to say anything out of fear of men.

For you say that all, friends and the devout, learned and simple alike, are [?] when they hear that it is a heresy. And you put forward this as proof: that since none of them opposes [the commandments] and teaches people to commit adultery and to absolve the unholy, how shall we call them heretics? Transgressors of the Lord's commandments, tramplers of the divine canons, unholy men: yes, it is just to call them that. How then can one not be astonished, first, at your persistence, which so often brings forward the same arguments of theirs and hears the truth in reply, a truth that could convince even children; and then again, as if it had forgotten what it heard before, brings up the same things with still more vehement perplexity and reproach against us, as though we were calling it a heresy without reason? This, then, is what astonishes [me] about you…

As for our opponents, I would say this. How can they say that they do not proclaim or teach what they proclaimed in synod, and confirmed under anathema against those who oppose the doctrine, that is, their economy, and what they still teach in practice every day? For what am I, the lowly one, confined here? For what has my Father the recluse suffered such hardship, first kept in isolation and then cast aside in the place where he is confined? For what is the archbishop, deposed as they claim, held in great straits, under orders and close security, so that he receives even his food by measure, the men who supply it having been so instructed; then shut up again in the palace, and now cast aside in a foreign place? For what are your honoured self and the brothers kept under guard in Thessalonica, Theosostus the abbot driven with his disciples out of the same city, and another abbot of that place flogged beyond measure? For what are the brothers Naucratius and Arsenius kept securely guarded until now, and Basil and Gregory [?]? For what did Stephen, the virtuous abbot, leave his own monastery with fifty disciples, together with a hundred and ten others along with a former bishop, anathematizing the adulterous synod for having abolished the Gospel, as the document he sent states? For what is Antony, the most devout abbot, in custody at Amorium, having likewise anathematized the adulterous synod with his brotherhood, as the former did? For what were brother Aemilian and his companions in Thynia bound and led away by the bishop of Nicomedia, and made to taste scourging and mockery, while those who fell upon them plundered the monastery's goods as spoils of war? For what is Leo, the most God-fearing bishop surnamed Balelades, persecuted in Cherson, and Antony the honoured abbot kept under guard with two others? For what are our brothers held in prison on Lipari, beyond Sicily? For what were [?] and his companions kept under guard in Cherson, and sent from there in custody to the emperor, then guarded

in Byzantium and held in monasteries? Shall I speak again of what was done to us three? For what was it declared to us at Agathou's by the emperor through the spatharii: “You are anathematized and deposed by the synod”? For what the imprisonment at St Mamas, with the three of us kept apart? For what the arrival there of the same spatharii with three men brought by the heterodox one to read out the sentence of our deposition and anathema, again, even when we had stopped our ears so as not to hear? For what are we exiled, each to a different place, and shut away, both the steward and Arsenius, our brothers, while the others were driven twelve miles from Constantinople, so that some, having changed into lay clothes, hid in a cave because of their secret service to us, and others crept under a slab [?] all day long, and since they could not show themselves by day, ran to one another by night? For what were those who were found seized by soldiers, imprisoned in the praetorium, and then banished from the city?

And to speak of how it all began: for what was the Studios placed under guard by a troop of soldiers who came upon it suddenly, so that we could not even breathe; and why did the bishop of Nicaea and the bishop of Chrysopolis come there, to make us accept the adulterous wedder, on the grounds that he had been permitted by the previous patriarch to perform the adulterous marriage? “Since”, he said, “the one who permitted it is a saint, as Chrysostom says, it is a saint's economy; so accept it.” For what were the four of us removed from there by night by an official and soldiers, and led off to Symeon, whom I do not know how to describe; and for what was it declared through him by the emperor that we should accept [the adulterous wedder] and repent, the very thing against which we have stood firm until now, as if economy had taken place? For what were we shut up again in St Sergius, and why did Symeon come there again from the emperor for this very purpose? For what were we brought by officials before the crowded synod, with three of the highest dignitaries sitting in it? For what was I, the lowly one, insulted there, surrounded on every side, and made to hear: “You don't know what nonsense you are talking, what you are saying”, while I cried out: “The Forerunner falls! The Gospel is abolished! There is no economy!”, and they answered at length that it was economy, and that the saints exercised economy in this way, as did the late patriarch of saintly memory? See, here are witnesses that he permitted the adulterous marriage, though they did not call it that; indeed, at the mere words “adulterous wedder” they gnashed their teeth as if to devour [me]. For what was the anathema shouted out slanderously against those who do not accept the economies of the saints, and why was I, with my Father and the venerable elder [?], excommunicated and removed from their midst by the hand of officials, and the archbishop shut away and, merely because he had celebrated the liturgy at Studios at my request, deposed by them as an ordinary presbyter? For the one deposed by Christ himself and by the divine canons as an adul-

[…] they acquitted the man who joined the adulterous union, declaring him blameless in every respect and saying that he had been their fellow celebrant even before. But the man who could not be deposed under the canons they subjected to deposition. In this way they confirmed by their deed what they had said: that hierarchs have authority to apply the canons however they see fit. They go on doing this all the time. Nor are they willing to see that, if this is so, then when they depose a hierarch, they themselves can be deposed by the very man they depose, and so the saying of the apostles is fulfilled: “Let these things concerning the canons also be ordained for you by us, O bishops. If you abide by them, you will be saved and will have peace; but if you disobey, you will be punished and will have everlasting war with one another, paying the fitting penalty for your disobedience.” What was the reason for what happened after the synod? Why did the emperor interrogate all the brethren, saying that we had been deposed, that the synod was holy and that he had set his seal on it? Was it not as though the adulterous union were an economy of the saints and the man who performed it beyond reproach? And when they did not accept this, why was each of them shut up in monasteries and fortresses, one by one, or two, or three, or more together? Why were some of them scourged and [?], while all this was noised abroad everywhere on land and sea? To sum up, what was the reason for all this? Was it not that they refused to say and agree that the transgression of the Gospel was an economy? Our opponents proclaimed it to the world as saving and equal to the economies of the saints, in deed and in word. They still proclaim it, and will go on doing so for as long as they persist in such words and deeds, by means of the persecution. How then can they say, “Since no one stands up and teaches it, are we to call them heretics?” Is all that I have described fantasy and dreams, or is it true? And since it is true, how can it be that they are not teaching and preaching it on every occasion, in deed and in word? And how is it that you, by obeying them, are not very nearly standing with those who say it, and drawing upon yourselves the fearful judgment that falls on silence? (Even if we keep silent, the ends of the earth cry out the truth.) For this reason I, the lowly one, am compelled not to keep silent, in writing and without writing, as far as my strength allows, with fear and trembling and prepared for death, even if one of you perhaps thinks that I do this needlessly, or I would even say wordily. But let me return to the matter at hand. You said, “Since no one stands up and teaches people to commit adultery and to absolve the unholy, how can we reasonably call them heretics?” It is true that they do not teach in words that people should commit adultery and absolve the unholy, for not even the nations that have no law teach people to commit adultery. Nor did we claim that they openly declare this. Our claim was this. They ratified the adulterous union and everything connected with it, and through it other transgressions of the Gospel, together with the setting aside of the divine canons. They declared it, under anathema, to be a saving economy. And they punish people for refusing it on every occasion with the exiles and prisons already mentioned. In doing so they have undone the Gospel, as the saints put it. They lay down that economy can in effect be applied to every transgression, and so the un-

-alterable commandments of God they have altered and shown to be changeable. And how would those commandments not be alterable and changeable, if their transgressions are laid down as dogma by a synod, in deed and in word, as saving economies? Let them not go so far in falsehood as to say that they did not hold a synod, or that they did not call the adulterous union an economy of equal weight with those of the saints, or that they did not anathematize those who do not accept it. If they say they did not anathematize, why did they cry out, “To those who do not accept the economies of the saints, anathema”? It is plain that the proclamation was made because some were refusing to accept something, unless we are drunk. And on what other matter was there any objection, if not the adulterous union? So the anathema was certainly pronounced on its account, as being in keeping with the economies of the saints. If the adulterous union is on a par with them, then the economies of the saints are lawless. But if the saints are not lawless, which is true, then the saints themselves have been anathematized for not accepting the adulterous union, however much our opponents contrive by their arts to make what is obvious seem obscure. What has happened cannot be hidden. Hear the great Basil cry out that the commandments of the Gospel are unchangeable: “Perhaps the Lord wished to brace my soul and make it more watchful for the future, so that I would not heed men but be shaped by the commandments of the Gospel. These do not shift with the times or with the circumstances of human affairs, but remain the same. As they came forth from that truthful and blessed mouth, so they endure for ever.” But those who proclaimed the opposite, that the adulterous union is a saving economy, what else did they declare but that God’s commandments are changeable? On their view the commandments are changed in some respects. In other respects they are not changed but operate without alteration. But at certain times and in certain human circumstances, as they themselves said about those in power, they are changed. Their transgression is not then counted as lawlessness. Indeed, these transgressions, which they call economies of the saints, have such force that those who do not accept them are anathematized in the Church. Nothing else follows from this than that God is changeable and alterable, since he would resemble his own word, and that the Gospel is undetermined as regards salvation and perdition. Does economy then apply to all people and to every transgression of a commandment, or only to some people and to some one thing? And what is the rule of allotment by which it applies to some people and to one thing, but not at all to others and to another? By whom, and by how many, is economy to be exercised? By hierarchs only, or by priests as well? By a synod, or by each one privately? And if it applies to emperors only, does it apply to adultery only, or to every lawless act? And how do the commandments of God give way before emperors? Do they not give way, as if God’s kingdom had an end? For not even an emperor’s law gives way unless another emperor succeeds him. But there is a further difficulty to raise. The divine Apostle says, “Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ also

loved the Church and gave himself up for her, so that he might sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word, so that he might present the Church to himself in glory, having no spot or wrinkle or any such thing, but that she might be holy and blameless.” How then could the Church remain without spot or [?] wrinkle, and not be befouled, if she has now admitted adultery and the adulterous union, and in the surrounding times other things on a par with them? I shudder even to say it. Let today’s evangelists decide this for us. They have admitted these things themselves, and they call themselves the Church of God, while they set apart those who do not admit them as her opponents. But truly, as the prophet says, “The fool will speak folly, and his heart will devise vain things, to do lawless deeds and to speak error against God.” This, then, is a most grievous heresy, and here one may repeat the words of the most blessed Apostle: “I am astonished that you are so quickly turning away from him who called you in the grace of Christ to a different gospel, which is not another gospel. But there are some who are troubling you and want to pervert the Gospel of Christ. But even if we ourselves or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be accursed.” And contrary to what was preached, not by the Apostle but by Christ himself, the adulterous synod has preached the adulterous union, from which comes adultery, and the many forms of being drawn over to the adulterers, as a saving economy. And it preaches this on every occasion, in deed and in word, even if it craftily pretends to lie low, so that after catching those it has deceived it may raise up its own Corybant again. May I, wretch that I am, escape its trial, and I pray, sinner that I am, that you may escape it too, even if you do not wish to heed me. See then, brother, I have shown you from the Gospel, from the Apostle and from the Fathers alike, if you are willing to be persuaded by words of truth, that the adulterous synod has beyond doubt brought a heresy to completion. It began from the adultery, even if it has lain low in the meantime, simply by naming, or rather proclaiming, the adulterous union as an economy taking place in the Church of God. And do not be surprised that a single word gives birth to heresy, when you hear the Lord say, “Not one iota or one stroke will pass from the law until all is accomplished.” And do not think of saying, “What need is there to be so meddlesome, and to rein in the speculations of knowledge over one word, and to put this and that together?” If you do, you may fall into the so-called heresy of the Gnosimachi, of whom the author says: “The Gnosimachi are those who oppose all knowledge in Christianity. They say that those who seek out certain kinds of knowledge in the divine Scriptures are doing something superfluous, for God asks nothing else of a Christian but good deeds. It is better, then, to walk more simply and not to busy oneself with any doctrine that involves the study of knowledge.” So say the Gnosimachi.

So you yourself, if you can, show me from the divine words that it is not a heresy. Do not bring a multitude against me, and do not boast of the God-fearing people who come by night, the ones you call learned, simple folk and friends. If they are God-fearing, where is their boldness of speech? And if they are learned (I do not say they are not, for I admit that many of them are far beyond me, a simple man), and if they want the truth, let them show it learnedly from the truth itself. Let them also show it from examples, but from fitting ones, not from examples that do not apply and are contrary to the truth and to the apostolic and patristic canons. And if they are friends according to God, how can they share in the communion of the heterodox? Friends of that kind are true and faithful. Pay attention then, brother, to what the divine Basil says to those who judge the truth by numbers: “He who does not dare to give an account of the question at hand, and has no proof to offer, and for that reason takes refuge in numbers, admits defeat, since he has nothing to equip him for bold speech.” And further on: “Let even one person show me the beauty of truth, and I am persuaded at once. But a multitude that claims authority without proof can frighten, but it can never persuade. How many tens of thousands will persuade me to think day is night, or to regard a copper coin as gold and accept it as such, or to take manifest poison in place of proper food? In earthly matters, then, we will not defer to a multitude of liars. Am I then, for the sake of heavenly doctrines, to follow nods that prove nothing, and to abandon what has been handed down from long ago and from of old with great agreement, and the testimony of the holy Scriptures [?]? Have we not heard the Lord say, ‘Many are called, but few are chosen’? And again, ‘Narrow and hard is the way that leads to life, and few are those who find it’? Who among the right-minded does not pray to be among the few who enter through the narrow way into salvation, rather than among the many who are driven through the broad way to perdition? If anyone had happened to be present at the contest of the blessed Stephen, who would not have wished to be on the side of the one man who was being stoned and was held up to ridicule by everyone, rather than of the many who thought they gained credibility from their evil agreement? One man who is approved by God is preferable to tens of thousands who pride themselves on their arrogance. So too we find in the Old Testament that [?] thousands of the people were falling under a blow sent by God. But Phinehas alone stood up and made atonement, and the slaughter ceased. If he had said, ‘How shall I dare to oppose what is being done in agreement by so many? How shall I cast my vote against those who have so decided [?]?’, he would not have won the prize, nor stopped the evil, nor would the rest have been saved, nor would God have granted his favor. It is good, then, it is good for one man to speak out boldly in the cause of justice, and to break up the unjust agree-

-ment of the many. As for you, if you like, prefer the drowned multitude to Noah who was saved; but allow me to run to the ark with the few. And again, if you wish, take your place with the many in Sodom; I will go along with Lot, even if he alone is separated from the crowds, to his own good. Yet even I respect a multitude, but not one that flees examination. I respect a multitude that offers proof, not one that takes bitter revenge, but one that corrects as a father does, not one that delights in innovation, but one that guards the inheritance of the fathers. And what kind of multitude are you telling me about? One hired by flattery and gifts? One stolen away by ignorance and [?]? One that has fallen through cowardice and fear? One that has preferred the passing enjoyment of sin to eternal life?” Many have openly confessed as much. Do you strengthen falsehood by numbers? Then you have only shown how severe the evil is. For the more people there are in evil, the greater the disaster. So much for this. It would be superfluous, beloved, to go on to your other propositions, since that would exceed the limits of a letter. Besides, those who receive these words with good discernment will find it easy to answer what is said.

Letter 49. To his son Naucratius. [225]

Whenever you speak and tell me something, my dearly beloved son, you say nothing superfluous or idle. What you say is timely and fitting and does the soul good, as it does now. I commend your vigor, and I welcome too the progress in your style, which you will make finer still if you are able to work through the commentaries on grammar. Whoever holds fast to orthodoxy and wishes to oppose the heterodox must have some share in skill and practice in speech. Those people think that the learning they gain from this gives them something great. They boast over those whose ears itch and tickle them. So it is best for the right-minded not to fall short in the power of speech either, and to beat back [?] their well-aimed siege engines. This is how I would like you to grow strong, my son. But I do not by any means wish for everyone what I wish for you, because each person is differently disposed by habit, and each needs what benefits him. You told me that brother Philip has fallen asleep, and Philo too. Well done, well done, for both came to a good end. I do not say that what came before the end deserved blame. How could it, for men who renounced the world, flesh and blood, and placed the easy yoke of obedience upon themselves? I say so because they attained the highest beatitude, being persecuted, afflicted and hard pressed for the Lord’s sake. No one disputes this except the ill-named Moechians, who have set aside the Gospel. As for Philo, I would like to stop my praise here. But good Philip had many achievements, which you yourself listed. Besides what has been said, I admire his unaffected and guileless character, his freedom from anger and from resentment, his compassion and brotherly love, his readiness to obey and his diligence. In short, I admire his freedom from the passions, from which came his readiness for compunction,

his hatred of the world and love of God, and his modest reserve. You speak, as you did before, of the man’s many tears, his love for the fathers and for the rule, his fighting spirit in dangers, his zeal and his complete freedom from grumbling, and the evergreen quality, as it were, of his soul with its many-flowered virtues. The news about the fervent [?] Gaius is also good. He has travelled through almost every place where the brethren are scattered. That they are in good health, thanks be to God our Master. That they do not lose heart in their afflictions but rather grow braver, glory to Christ who strengthens them. As for their being driven away and not even thought worthy of shelter by some monks, especially since nearly all of these have agreed together on this, do not be surprised. It is written, “And a man’s enemies will be the members of his own household.” Did not the wretches reject Christ our God himself, who said these words? Indeed the son of thunder says, “He came to his own, and his own did not receive him.” What difference is there, then, if those people did not receive Christ, the Redeemer of the world, while these do not receive those who for his sake and for the sake of his Gospel have endured persecutions and prisons? None, except the crucifying and killing. May this bond of iniquity not be counted against them. But as you said, they cannot bear the complaints of those under them. So that the light of truth may not shine on them, and they may go on walking in the darkness of ignorance, they send our brethren away, lest a holy word of truth and righteousness be heard by them, or rather serve to remind them. It shall not be; this counsel of theirs shall not stand. But the word of God, which they have trampled on, will be spoken and established for ever. For he says, “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.” And who can stand against this? Only Satan the tyrant and his spokesmen, who have ratified adultery as a saving economy for the Church of Christ, truly vain-minded and most hateful men. Now I must turn to your questions. You asked why the divine Cyril used economy and did not break communion with those of the East who commemorated in the diptychs Theodore of Mopsuestia, though he was a heretic. It was because the doctrines of piety had been preserved among them most correctly and in the most essential points. This is what is written by the one who recorded these matters, Eulogius, archbishop of Alexandria, who is among the saints, in his discourse On Economy. We also included a quotation from it in the treatise we wrote specially, On Economy in General. So the man who recounted the story has himself given the solution. It has not been stated anywhere else, and it is enough not to look for any other. But for the sake of clarity, let me add what we hold, keeping the same sense. Some of the economies of the Fathers were made for a time, while others are permanent. For example, it was a permanent economy when St Athanasius allowed the Italians to say “persons” instead of “hypostases.” Economies for a time include the Apostle’s concerning circumcision,

the great Basil’s concerning the Holy Spirit, and also the present one of the divine Cyril. Things done for a limited time have nothing blameworthy about them, nothing discordant and nothing unlawful in any respect. Even so, they are relaxed and not fully strict. That is what economy for a time is. A physician cannot quickly free a sick man from his disease. Nor can anyone at once make an unruly horse obedient to the bridle, or make a dry branch easy to cut straight. Even the most experienced in such matters must use, little by little, clucking and coaxing and gentle [?] appeals. So it is with the saints in their economies, as with the great Cyril in this case. He waited a little for the Easterners, who were slow, or attached to the man, to recognize as a heretic one who truly was a heretic. For what else stood in the way? They preached the faith in an orthodox manner, and in doing so they anathematized the very man they commemorated. For everyone who is orthodox in all things anathematizes every heretic implicitly, even if not in words. Then, when full understanding dawned on them, the saint was perhaps united with them in every respect. Or do we not plainly do the same thing ourselves? Sometimes people who share our views differ from us on some point, where the matter is not very grievous and does not depart far from strictness. Even so, we accept communion with them, so as not to lose everything for some small matter that can be put right a little later. To act otherwise belongs to the unskilled, not to stewards of the mysteries of God. This is what it means to use economy for a time in words and in conduct, with judgment, truth and law. But it is never done in lawlessness and falsehood. Let the Moechians not thrust their tongues forward here. Let them not think that the guide is pushing people over a cliff, or that the helmsman is drowning them, or that the physician is causing disease. That is what they themselves have become like. They committed adultery along with the adulterer, joined the union along with the man who joined the adulterous union, accused God along with the accuser of God, and undid the Gospel along with the undoer of the Gospel, like dogs, for that is the more fitting way to put it. And where, or how, did the divine Cyril receive Dioscorus, the heretic of Alexandria, as the Moechians claim? They are dark around the light, accusers of the saints. Such a thing was never heard of, and their lie is impossible by its very nature, because Dioscorus came after the divine Cyril. How then could the saint, who had already received his lot beyond this world, have received a man who was recognized as a heretic after the saint had fallen asleep, at the time of the robber synod at Ephesus, after the third holy council? This is how they lie and tell tales, to hunt down souls that walk in simplicity. Therefore become skilled and well informed in everything, so that you may flee the serpent and those who speak with the serpent’s voice, by whom very many have perished from generation to generation. As for your other questions: if the bishop was not present at the adulterous synod, but calls it

…his metropolitan. As for whether one ought to receive communion from the priest when his bishop is orthodox, I have answered in other letters to Evodius as well: Yes, for the sake of economy, provided only that he does not concelebrate with heretics. For it makes no difference, when the bishop he commemorates is orthodox, even if that bishop, out of fear, commemorates his own metropolitan, who is a heretic. If such a priest invites you to an all-night vigil, you should go. If he offers a church, it should be accepted. When he comes into it to celebrate the liturgy, he should be allowed, and he may also be permitted to commemorate a dead person, provided the person was orthodox. Nothing should prevent the one who has received the church from celebrating in it. But if he commemorates a bishop who is a heretic, even if he calls him blessed, and even if he himself is orthodox, one must abstain from divine communion, but from the common table [only] if it is necessary to commemorate [the bishop] there [?]. On these terms one may perhaps also accept him when he gives the blessing and chants with us, as long as he does not concelebrate with a heretic, or with his own bishop, or with anyone else [of that kind], or knowingly give communion [to such people]. If someone eats indiscriminately with the one who joined the adulterous marriage, or with any other heretic, you must take care not to dine with such people, even if they pretend to be orthodox. For they do not keep the command of the Apostle, who says: "With such a person do not even eat." Beyond that, you must not investigate further, or ask with whom the person who dined with the heretic has dined, and then with whom that person has dined, and so drag the argument along and separate yourself from everyone. That is a self-willed course, not the way of the saints. "Up to this point," it says, "stand, and you shall not go beyond." Did they not know how to investigate these things and pass them on to us? Of course they did. But they knew that it is not good to move the boundaries which our Fathers set. We should not accept a gift from someone we do not eat with, if after being taught once or twice he remains indifferent and does not listen to us. I am not sure whether it might be permissible to accept things from the guards, not as blessings but as necessities. Perhaps, for the sake of economy, we may also accept things from other people, provided they avoid dining indiscriminately with heretics. I am not sure whether circumstances might even require us to accept from these people and dine with them too. But we should not hesitate to give food and drink to such people and to the guards, since we ought to share with every human being. As for the church of lord Gregoras, our child, I do not dare to say that our priest should celebrate the liturgy there. It was consecrated after the adulterous synod, by a man who concelebrates and has concelebrated with the one who joined the adulterous marriage and who was ordained [?] by the arch-Moechian…
50. To the same. [228.] You are eager, beloved child, to ask about useful things and to learn them, and that is praiseworthy. I am not competent to resolve your difficulties, but

for the common good I must contribute now what I can. Your question concerns those who marry a second time. You say that their union is disputed: should they be crowned, as is done for those marrying for the first time, or not? And if they are not, how could there be a union, since the priest has not joined them? You also say there is a story that the custom of crowning second marriages took hold from the days of the impious Constantine, because of his own third marriage, and that it did not exist in the times before him. I do not reject the idea that the story is credible on this ground. But lovers of truth must not establish matters on the strength of a passing rumor or human custom. They must establish them from the divinely inspired Scripture itself and from the patristic and canonical tradition. A second marriage has clearly been permitted by the holy Apostle, and through him by Christ. But it is not a law, as Gregory the Theologian says, but a concession. A concession is not granted for something blameless and without fault. How could it be, and why would it be? It is granted for a kind of defeat and a fall. The divine Apostle himself hinted at this when he said: "If they cannot exercise self-control, let them marry." Incontinence has lost the strength of manliness, and it is the offspring of defeat and falling away. Starting from this, the divine Fathers placed those who marry twice under penance. The Fathers of the synod at Laodicea did so without fixing a term, when they said: "After a short time has passed and they have devoted themselves to prayer and fasting, we have decreed that communion be restored to them by indulgence." The great Basil, however, fixed a term. He says: "For those married three times and many times the Fathers laid down the same canon" (that is, the same as for those married twice, in proportion), "for those married twice, one year; others say two years." It has been shown from what has been said, then, that a second marriage falls in the category of faults and has received a penance. This is also why the holy Fathers of the synod at Neocaesarea forbade a priest even to feast at the wedding of someone marrying a second time. They said: "Since the man marrying a second time is asking for penance, what priest will consent to the marriage by feasting at it?" What, then, necessarily follows? The first marriage is properly the law. It is fittingly crowned by the priesthood as untouched, unstained, not taken captive by the passion of fornication, and so it is crowned as victor over sin. After this comes the partaking of the holy things, and the one who crowned the couple, along with every other priest, feasts at such a marriage. So too our Lord and God deigned to dine at Cana of Galilee, and by feasting there he blessed every wedding feast. And even earlier, in anticipation of the crowned union, he placed the blessing upon our forefather Adam. How? "And God made man; in the image of God he made him; male and female he made them. And God blessed them, saying: Increase and multiply, and fill

the earth, and have dominion over it." This, then, is the blessing of marital union, and from it comes every blessing of the union of a first marriage, since Adam too married only once. Note also that the prayer of crowning starts from there, recalling the forming of the first man and his union with the woman taken from his side. A second marriage, even if it is permitted, is still under penance. How could it be worthy of crowning when it has been defeated and has not conquered? What priest will crown it, when the Fathers have forbidden him even simply to feast at its wedding banquet? How will someone share in divine communion when he is barred from the holy things for one or two years for this very reason? And what blessing prayer, or what kind, would be said over his union, since there is no other prayer than the one for the first, single marriage? So from all this, both from Scripture and from the Fathers, we conclude that a second marriage has no share in crowning. For this reason it is not joined by the priest, nor has any such rite been handed down for it. It is accepted when the penance, given in whatever measure the priest has judged, has been completed. After that the couple will also partake of the divine gifts and in this way receive a blessing, as if from a crowning, in a secondary sense, after the concession. For the gift is a blessing, and at that point it is also a sign from the priest of their union. From then on the priest is not prevented from feasting with those who have married twice, just as with those who have married once. In this way a second marriage proceeds by a law of concession, as the Apostle says. It knows that it holds second place to a first marriage, and it does not unreasonably demand the rights of the first marriage, which the person has already enjoyed. But you might say: "How, then, are they to enter into the union?" By the customary human formalities, just as those marrying a third time and many times do, for that is what the Fathers called marriage after a third. Or else let those be crowned too! But in truth, the utter dissolution of the canons, or rather of the Gospel, has now led priests to crown not only those marrying a second and third time, but even adulterers. It persecutes those who hold fast to the divine law and refuse to cooperate in this, and it anathematizes as strangers to Christ those who stand up for his commandment and his truth. Be astonished at this, O heaven! Everything is turned upside down: righteousness has become lawlessness and light has become darkness, as what the Moechians say and do makes plain. This is for those who are blind and deaf in soul, and so they carry the forerunners of the Antichrist. Perhaps you might also ask this: "If one party is a virgin, why do some say that the virgin is crowned on the head and the one coming from a previous marriage on the shoulder, while the prayer of crowning is said?" To me this seems not only absurd but laughable. Suppose it is a third marriage: where will the crown be placed? On the hand, or on the knee? And if the bride too comes from widowhood, she will receive the crown on her shoulder. Away with such things!

Who will perform the crowning, and how will the undivided prayer be divided, so that one party is blessed as spotless and victorious and the other is not? That is laughable and impossible. How will one partake of communion and the other not, since the other is under penance? And if the latter is the husband (and the husband is the head of the wife, and the two who have come together are one body), will the rest of the body partake but not the head? What has been joined will be cut apart at once by the very priest who joins them, even supposing he is permitted by concession to do it. For the chief point and goal of the union is the holy and undefiled body and blood of Christ. Or would you give it to both? Then we are done with idle talk, for such a man will clearly be not a priest but a transgressor of the divine ordinances, and therefore fallen from the priesthood. He is not even allowed to feast at such a marriage, much less to commit so great a lawlessness. "What then," you might say, "does the virgin party lose the victor's crown along with the blessing? Does the undefeated party not rather prevail, and bring along with it the party defeated through a second marriage, so that it shares in the crowning and in communion?" If this were so, it would have been laid down by the canons of the Fathers. But no such distinction has been made. Anything that has not been distinguished and laid down by the testimony of the Fathers is treading on empty air, whether in thought, word or deed. What I say is this: the virgin party rightly misses out on the rite handed down for a first marriage. That party could have enjoyed it by marrying someone of the same rank, since pure must be joined to pure, virgin to virgin, victor to victor. But a person who chooses to be joined to a non-virgin falls away from it and thereby dishonors the glory of virginity. Perhaps he never had it. Or if he had it, he threw it away in some fashion through his passionate attachment to the one marrying a second time. As a result he does not raise the other up, but rather brings himself down into the penance of the party marrying a second time. This is what I have been able to find and say, my good son. But if the truth seems otherwise to you or to anyone else, provided it is shown from Scripture, from the Fathers and from the canons, together with one's own contribution of reasoning, then we for our part are ready to be guided and eager to be illumined by the torch of others, since we are in need of light.

51. To the same. [229.] Your present letter, beloved child, has made me feel three things at once: I was astonished, I was delighted, and I [gave glory?] [?]. The first was because of the lawless, the second because of the law-abiding, and the third because of God, who strengthens those who rely on his law. As for my holy Athanasius and the thrice-beloved brothers with him, and also my most courageous Theosostus and his God-strengthened band of [seventeen?] [?], what I have written to them is enough, and I will refrain from speaking of them here. They deserve more words and praise, however, since they have contended divinely and like athletes

and are still contending. I turn now to the crowning point of my letter. What Christian has ever heard of anything as lawless and outrageous as what has been done by the ill-named Moechians? They are called hierarchs, but every apostolic and patristic voice declares them unhallowed, even apart from their heresy. What human hand (I do not say a Christian hand, but a barbarian one) has ever struck a man like this: two hundred and sixty-six lashes, and then shortly afterward four hundred blows with ox-sinews on the back? That is what the noble archbishop of Thessalonica, or rather the alien bishop, did. And he did it not to one of the common people but to a monk, and a hegumen at that, a most pious man named Euthymius, who truly bears the name of good cheer. Heaven was astonished at this, and I, wretch that I am, shuddered. So too, I think, does everyone who has natural gentleness and mercy and hears of it. He who ought to stand as a type of Christ, who when struck did not strike back, has become more savage than wild beasts. He bears no trace of a Christian at all, still less of a hierarch. And what was the beating for? To persuade Christ's athlete to agree to commemorate him as hierarch. But oh, the nobility and strength of the blessed man! It is right to put it this way: after so many blows, and after so much holy blood had flowed that the soles of the feet of those present were reddened, and the crimson mortar was turned into clay, as it were, for the building of God's Church, he lay for a while breathless and speechless. Then those deceivers asked him to commemorate the tyrant (I call him that, not archbishop). "No," said the blessed man. So, almost to the point of death, he did not turn his mind aside or depart in any way from what he knew in orthodoxy. I almost passed over something important: the temple of God became Pilate's praetorium. You said that the martyr was beaten there, namely in the sacred house called the Archangel's. The savage tormentors left him half-dead, but someone imitating Christ took him to his own house. He laid the fleece of a freshly slaughtered lamb on the bleeding and flayed flesh and brought the man back to life. When he had restored him little by little, he sent him away secretly, in keeping with the commandment that bids [us flee] [?]. So the one who had died escaped and was wondrously raised up as a pillar of orthodoxy and a triumph over the heterodox. What could be more impious than this? What orthodox person has ever done such things to a heretic? But this too shows how great the impiety of the Moechianizers is, and whose disciple each man is. The one who was beaten and bore it is a disciple of Christ, while the one who did the beating is a disciple of the devil. Such is this hierarch, who wishes to terrify by these means and to avenge his own cause. May we be rescued from his portion, brother, and may we belong to the first man's portion with all the pious. See, Lord, Lord, this affliction, and spare your people, and preside over the peace of orthodoxy in our Church. We have nothing else to say about the present situation, except that we should bear everything readily for his name.

But you, my beloved child, rejoice, even if you have been moved to another place of custody, as you indicated, because more crowns are being woven for you. And even if Leontius, once a disciple and now a denier, becomes hegumen over those among whom you are shut up, do not be surprised. The present is a time of God's long-suffering, so that those who are approved may be made manifest, and so that the son of Tabeel may rule over Bethlehem. As for the man who confessed and asked for a penance, it was rightly given. I agree with what you told him: if he does not wish to be placed under penance for killing enemies, let him not stop killing, and then we are free of judgment. But if he chooses to submit to the canons of the Church, he must choose one of two things: either to be placed under penance for having killed, or not to remain without penance [?]. That is no reason to condemn the first course, for such men are worthy of praise, as the divine Father says. But they must also accept the penance. Long ago Moses, who saw God, set Israel apart outside the camp for seven days when they returned victorious from the war against the Midianites. He was clearly moved by God to do this, and said: "Everyone who has killed a person or touched the slain shall be purified on the third day and on the seventh day, you and your captives." It seems to me that the great Basil took this as his starting point, or rather was divinely inspired, when he gave the penance of three years, giving it as a matter of economy. For imposing such penances is permissible, and not necessarily bound in every case to the letter of the text. Farewell in the Lord, my [?] child, and pray for me the sinner. My beloved child Gregory, your brother, joins me in greeting you. 52. To Philip the Deacon.

Do not think, holy man, that I am closing the gate of repentance, for that is what the Novatians do. I simply do not wish to open a door to sin for those who want it. Is that not the very situation you described in your earlier letter? A young woman vowed that if her betrothed recovered, she would be espoused to Christ. Then, when he did recover, she wanted to be joined to him and sought a remedy for breaking the second [commitment]. So our answer to you was entirely right. Anyone who puts the things of God before the things of men can give no other answer. Who would impose a penance on someone who has not yet sinned, except in intention? What physician dresses a wound before there is any illness, rather than keeping the one who is inclined toward illness from falling sick? The rule of medicine is either to preserve the health one has or to recover the health one has lost. But it is unreasonable, forgive me, to treat a sickness not yet present but only contemplated as though it already existed. That is the work not of a physician but of one who causes a fall [?], dragging what is still free of passion into passion. Such, I think, is the case of the girl as well. And I am not yet saying that if someone has thought of some good, …not this… [?]

But here what was planned has, as it were, already been carried into action through the petition and the sacred commitment. So refrain, my dear friends, from playing with such things, and listen to the one who says: "It is better not to vow than to vow and not pay." "While it remained, did it not remain yours?" he says. "Why have you lied to the Holy Spirit?" What follows I pass over because it is too dreadful to say. It is not that I look down on the girl. I care for her as the apple of my eye, both for her own sake, since she wishes to be cared for by my lowliness, and for the sake of the lady her mother, whom I revere and cherish as my own holy mother. But I fear the judgment that will confront each of us on the day of judgment, both the one who asks and the one who answers, since we must avoid even a chance idle word, lest we have to give account for it to the impartial Judge. So if the girl is not yet married, our word remains the same, and no other, before God and men, and you too ought to heed it. But if she has already married (alas for my wretchedness!), let me know, and then we will give the penance. For nothing is incurable for those who wish to be healed.

I have received the letter of your love, zealous for God. Its heading says it was sent by one person, but in substance it comes from several. Whether from one or from many, having been asked, I owe you as worthwhile an answer as my ignorance allows. First, this: the praises your eloquent tongue charmed me with do not belong to me, for I am a sinner and my life has not been set right. If anything good has come about, it is God's gift. It was granted through the Father who begot me in the spirit, and through the supplications of you lovers of piety it will be kept unharmed from now on. Second, I do not know how I am to give my explanation, since the question was not put clearly. On the whole I have reckoned that the issue centers on Tarasius, who was patriarch. I have long given careful attention to the matter raised. I have turned it over at length in my mind and have reviewed how events turned out. I certainly hold in praise and esteem those who stood firm for what is good and suffered for many years. Yet, as I am about to show, I do not altogether wish to have them share my view. For how could I not, when such men have proved so courageous for piety…
but with the word of truth and with the [?] and fitting power. So I would put it this way: what is the difference with respect to Tarasius

[?] to us [Reg. ms.: to you]? His faith? As far as is evident, it is orthodox. He has followed the holy councils and agreed with the other patriarchs, and earlier he even fought hard on behalf of the faith. The reception of those returning from heresy? That too was no innovation of his, for the holy Fathers before him received such people in three ways: by rebaptism, as with the Pepuzenes; by anointing with chrism, as with the Arians; or by having them anathematize their own opinion, as with the Nestorians. Ordination for money, which by necessity incurs deposition? Yes, that is entirely true. And indeed at that time shepherds were seen to be savage wolves. Altars were torn down, holy relics were dishonoured, and sacred books were burned. What more? The very image of Christ, along with other most venerable images, was insulted and trampled underfoot. And who could briefly recount things that would need a long history? But what of the fact that the prelate who came afterwards, having been quickly advanced from secular life to the dignity of the hierarchy, was not able to fight adequately on behalf of the Spirit [?]? From this came the scandals, and from there the troubles now disturbing us have taken their origin. As for you, you know how you stand toward him. But we heard from him that, regarding those ordained for money, he does not admit them to communion, even if this was not what was suspected. So for the sake of the good of peace we thought it expedient [to keep] concord with him [?], since the Theologian also says: "As far as it is possible, one must incline toward this." And where what grieves us is only a suspicion, accommodation is better than obstinacy. We do not drag you away from your conscience, and you for your part should not demand of us a judgment that is not evident to us. For person, time and experience make people differ when they have not come to the same matters in the same way. But what is this going back to the divine Germanus, and insisting at all costs on tracing ordination from there? For what of the three heretics in between? Is there anyone who was not ordained by them, or by those ordained before them, since ordination has been passed down in succession as far as Tarasius? How many clergy have come in the meantime from east and west, from the north and from the sea, and been joined in communion with our Church? And how many were ordained at that time without money, and have ordained others, even if they held heretical views? To know all this belongs to God alone; it is not for a human being to affirm it with certainty, and on that basis to suppose that all are deposed. But since we are human, let us, I beg you, look at things as humans do. For man looks on the face, but God looks on the heart, and only the confession of the mouth should be required, as long as it is not plainly false. It was on this basis that Tarasius too received ordination, and on this basis the zealous and strict men of that time joined Tarasius and were of one mind with him. Soon after the council they parted from him, over what they regarded as the acceptance of ordination for

money, and over certain other questions. If this seems right to you too, we shall go on to what follows, for the same things will be said of the period from Tarasius to the present. What, then, is the conclusion? To take communion from any priest who is blameless, according to the Theologian and Chrysostom. For the one says: "Let anyone be trustworthy to you for your purification, provided only that he is one of the approved, not openly condemned and not estranged from the faith." And the other says: "Inquire, investigate closely, for communion without examination is not without danger. For the danger concerns great things [?]"

Let us therefore seek out and investigate [?] with whom to communicate: whether he confesses the right faith, whether he has not been ordained for money, and whether any of the other dangerous things suspected and reported about his life is true. But suppose his ordination is derived from such-and-such a person, whether from a heretic or from one ordained for money, while he himself is neither a heretic nor knowingly ordained by one who received money, that is, by a Simoniac. If he nevertheless confesses the whole truth, promises to keep both the faith and the canons inviolate, and rejects those who have violated either, then we have no reason to keep away from him. For such a man is blameless according to the saints cited above, and through them according to all. This, then, is how we communicate, and we have advised you to do the same, sons [ms.: "if we will not hear"; Lat.: "if you do not hear"] [?]. For if one investigates further, the precepts of the Fathers are rejected, as has been shown. And the gift of the priesthood, by which we are able to be called Christians, fails so completely that we fall back into pagan worship, which is absurd. Besides, those who are so strict would not find what they seek even if they went to the West and the East, since everyone would be deposed in turn, all the way back, through mutual concelebration. For clearly the apocrisiarii sent from here concelebrated with the prelate of Rome in the time of Tarasius, and he in turn, perhaps, with those of the East, and so the priesthood would vanish altogether. Rejecting this entirely, we have chosen to stand [?] by the measure mentioned above, in accordance with the saints.

For many such lapses have occurred and still occur in the Church, and none of the saints is found to have investigated them in this way. It is not even possible, and they did not hand it down to us to observe. So much for that. As for the claim that our stand [Reg. ms.: your stand] is more important to us than [opposing] the adulterous synod [?], I was astonished to hear it. For the latter is as much more to be preferred as the Lord's voice is to an apostle's. And I do not yet say that Tarasius never proclaimed that ordination for money was permitted. On the contrary, he confessed that such men were not to be received, at least openly. But here a dogma contrary to the Gospel, to the Forerunner and to the

canons has been proclaimed synodically through the acceptance of the priest who joined the adulterous couple. It confirms lawlessness as "economy" and gives hierarchs and priests authority over the canons whenever they wish, and it anathematizes and casts out those who do not think the same, as you know. Though this comes second to the iconoclast heresy, it is no less serious in the eyes of those who consider it piously. Through their prayers may the Lord remove the evil and grant peace to his Church as in the beginning. Except that, as you wrote, the one is struck by the other, and the recognition and the undoing of this lawlessly bound deed depend on each other [?]. May the Lord keep you in good health, together with all your household, and praying for our lowliness, you who are foremost among friends and zealots.

54. To Anna, abbess. [274.] Why have you held back from writing and letting us know how your holiness is? We, for our part, will all the more not stop writing, partly because we have once opened our lowly mouth, and partly because of your godly zeal and fiery piety. For I learn that you never cease doing good to our brothers. You run about here and there, receive kindly everyone who comes your way, and send each one off with words of prayer, as a servant of Christ. Oh, this most beautiful work of yours! Oh, your holy soul, so watchful in divine things! For these deeds are not orphans. They are the offspring of other virtues, or rather shoots of your spiritual fruitfulness, since one who carries perfumes cannot fail to give off fragrance, nor can one who bears light fail to shine. So it is always and in every way made plain, and above all in persecutions for Christ, who are the lovers of holiness and blessed by God, and who are the base and those without share in the good, even if by their outward habit they pretend that all is well within. ... 55. To Irene the patrician. A written greeting is something that kindles love, creating attachment in the souls of those who love. It does so all the more the more frequent the exchange is, as though raking up the sparks of love lying stored within and kindling great affection. Just such an effect has your gracious letter produced in us lowly ones. It has multiplied our spiritual friendship for you and set the embers of memory glowing more brightly. So, most God-fearing lady, make use of this remedy of love, and let us know of your good health and well-being. For we know that your virtue is evergreen and productive of piety, from what we have heard and still hear, and from the kindness we ourselves have received and still receive.

Whether you borrow another's voice or speak with your own tongue, we listen to your letter with sweet affection rather than attending to the mere sound. At the same time we know that nothing portrays a soul as well as the word that comes from it, whatever kind that may be. We were grieved to learn that this has happened to the lady your daughter. But what prayer, or what sort of anointing [?], could we give, sinners as we are? Yet be assured of this: such sorceries have no power unless we give room to some carelessness. Just as a place lit up by the sun cannot admit the opposing darkness, so a person supported by divine light, that is, by understanding and virtue, cannot suffer any of the sinister and demonic trickeries. So may the girl be healed in the name of the Lord, who heals every disease and every infirmity. May the hand of God hover over her and overshadow her head, and drive away every harmful influence, so that, restored to health, she may offer her prayers in thanksgiving together with her God-bearing mother.

56. To Antonius, abbot of St [?], and those with him. [?] We have received the letters your paternal holiness wrote to us out of great distress and affliction of heart. What need is there even to say how much we groaned? We were moved by brotherly compassion, unworthy though we are, and since we suffer the same things, we could imagine your hardship and share in it. For pain is known to no one except those who are held fast in the same griefs. But our sins have so multiplied in this present generation of lawlessness [Reg. ms.: "lawlessness has so multiplied"], love having grown cold according to the Lord's word, that those who ought to clear away obstacles and stumbling blocks can be seen doing the same things as those in secular office, or perhaps worse. You say that you have suffered, and still suffer, prisons, arrests, insults, persecutions and hardships at the hands of those who govern the Churches of God. Yet even if you had not been standing firm for a commandment but had been caught in ordinary human failings, it would in no way have been right for you to suffer such things from shepherds of God. How much less when you are contending for the truth! You are owed praise and blessing, and you are adorned with the monastic profession besides. "By their works you will know them," said the Lord. Surely nothing of this kind was ever known among the saints. On the contrary, they were shown to be the ones who suffered, taught by the apostolic voice, which says of the Lord: "When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten." He even graciously offered his divine cheek to the one who struck him. By this Christ's shepherds are recognized, and by that the strangers [?]. But what can one do, given the wickedness that has fallen upon people in our

lowly generation? They even boast of it and pride themselves on it, reckoning the unlawful lawful and exercising their leadership in opposition to the divine commands. Let them, then, receive the due reward of what they have done and are doing, or rather, may they be forgiven by the impartial Judge, who on the day of judgment will not overlook anything as unexamined and unaccountable. But you, most honoured brothers and most venerable Fathers, rejoice and be glad, for you have carried off the glory of the divine beatitude and have honourably received the dishonour of Christ, being repaid for small labours and struggles with things that are very great and eternal. And since, as we wrote earlier, by the good pleasure of the supremely good God the man through whom division arose in our Church has been removed, peace has been established by the assent, influence and kindness of our gloriously victorious and Christ-loving emperors (and I would add, by their entreaties), and by the cooperation and defence of our most holy patriarch, for from now on we must call him so. Let your holiness also accept what we lowly ones have judged and settled after much consideration and investigation, and after comparing the precedents of the Fathers [?] and the scandals that have from time to time occurred in the Church. In this way, in our [Reg. ms.: your] Church of Christ [Reg. ms.: of God] too, the peace of God may rule the hearts of all. For if we do not do this, it will not be reckoned holy before God, nor will victory be ours. Instead, by seeking more than what is right, we may perhaps lose even the good we achieved by our earlier labours. Therefore we beg you: receive and welcome our most holy patriarch, and be in communion with your own bishop as well, in matters where lawlessness is not manifest, leaving what lies in between to the Lord, who examines and repays what is done and what is said. To this very end we have made our entreaty and urged our most holy patriarch [?] that you too may be released from prison. And once you have made a pact of peace with one another, may anything that is in doubt be resolved at once. Or if something proves incurable, may the ailments be healed when we and the most honourable bishop come here, in the presence of the ecumenical patriarch himself, so that everything may come together in the joy of peace and the sincerity of concord. 57. To Plato, his own Father. Why, holy Father, do you command wretched me to do things beyond me? I need to be enlightened by you, and you seek to be instructed by me, who am in darkness. But in this too you are shaping me toward humility. I do not know what to say that suits the moment, except that God has ordered our affairs well. For if some men, out of love of God, left the high offices they held and ran far away, and were called blessed for the solitary

life, how can we lowly ones, held under guard in exile for the sake of God's law, not rejoice in the Lord? We should count it a grace and the greatest of gifts that we have been found worthy to reach such a measure, which many desired and did not attain. So sit, my holy Father, in the place where God, not man, has confined you for the time being, since we do not know what the coming day will bring, whether providence orders things this way or otherwise. And glorify the Lord who glorified you through your martyr's stand. ... [lacuna] ... your bread with thanksgiving and joy, though men thought they were giving you something bitter. You no longer have strength in your old age, having laboured [?] beforehand in ascetic struggles in your youth, by the grace of Christ in all things. Therefore I beg you and [?] to support your worn-out body with food and drink. Do not refuse. The solitude is enough for you, and the confinement, the desolation, the deprivation, the weakness of old age along with illness, and your care for us sinners and for the others. Be content to endure in these things, pursuing purity of thought through the soaring of your precious soul. Now that the solitary life is at hand [?], the mind can easily rise from earthly things to heavenly ones, like water forced up through a pipe. This is what we seek: to be with God forever, free of attachment. Yet our Fathers define wars as the cause of crowns, so that if we stand firm while under attack, we carry off the glory of victory over the vanquished

I am ashamed to say such things to you, my Father, disgraced as I am by the passions, but I have been compelled to do so out of obedience to you. It is good to be loosed from attachment with its many bonds, and to be bound by the insatiable love of the Lord. It is profitable, my Father, to keep away from the stench of the passions and to breathe the fragrance of the Spirit. Blessed [?] is it to be pierced with compunction here, and to weep for ... [lacuna] ... and exultation to the one who in all things puts first ... [lacuna] ... of God. When this comes into the soul, like fire it naturally drives off [?] the assaults of sin. And how should he not be feared, at whom angels shudder, at whose glance creation quakes, before whom we shall all stand naked and laid bare, and from whom a little later we shall receive the recompense for how we have lived? But I,

wretch that I am, find myself in none of the things I have described, and so I am downcast. I ask the help of your holy prayers for the opening of the eyes of my soul and for a taste of the true love. But as you know, my body is weak as well as my soul, and I do not know what to do. For if I try to force myself even a little, I lose even the little I have. I have found one consolation, and I must put it before you, my Father. I learned from reading and from the practice of the Easterners that those living in stillness ought, if possible, to partake of divine communion every day. I did so, and wretched as I am, I found help: my mind is held back from passionate impulses by the awe-inspiring majesty of the gift. For what could bring the soul greater exultation and illumination than divine communion? I pour wine into a glass cup set apart for this purpose, say the customary prayers, and, unworthy as I am, partake of the gift. Tell me whether I am doing well or not. ... [lacuna] ... to eat of your fruits. Blessed are you, my Father, and it shall be well with you, for you have been called the father of many, and you have led them so far into the heart of virtue that now all are in exile for the commandment of the law of the Lord. But pray for them all, that he may complete for them the

A selection from his various letters of the third exile. 1. To the iconoclast synod, written as in the person of all [?] the abbots. We follow divine laws and canonical decrees which say that one must not do or say anything bearing on the good order of the Church contrary to the judgment of one's own bishop, still less anything that draws one into doctrinal disputation. For this reason, when your authority once and again summoned our insignificance to such proceedings, we did not dare to come and do something outside what is lawful, since we are under the sacred hand of Nicephorus, the most holy patriarch, by the divine Spirit. But some abbots of the same rank as ourselves, making a trial of it, decided to attend and enter into debate. And what else have we heard but things that dismay our lowly heart? For they say that the summons is for the overthrow of the holy second council at Nicaea, that is, for the abolition of

the veneration of the venerable image of our Lord Jesus Christ, of the Mother of God and of all the saints together. Oh, who on hearing this would not groan bitterly from the depths of his heart, since the saving dispensation of our Lord Jesus Christ is now being overturned by these things? "Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth": let the most loud-voiced Isaiah cry out with us, along with everything that follows in that passage. Or rather, to speak more fittingly: Hear, East and West, North and the regions of the sea, where our affairs now stand and against which [?] they have dared to sit in council. We, then, the least, both those who attended and those who did not (for one statement serves for both, since we are of one soul in one divine mind), hold a faith in agreement with the Church under heaven. That is, we honour without distinction [?] and venerate the divine image of our Saviour Jesus Christ himself, of his all-holy Mother, and of any of the saints. We do not claim to have our security only from the holy second council at Nicaea, or from the council before it that decreed in a most divine manner. Rather, grounded both in written and in unwritten tradition from the very coming of our Lord and God, we have stood securely on that seat of which Christ says: "You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of Hades shall not prevail against it." For what argument could anyone find who chose to speak against so great a power of truth? For if, as is agreed, our Lord Jesus Christ was seen in human form and in a shape like ours, he is ineffably [?] circumscribed and depicted as we are, even though in the divine form the same one remains uncircumscribed. For he is the mediator between God and men, preserving unimpaired the properties of each of the natures of which he consists. But if he were not circumscribed, he would no longer be man, much less mediator, since the abolition of circumscription abolishes along with it all the properties of the same order. For if he is not circumscribable, neither is he tangible; but if he is tangible, he can also be handled, and to deny this is folly. For these belong to a body that is subject to touch and colour. How, then, is he not also circumscribable, and therefore capable of suffering? And if he is circumscribable and capable of suffering, he is certainly also to be venerated, namely in the form in which he is circumscribed. For the glory of the prototype is not divided [?] in its copy, according to Basil the Great: "the honour of the image passes over to the prototype." This holds for any image whatever, natural or artificial. The same principle must be understood of the figure of the precious cross. For when the figure is venerated, the life-giving wood is venerated along with it, just as, conversely, abolishing the one necessarily abolishes the other. Or is not the confession of the figure a confession of the life-giving cross? And denial works the same way in reverse. Anyone with understanding must apply the same reasoning to the image of Christ and to Christ himself. And it is not yet the time for dogm-

[?]… unfolding, which persuades even the very dull of mind to look up readily to the rays of the truth. This is the evangelical faith of us sinners; this is the apostolic confession of us lowly ones; this, in short, is the religion handed down from the fathers to us, the least. Apart from this faith, not just this person or that, now or in the past, but not even Peter or Paul (for we are speaking of the impossible as if it were possible), not even someone who came from heaven itself teaching doctrine and preaching the gospel, could we accept as a partner in communion, since he would not be keeping in step with the sound teaching of the faith. Whatever your authority decides about this, our humility is ready to undergo even death rather than deny this sincere confession of ours.

2. — To monks. [209] At this time, when Christ is being persecuted through his image, it is not only the man who excels in rank and knowledge who must join the struggle, speaking and teaching the word of orthodoxy. Even one who holds the rank of a disciple is bound to speak the truth boldly and with a free tongue. The saying is not mine, a sinner's, but that of the divine Chrysostom, and of other Fathers as well. The lord abbots, however, when they were detained by the emperor, did not do what I have just described, although [?] they surpass in rank and knowledge all the superiors of this land. On the contrary, they kept silent. Bad as that is, they did more: they also signed a written undertaking neither to meet with one another nor to teach. This is a betrayal of the truth, a denial of their office as leaders, and the ruin of those under them, and of their peers as well. When the Jews ordered the apostles not to teach in the name of Christ, they said: "Judge for yourselves whether it is right to listen to you rather than to our God." And again: "We must obey God rather than men." The abbots should have said such things to them. Then God would have been glorified through them, the orthodox built up, the monasteries strengthened, and those suffering in exile given new strength. But why do we value the monasteries above God, and the [?] of this world above suffering for the good? Where is "I spoke before kings and was not ashamed"? Where is "Behold, I will not restrain my lips; Lord, you know"? Where is the glory and strength of our order? Think of the blessed Sabas and Theodosius. When the emperor Anastasius chose impiety in their day, they rose up and fought fervently for the faith. They did so first by joining others in anathematizing the heterodox in the church, and then by what they wrote to the emperor, solemnly declaring that they would choose death rather than disturb anything that had been established.

And, as they report, the lord abbots say: "What are we?" First, Christians, who ought by all means to speak now. Then monks, who must not let even the smallest thing be snatched from them, being unbound by the world and not subject to its hold. Then abbots, who also remove the stumbling blocks of others and are bound to give no offence in anything, "so that," it says, "the ministry may not be blamed." Yet what offence and blame, or rather what consent, they have given by their own signatures, why even say? If silence is a kind of consent, how much graver is it to ratify that silence in writing before the whole Church? And you say that, while celebrating in secret, they commemorate Nicephorus [?] secretly, and that all the patricians, [?] the others, hold the orthodox faith. But what does Christ say? "Whoever confesses me before men, I too will confess before my Father in heaven." And the reverse holds for denial. Even if the only thing they signed was an undertaking not to meet with one another, it comes to the same thing. For how will they keep what Christ says: "Whoever comes to me I will never cast out" [?]? Suppose someone comes, asking questions and seeking to learn the truth, whether an abbot or anyone else. What will the abbot answer? Obviously: "I have received an order not to speak." Would that it stopped there! But he will also say he cannot receive you into the monastery or eat with you. Christ says: receive and teach. "For if he draws back," it says, "my soul takes no pleasure in him." So they bound themselves in writing to obey [?] in opposition to Christ. These, brothers and Fathers, are the things I know for certain that they have done. And since you required me to say what I knew [?], I have reported it, [?] asking that it be kept secret, out of caution because of the trial. For the rest, may you save your own souls and keep them safe, praying also for me, the lowly one.

3. — To an abbot.

4. — To Theophylact of Nicomedia [?]. [195] For two years I have been anxious and labouring in my thoughts to write to your sacred head, and only now have I, the lowly one, barely satisfied my longing. But it is good that through this letter I am counted worthy to greet you: my Father, the pillar of the truth, the foundation of orthodoxy, the guardian of piety, the support of the Church, the victorious man, the Christ-bearing high priest, the martyr for the confession of God. For is the crown of martyrdom not yours? You are an exile for Christ, homeless and much-enduring. And you bear this in a body that is delicate by nature and, I know, already worn out by the ascetic race toward God. The company of the right-minded boasts in you. The land of Nicomedia rejoices and freely gains glory by putting you forward before all under heaven, shaking off the things long noised abroad about those who presided there before you.

[?] But if something more personal should be said, [?] Tarasius, now among the saints, saw that the man who was first a sheep of his own court and hand, then a renowned shepherd, is now struggling and facing danger for orthodoxy. Tarasius had made his own contribution in synod, by the grace of God, in the days of a reign whose name meant peace and which brought peace, so that the events fittingly matched the names. But that is how things were then. The present is bitter and painful. How could it not be? Altars are being destroyed and churches ravaged, while the heresy stirs everything upside down and persecutes Christ together with his mother and his servants. For are these not persecuted when their holy icons are ravaged? Or when the figure of the life-giving wood is destroyed, would anyone say that the cross has not been done away with? And if that cannot be granted for the cross, how can we not agree that the same holds for the icon? For a figure is also an image, as the argument runs the other way as well.
