But who am I, wretched and uninitiated, to explain these things to a divine Father and teacher? Teach us, most holy one, the more perfect things, as one initiated by God. And teach us by your example to bear firmly the present ordeal, whether it is chastisement or testing: chastisement in our case, because of our sins, and testing in yours, because of your divine love for Christ. Do not cease [?] to pray to him to turn the shadow of impiety into the dawn of a peaceful orthodoxy.

5. — To Naucratius, my child. [215] News upon news, word upon word! What shall I say, and what shall I speak? How should I, wretched as I am, feel about what has happened? Joy and grief, relief and lament: I am caught between two emotions and do not know which to choose to express. Yet he wins who conquered Satan and the rulers and torturers of this age. The lamb of Christ has been put to death for Christ under the scourge: Thaddaeus, my sapling, my own heart, the son of obedience, the stock of piety, the namesake of the Apostle. The joy is beyond bearing, the gladness unsurpassed, not for me, the lowly one, alone, but for angels and men. How great are your works, O Lord! Even now, in this lowly generation, you have shown forth a witness to your truth whom none can challenge. And you chose him not from the wise and well-born of this world but from the opposite, so that the word of the Apostle might be fulfilled: "He chose the low-born and despised things, and the things that are not, to bring to nothing the things that are." Where have you gone from me, blessed child? Where have you been so quickly exalted and numbered among the martyrs? O your good fortune! O your nobility! O your good counsel! In one day you gained endless ages; in torturing pains you acquired unspeakable joys; through a hundred and thirty blows you received the perfect

reward for your labour, with the martyrs, from the Holy Trinity. For one number stands for perfection and the other corresponds to the Trinity, so that God might show your greatness of soul even from your very punishment. Your blood is myrrh; your remains impart sanctification to those who touch them. I beseech you, Thaddaeus, saint of God, intercede for me, your unworthy servant, for I no longer dare to call you [?] child. See, my brothers, what has happened: we possessed a [?] treasure and member. Thaddaeus, the martyr of Christ, is enough to give glory to God, to be our boast, and to be the joy of the whole Church. What [?]? "The first," it says, "will be last, and the last first." I say this of James and Lucian. The one has contended, and may he contend to the end, with Dorotheus and Bessarion. The other, because of my sins, has been shipwrecked along with those like him. Oh, how they have fallen in the midst of the luminaries, the [?]! They forgot, then, the one who said: "Do not fear those who kill the body." For has not the only Sovereign, who gives strength to the weak, measured out what is possible? And the martyrs are close at hand. Does he not, of necessity, exempt those who are not yet strong by nature, though not those who lack the will? And the martyr Thaddaeus is faithful in heaven. So, my brothers, let us not be terrified or grow fearful at the fall of the defeated, as though we too [?] will not endure the blows. We shall endure them by the power of God. We shall pass through, whether it be fire or sword, with God going before us and calling us to enter the kingdom promised to us, as he did Israel into the land of promise. Do you not know what happened to those who stirred up the people back then, saying: "We will not be able to cross over, for there are cities walled up to heaven, and giants, among them Anak"? And what came of it? Was it not for this that they themselves were consumed by fire, and the whole grumbling people perished, whose bodies fell in the wilderness? Let no one be such an agitator; let no one be faint-hearted; let no one lose hope. Let us pass through, then, brothers, let us pass through like Caleb, I say, and Joshua son of Nun, the heirs of the promise. Spiritual walls will be shaken down for us, as the walls of Jericho were then, by the trumpet of thanksgiving that blessed Thaddaeus sounded when he sang from the starting line of his labours: "This is the day that the Lord has made." So I exhort you, so I entreat you. "For we are ambassadors for Christ," it says, "as though God were appealing through us." We beg you not to shrink like cowards from death for him and with him, if it must come. The letter is to everyone, even though it is addressed to you, good child. Therefore I greet everyone and rejoice with everyone in their sufferings. And who is worthy to fill up what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ in his flesh? And woe to the one who denies and has turned aside, even if death threatens; for eternal death will be his shepherd, and the upright will rule over

him in the morning. The peace of Christ be with you, and might, strength and comfort, as you pray for all the brothers, and for me, that by God's mercy I may be shown to fulfil what I urge on others. The brothers with me

6. — To a priest who signed. [144] What your reverence has suffered in the shipwreck of signing! And how much you have wept over your fall! For truly it is a fall to stretch out even just the hand against the holy icon of Christ. I learned of it through your note, man of God, and I have suffered with you, wailed with you and grieved with you, crying out in distress as befits [?] one who loves his brother. For we are members of one another. And: "If one member suffers, all the members ought to suffer with it" (these are the Apostle's words); "if one member is honoured, all share the joy." But oh, the abuse! We were despoiled, alarmed and frightened by things that should neither frighten nor alarm us, if we indeed read: "Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot harm the soul." Why then, my friend, have you brought the matter to me, a useless man? Who am I to heal, when I am sick with sins and not one of those entrusted with healing such fractures? For God has [?] assigned to bishops the task of setting right and healing the affairs of presbyters, that is, of priests. How could you ask of me what is beyond me [?]? It is not possible. Still, so as not to leave you entirely without an answer, I offer this as advice and in love. God is good. He does not want a man to die but wants him to turn and live. If, then, your repentance is genuine, abstain completely from celebrating the liturgy. I do not know whether you might give some of the holy gifts to anyone, except under the present necessity. For in necessity and want it is permissible for anyone to receive communion even by himself, because the heresy must be shunned. Whatever you have done, then, whether on your own or by assigning it to another, is good and praiseworthy for moving God to mercy. But nothing at all can release you to celebrate the liturgy, even if the release should seem to come from some bishop or other. This holds [?] until the Church of God is at peace. Then, as is proper, every such case will be regulated by the judgment of a synod and will receive a judgment measured by God. You may say: "While I was signing, I cried out that I venerate the holy icons." Forgive me, brother, but Pilate also [?] declared with his mouth that he was clean of the slaughter of Christ, and yet with his pen he confirmed the death. This is what I, [?], say to you before God. But I beg you, remember my salvation in your repentance [?]. And please greet, where you said you see my holy Fathers among the bishops, as from me, the

7. — To John, my child. [148] I am delighted with your letters, child and brother, because they come in good order and refuse the nausea of wordiness. For a letter's virtue is to take up the subject at once and to say only what is necessary, without circling round what is not. Well, then. As for what you asked: this is not the time to be curious about such matters, nor are you to be initiated into them by me, good child, since I too, like others, am uninitiated in things hard to reach. But so as not to grieve you by saying nothing, I say this about the first question: none of the other God-bearing Fathers has yet clarified the problem as well as Gregory of Nyssa. So let us be content with the spiritual contemplation, a contemplation lifted very high. For, as the saying goes, what lies beyond Gades cannot be crossed. As for the second: "He who understands will keep silent at that time, because it is an evil time." This does not seem crooked or twisted to me. For the divinely inspired Scripture has set for us a time to speak and a time to keep silent, depending on the need at hand, as we consider and manage the word of truth. Have we not been commanded not to throw holy things to dogs or cast pearls before swine? Look at the God-bearers, and you will find them sometimes putting the word under the bushel of silence, when speaking is unprofitable or rather harmful, and sometimes raising it up on the lampstand, when the sowing is fruitful and not on stony ground. That is as much as I can see in the question. If you discover better answers by yourself or through others, do not [?] hesitate to share them [?] with your father and brother, who is short of ideas. Farewell, and pray for me much.

[To] the communities scattered everywhere for Christ's sake, together with those held in prisons and exile: greetings in the Lord. [150] Grace and peace to you, to speak as the Apostle does, from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, our hope. It is for him and because of him that we suffer persecution, affliction and distress, desolation and flight, prisons, punishments and all the other trials and misfortunes that daily bring us hardship. For this reason, my beloved brothers, we have thought of some consolation for the absence of our lowly person and are sending you this letter. We want you to know that we make mention of you unceasingly in our lowly prayers, recalling and thinking of each one of you, and raising our hands to God with tears and groans. We pray that, just as we took up the contests for the truth and came

[Notes: ¹⁰ [?] ¹¹ Gal. 1:5. ¹¹ Rom. 1:9.]

out of our holy monasteries in one spirit and one soul, as if from a nest, so we may remain to the end by the power of the Lord. May we have the same faith and the same love, being one in soul and of one mind, holding fast the doctrine of the truth that has been preached and set down, for eye and ear, in all creation under heaven. That doctrine is this. We worship Father, Son and Holy Spirit, the much-hymned and blessed Trinity, according to the teaching of theology. And we confess that one of the Trinity, the Son and Word of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant and being born in the likeness of men. He is therefore portrayed in a form like ours and marked by the features of a body, since the same one was at once perfect God and man. He came within the bounds of circumscription, like us, whose nature he also took, in so far as that nature has been united to the [?] of the divine nature. For surely, as the Scriptures say, it is not angels that he takes hold of (though even angels can be depicted, as they have appeared to those who see by the Spirit), but he takes hold of the seed of Abraham. Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect. So let the enemies of Christ tell us how the seed of Abraham can possibly not be depicted. And how can he [?] be like us in every respect, he who is called our brother, if he is not shown to have taken on the property of circumscription, as we his brothers have it? Then he is not a brother, nor indeed like us, and for that reason not a man either. This is what follows from their refusal to say that Christ is depicted as we are. In this way they do away with the saving dispensation, just like the Manichaeans, Valentinians and Marcionites. Let us flee from communion with them, brothers, as from the venom of a serpent, which blackens not the body, as the Theologian says somewhere, but the depths of the soul.

We think the same as the apostolic Church throughout the world, for this Byzantine church is a heretical fragment, as it has often been in the habit of cutting itself off from the others. We depict our Lord Jesus Christ in bodily form, following a succession handed down from the beginning, from the very time of his appearing, by apostolic practice. We copy image from image, just as we do with the life-giving cross. We do not portray the cross, which is Christ's weapon against the devil, while refusing to depict Christ, who is the warrior and destroyer of Satan. For where could a true and victorious weapon be painted without the warrior who bears it being shown before our eyes? We also venerate his holy icon, venerating in it Christ who is depicted. For he came forth from the womb of his mother, the Theotokos, with a form that could be depicted. Otherwise he would be some miscarried fetus, a man without form, you enemies of God! But if the infant comes forth with such a form, as is true of the one of whom the prophet says, "Every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord," then it must certainly be possible to depict him as well. Hear, you deaf, and you [?]

[Notes: [?] 2:15. Isa. 42:18.]

[?] … in one thing only did our nature undergo something new in Christ: he was conceived without seed in the womb of a Virgin, and was born without corruption; for, as Scripture says, he did no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth. In everything else he was as we are: he ate, he drank, he breathed, he grew, he walked, he sweated, he grew weary, he was crucified, he died. And although, as God, he rose on the third day, even after the resurrection he kept our form, which can be depicted, now deified and made incorruptible in him. In that form he was seen by the apostles; after he had risen he ate and drank with them, and Thomas touched him. And to all those who suspected that he was a spirit he said: “Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.” So too he was taken up in glory, and in the same way he will come in the same form, the form of our appearance. All flesh will see him coming from heaven with the angels of his power in flaming fire, inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God and on those who do not obey his Gospel, as it is written. With them the Jews who crucified him will mourn, and so will the Iconoclasts, who cannot bear to have him portrayed. These, brothers, are the proclamations of the Gospel; these are the teachings of the apostles. But those who hold the opposite view try to turn the people of God to another gospel, which is no gospel at all. They bring forward spurious writings, speaking from the belly and not from the mouth of the Lord. For tares are always sown among the wheat, and falsehood is always set beside the truth. How else could the truth be shown, if no one spoke against it? “But even if we,” says the Apostle, “or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be accursed. As we have said before, so now I say again: if anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to the one you received, let him be accursed.” As for the Mother of God, or any of the saints, and the fact that they are portrayed, there is no need for me to write to you. I would call it foolish to say that any human being whatever cannot be depicted. But those who refuse to let Christ, the head of the body of the Church, be circumscribed have also seen fit to take away the members of Christ along with him, so that they too are not portrayed, since we are all the body of Christ and members of it individually. For it convicts them to allow the Mother of God to be portrayed but not the one born of her, who was seen at her breast, nor anything that belongs to his bodily presence; or again to let the eyewitnesses and servants be depicted on columns, while the one they served and lived with is not depicted. They show themselves worse than the Jews, for they will not accept an image even of Moses or of any other of the prophets, though those men who lived before grace accepted images, being men of the Law and not Christians. But these men are so senseless that they fight both against themselves and against the Jews. They are neither Jews keeping the Law nor Christians, since they do not depict Christ, whom they have acknowledged to have become man. The word of Peter the

apostle is found in the account of the martyrdom of Saint Pancratius: “Joseph, my child, bring out the image of our Lord Jesus Christ and set it up in the little tower, so that the people may know what form the Son of God took. Then, when they see it, they will believe all the more, beholding the representation of his form, and they will be reminded of what we have preached to them.” The word of Paul is: “O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you so that you do not obey the truth, before whose eyes Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed among you as crucified?” The word of Basil the Great is: “Let Christ, the judge of the contests, also be painted on the panel.” And again: “The honor paid to the image passes over to the prototype.” The word of Athanasius, who endured so many struggles, is: “We the faithful do not venerate images as gods, as the Greeks do — God forbid! We only show our relationship to the features of the face in the image, and the longing of our love for them.” The word of Chrysostom is: “I too have loved the painting in poured wax, filled as it is with piety. For I saw an angel in an image driving off hordes of barbarians; I saw the tribes of barbarians trampled underfoot, and David proved true: ‘Lord, in your city you will bring their image to nothing.’” This is exactly what those who now war against the icons of Christ are doing to the Mother of God and the saints as well — O fearful thing to hear! — bringing their holy images to nothing. I will pass over the words of the others, for they are many. Adding just one more, I will turn my discourse to another matter. The word of the God-bearing Fathers of the sixth holy council is: “In some paintings of the venerable images a lamb is depicted, pointed out by the finger of the Forerunner. It was received as a type of grace, foreshowing to us through the law the true Lamb, Christ our God. While we embrace the ancient types and shadows that were handed down to the Church as symbols and prefigurations of the truth, we give preference to grace and truth, receiving it as the fulfillment of the law. So that what is perfect may be set before the eyes of all even in paintings, we decree that from now on the Lamb who takes away the sin of the world, Christ our God, be set up in images in his human form instead of the ancient lamb. Through it we may grasp the height of the humility of God the Word, and be led by the hand to remember his life in the flesh, his passion and saving death, and the redemption that came to the world through them.” Since we have these testimonies, beloved, together with the indisputable proof that comes from our own resources and from the truth itself, as has already been shown, I urge you: be watchful, stand firm in the faith, be courageous, be strong. Do not be frightened in anything by the adversaries, nor again

by those who have been tripped up and deceived [?]. This is a sign of destruction for them, but of salvation for us, and this comes from God, as it is written: “For to you [Reg. MS: us] it has been granted by God for the sake of Christ not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him, since you have the same struggle” that you saw in me, the sinner, and now hear of. Be of one mind and one soul, striving together for the faith of the Gospel. Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, so that I, the sinner, may rejoice when I hear news of you. Beware of Satan; beware of overconfidence; see that no one provokes God in any way. For the great dragon has many offspring and much experience. Where he finds no means of destroying us through our faith, he hurries to work the same evil in us through transgression, by means of the law of sin that wars against the law of our mind. He roars; like a lion he watches for a chance to snatch his prey; he tickles; he kindles fire; he longs to burn down the house of the soul. We have from God the defenses that bring him down: water for the head, a fountain of tears, supplications, prayers. Above all, let the fear of God pierce our flesh like iron and nail it down. Let envy find no lodging anywhere, nor strife, nor vainglory, nor any of the works of darkness. While the passions are still skirmishing at the outposts, let them be beaten back, so that they do not settle in, poison the soul and become hard to get rid of. Everyone who competes exercises self-control in all things. Run in such a way that you may win the prize. You who are last, yield to the first. For God is not a God of disorder but of peace. You who lead, love those who follow you with a godly love, and require submission and obedience not by authority but by virtue and goodness. Do not separate from one another, changing from one superior to another and being of use nowhere. Paul did not choose to take Mark the evangelist with him, as it is written, because Mark had not gone on with them but had earlier gone back home. How much more are we bound to be content? Let each of you, brothers, remain in the state in which he was called. Let us always cleanse ourselves, beloved, from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God. Hold fast to the traditions you were taught. Instruct one another. Always keep death in mind. Pray, therefore, I beg you, for everyone. Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse. You go about from place to place, destitute, afflicted, ill-treated, wandering in deserts and mountains, perhaps even creeping into holes in the earth. Boast that this is for Christ's sake, and that the world is not worthy of you. Bear up, my little children, little children, bear up a little longer, and the Lord will come, the giver of crowns, the one who pays the reward. We have been promised that we will be his fellow heirs, “if indeed we suffer with him, so that we may also be glorified with him.” Above all, pray

for me too, wretched as I am, that my heart may be strengthened to bear until death whatever is brought upon us; that Christ may not reject me because of my unworthiness; that I may always be delivered from the evil one in every way. Now I live, beloved, if you stand firm in the Lord. For what is our hope, or joy, or crown of boasting? Is it not you, both in the present age and in the age to come? Yes, for you are the consolation of love and my comfort. May the God of peace himself sanctify you completely, and may your spirit and soul and body be kept blameless. Our God is faithful, and he will do it, brothers. Greet one another with a holy kiss. I, the humble Theodore, send my greeting to all my members from the lips of my heart. The brothers with me greet you. Grace be with your spirit. Amen.

9. — To Joseph, brother and archbishop. [151]

I always long to write to your holiness, and the longer the distance of my banishment, the more I long to do so. For it brings me near to your honored face, and addressing you gives me relief, as it does now, when I am grieved at the betrayal of the truth by certain abbots. I want your holiness to know this: the old guard — I mean Joseph the joiner of adulterous marriages, the abbot of Photeinoudion, the abbot of Heraclea, the abbot of Medikion, the abbot of Mylianos, the abbot of Hypolichnion, the abbot of Goulaios, and, alas for my sins, even the abbot of Phlousouta [Reg. MS: Phloudoutinos], who was caught by his foolish simplicity — all these together, after resisting only a little, supposedly for the sake of economy, have turned aside after Satan. They were egged on by Joseph, who is used to bringing such things about, and they have taken communion with the impious once and again. For this they were kindly set free, and now by their own fall they are catching the unstable. And it seems that the bishop of Nicaea too lies fallen among the bishops. For they are recalling those in exile so that they may do the same. Unless the hand of God comes first to hold us up, we who are left will perish as well. Why is it, then, that the drama seems once again to have come round to us humble men, along with a few others? Arise, then, O man of God, as high priest of Christ the true Chief Shepherd, all the more since you surpass everyone in the headship of the priesthood, except the one who lies in transgression. Glorify God in your body and in your spirit. You will surely not be left alone on the island; perhaps you must be tested as in former times, so that here too you may be proclaimed a still more glorious victor. Alas, alas, brother, for what times we have been kept! Yet thanks be to the one who kept us for them, “and this is from God,” says the Apostle, “for to us it has been granted for the sake of Christ not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him.” The Lord did not overlook our lowliness in times past, and I trust that he will not neglect your honor now either. As then, so now too Christ will be magnified in your body, making his mercy overflow to display your vir-

tue. Stretch out to me too, then, a hand of intercession, holy father, so that I may be strengthened and saved from the bitter storm that is upon us. Stand and pray for God's mercy, that the tempest may be turned into a breeze of the Holy Spirit. May it be so! I greet the brothers most warmly and beg them to pray for my lowliness. Those with me fall at your feet.

10. — To his child Naucratius. [152] [?]

The news in your letter is grievous, my child. It touched my humble soul and truly pained it, and drew tears from my heart. It almost made the night on which I received the letter into my hands a sleepless one. This was because of all who have fallen, but especially because of the abbot of Phlousouta. For the others have now done what they did before, but he was known as one of those who seemed to be standing firm. While they were still standing, I used to wonder that they had taken up the present cause without confessing their earlier defeat over the adultery and the adulterous union, and I supposed that perhaps they had repented privately, among themselves. And I, humble as I am, rejoiced that they were walking upright. But it seems they built their house on rotten foundations, and in the hurricane of the heresy that broke upon them they have fallen a most grievous fall, once again calling the setting aside of the truth “economy.” These same men were a stumbling block to the Church of God before, and now again by what they have done they invite everyone to destruction. Indeed most people are ready to share in evil, seeking in times of pressure to find some pretext by which the struggle for true piety might be made free of affliction and hardship for them. These men have joined in communion with the denial of Christ, of the Mother of God, and of all the saints, for that is what denying the image of anyone at all amounts to. Alas for the calamity! Alas for the deception! Woe is me! Having begun well, how they have turned to the worse [?]! Woe is me! For how many will they be a cause of ruin — their equals and their superiors, laity, clergy and monks alike? But the ancient plague, the evil we nursed in our bosom, Joseph, once fittingly called the Joiner of Adulterers and now the Mocker of Christ, is himself the guide of the old guard. What shall we say to this? Shall we lose heart? Shall we fall? Shall we grow weary of confessing Christ and resisting? By no means, brothers, by no means! For if the righteous are afraid when the impious fall, still the fall of a neighbor brings the greatest security to the one who stands. So let us stand more firmly in the Lord, rather, I beg you, not frightened in anything by the adversaries. For is our confession made for the sake of those who have been tripped up? Were we made firm by leaning on their standing, so that we must be shaken down when they trip? God forbid! Christ is our foundation, not they nor anyone else. In him we stand; in him we boast, saying with Paul: “Who will separate us

from the love of God? Will affliction, or distress, or famine, or persecution, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us.” So whoever is not drawn up in the battle line will not fight for Christ, and cannot be a Christian. Were the contests of the martyrs, their prizes, their tortures, in vain? Were they not of the same flesh as we are? Did they not feel pain when they were subjected to so many punishments? Did they not despair even of life, as the Apostle says? But out of fear of eternal punishment and longing for heavenly rewards, they chose instead, like sensible men, the death of the flesh, and endured it in place of eternal death. They were not terrified; they were not dismayed. Picturing the things to come as though they were present, they went with joy to their tortures and counted their many sufferings as gifts. “For to us it has been granted for the sake of Christ not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him.” And again elsewhere: “For in a great ordeal of affliction their abundance of joy…” So all the saints rejoiced; so they exulted as they suffered for Christ. Let us too, beloved, taste the love of Christ. Let us walk in the footsteps of the saints. Let us break our attachments to this age. We have no lasting city here; the Jerusalem above is our homeland and our city. O men mighty in the Spirit, O children of God — for you are not children of me, the sinner — let us not give way, even if everyone else should turn back, which God forbid! As we were strengthened by God of old, let us now too fight on alone if we must. God is with us, and all the saints from the beginning of time. East and West are with us. Only a small part has broken itself off from the Church under heaven, and it did so out of fear, for the sake of temporal things, for the sake of the flesh — which, a little later, we will hand over to eternal fire together with the soul, if we do not hold fast to the truth. Suppose we are tested and scourged, and that many times; suppose in the end we even die. Is it not then joy unspeakable for us to attain the kingdom of heaven and to win immortal glory from it? Or, on the contrary, would we rather flee these things, and so be mocked to the end and bear endless shame? I beg you, my little children, whom I begot in the Lord, whom Christ has raised up through labors and toils, not only ascetic but also those of the contest: complete my joy by being of the same mind, having the same love, being united in soul and intent on one thing. Do nothing from selfish ambition or vainglory, but in humility count one another better than yourselves. These are apostolic precepts, even if it is I, the wretched one, who remind you of them. Pray for me too, I beg you, that strength, power and speech may be given me for your sake, unworthy though I am of divine grace, so that with one accord and in one spirit God may be glorified in our body and in our spirit. Send to the archbishop [?] the good Dionysius. Greet the abbot Peter,

the abbot Ignatius and the abbot Tithoes, and show them this letter. Further, prepare yourself along with the rest, and especially those named above. For since those near us have slipped, we [Reg. MS: you] will not be left alone by those very men, but will be slandered. May the Lord give you strength, might, mind, sight and understanding to do everything well, to the praise and glory of Christ, as my boast, and for your eternal renown. Those with me greet you both. Christ be with you.

11. — To the same. [154]

I received your letter, beloved child, and the brothers, sooner than I expected, for you did not wait until September as I had written. Nevertheless I welcomed your eagerness, your irrepressible love, the ardor of your longing, your love of God in everything — and I would add, your love for your father. You are my joy and comfort. In the Lord you are my support in all dangers and afflictions, and my crown of boasting, together with all your fellow contestants, and above all our brothers and children in Christ Jesus. So I rejoice and bless the God of my father that you are healthy in soul and body. God has so arranged it that you are free from bonds, so that you may anoint those in bonds and strengthen those who have been released, binding them together. This you are indeed doing by the grace of Christ, exhorting, admonishing and comforting each one. You are truly a steward of God. I beg you, then, not to grow weary of working at this very thing, for the glory of Christ, for the gaining of your salvation, and as a boast for me, who am lacking in every good. But [?], we did not run and are not running in vain, either in the past or now, nor do we labor in vain. For it is for Christ and because of Christ; for his sake suffering is a Pascha, and for his sake grief is joy. “If indeed we suffer with him,” he says, “so that we may also be glorified with him. For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us.” And rightly so. For the affliction here, whatever it may be, is shadowy and dreamlike, but the recompense there is endless life with eternal glory. So let us not be ashamed, my child, of our present witness, for it belongs to the Lord. Many out of love for Christ have longed to see this, but did not obtain it, while we have been counted worthy. What is it? To suffer for him, to be persecuted, taken captive, imprisoned, banished from place to place, perhaps even beaten; to become a spectacle to angels and to men. And if they have also cast out our name as evil, anathematizing it in private and in public along with the saints, is there not joy in that? Is there not cause to leap for joy? I know, my child, the Lord's beatitude. Rejoice in these things yourself as well, and delight in them with all the children. For you are the body of Christ, and members of it individually. And whether one member suffers

…one member [suffers], all the members suffer with it; or if one member is honoured, all the members rejoice with it. “Seek,” he says, “what is still lacking: spitting, blows, and finally the cross, the nails of Christ that are sweet to me.” Who would be counted worthy to be crucified with him, to be pierced with the lance with him, a slave with his Master, to mingle his blood, a man's, with the blood of the living God? With such a disposition the saints went forward, rejoicing as they were cut and glad as they were torn limb from limb. Our joy too has now arrived: we have tasted it in part. May we taste it fully, by the grace and love for mankind of Jesus Christ our Lord. For to grace be the victory in anything whatever, so that no one may boast of having anything of his own. So we draw down the mercy of God in Christ Jesus through humility and active trust. If then there is any encouragement in Christ, any consolation of love, any fellowship of faith, any affection and compassion, make my joy complete (to say, wretch that I am, with the Apostle) by being of the same mind, having the same love, united in soul, thinking one thing, doing nothing from rivalry or vainglory, working against one another and setting yourselves up against one another. For know that love of preeminence and contentiousness creep in even into the very contests for piety. But you, as ministers of God (for together with you I include those who are senior, who may also read this letter), give no offence in anything, so that your ministry may not be blamed. As for those who, you wrote to me, have come to repentance: we are, though unworthy, nonetheless physicians to the members of our body. So the penance that we gave to Orestes when he came here, through the voice of the brothers (for we did not judge it good to see him face to face, for many reasons), let the others have too: to have no share in the holy things, and in the other observances. You ask, until when? Until the clear sky of orthodoxy shines out. “What if,” he says, “death should come?” Let them receive communion. We believe the sin has been forgiven them. But since you have written that you are disputing this and that with one another, settle your questions and be at peace among yourselves. These are not to be received like those returning from heresy, since there too an observance of no small difference [is required]…

…[?] those banished from Egypt to Mesopotamia, reproaching them for having admitted them unguardedly. Or do you not know what the same Father says in another letter? “I do not recognise as a bishop, nor would I count among the bishops, one who has been promoted to the presidency by profane hands for the overthrow of the faith.” Such are those of the present time, who, not through ignorance but through love of rule, leap upon the thrones, having willingly abandoned the truth and taken the presidency of impiety in exchange. “If, humanly speaking, I fought with beasts at Ephesus,” says the Apostle, “what gain is it to me?” I too say: if, according to you, such people are to be received at once and without penance after their denial, that is, their communion with the fighters against Christ, why do I put myself in danger every day for nothing? Why should I not desert to the opponents, and then, through repentance, be ranked once more with the orthodox without penance? Do not be deceived: bad company corrupts good morals. Sober up in the Lord. What fellowship has light with darkness, that our affairs should [?] side by side with those of the fighters against Christ? For, he says, they themselves receive with joy and without penance those who come over to them from orthodoxy. Then [?] we ought also to crown those who have denied Christ, and to celebrate some of them as those people do. Brothers, I beg you, do not be children in your minds, but become mature through true knowledge. As for those outside our brotherhood, who am I to give rulings? But if someone should press me, since love, being the fulfilment of the law, also carries persuasion, I say the same as for our own; for they too are our people. A presbyter who either signed, or entered into communion out of fear because he could not bear the ill-treatment, is to be barred from communion. For having communicated against Christ, how could he communicate with Christ? The lifting of the suspension from priestly ministry belongs to synodal examination. One who after his defeat appears to have returned to the struggle is to withdraw from the place in which he sat before; for otherwise how will the denial he committed be made known both to himself and to others? I cannot permit it, especially if his return to the struggle did not take place in some notable act, as in the case of the [bishop] of Laodicea. Even to him I for my part would not advise celebrating the liturgy, but only receiving communion, because of the notable character [of his act]. So too with an ordinary monk, and so with a layman: exclusion from communion, together with the other fruits worthy of repentance, and waiting for the time of orthodoxy. However, since it is possible for the one imposing the penance to make it either lighter or heavier (I mean in regard to communion), as the time of the heresy is prolonged according to the unsearchable judgements of God's just wrath, it is possible to grant release in the Lord even before a synod, according as the person's fault is heavier or lighter, and again according to the repentance he shows. And as for sharing meals with them, both for our own people and for those outside, this is not to be forbidden,

but not so that they give blessings, until their release. This is how these matters have seemed to me, in the fear of God and in truth. But if anything better is offered by you or by others, I shall be taught. For I confess that, as one who sins much, I also admit to being ignorant of much. Greet your brothers and my children, [?], Peter, Ignatius and Tithoes [Codex Reg.: Tidoios], my beloved ones and fellow workers in the Lord. Greet my dear ones of the holy community. Greet the guardians of the mysteries, my own beloved heart. Greet her who labours in the Lord, from whom I have received in full and abound in good things. Greet all the brothers in Christ, even if they are lay people, among whom is Sergius the pious and holy. The ever-longed-for brothers who are with me greet you and the others. Remember my lowliness. Our Lord Jesus Christ be with you, brothers.

12. To Paschal, Pope of Rome.

[?] …a parable and a byword among all, to speak in the language of Scripture; yet perhaps the report [has not reached you] fully and in the form of a letter. Therefore we, the least, though we are perhaps the last member of the body of Christ, nevertheless, since our head is confined and those foremost in the brotherhood are scattered here and there, have managed somehow, by being near one another and by informing one another, to become one in spirit and in word, and we write these things, boldly though it be. Hear, apostolic head, shepherd of Christ's sheep appointed by God, keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven, rock of the faith on which the catholic Church is built. For you are Peter, adorning and governing the throne of Peter. Fierce wolves have burst into the fold of the Lord; the gates of Hades, as of old, have dashed against it. What is this? Christ is being persecuted together with his Mother and his servants, since an assault on the image is persecution of the prototype. Hence the deposition of the patriarchal head; exiles and banishments of bishops and priests, of monks and nuns; prisons and chains; tortures and, at last, deaths. O fearful report! The venerable icon of our Saviour God, at which even demons shudder, has been insulted and treated as nothing, not only in the imperial city but in every land and town. Altars have been destroyed, churches darkened, sacred things profaned; the blood of those who hold fast

to the Gospel has been shed and is still being shed. Persecutions and flight for those still left. Every pious mouth has fallen silent for fear of death; the hostile and blasphemous tongue has been loosed; all flesh has been shaken, wavering. “Woe is me,” he says, “for I have become like one who gathers stubble at harvest, and like gleanings at the vintage when there is no cluster.” All these things, blessed one, have come upon us. Who would not grieve within himself as he contemplates the sufferings of his neighbour? Who would not reckon them as preludes to the coming of Antichrist, differing from it as much as an image differs from its archetype, [?] he rages? Come then from the West, imitator of Christ: Arise, and do not cast us off for ever. To you Christ our God said: “And you, when once you have turned back, strengthen your brothers.” Behold the time and the place: help us, you who have been appointed by God for this. Stretch out your hand as far as you can. You have strength from God through being first of all, the rank in which you have been set. Terrify, we beg you, the heretical beasts with the pipe of your divine word. Good shepherd, lay down your life for the sheep, we implore you. Let the whole world under heaven hear that those who have dared these things, and who even anathematize our holy Fathers, are anathematized by you in synod. May this be acceptable to God, a joy to angels and saints, a support to those who are shaken, a seal for those who stand firm, a raising up for the fallen, a cause of exultation for the whole Church of the orthodox, and for your preeminence an eternal memorial, like those who led before you of old, who in similar times, moved by the Spirit, did what we sinners now ask, and are both remembered and called blessed. But we firmly believe that, moved by tender mercy, you will receive our humble letter, imitating Christ, who, though God of all, did not disdain to receive the letter from Abgar and to write back in reply.

13. To the same. [201]

To the all-[holy?] Father, chief luminary of the world, our [?], apostolic master, [?]: John, Theodosius, Athanasius and Theodore, the least presbyters and abbots of the monasteries of Kathara, of Pikridion, of Paulopetrion and of Studios.

The Dayspring from on high has visited you: Christ our God, who has set your blessedness in the West, like a lampstand shining with divine light, upon the first apostolic throne, to illuminate the Church under heaven. For we who were held in the darkness and shadow of death of the wicked heresy have perceived spiritual light; we have put away the cloud of despondency and looked up to good hopes, having learned through the brothers and fellow servants whom we sent what things, and how great, your holy preeminence has done and said: the heretical

envoys it treated as thieves, not even admitting them into its sacred presence, but justly sending them far away; while over our miseries, on hearing the letters and the account of those who were sent, it grieved and groaned in imitation of God, as over its own members. And truly we humble ones have recognised that a manifest successor of the chief of the apostles presides over the Roman Church. We are truly convinced that the Lord has not forsaken our Church, since by the providence of God it has had, from above and from the beginning, one help and one only in the crises that befall it: help from you. You then are truly the unmuddied and unadulterated fountain of orthodoxy from the beginning; you are the calm harbour of the whole Church, sheltered from every heretical storm; you are the city of refuge for salvation chosen by God. But since it is bold for us, wretched and unworthy as we are, to heap praises on your divinely named [holiness], long since called blessed by divine tongues, we must turn to the task at hand. The impious do not cease doing their usual things with all eagerness and frenzy, dragging and pulling everyone down into the pit of heresy, men who are afraid of death. For whoever does not yield must inevitably be subjected, together with his followers, to the wicked flame of the whips, so that little by little (most grievous of all) some slip away even from among those who have contended. But we, again, the humble and last among the members, on behalf of our own sacred head and of the eminent fatherhood and brotherhood now present, boldly make our appeal and entreaty that your holy and apostolic soul may be moved: first, as we believe you are already doing, not to cease from the prayer that inclines God, for the strengthening and preservation of all — yes, we beg your most sacred heart — and then, with God, to bring to completion what it has resolved and decreed under the Spirit's prompting, for the benefit of us humble ones and for the eternal blessedness of your own virtue.

14. To the Pope of Alexandria. [204]

To the all-holy Father of fathers, light of lights, my lord, most blessed master, [pope?] of Alexandria: Theodore, least presbyter and abbot of Studios.

It is a very great gift to my lowliness, and the fruit of the highest prayer, to be deemed worthy to converse by letter with your apostolic preeminence. This is so not only because of my utter insignificance, which is unequal even to writing to its equals, let alone to so great and divine a head, but also because of the passage across so great a distance, barred above all by the wall of the pagans. Yet by the good pleasure of the supremely good God it has been granted to me, for two reasons: first, so that I, the sinner, might fulfil the desire I have long had

by touching your sacred footsteps in spirit, for there was no other way for my heart's wish to be fulfilled; second, and more pressing, to make better known to your most divine preeminence, as one that suffers together with the members of the whole body of the Church, the terrible things that have befallen us here. These things, I think, have been heard even to the ends of the world, so notorious is the wickedness. Persecution has overtaken us, most blessed one, and the heaviest of persecutions. Of old, Ahab, seeking Elijah the prophet, is said to have set fire to every place, the burning revealing the wrath of the [?]. But now the one who is an Ahab in both rank and heart seeks out not only Elijah in painted form but also his Master Jesus Christ, our Lord and God, the Mother of God and every saint; he hunts them down, and when he finds them he wipes them out in great wrath from every city and land under his hand. Hence altars have been torn down and churches of the Lord made useless, both in houses and in the public churches, and in monasteries of men and of virgins, old ones and newly built. It is a pitiable sight: like men disfigured [?] into monsters, so are the Churches of God to behold, stripped of their proper adornment and left formless. Who ever heard or saw such a thing among the impieties of old? Perhaps the Arab who presses upon you shows respect and behaves more like a lover of Christ in this. But not our Tabeel. Spare, O Lord, and do not give your inheritance wholly over to reproach. And if he mocks, ridicules and disparages as abominations the figures on panels, those on sacred offerings, and the books that record them, treating as hateful to God the things that are dear to God and bring salvation to the world — oh, who would not shed a tear? Who would not let out a groan sent up from the depth of his heart? The roads of Zion mourn, because there are none who travel them piously. And indeed, all have turned aside, together they have become worthless: those who are thought to be bishops and priests, monks and lay people, every race and every age. Some have made complete shipwreck of the faith; others, even if not sunk in their thoughts, yet through communion with the heretics share half the danger, out of fear of bodily death. Yet there are some left who have not bowed the knee to Baal, as many as are numbered by the Lord. First of all, our foremost, our sacred head, equal in rank to your perfection; bishops and priests of the Lord, monks and nuns. Of these, some have experienced mockery and scourging, others bonds and prison, fed on meagre bread and water. Others have been confined in exile; others live in deserts, mountains, caves and holes in the earth; and some, scourged on the spot, have departed to the Lord as martyrs. There are also some who were sewn into sacks and thrown into the sea [?], as has become clear from those who saw them.

What more? Our holy Fathers are anathematized; the impious are proclaimed; children are brought up in the doctrines of impiety through the volume given to the teachers. There is nowhere in the inhabited world a refuge for the body; it is impossible to utter a single pious word; and the hunt is close at hand, so that a man guards himself even against his own wife. Informers and betrayers, hired by the ruler for this very purpose, [watch] wherever anyone still says something displeasing to Caesar, or does not communicate with the impiety, or has a book about icons that contains something said on the subject, or the icon itself; or takes in a fugitive, or ministers to those imprisoned for the Lord's sake. And if he is caught, he is at once seized, flogged till he bleeds, and exiled. Hence even masters cringe before their slaves for fear of being informed on. It befits us to say that at this time there is no ruler, nor prophet, nor leader, no place to offer firstfruits before the Lord and find mercy. That is why we unworthy ones have cried out these things to your holy soul, as from the mouth of all who hold fast to the truth, calling on it for help and sympathy. For we know that even if it cannot help us otherwise, by the aid of its prayers it will bring us great benefit in our most urgent needs, since it has God's favour. And so that you may know in part what sort of impious doctrines the godless hold, I have sent these too along with the letter, in quires; I, unlearned as I am, ventured to refute them at the urging of pious people. I ask that they be examined by your divine magnanimity and that whatever is lacking be set right, that I may receive pardon for my debts, and that I may be remembered in your prayers that incline God, as a useless child. The same letter was also sent to the patriarch of Antioch.

15. To the all-holy Father of fathers, light of lights, my lord, master, patriarch of Jerusalem: Theodore, least presbyter and abbot of Studios. [?]

“Who will tell Abraham that Sarah is nursing a child?” says the sacred word somewhere. And who will bring me, the unworthy one, the good news that my humble letter has reached the sacred hands of your apostolic and most blessed preeminence? Yet I believe it will happen. For it was not an unreasonable desire but a necessary cause that moved me, a sinner, to dare to send this letter, and to send with it as its bearer Dionysius, our most beloved brother, who is trustworthy and able to explain on his own whatever is missing from the letter. So, absent in body but present in spirit, I first humbly kiss your God-trodden footsteps, for this is a blessing and a sanctification to me. Then, as though permitted by you, I go to the venerable places. I embrace the divine ground where the divine feet have trodden, the life-giving tomb

in which the all-holy body of our God and Saviour Jesus Christ was laid; the place of the holy Skull, where the Lord of glory was crucified. I pass on elsewhere: I see holy Bethlehem as Eden; I venerate the divine manger, greater than the golden jar, for in it was laid not manna but the bread of life. And I see the holy mountain where the most divine Transfiguration took place; the Mount of Olives, from which the Lord of all ascended to heaven; holy Gethsemane, where the tomb of our all-venerable Lady, the Mother of God, lies; and this place and that, so as not to draw out my words at length. Oh, how even the mere remembrance of them gives a share in sanctification! Oh, how great and awe-inspiring are the holy things over which your blessed preeminence presides! You are first of the patriarchs, even if fifth in number. For where the Bishop of souls and High Priest of all was born, did all his divine works, suffered, was buried, rose, lived again and was taken up, there clearly lies the dignity that surpasses all. But on these matters I have dared to speak this much, with longing and trembling; now I shall turn to my other report. Persecution has overtaken us, most blessed one, and of all persecutions the most like those of the pagans. For when Satan perceived that the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ was at the doors, he kindled greater flames of heresy, preludes to the coming of Antichrist. What is this? The impiety stirred up long ago under Leo and Constantine, which raged for a long time and was broken by divine rebuke, has now been renewed by the present ruler, who shares both the name and the impiety [of his predecessor], and to such a degree as to put their fury in the shade. He persecutes Christ in his painted image, together with his Mother and his servants, and wherever he finds them he destroys and burns them. Hence altars have been torn down, sacred churches darkened, sacred vessels burned; there is no part of his empire left unpurged. And if anyone is found to have hidden an icon, or a book with something said about icons, he is at once seized, torn with whips, and made to suffer every other horror. Hence fear, trembling and bewilderment have come upon everyone, so that brother avoids greeting brother, and friend friend. A synod has ratified the most impious one of old and anathematized the orthodox one. The priests have become senseless and have not sought the Lord, but have endorsed what pleased Ahab. All have turned aside, together they have become worthless, except a very few. Who are they? Bishops and abbots, monks and nuns, and, by the grace of God, our supreme high priest himself. Of these some have been scourged, others banished, others imprisoned. And some have departed to the Lord on the spot from their punishments, winning the athlete's crown. And what of the blasphemy? The venerable and

…the awe-inspiring image of Christ is treated as the abomination of desolation and an idol of error, and so is every other image, whether of our Lady or of a saint. “Now at last,” they say, “the faith is pure and blameless”; “now at last,” they say, “the Lord has spoken peace to his people, and to his saints, and to those who turn their heart to him.” They talk as though peace had been taken away from the moment Christ said, “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you,” until now. They talk as though his Church had been defiled, the Church that the holy Paul proclaims has no spot or wrinkle or any such thing, but is holy and blameless. Some have made complete shipwreck of the faith. Others have not been drowned in their thoughts, but they still perish along with the heresy by sharing its communion. Even those who are orthodox in mind grow dizzy about the truth because the persecution goes on and on, like people with no experience of sailing whose sight grows dark among the great waves of the sea. Everything about us is pitiable and deserves lament. The psalmody handed down from of old, in which anything about images is sung, is set aside. The impious new doctrines are sung in its place and set out for all to see, and children are taught other things by their teachers. It is a most godless overturning of everything. To put it plainly, our sins have made us like Sodom and Gomorrah. The storm of heresy swells and rises higher every day, and no one can be found to wake Christ our God and have him rebuke this evil sea. But you, most blessed one, become one of the twelve apostles for us. Rouse the sleepless Eye that sleeps for a purpose, for we are utterly perishing. If there is any other remedy to help heal the sick, then hasten to it, skilled physician that you are. Yes, most holy one, we beg, we entreat, we implore. We are your members, for all the faithful are the body of Christ and individually members of it. Urge our other holy Fathers too to stretch out a hand of intercession, so that mercy may come to us from God through many people. That is why this letter is written, and why the letter-bearer is sent by the will of all, even though it is only we, the least, who stand in for the rest. So that your preeminence may learn in part what the doctrines of the godless are, I have sent along with the letter these writings in quires, which I, unlearned as I am, undertook to refute [?] at the urging of others. I beg that your divine wisdom examine them and set right what is lacking, and that you pardon my faults. I also ask that our fellow servant and brother be given help, both to deliver the letters we have written to other holy persons and, God willing, to make his journey back to us here. 16. To the Lavra of Saint Sabas. To my God-honored, beloved and spiritual father, the lord abbot of the renowned lavra of our all-blessed holy father Sa-

-bas, and to my holy fathers under him, from Theodore the least, priest and abbot of the Studites. [216] It is a great joy to me, unworthy as I am, and a robe of glory, that I have been found worthy to send my poor little letter to a holy place, to the tents of the saints, to your fatherhood whom I so long for. I could not come in person to walk in your footsteps and see the holy precinct, your sacred enclosure, which I, the lowly one, revere as a city of God. So the good God has been pleased to fulfil the desire of me, a sinner, through the visit of a letter. And so, as though present, I fall at your feet and embrace you with holy longing. I venerate the divine ground in which the chosen vessel of God is laid up: the light of monks and the lamp of the world, the one who drowned the spiritual Pharaoh and led the holy nation, the master of the holy land and founder of the divine monasteries. I greet as well the other venerable tombs that hold the sacred bodies of the saints, whose wealth of virtues shines like God-lit stars in the night of this life. I see the place where the pillar of fire appeared to the host of the virtues. I see the victorious wrestling against the invisible enemies and the drama of wonder-working, all of it adorned with the workings of the Spirit, each in its own season. Oh, how much my longing urges me to say, and how propriety restrains me from letting the letter run on without measure! Oh, how many tokens and memorials of good deeds are among you, able almost by the mere sight of them to spur the soul toward progress in virtue! But let my first word go only this far, even if it falls short of my desire. I shall pass on to another, one of mourning rather than joy, and it was for its sake that the first was set in motion. The wrath of God has overtaken us, most holy fathers, because lawlessness has multiplied and love has grown cold, as the Lord said. We suffer a persecution like those of the pagans, and it is very grievous. Our chief shepherd has been driven from the fold. Christ's sheep have been scattered. Savage wolves have broken in among the flock, and a wild boar has fed on it. What more [?]? Here once again the venerable image of our God and Savior Jesus Christ has been dishonored, and that of the Theotokos and of every saint whatsoever. For this reason the shepherds have become senseless. To speak with the prophet, it is not only that they have failed to seek the Lord, which would be a lesser impiety. They have gathered together, as the Jews did, against the Lord and against his Christ, rejecting his holy image and those of his Mother and his servants. For this reason holy altars have been destroyed, and churches of the Lord darkened in every city and region under this rule. Stripped of their proper adornment of divine beauty, they stand as a cause of mourning to all who see them. For this reason sacred vessels are being melted down, and divine vestments

are handed over to the fire, together with the figures on panels and any books in which something is said about images. For this reason the great mystery of the incarnation is laughed at. The likeness of Christ that saves the world has been called an abomination, and I shudder to say it. Or rather Christ himself has been called so, with his Mother and his servants, since image and prototype are one and the same in honor and in name. For this reason there are searches and inquisitions, man by man and house by house, with terrors and threats, so that no one, and no image at all, may be left uncaptured by the heresy. For this reason priests act lawlessly, and monks who are no monks turn on those who wear the same habit. Disciples turn against their abbots and carry off promotion as the prize of apostasy, and whoever has raged most against Christ is granted the most honors. For this reason scourges, chains, prisons, starvation, exiles and deaths fall on those who resist. To the impious the episcopate is not venerable, gray hair does not move them to pity, the practice of piety earns no respect, and nothing else that deserves to be spared is spared. There is one law, the will of Caesar, and one aim, that everyone be caught by it. The deserts hold those who have escaped; the rocks and caves hold those who have been saved. Oh, how we have become like a pelican of the wilderness! Oh, how we have been handed over to the teeth of the ungodly! I have left out the rest so as not to weary you. But groan for us, most compassionate ones, as members of one body; stretch out a hand of intercession, as lovers of the brethren. What we suffer is more barbarous than what you suffer there. We have already become like Sodom, and we have been made like Gomorrah. That is why we, the lowly, have cried out to your holiness, as if with one mouth for all the brethren who suffer with us. For we know that a righteous prayer has great power when it is at work. By its atonement may the slaughter of the heretical sword cease, as the Lord brings our Church too back to a peaceful orthodoxy. So that you too, venerable ones, may know in part what the impious doctrines of the godless are, I have sent along with the letter these writings in quires, which I, unlearned as I am, undertook to refute at the urging of pious people. I beg that your divine sagacity examine them and set right what is lacking, and that you pardon my faults. I ask too that you remember me in your prayers lifted up to God, and indeed that I be counted as the last member of all in the fullness of your holy
The same letter was also sent to the monastery of Saint Theodosius. 17. To my God-honored, beloved and spiritual father, the lord abbot of the great lavra of our all-blessed holy father

Chariton, and to my holy fathers under him, from Theodore the least, priest and abbot of the Studites. [227] Since the delivery of this letter comes beyond all hope, I cry out in wonder: How has this happened to me, that I, a worthless man, should be found worthy to write to you, my holy fathers? For see how this most grievous persecution has overtaken us because of our sins; surely the report of it has reached even you. I, the lowly one, kept considering and searching how, and through whom, I might lament to you saints the terrible things that have befallen us. My only purpose was to call your holy souls to sympathy and to help us through your prayers, since you know how to suffer with others, as the apostolic teaching says, if indeed we all are the body of Christ and individually members of it. While I was still thinking this over, the letter-bearer suddenly arrived from your region. He is my son in the spirit and utterly trustworthy. How could I, a sinner, not be astonished at such a windfall? How could I not give the Lord my God the thanks that are fitting? But before I tell of painful things, I, the lowly one, shall pay my debt of longing toward you. Hail, most blessed Fathers, dwellers in the holy land, the golden race, most proven in faith and tamers of the passions! Hail, renowned assembly of Christ, workers of the Lord's commandments, who imitate the godlike life of those who dwelt in paradise! Hail, chosen city of God, since the Lord is in your midst and is served by your taking up of good works! I wished to take in your divine enclosure with my own eyes [?] and to touch your sacred footsteps, to see the holy precinct, to venerate the divine ground, and to look closely at each place. I wished to see where God's saint Chariton, full of grace as his name says, struggled as a martyr and an ascetic at once. I wished to see where his sacred body is laid up, the true treasure of virtues, the citizen of the desert and lamp of the world, whose honored seed has not failed and will not fail until the end of the age. Would that I had seen these things and embraced the dust as though it were alive! Would that I had been led among the other tombs of the saints and made holy by the mere sight of them! But since I have sung of these things briefly, come, let me tell of things full of grief as well. “Another king arose,” the sacred Scripture says somewhere, “who did not know

Such then is our Pharaoh, most holy ones. He is not ignorant of Joseph; he denies the Master who bought him. For it is clear that whoever rejects his image rejects him. In the same way he rejected the Theotokos and every saint. Being a denier by nature, he could not bear to remove the head without removing all the members along with it, so that his own image alone might be displayed, as in the decree of Nebuchadnezzar. Hence the desolation of all the churches of God, as

every venerable image is wiped out everywhere. Hence the burning of sacred offerings that bear an image, and of books in which anything is said about it. Hence written pledges of impiety are demanded, and with much searching and inquiry people are made to share in the godless communion, so that no one at all may be left uncaptured. One of two things is required: either worship the golden image, or be thrown into the evil flame of tortures. And yet those who will not bend are few enough to count. Who are they? Our [?] holy patriarch, bishops and priests, monks and nuns. For the harlot's face was not ashamed to let the scourges loose even on these. How could I vividly set before you the afflictions, the prisons, the chains, the starvation, the exiles, the abductions, the deaths? To this day there are flights into the mountains and hidings in caves and holes in the ground. It is said that the prophet Obadiah, while he was still Ahab's steward and Jezebel was murdering, hid sons of the prophets, fifty in each of two caves, and fed them. Here, if anyone is caught having hidden even one person, he is in great danger. Indeed, even if [?] anyone is found fleeing the impious communion, or keeping an image, or a book containing anything about it, the same danger awaits him. The mouths of the pious inside the country are silent. The blasphemous tongue is let loose, and the great mystery of the incarnation is ridiculed. “Now at last,” it says, “the Lord has spoken peace to his people, and to his saints, and to those who turn their heart to him.” Yet it was he who at the beginning said to his own disciples, “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you.” “Now at last,” they say, “the abominations of Greek polytheism have been removed.” Yet the Apostle cried out from the beginning, “An idol is nothing in the world.” “Now at last,” they say, “the Church has been cleansed.” Yet long ago the same Apostle declared that it has no spot or wrinkle or any such thing, but is holy and blameless. “Now at last,” they say, “the light has dawned on Christians held fast in the darkness of ignorance.” Yet to these Christians Christ said, from above and from the beginning, “I have come as light into the world, so that everyone who believes in me may not remain in darkness.” Holy brothers, see the apostasy that must come first, as

by its atonement may the slaughter of the heretical sword cease [?], as the Lord brings our Church too back to a peaceful orthodoxy. So that you too, venerable ones, may know in part what the impious doctrines of the godless are, I have sent along with the letter these writings in quires, which I, unlearned as I am, undertook to refute at the urging of pious people. I beg that your divine sagacity examine them and set right what is lacking, and that you pardon my faults. I ask too that you remember me in your prayers lifted up to God, and indeed that I be counted as the last member of all in the fullness of your holy Church. The same letter was also sent to the monastery of Saint Euthymius. 18. To Nicephorus, the most holy patriarch. [215] I have often meant to write to the sacred head of your blessedness, but I held back. Partly I considered my own unworthiness (another manuscript reads “perceiving”), and partly I was unequal to the trials. Now, setting both aside and taking courage in the Trinity, wretch that I am, I say this. Hail, true trophy of victory for piety [?], who run the course of faith in a four-horse chariot of virtues! Hail, great sun of orthodoxy, whose confessing rays light up the world! Hail, champion of the truth, distinguished by the beauty of virtue like the God-bearers of old! You left the lofty throne for the sake of him who humbled himself to the point of death, even death on a cross. You left the services and comforts of the high priesthood, choosing rather to share ill-treatment as a confessor than to enjoy the passing pleasure of sin. Even while you were among those comforts you did not live by them, but put your members to death through the life that is in the Lord. Yet you bore the loss of a holy Mother and of honored brothers, stripped of everything at once. And I have not yet mentioned the reproaches you bore like Christ, the attacks from those in power, the mockeries, the hardships and what amounted to strangling. You were carried off with Christ by night, since he too was betrayed. You were confined and then moved elsewhere, and now you sit on some hill, martyr of Christ. But well done, for all things work together for your good. Lift up your eyes round about from the watchtower of the mind and see your children, or rather your sheep, O good shepherd. They are scattered in body but united in spirit, spread through almost your whole Church, one here and another there. Like stars, by the rays of their confession, they signal the light of orthodoxy to those fighting the night battle against heresy. Some have been offered to God through a martyr's consummation. Others are still contending, shrinking from nothing in the present troubles and strengthened by your prayers lifted up to God. This is your glory in the Church; this is your

distinguishing mark of witness. May the age to come receive it and glorify God in you, as the present age does [?]. Many praises are owed to you who contend for the image of Christ. But forgive me, inimitable one, for daring out of longing to say what I have said. I ask for your sacred prayer, that I may not fall from being your least child, I who because of my sins am the most worthless of all. 19. To nuns. [221] I, the lowly one, rejoice to hear a good report of your honorable selves, especially since you are the blood and spirit of the man of God, our common Father. I am still more delighted, and I glorify God, to learn that you have remained untainted by the communion of the heretics until now. Indeed, those who keep their bodies untouched must also be virgins in faith. For sharing in that communion is adultery too, most wise ones. May the Lord, who betrothed you to himself through your profession of virginity, keep you untouched by it to the end. That is my first word. But why do you ask for teaching from me, a sinner? By the grace of Christ you are taught by God. Both of you come from pious parents, both excel in knowledge, and both of you hold up the teaching of the commandments in your way of life. If you need anything from us, unlearned as we are, what you should seek is the fear of God. When it is present in the heart, it makes light shine and lessens the passions. From it come compunction, tears, hatred of the world and desire for heaven; indeed, what good thing does not come from it? This is the indwelling of God, and where God is, there is the fountain of good things: peace, joy, love. So I, the lowly one, beg you not to look to the examples of those around you. Above all, do not look to the way of life that most nuns put on for show, lukewarm, so to speak, and muddled. Look instead to the archetypal beauties whose Lives are in your hands, and carry off [?] their divine loves, just as a painter copies an image not from poor models but from beautiful ones distinguished by their antiquity. What did you learn from those women? The loosening of the bonds of attachment; flight from the sight of men as far as possible; a humbled mind; a shabby garment; eyes cast down; ears that flee useless talk; a mouth that speaks godly things; the bruising of the body. This is how they overcame the mind of the flesh. For the flesh desires against the spirit, as it is written, and the spirit against the flesh; these are opposed to each other, and the war between them admits no truce. Every day, I would even say every hour, we must arm ourselves manfully against the passions with God's help, and in a long struggle conquer the enemy who always thirsts for our destruction. His swords have utterly failed against those who keep watch

carefully. Still, no one who struggles can avoid ever being defeated or wounded, in word and thought and the like, in sins that do not lead to death. But one must quickly wrestle back and soar up again to the state one ought to be in. For who can discern his own faults? And who will boast of having a pure soul? [?] The one who lives in the Lord is indeed in affliction, since narrow and hard is the way that leads to life, just as the opposite way leads to the opposite end. But when the end of the contests comes, then, brides of Christ, you will know what your way of life has won for you. Good angels will carry you up with inexpressible joy, and you will enter the bridal chamber not made with hands, the heavenly bridechamber, and follow the Lord forever. There was more to say, but since I suspect I have gone beyond the proper length of a letter, I shall end my words here. In return, grant me, the sinner, your holy

20. To Macarius, abbot. [?] What are you doing, divine Father, humbling yourself when you are lofty in virtue, and exalting me in your honorable words when I am low in wickedness, besieged every day by countless passions? I am your servant and child, eager to be a disciple rather than able to teach. Yet the good man brings good things out of the good treasure of his heart, and that is what you are, both when one sees you and when one reads you. As for the man from Demetrias and the disciples who have gone off: know the tree by its fruits. Pray for their repentance, and for me, wretch that I am, pray for steadfastness against those who make war on me, both unseen and seen, so that I may be found worthy to follow behind all the present confessors of Christ. For everyone who resists is a confessor. As for the other two points, this is my view. A priest who has signed in favor of the impiety ought to repent and weep fervently that the impiety be forgiven him. But he must by no means celebrate the liturgy, even if he does not commemorate the impious one. He is to be barred from sacred ministry until the Lord looks down and grants the occasion for an orthodox synod, at which each will receive what he deserves by God's judgment. I also advise that, if he took part in the impious communion, he abstain from receiving the holy things for one or two years. For it is written: “You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons; you cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons.” The same holds for churches: “What agreement has the temple of God with idols?” So we must not enter the shrines of the heretics; the holy synod has commanded us so. The only exception I know of is when a church passes entirely into the possession of an orthodox person, so that it is no longer served by a heretic, for then one may enter.

…and the Orthodox man should celebrate the liturgy, since what went before does not prejudge the matter. This is what I, your humble servant, think, my Father, after reviewing the examples given by the divine Fathers. It would be for your perfection both to see what is better and to show it to my eyes. May you still be kept safe for me, in good health and contending for God, you who are renowned among the Fathers, and may you also pray for my unworthiness, partly out of love and partly because the commandment bids it.

21. — Theodore to the beloved brothers held for the Lord's sake in various prisons

How do things stand now? With joy and gladness, because we have been counted worthy to contend in the struggles of martyrdom for Christ; because we have been handed over to prisons and afflictions for the word of God; because we have been subjected to blows and insults for the sake of Christ, who was scourged and reviled for us and then crucified.
