Who would not [?]? Who would not give glory? The East is delighted, the West rejoices; every Church of the four-cornered creation exults. And why do I speak only of the world on earth? Heaven itself is filled with delight, because not only the chief of our hierarchs, but hierarchs and priests, abbots and disciples, and even nuns with their superiors, have chosen the arenas of martyrdom. I pass over those in deserts and mountains, in caves and holes of the earth, afflicted by exile, destitute, ill-treated because of the persecution for Christ. Rightly then, my beloved and longed-for brothers, my joy and crown, I rejoice and rejoice with you; and in the same way you also rejoice and rejoice with me. These are the words of blessed Paul, but they suit the present time, since all things were written for our instruction, and he implores us to become his imitators. First, this much is true to say: we are not handed over to afflictions and hardships as far as those who maltreat us choose and wish. If we were, the trial would be unbearable, as is the trial that the demons invisibly launch against us. Rather, we are handed over as far as Christ permits, who presides over the contest and contends with us. By the measure and weight of each one's strength, and in just judgment, he lets the contests loose upon us, either for the paying off of sins—even if we came of our own free will to [?]—or for the reward of victors' crowns for those who advance from glory to glory. For we are not tortured as Peter or Paul were with those of their rank, or George and Theodore with those of like renown, or Thecla and Febronia with those of like glory. Because they loved much, the sufferings of Christ were granted to them in proportionate abundance. But those whose love is small are given less to suffer, so that we ought to grieve and be distressed that we do not suffer much, and not

waver and grow weary in the moderate punishments we are receiving. And if we fall away—God forbid we should even think it—it will not be because of the trial God has decreed, but because of the weakness, faintheartedness and cowardice of the one who has gone soft. For God has given the strength to stand against the power of the evil one, wishing the contestant to be victorious; but such a man, through negligence, has thrown away the weapons of endurance and perished. A witness to this is the one who cries out: "God is faithful, who will not let you be tempted beyond what you are able, but with the temptation will also provide the way out, so that you may be able to bear it." Here is endurance, brothers; here are the crowns of faithfulness woven by God. Let us not, then, be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, nor fall short of Thaddaeus, the newly chosen martyr, and those who confessed with him and departed this life after him, whose names you know. With the blood of martyrs the Church of God has now been watered once again, since it is watered also by those who are still contending and are pressed in many ways by afflictions. He sheds blood who is shut up, isolated, hemmed in, snatched away from every face, lacking necessities, hungry, thirsty, never receiving a ray of the sun, dying daily, as Paul cries out, and being put to death all the day long, as David sings. But if we die with Christ, we shall also live with him; if we endure, we shall also reign with him. In former times grace chose whom it chose for the testimony of Christ. In generation after generation martyrs arise. "For it is necessary that scandals come," Christ said, so that the elect may shine like the sun and the tares be shown up for the night they are. May we, brothers, in this crooked and perverse generation, be as lights shining in the moonless night of heresy, since Christ has chosen us for his boast, for the glory of Orthodoxy. As those of old were to us, so may we be shown to those after us as a support and a pattern; and may we be found dancing on the day of Christ. And indeed we have a more manifest testimony than those who came shortly before us. For the dispute is not about the natures and wills in Christ and whatever else was disputed along with them, where the error lay in concepts and so offered no proof perceptible to the senses. Now, besides the concepts, what is disputed—or rather impiously assailed—is also before our eyes. For the adversaries not only say and perversely think that Christ is not to be depicted, nor the Mother of God, nor any of the saints, but they also destroy those already painted, teaching that the divine images are error and the ruin of souls. O impiety that has rivalled [?] the impiety of Jews and pagans! So in the matter under discussion the difference is nothing at all, unless it be [?] a difference of substance. The Jew or the pagan says to the Christian: "Deny Christ, deny Mary." So does the Iconoclast. For the

image of Christ, like that of the Mother of God, is called by the same name, "Christ" and "Mother of God." So the one who says to deny the image would in effect be demanding outright the denial of the one whose image it is. This argument is not mine, a man of no account. Hear what the God of all says to Moses: "Make cherubim." Yet what he commanded was to make an image of cherubim; for no one in his right mind would say that Moses produced the nature of the cherubim. And again: "Make a bronze serpent." Here too he commands him to make an image of a serpent. But this is the nature of prototype and derivative: what is derived, that is, what is depicted, is called by the name of the archetype, and when the one is abolished the other is abolished too, since they exist together. There was an angel, and therefore also an image of an angel; there was a serpent, and therefore also an image of a serpent; and likewise with anything else that exists. In one sense they are called images of those they represent; in another, because of the relation, they are named as the archetypes themselves and not as their images. So also the holy Apostle says: "Above it were the cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat," using the name of the prototypes for the images. Hear also Basil the Great: "Let Christ, who presides over the contests, also be painted on the panel." He did not say, "Let the image of Christ who presides over the contests be painted," but "Christ." Hear also Gregory of Nyssa: "Isaac lies before us," calling the image of Isaac "Isaac." Hear Chrysostom: "I saw an angel in an image." He did not say that he saw the image of an angel in an image, but an angel. For in the image the archetype is made manifest, just as the life-giving cross is in the figure of the cross; and since the one cannot be separated from the other in veneration, the image also bears the name of the prototype. For the figure of the cross is called a cross. So too with an emperor, with every man and with every form, it is true for us to say that the emperor's image is also called emperor, as the divine Basil says; and Peter's image is called Peter, and Paul's image Paul. Let me say something loftier still: man too is called god, as the image of God. Therefore, as Basil said, the image of Christ is also Christ. For he said—and I say it again—"Let be painted on the panel" not "the image of Christ" but "Christ." If the quarrelsome will not accept this, they first set aside the divine words, and then, as a consequence, they teach that Christ did not in fact become man, even if they do not say so. For if he is man, he is clearly depicted, since to be depicted is the first property of man; but if he is not depicted, he is not man but fleshless, and Christ has not yet come, as the Jews are deluded into thinking. That is why they also banish the Mother of God and every saint when depicted, as though she were not the Mother of God, nor they the servants of Christ. And the golden-mouthed one cries out: "Your deeds are more credible to me than your words." It follows, then, in truth, that the Iconoclasts Judaize; and the one who suffers at their

hands for Christ and on behalf of Christ, for the Mother of God and on behalf of the Mother of God, for every saint and on behalf of all the saints, is an incontestable martyr and confessor of Christ, as one who contends and resists. No argument will gainsay this. The Maccabees were martyrs because they refused to taste swine's flesh against the law. The Forerunner was a martyr for rebuking in the cause of truth; another for refusing to contribute an obol to the building of an idol's temple; and another for another commandment. Why need I say more? Is the one who contends for Christ in this case plainly not a martyr, as some wretched people say? He is a true martyr, lacking nothing of those who bore witness under pagans or Jews. "And the witness in heaven is faithful." For if the one who rejects the figure of the cross directs that rejection at Christ, much more does the one who denies the image of Christ send that denial up to Christ. So the one who bears witness in either case is a most true martyr, and still more so in the case of the image, for the one is a sign of Christ, the other his form. I beseech you, my holy brothers, sharers in a heavenly calling, first to remember me, the humble one—I mean, to pray that I may prove in deed that I in no way slacken under the invisible and visible attacks; and then to look to yourselves and to the contest now upon you. Do not let your thoughts inflame you through poverty of understanding at the course of events, which are governed by providence in depth and beyond the reach of the human mind; and do not suffer what you sing: "But as for me, my feet had almost slipped, my steps had nearly gone astray, for I was envious of the lawless," when you see this or that. Rather, listen to the Lord saying: "Wait for me until the day of my rising." And: "He who endures to the end will be saved."

22 [?]. — To the absent brothers [?]

A Christian should always be setting his affairs in order for death, and above all when he falls into trials that threaten death. Since this is our situation, because of the seething madness of the persecutors against us for the love of Christ, with the martyrdom of confessing him set before us, and since I do not know what may suddenly befall me, isolated as I am and shut up somewhere far from all of you, my brothers and Fathers, I thought it right to set this letter before you as a kind of last word, and through you before the whole brotherhood. For it is good to make one's dispositions often and live on, rather than, while expecting to live, be suddenly snatched away and left without a testament through lack of forethought. What, then, do I have to say now? I have often set out and recorded in writing what needed to be said, whether when gravely ill or when persecutions were impending, so there is no need to repeat what has already been said. First of all this, my brothers: that you

grant me pardon for whatever I have said or done unreasonably toward you in my leadership, in word or in deed. For who can understand his sins? And: we all stumble; and I most of all, the most useless of all men. Therefore I ask your prayers, first that my wretched soul may attain salvation, and then for the brothers who, on account of my sins, have broken away from our union in the Holy Spirit. Their just judgment before God is plain to all; nevertheless, since they are our children and members, we must suffer with them and still bear solemn witness to them. I mean brother Leontius, Maximus, Clement, and all the others who have split off on any vain pretext whatever. As for what they did against me, I said long ago and I say now: they are to be forgiven. But what concerns God, it is not for man to loose while they remain unrepentant; and they clearly do not appear to have repented, but have gone on to do this and that besides, as they well know. So I beseech you, either now or after my death, given the fear of trials, to send them word: "You see, brothers, the judgment is fearful and inescapable unless you appease God by a repentance worthy of the name; for as far as it concerns me, the sinner, you are forgiven." This is what still grieves me and stays before my mind; and I implore you to carry it through with all of them. Farewell in the Lord.

23. — To an abbot [232]

I have been slow to write to your fatherly holiness, hindered somehow by the guard that surrounds me, although I heard long ago of your struggle in prison and suffering for the Lord. But blessed be God, who has called your holiness to the confession of his Son Jesus Christ, our Lord and God. For to contend for the image of his bodily likeness is nothing other than to bear witness about him, since the image is one and the same with the one depicted in the hypostasis of the likeness. That Christ is depicted, even the stones have cried out. For he became like us in all things except sin, as it is written—"except sin," because he took flesh without seed and was born virginally of his all-holy mother, the Mother of God. Since, then, all of us are depicted, whoever is not depicted is not a man but some kind of abortion. And since every living thing that comes into the light is by nature depicted, Christ is clearly depicted too, even if the godless do not think so, denying thereby the mystery of the saving dispensation. For how could the Son of God be confessed to have become man like us—he who deigned to be called our brother—if he were not circumscribed just as we are? And how could he have been born according to the law of nature if he did not resemble his own mother? If, then, contrary to what

is written, he was not formed from her virginal blood, out of which he fashioned a temple for himself, but bore a heavenly body, as Marcellus the heretic thinks, and the impious men of old before him, then it follows that his mother is not truly his mother but falsely so called; nor is he like us, but of a different essence. Nor, indeed, has Adam been restored in him—for how could he be? Will what is of the earth rise again in a body of a different kind? For it has been shown that like is saved by like. Nor, consequently, has death been swallowed up; nor has the worship of the Law ceased; there is need of circumcision and of the…

Do you see, man of God, into what pit of impiety they have been driven and impaled through holding that Christ is not to be painted on a panel? The Iconoclasts, then, certainly Judaize. Hence they accept neither the Mother of God nor any of the saints: by denying their images, they show their loathing for those depicted. For the honour and dishonour of the image passes over to the prototype, as Basil the Great says. Loathe the figure of the cross, and whom do you loathe? Is it not the life-giving cross? So with the emperor, so with any man at all, and so also with Christ, his Mother and every saint. Christ is now denied, persecuted and set at naught. And blessed are you, Father, for contending and holding fast to Orthodoxy. But pray also for me, the wretched one, that I may follow [?] after your holiness and not be cast away because of my sins.

24. — To his son Ignatius [?] [237]

I have read what you wrote, beloved child, and I rejoice to hear your voice. But my affairs are not as you suppose, for they are stale and worthless—unless you mean that you profit from my words. Write, and receive replies; there is no grudging. I understand that you are living a cramped life in the present persecution, as are those who are in hiding like you. But let hope lighten it. Keep your affairs secure, together with the good Eusebius, whom I also greet. Communion received from the heretics is no ordinary [?] poison: it does not harm the body but blackens and darkens the soul. As for throwing it away secretly, it is not for me to say. But of those who do this out of fear, one may say: "Many of the rulers believed in him, but did not confess him because of the Pharisees, so that they would not be put out of the synagogue; for they loved the glory of men more than the glory of God." And if the prayers of the service are those of the Orthodox, what does that matter if they are said by heretics? For they do not think as the one who composed them, nor do they believe what the words themselves signify. The whole rite glorifies Christ as truly having become man; but they deny it, even if they say the words, because they hold that he is not to be depicted.

It is as if someone were to say, "I believe in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit," while thinking that the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are a single hypostasis with three names, which is the doctrine of the vain-minded Sabellius. What then? Shall we say that such a man believes in the Trinity? By no means, even if he says so. In the same way, here too he does not believe what he says, even if the rite is orthodox. Such a man [the manuscript reads: each of the two] speaks idly, or rather insults the liturgy by making sport of it, since sorcerers and enchanters also use divine hymns in their demonic rites. If no Orthodox minister can be found to baptize, it is better for the unbaptized person to be baptized by a monk, or, if there is none, by a layman, who says, "N. is baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit," than to depart this life unenlightened; and he has truly been baptized. For of necessity there is also a change of the law, as happened in the past and has been demonstrated.

25. — To Peter of Nicaea [242]

Knowing that you, my holy head, like me—a man worth nothing—to speak to you, I now speak for friendship's sake, not out of any need. It seems I also spoke earlier through another letter, though I do not know whether you received it. In both, then, I have one message: that you, my Father, may be well in body—you, the firm foundation of truth, for the grounding of many, for a seal of faith, for the praise of Christ, for the glory of the whole Church. For you are a conspicuous eye among the rest, known in East and West, possessing along with a holy life a great abundance of learning. Because of this you have become dear to emperors, beloved of rulers and praised by monks. And what need is there even to speak of your own Church? It calls you blessed and longs for you, for the very many great achievements you accomplished, as infants long for their mother's breasts, as nestlings for the one who feeds them, as lambs for the true shepherd. And how could it not? Your life-giving words still ring in their ears, and they see before their eyes the temples of God you restored. And I say nothing yet of the abundance of your almsgiving and your other holy works. Do not think I am flattering you out of friendship. For even if I did not witness these things myself, I heard of them from those who know. And if now an outcast, truly one-eyed in both his outer and his inner eyes, holds these things, do not grieve, blessed one, and do not be surprised. The apostles were in the upper room, while the god-killers held the famous temple. Such too is the state of the Iconoclasts and Jewish-minded men now. May the Lord turn them back, and may he keep you safe as you pray for me, your child. I have long wanted to write to your blessedness, and it was not possible for me, the humble one, for want of a letter-

[?]-bearer. But now that I have obtained God's good pleasure, I am satisfying my longing, which I have every reason to feel for you. This is not only because of our shared confession in the Lord, but also, in particular, because of your character, which sets you apart from most people: your gentleness, your simplicity, your graciousness, the sweetness of your conversation, your friendliness when we meet, and your kindness in everything. From these the character of your holy soul can be seen even though it is not visible, made beautiful by the variety of its virtues. But enough on this, since this is no time for praise. How do the present events look to you, blessed one? Are they not little short of Judaism, or even paganism? The Church has been stripped of its adornment and the holy churches of their appearance. The holy things have been handed over to fire. Christianity now wears a different face, if we should even call it Christianity and not Judaism. Now too it is fitting to say: "Lord, they have killed your prophets and torn down your altars." They have indeed killed, and they have indeed torn down. Is it not plainly tearing them down to scrape and gouge out their faces? Take away a man's face and he is no longer a man but some kind of miscarriage, if it can even live. "They have set your sanctuary on fire." This too is true, since they have burned every divine image engraved in every material. A blasphemous tongue has been opened, calling Christ an idol, and the Mother of God, and every saint. For the copy has the name of the archetype, since it also has its veneration. That is why we call every figure of the cross a cross, and when we venerate it we embrace the life-giving cross. In my lowliness I have poured out these laments, not as though your all-wise perfection did not know how ruinous this error is (may I not be so foolish!), but to console the crushing grief of my own heart by telling these things, since speaking of them somehow naturally eases hidden pain. At the same time I wanted to urge your heart to approach God more fervently, so that he will swiftly rebuke this wicked heresy for the salvation of his people. Pray for me too, your least child, my most holy Father.

27. To his son Timothy. [244]

Your letters are like your soul, my beloved child: bold, cheerful, eager, God-loving, martyr-loving. Words are indeed images of the soul, and each person brings out his words from the abundance of his heart. So when we heard your words we too were strengthened, made more courageous, and spurred on to the contest. Brother Adrian amazed me still more when he told me of your courage, your steadfastness and your boldness of speech, and also your skill in arguing with those who provoke you. Where did you get these things? Was it not from God, with your good resolve leading the way and God's protection? Through these you endured what came before, and you stand firm in the hope of the glory of God, preparing yourself even for

death. Rejoice and be glad! With God you will be able to bear everything, once you have put on the victor's crown. But pray that I too, brother, may follow you and anyone else like you. By the grace of Christ we are equal to it. For as the stadium is splendid and in full view, so the martyrs are very many. Do not imagine that the present events are anything other than a denial of Christ on the part of the persecutors and a witness to Christ on the part of those who endure the contest. This is obvious. For just as the life-giving cross is both confessed and denied in the image of the cross, so exactly the same holds for the image of Christ. The world has been blinded, and in denying Christ it makes a game of its outrage, because of the patience of the one it outrages. And what wonder is it if he endures it, seeking the conversion of those who rage like drunkards? Did the soldiers not put a crown of thorns on his head? Did they not also throw a purple robe around him, saying, "Hail, King of the Jews," and striking him? Yet he bore it all, being laughed at and mocked, and everything else he suffered on the cross. He is suffering the same things now through his image and in his image, since the archetype shines out in the image, as the saints have said. But may mercy come swiftly to his Church and strengthen those who confess him. I hear that you are keeping a long fast. I rejoice at it, but I advise you to eat every day after vespers. For this is the royal road, and this is praiseworthy self-control in the

28. To Basil, abbot. [?]

When I learned everything your holiness suffered for the Lord's sake together with your holy flock, I gave great glory to our good God. For you too have risen as a light in the world along with other lamps in the present night-battle against the heresy: a chosen vessel, a pillar and foundation of the truth. How wonderful the two of you are! How dear to Christ, having endured beatings for him, arrests and prisons, and that up to the present! But why is it that before your trial you came to me in my lowliness, as you have told me, and did not get to meet me? Well, that was natural. Since, as you supposed, it was not [?], for I am pitiable and obscure, what harm did you come to? Besides, you have now joined yourself to us through your letter. We already see each other in spirit, and we have come together in spirit, having become one soul in the Lord: I in my lowliness in you saints, and you in me, since Christ is in the midst of us both, as he faithfully promised. What remains, then? That, as we began in our witness for Christ, so we may finish the contest set before us, shrinking from nothing: not beatings again, not chains, not the rack, not fire, not the sword, not water, nor

the knife. This is what the word of God counsels us; this is what the Apostle cries out; this is how all the martyrs were made perfect. We are not less noble than they. Even if I am wretched, we too were born of God, and we have the same mother of adoption. They won their contests: shall we disgrace ourselves? Women and girls were crowned: shall we love our flesh? Old men and infants overcame tyrants and kings: shall we grow faint? Certainly not! Let us give our flesh to those who love flesh; the soul cannot be seized. Let us not fear those who kill the body, but him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna. Now is the time for exultation and delight. For if we suffer with him, we shall also be glorified with him. Let the devil lament, and his servants too; that is what they suffer at the fearless resistance of those who bear witness to God. You say that you have never seen an emperor or stood before rulers, and that this makes you somewhat afraid. Not at all! Father, you have put on Christ: despise them both. Let the emperor cower before you, as the demons do. Open your mouth when you stand before him, for words will be given you; Christ has promised it. Refute him if he talks nonsense. Did not Elijah refute Ahab? Did not John refute Herod? Did not others refute others? I will not lengthen my letter by naming them. The God of then is the God of now. As he loved them, so he loves us, and we are disciples of the apostles, martyrs, prophets, Fathers and saints. Let the fruit resemble the tree. If we do not walk in this way, we are perverse and not disciples, nor sons, nor fruit, but belong to the opposing party, I mean the lovers of the world and the servile. May we flee from imitating them and attain to God, contending with perfect resolve in Christ Jesus our Lord, who said: "Take courage; I have overcome the world."

29. To Megalo and Maria, nuns. [?]

Your letter is precious, and your way of addressing me is wise. But the news: what shall I call it, painful or joyful? My Father has departed: the confessor of Christ, the second Job, the ornament of monks, the craftsman of love, the man loved by all, the man of God, the eye of many tears, the mind that loved learning, enriched with divine knowledge, great in humility and abundant in understanding, distinguished before he took the habit and still more eminent after his monastic profession. He was bound by love of God and therefore hated the world. He gave all his great wealth to Christ as a dowry, then parted from his wife, his family, his friends and acquaintances. He left behind earthly rank, house, city and homeland, and did so in the prime of life, with a handsome face, tall stature, bodily strength, and skill in both kinds of conduct, the spiritual and the visible. Whoever said more than this would still fall

short of the man's virtue. He has gone; he has ascended to the Lord. Where and how? He was taken [?] (sic) from his flock because of the grievous disease, imprisoned in the city for two years and more, then exiled to an island, and there he finished his course of confession for Christ. So his passing is not painful to me but a cause of great joy. He has not died but has passed over to eternal life. Earth has not covered him; heaven has received him. The choir of confessors has welcomed him, the fellowship of ascetics, where the true light is and the blessed places of rest, in return for the toils and labours he chose in the flesh, both as an ascetic and as a confessor. For me it is now a festival, a feast, a delight, and indeed for all the orthodox, who have sent on to God a protector who now runs alongside the martyrs who went before. Let the Church exult that it still gains pillars. Let the holy company rejoice that lights are again rising in the world, sending signals to those in the darkness of the heresy. O Father, Father, how fair your course! How holy your memory! How blessed your remembrance! You are all radiant, all gracious. Who saw you and did not love you? Who met you and was not sweetened? Your company was longed for; your virtue was plain to see. What remains? Remember your flock, and me your son, though I am the least and cast off. You know your longing for me, as I know mine for you. Help [variant: Cry out] for the whole Church before the Lord. Pray for wretched me too, that I may come to you soon, in the same way that you were made perfect. These are my words to our common Father. As for you, I beg you not to betray the faith, and to live holily as women who belong to him, each in her own way: the one as his wife, the other as his wife's sister. Then you will enjoy eternal glory with him.

30. To Symeon, monk. [?]

I received your holiness's letter, read it, and learned everything that happened to you and to our holy Fathers with you, whose names are in the book of life: the holy flight of you all, your banishment to foreign parts, trying and painful, as you were led off here and there and held under guard by the godless. I, in my lowliness, groaned at seeing what trials the times have brought upon the Churches of God. At the same time I called blessed the contests of those persecuted for Christ's sake, and then you as well, who have become our messenger of everything that took place, and did not hesitate to set your hand to writing to me, who am worth nothing, and to trace out the whole story of the ill-treatment. For this may the Lord bless you,

strengthen you still further, and confirm you in your unyielding stand of witness to Christ. For I learned that when you encountered John, the ringleader of impiety, after you had taken your stand, you did not shrink back or come off worse in the debate. You stood firmly against him, overcame him and boldly silenced him with the word of truth given to you by the working of the Holy Spirit. For those who have been deceived have no power of argument, since they have no light either, no proof of the truth, nothing upright or holy, walking as they do in darkness with a senseless heart and a foolish wisdom, or rather, to tell the truth, with unwisdom, ignorance and blindness. They have one thing only, first and last: the power of darkness. This is their argument, their definition, their faith, their doctrine and their weapon. "By their works you will know them," said the Lord. For what impious and Jewish deed have they not done? They have insulted Christ, the Mother of God and the saints. For when the bodily likenesses are dishonoured, the insult passes up to the prototypes themselves. That is why the iconoclasts might reasonably be called Antichrists, since the Theologian and evangelist says: "And now many Antichrists." These words are slight for one of your understanding, but they are tokens of the love God has given us in one mind and one soul. But pray for me, good [?], that I may contend as you do. And please let me know again how you are, and how things stand and will stand with your holy community.

31. To Joseph, his brother and archbishop. [262]

[?] As far as letters go, I have heard nothing about your health. But alas for my sins that it should have turned out so! The brothers told me that these letters were lost along with others, and that this was the work of the devil. But glory to God, who hid them from those in power, for many would have been in danger. And the iambic verses you did well to compose against the iconoclasts were lost with them too. Surely you would not have sent them without making a copy and taking notes? These things grieved us, naturally. But I, the lowly one, greet your holiness once more, longing for your honoured face. Whose face would I long for before yours? And would I not long for it always? This is not so much because we are kin by nature as because of our fellowship, which does not spring up from the ground but is worked from heaven, almost from the starting line until now, as everyone knows. Our parents shaped us so, shall I say, both in body and in spirit? May we remain the same in what lies ahead. May I not be separated from your virtue by the multitude of my sins, but may we be held together by God's love for mankind and the intercession of those who brought us into the light. Such is my prayer. As for the rest, what things are happening in the Church of God, and how many, deserving groans and laments, you have surely already

made his stand, been taken away and imprisoned, and then exiled; and so he completed his martyrdom. The Lord therefore did not overlook his labours under obedience, of which you know how many there were. It is true that, because of my sins, he was caught up among the Moechians, sparing his body but not sharing their mind, as events showed. That is why God tore him away from their faction and he turned the victory the other way, as did the abbot of Medikion too, and also the bishop of Nicaea, as I was assured by their own letters. But why do I speak of this one and that one? I am convinced that every one of those standing firm is of the same mind. Indeed our true patriarch himself confesses the truth, as I learned from the mouth of someone who heard it from him and praised the stand he made at that time. I have said these things both to honour the departed as is fitting and to inform your holiness of what you ought to know. But you know about Leontius, that evil in our own bosom, once one of us: just as he was carried off with the Moechians before, so now he is a champion of the iconoclasts. That is why he has taken over the Stoudios property and unlawfully rules Sakkoudion. From the unclean nothing clean: as the father is according to the flesh, so is his offspring. May God turn him back through your holy prayers, and establish me, the sinner, in his fear. I greet those who have been found worthy to serve your honour. The brother with me bows before you as your servant.

32. To his son Thaleleus. [?]

You did well to write to me, beloved child, for in this you showed your faith and love. But why do you sing my praises, when I have no share in them at all? Do you not know that I am a sinner and unskilled in speech? But love is a great thief, attaching to those who deserve no honour what they do not have, at the hands of those who love them. So stop praising me and pray instead, child, that I may be established in the Lord and saved in every way from the Evil One. May you bear your bodily illness with thanksgiving to God, and do not be distressed at the way it came. The Lord knows how to arrange what is good for each person, though I do not know where it came to you from. Treat the blasphemy with contempt and it will go away all the sooner; if you are afraid of it, it comes all the more. May you be delivered from it by God's strength. Even if the persecutors wear you down greatly, the prize is in heaven. If then we suffer with him, it is so that we may also be glorified with him. For this is not a time for comfort but for martyrdom.

Now the question about the priest who appears to be orthodox but eats with the bishop, as you described. If he stops such table-fellowship, and accepts as a penance exclusion from celebrating the liturgy for a time, and no longer falls into the same slip, he can be restored to offering the liturgy to God. But if he is indifferent about it, God forbid! "A man's own wealth is the ransom of his life": that is, by paying it he may escape both communion with heretics and any other sinful act. But he must not make an exchange in which he gives up the good and takes the worse, like giving up light and receiving darkness. Even if someone offered all the money in the world, if he were in communion with the heresy he would not be made a friend of God, but an enemy. And why do I speak of communion? Even if he only joins the heretics in food and drink and friendship, he is guilty. This is the judgment of Chrysostom, and indeed of every saint. And how can it be involuntary, and not the deliberate act of one who appears to be orthodox yet still communes with the heresy? It is involuntary when someone forcibly prises open the mouth of an orthodox believer and pours the heretical communion into it. The heretics of old did this, and, as I have learned, the present fighters against Christ do it too. But to partake of one's own accord is voluntary. And if it is done out of fear, which is the point in question, even then he will have no defence. "Do not fear those who kill the body, but God," who sends both body and soul together into the Gehenna of eternal fire. Do we hear this? Truly the whole world is not worth as much as one soul that keeps itself free from heretical communion and every evil. But those who share in both are worth no more than grass, wood and straw. The testing fire of judgment will burn these up, but it will keep those who did them burning forever without being consumed.

33. Against those who say that Christ cannot be circumscribed. [288]

Whoever says that Christ cannot be circumscribed in bodily form must surely have based his objection on some natural chain of reasoning and logical proof, to confirm the truth and make it clear to the uninitiated. So let him come forward and teach us how the matter stands by nature, and what makes Christ impossible to depict. Is it that he was not formed in our shape? That his body was not framed with bones? That his pupils were not set with eyelids and eyebrows? That he was not equipped with ears and their spiral passages? That he did not have nostrils fitted to perceive smells? That he did not have youthful cheeks? That he did not speak, eat and drink with mouth and tongue, lips and teeth? That he was not formed with shoulders, arms and hands attached? That chest and back, shins and feet did not grow on him? That he did not pass through time, advancing and growing in stature? That the movement of walking, up, down, in, out, right, left and around, was not seen in him? That with toils and

[?] and the other blameless passions he did not live? That his head did not grow hair and his whole body was not covered with clothes? But if he was admittedly seen in all these things, which together make up a true man, and whose portrayal in bodily form is a truthful drawing, and without which no composite body can even exist, since such a body exists in touch and colour, then what utter blindness and godless quarrelling it is to call Christ undepictable, when he appeared consubstantial with us and like us in every respect! And if the ability to be depicted is gone, how will all the corresponding properties not go with it? For a property, says the Theologian, is unchangeable; or how could a property remain a property if it changed and shifted? Let the opponent tell us.

34. To his son Naucratius. [?]

What could delight me more than for me, the sinner, to hear that you, my beloved son, together with seven other brothers of yours, whose names are in the book of life, were flogged for Christ our good God? Glory to him who called you to confess his truth! Glory to him who made your honoured souls firm to face danger ahead of the others, so that you did not cower or retreat before the face of the avenging fiend, but confessed your good confession, and for its sake gave your backs to the whips along with Christ. You have been added to the Church of God as another choir of confession. You have increased the renown of the brotherhood in Christ. You are truly blessed, my beloved ones, thrice blessed! Blessed too are the wombs that brought you into the light. And if I may say something about myself, I too am blessed, though I am unworthy of blessing and wretched, because I hear such things, the father of children who are sons of God and heirs of Christ. What is this joy? Is it not more delightful than any joy? What is this glory? Is it not more wonderful than that of those who wear diadems, to bear the marks of Christ, his saving sufferings, as crowns? So heaven has praised your deeds, and earth has heard of them. Our own affairs are small and sinful, but they are as brother Adrian reported, for he has surely arrived safely. If anything needs to be added, we will tell you now. After the beating they shut the two of us in an upper room. They blocked up the door and took away the ladder, with guards all around, so that no one might touch the room or come near it. Indeed, the guards meet everyone who enters the fortress and do not let him turn aside anywhere except to his own house until he leaves again. There is a strict order that we be given nothing but water and wood. So they simply put us away as if in a tomb, even to the point of killing us. But God, in the mercy of his love for mankind, provided for us, through the supplies we had brought in beforehand and also through [?], and what was permitted has been handed to us through the opening of the little window

[?] …feeds us, climbing up by a ladder that is set in place at the appointed hour. We do not dare to say what Daniel said when he received his meal from Habakkuk: 'For God has remembered me.' Yet he has remembered us sinners too; he has mercy on us, cares for us and shelters us. So as long as we can be fed from what is inside, or somehow, when one of the porters secretly passes in the weekly ration from his own house as well, he feeds us, and we glorify God. But if the necessities run out, by God's dispensation, we too will leave life along with them, and we rejoice in this; this too comes from God's great bounty. And who am I, wretched as I am, to have been seized in this way for his name's sake, and for what follows, if he so commands, to be deemed worthy of greater glory together with my brother, unworthy of honour though I am? I beseech you therefore, brothers, strive together with me in your prayers to God, that I may be delivered in every way and at all times from the Evil One. He began in us the work of confessing him through his tender mercies, not because of any works of mine, for I have done nothing good on earth, but the contrary. May he also bring it to completion in us both. We lowly ones also do not cease to ask this with tears for you who suffer the same things. We greet in the Lord not only the eight, the Lord's chosen, but also the [?] Peter, the good Letoius [?], and anyone else.

35. To his son Epiphanius. [?]

Here, my beloved child: you were eager to set out for the West when I told you to take these letters. I have sent two letters, one to the apostolic lord and one to the lord Methodius. By God's good pleasure, those who went with brother Dionysius arrived safely there and brought back good hopes, and in reply to these I thought it well to write again. I wrote not as from myself alone but, as before, from both of the abbots whom the letter names, except the abbot of Eukairia, for he, as I have learned, has fallen, as my sins deserved. At that time we wrote with their knowledge and common consent, through a secret message and after the letter had been read to them, as the letter that went out made clear. Now, although I have not been able to do this for safety's sake, this letter too is sent, since both are already of one mind. Perhaps they may also come to know of it afterwards. Go then, good Epiphanius; appear [?] to the West as a faithful messenger, prudent and long known. Deliver the letter, and, in keeping with what was set out under divine inspiration in the holy apostolic letter, by way of suggestion and at the word of the sacred Methodius and of the holy bishop of Monemvasia, join in the embassy yourself and plead that these things be brought to completion by the good pleasure of God, who is able both to keep you safe and to present you to the sacred and blessed

[?] head. Do not be afraid; your reward is great, and great is the contest. Christ is with you. Greet all the saints, especially those best known to us, and above all my holy Father the archimandrite. Greet also my master the Chartophylax, whose love is set in my lowly [?]

36. [?] To his son Naucratius.

I rejoice over you, my brother Naucratius, because you are called a son of joy, which means suffering for Christ. What could be more delightful than this? What more glorious? You were scourged, then, in imitation of Christ; you were taken from prison to prison and handed over into the hands of the impious John, at which I, lowly as I am, [?] was in anguish. But when he attacked you, you were not overturned; on the contrary, you refuted the vain-minded man and sent him away. At this I, wretched as I am, was very glad and took heart. May you have help from the Lord for what follows, too, against whatever may happen.

You said that in the debate he put forward statements aimed at overthrowing the holy icons, namely those of Asterius, Epiphanius and Theodotus. So I thought it necessary, for the instruction of us both, to set out here the statements of those men themselves, together with their refutation, made with God's help by us unlearned ones, even though this goes beyond the style of a letter. The statement of Asterius (1), then, runs word for word as follows: 'Do not depict Christ. The one humiliation of the incarnation, which he willingly accepted for our sake, is enough for him. Instead, carry the bodiless Word about spiritually in your soul.'

Let the writer be asked, then. Having forbidden Christ to be depicted, he says that the one humiliation of the incarnation is enough for him, as though Christ shrank from a second manifestation of his humiliation as inglorious, having once chosen the first. But how can it be voluntary if it is inglorious? What is voluntary is glorious; it does not have the ingloriousness of what is involuntary. And if that is not his point, but rather that a picture showing by likeness the same thing as the original is a repetition, how will he not also reject its being recorded through hearing, if being displayed in triumph through sight offends him as a repetition? Each accompanies the other and is of equal force, as the divine mouth, Basil the Great, declared. By the same reasoning it will also be reckoned that a cross, once depicted, is the repetition of another cross, and likewise with the Gospel. And since both are always being written and drawn, there would be countless crosses, and Gospels too, not one of each. But if the cross is one and not a second, even if it is drawn ten thousand times (2), and the Gospel is one and not a second,

(1) Asterius is anathematized by the most holy Sophronius in his synodical letters, and by another Father is ranked with Apollinarius and Eutyches. Scien-

even if it is written countless times, then Christ too is one and not two, even if he is depicted in the same way. For he is depicted just as he is read. And the ear will not be filled with hearing, nor the eye with seeing, that God has become man; that the eternal one was seen as a baby; that he who feeds all things is fed with milk; that the uncontainable is held in arms; that he who is beyond God is called a man; that the abyss of wisdom is baptized; that he who is beyond being does things befitting both God and man; that the Lord of glory is crucified; that he who gives life to all things is buried and rises again; and that he whom nothing can contain is taken up in human fashion. Let him stop forbidding this manifestation, so saving for the world, by both means, treating the glory of the Lord as disgrace and making out the voluntary humiliation to be involuntary. And let him stop opposing the great Basil, whose voice is the voice of God, and who somewhere gives this command: 'Let Christ, who presides over the contests, also be painted on the panel.'

Along with this denial, let the affirmation that follows be thrown out of the divine choir too, since it is just as absurd. For what does he say? 'Instead, carry the bodiless Word about spiritually in your soul.' What irrationality! Where has any divine mouth called the Word bodiless after he became flesh? The holy Apostle did say that Christ is no longer flesh, but he did not say that the Word is bodiless. He says: 'From now on we know no one according to the flesh; even though we once knew Christ according to the flesh, we know him so no longer.' Gregory the Theologian, interpreting this, said it refers to the passions of the flesh, which are ours too, though without sin; and elsewhere he says: 'No longer flesh, yet not bodiless.' Whoever calls the Word bodiless is fighting not only these two but all the God-bearing Fathers. So it has been shown that by the logic of nature one absurdity follows from another. With the falsehood overthrown, let the truth be laid down in its place. How? Depict Christ where it is fitting, as one who has him dwelling in your heart, so that, read in a book and seen in a picture, and so known doubly through the two senses, he may enlighten your mind, since you learn to see with your eyes what you were taught by word. And when he is heard and seen in this way, it cannot be that God is not glorified and that a devout person is not moved to compunction. What could be more saving than this, or more acceptable to God? This, then, is how we nobodies understand the truth, even if some of the holy Fathers before us took the problem now refuted differently.

Now that this man's statement has been dealt with, what does Epiphanius (3) say? 'Let your piety consider whether it is fitting

for us to have God painted in colours.' Look at the liar! He did not say 'Christ', a name by which the circumscribed is signified together with the uncircumscribed, for in this way both natures are indicated. He said 'to have God painted', stripping the Word of his humanity in the Manichaean way and putting forward God naked, so as to shock the hearer with the absurdity of the proposition. In the same way it would be out of place to call God visible, since the divine oracles say: 'No one has ever seen God.' And yet the only-begotten Son, who is God and was seen, has made him known. Clearly, then, no one has seen God naked of humanity. But since the Only-begotten is not naked after the incarnation, for this reason he is also visible. And the holy Apostle proclaimed: 'God was manifested in the flesh, vindicated in the Spirit, seen by angels, preached among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory.' So the words 'in the flesh' must be understood as applying in common to every statement. The first phrase is a kind of link connecting not only the statements that follow but all the properties of the embodiment. As God was manifested in the flesh, and so in each of the things just mentioned (for he could not have been seen or taken up unless 'in the flesh' is understood), so clearly he is also suckled in the flesh, grows in stature, walks on his feet, sweats in agony, speaks with his tongue, and everything else in the same series. If this is so, then since circumscription is also one of the properties of the body, it is clear that God is also circumscribed in the flesh, whether in colours or in some other way. Of the two, each necessarily follows: if he has been seen in the flesh, he is also circumscribed in the flesh, since each corresponds to the other and each implies the other. If then the second were not true, neither would the first be. But the first is true; therefore so is the second. So both by the divine oracles and by ordinary reasoning it is foolish not to confess that God is depicted in the flesh, if he has been seen in the flesh.

Elsewhere the fine fellow says: 'I have heard that some even profess to paint the incomprehensible Son of God. [?] even to hear.' What person with any sense would not laugh at this vain-minded man? Has he not read: 'They seized Jesus, bound him, and led him first to Annas the high priest'? And again elsewhere: 'They took the body of Jesus and bound it in linen cloths with the spices'? Does he not confess that Jesus is God? If he is God, how was the incomprehensible one seized and bound, unless, clearly, in the flesh, as the [?] Paul confessed? So let this deceiver too stop raving against Christ and be silent. If he were to hear somewhere that we have God even as food to eat, perhaps he would not only shudder but burst, unable to bear what he

heard. But what does Christ say? 'Whoever eats me will live because of me.' He could not be eaten except in the flesh. For since Christ is at once perfect God and perfect man, he may be named after either of the natures from which he was composed, and may be spoken of as properly understood according to each, the property of neither being diminished or confused in the oneness of his hypostasis. The God and Word himself bears witness to this. At one point he says: 'Why do you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth?' And yet the speaker was also immortal God. At another he says: 'You say, "You are blaspheming," because I said, "I am the Son of God."' And yet the speaker was also son of man. So when we assign what naturally belongs to each name to the other nature, we are in no way mistaken.

Since this man's statement too has been dealt with, what does Theodotus (4) say? 'We have not received a tradition of portraying the likenesses of the saints in images made of material colours. Rather we have been taught to reproduce their virtues, as a kind of living images, through what the Scriptures tell us about them, and so to be roused to a zeal like theirs. Let those who set up such forms tell us what benefit they enjoy from them, or to what spiritual contemplation they are led up by remembering them. But it is clear that such a notion is futile and an invention of diabolical cunning.'

The opening of the statement is not objectionable in itself, even though it prepares the way for the absurdities that follow. For many of the holy teachers rank the account given in words above the sight of images, without disparaging the other, while others do the reverse; but the two would be equal, as Basil the Great says: 'What the account of history presents through hearing, painting shows silently through imitation.' And not all are painters, nor all are writers, but each according to the measure of grace God has apportioned. So let him pass over this proposition and state the next: 'Let those who set up such forms tell us what benefit they enjoy from them, or to what spiritual contemplation they are led up by remembering them.' Let the fine fellow be questioned in return: what benefit and what sacred contemplation is not to be found here? If the nature of an image is to be an imitation of the archetype, as Gregory the Theologian says, and in the image the archetype is shown forth, as the all-[?] Dionysius says, then it is clear that from the imitation,
These [?] four are anathematized by holy Sophronius; three of them are well known, while one is unnamed, but by another Father, as I have read, [?]

that is, from the image, much benefit comes forth, and through the imitation the fullest spiritual contemplation rises up to the archetype. The same divine Basil is witness to this, saying somewhere: 'The honour paid to the image passes up to the prototype.' And if it passes up, clearly it also comes down from the prototype to the image. No one who is not out of his mind would call that honour useless, or deny that the imitation is an imprint of what it imitates, so that each is in the other, according to the divine Dionysius. And what could be more beneficial or more uplifting than this? The image is a reflection of seeing with one's own eyes, something like moonlight compared to sunlight, to use an illustration of my own. Otherwise, what use was the tabernacle of witness to the people of old, since it was an imitation of heavenly things? For there too, along with everything else, were the cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat, that is, images fashioned in human form. All these things lift the mind upward and are objects of contemplation for worship in the spirit. As far as this proposition goes, then, the image in the shape of the cross is useless to us; useless too the image of the lance, useless the image of the sponge. For these too are imitations, even if not in human form. Useless too is everything else that has been handed down to us in sensible images, to use Dionysius's words, through which, he says, we are led up as far as possible to intelligible contemplations.

Again, one of the five powers of the soul is imagination, and one might take imagination to be an image, since both are representations. So the image, which resembles imagination, is not useless. And if the more excellent of the two is useless, then much more the lesser, existing in our nature to no purpose. And if it is useless, so are its fellow powers: sense, opinion, discursive thought and intellect. So the argument, reasoning from nature by a more inductive line of thought, shows that whoever despises the image, or imagination, is without intellect.

I also admire imagination for another reason. Some say that a woman who imagined an Ethiopian at the time of conception gave birth to an Ethiopian. Such too was the case of the patriarch Jacob and the peeling of the rods: from that imagination the young born among the flocks were speckled, and, what a wonder, an imagination in the form of an image was seen to produce a real effect. But back to our subject: 'Let those who set up such forms tell us what benefit they enjoy from them, or to what contemplation they are led up by remembering them.' My good sir, who, if he gazes intently at the form of an image, does not go away carrying impressions in his mind, whether for good or for ill? From the best, the best; from the most shameful, the most shameful; so that often, even after he is back at home, he is moved to compunction by the one and stirred to passion by the other. Does not someone sometimes wake from dreams in the night and get up full of joy or of grief? If it is so there, much more is the beholder affected

one way or the other by images seen while awake. Have you not read, my excellent friend, that the people of old served a copy and shadow of the heavenly things? Well then: is not each of these an image? Were they not led up through an image to the contemplation of heavenly things? Does not every man walk about in an image, to speak in David's words? Are you yourself, the iconoclast, not an image of God, born in your father's likeness, and depicted as an image on a panel? Or are you alone beyond being imaged, as not a man but an abortion, and for this reason think the saints are the same? But so that the argument on this point may be more convincing, I will leave aside teaching from my own resources and bring forward the very luminaries of the world to answer your question.

Gregory of Nyssa: 'I have often seen an image of the Passion in a painting, and I did not pass by the sight without tears, since the art brought the story vividly before my eyes.'

Chrysostom: 'I too have loved the encaustic painting filled with piety. For I saw in an image an angel driving back hordes of barbarians; I saw barbarian tribes trampled underfoot, and David speaking the truth: "Lord, in your city you will bring their image to nothing."'

Cyril of Alexandria: 'I saw a painting on a wall of a girl contending in the arena, and I did not look upon the sight without tears.'

Gregory the Theologian:
'Polemon was there in an image, leaning over her.
Seeing it, the [?] courtesan (for she was a courtesan) [?]

went off at once, overcome by the sight,
ashamed before the painted man as if he were alive.'

Basil the Great: 'Rise up now, you illustrious painters of athletic achievements! Magnify with your arts the image of the general that I have left incomplete. Illumine with the colours of your skill the crowned victor whom I have depicted too dimly. Let me go away defeated by your painting of the martyr's exploits. I rejoice to be vanquished today by such a victory of your power. Let me see the struggle of the hand against the fire depicted more exactly by you. Let me see the wrestler painted more brilliantly in your image. Let the demons weep even now, struck by the martyr's exploits as you show them; let the burning and victorious hand be shown to them again.'

Do you see how the one places painting above writing, and how great is his exaltation of it, so that even the demons weep? How the other calls image-making revered, since it brought a courtesan to her senses? Then again, how another does not come away from the painted scene without tears, seeing the martyr contending in the painting? Again, how another calls the encaustic painting beloved, as having seen the prototypes in it? And then the one after them, how he too does not come away from this painting without tears,

as if he had taken it to be the very sight of the thing itself? See how many are the advantages; consider how great the benefits. And since you asked and have heard the answer, not from this or that petty and worthless man, but from those who spoke by the Spirit of God and thundered over the whole earth beneath heaven, now state the conclusion of your argument, you dogmatist: 'But it is clear that such a notion is futile and an invention of diabolical cunning.' This is the moment to cry aloud: 'Be astonished, O heaven, at this!' that the sacred doctrines of the God-bearing Fathers have been declared a futile notion and an invention of the devil's cunning. But it is not so, greatest of deceivers! On the contrary, the dazzling flashes of your tongue must be laid at your own door.

Since this treatise is now at an end, I want you to know this, brother. Of the citations the iconoclasts bring forward, some are plainly from heretics, for it cannot be, it simply cannot be, that falsehood does not spring up alongside truth, like tares among the wheat. Some are from holy Fathers but are twisted by their darkened minds. And some are entirely out of place, applying to the image of Christ what was said against idols. One must not accept their statements at random, nor join in discussion with heretics, contrary to the apostolic law. For the rest, keep well, my child, and pray that I too may be kept safe (1).

37. Theodore to the brotherhoods scattered everywhere. [?]

Grace and peace be multiplied to you. For it is right to address those persecuted for Christ in the words of the apostles. Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has opened a door for us lowly ones, closely guarded though we are, to join with you, beloved brothers, in conversation by letter. Truly the word of God is not bound, even if the rulers think they can bind it. Truly we ought to rejoice greatly, because in ourselves, sinners though we are, we see the divine predictions fulfilled. Come, brothers, let us say with the Apostle: 'Who will separate us from the love of God? Shall affliction, or distress, or famine, or persecution, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword?' For he did not say these things for himself alone, but also for us, so that we too might have such a disposition toward God that we do not lose heart in our afflictions, but gladly bear with joy the sufferings that remain. For it is joy beyond words to suffer for Christ and with Christ. All the [?] have shown this, down to Thaddaeus our martyr and every other confessor who has departed after him, whether from prison or from some other place of exile, with noble zeal and [?] action.

My brothers, let us too become martyrs in this way, by always being ready to be arrested, to confess, to be scourged, to die. This is to bear witness daily; this is to die daily. From this it [?] follows that the soul is purified, withdraws from the passions, draws near to God, hates the world, and pictures heaven and the good things laid up for eternity, though these are also sombre things. For such readiness would not give the mind leisure to love pleasure and to be swayed by passion this way and that. Rather, it braces the heart, pricks the eyes to stream with tears, and makes one long for departure from the body as from an oppressive prison. So let us examine what sort of people we are. If we are like this, well and good; if not, let us recover ourselves and be purified. Let us flee the savage dragon, the devil, and the fiery darts of bitter and deadly desire. Desire is not pleasure but pain, not sweetness but gall, not well-being but hostility, slavery, corruption, possession by demons, a perversion of our natural state. If it were good and pleasant, how is it that it immediately shows those it captures to be foolish, brutish, disgraced, servile, without hope, enfeebled, and liable to eternal death? It bewitches, then, deranging and altering us. It is not what it is supposed to be [?]; it is the chief of sorceresses, and its victims are like the possessed, who do not understand what they are going through until they come to their senses. So, beloved, let us look to our retreats and our ways of life, where and with whom we live. If a place is harmful, we must move elsewhere. If we live with someone who causes scandal, we must cut him off. If we live with no one, we must take a companion, since solitude is accursed, unless some necessity requires it. We must watch over everything else as well: food, drink, sleep, work, so that all is kept in measure, strengthening the body to serve the commandments but not making it wild enough to rise up against the soul. It is [?]; if it is overfed, it grows unruly and throws down its rider, the mind. From our own case we speak of yours too, since all people have received the reins of free will from God alike, to rule themselves, and there is always war, with soul and body set against each other. Let this be enough on that subject. What comes next? The faith, unswerving and unalterable, as I handed it down to you and as I received it from the saints; or rather, both of us from one and the same [?]. Christ is not Christ unless he can be depicted. For to say "Christ" is to have in mind the mystery of his taking a body. Christ would not be spoken of [?] if the Word were thought of as bare of a body. But since the Word became flesh, he would plainly be circumscribed in the flesh; and with the name "Christ" the property of circumscription is also brought in and understood along with it. So those who say that he is not depicted, that is, not portrayed in images, suppose him to be without flesh. And they are outside [?] the fold of Christ, even if they were Peter, even if they were Paul, as

Peter and Paul themselves declared for our safety. It is not that any of the apostles, or any of the saints after them, said that Christ is not circumscribed in the body. Far from it! That is what the impious claim when they bring forward their spurious texts. Let us hold this pure faith, brothers; let us confess this good confession, not being swept away at all. Those who do not hold it are deniers of Christ; those who stand firm are Christ's martyrs, along with the Forty and with the assembly of champions from every age. [?] The Maccabees' refusal to taste pork, which was then unlawfully forced on them, was martyrdom; and are you, dying because you will not deny Christ depicted, not a martyr? John the Forerunner, put to death for reproving Herod with the truth, is the glory of the martyrs; and are you, dying for Christ, not among the martyrs? Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of these the wrath of God comes on the children of disobedience. One who confesses is a martyr beyond dispute, and all the more so the more he abounds in sufferings. Do not let the persistence of the persecution shake you. We have not yet endured many years, as the confessors before us did. We have not yet been refined in the lasting fire of the most searching trial [?]; there is still lead mixed in, still a wrinkle of sin. Who are you to pry into the depths of judgments beyond our sight? Think about what has been commanded you. The seed promised to Abraham with God's blessing, to inherit the holy land, God arranged to be enslaved first for four hundred and thirty years under Pharaoh's hand. Christianity, from the beginning of the apostles' preaching, was in roaring persecution for more than two hundred years, until Constantine, the first Christian emperor. The persecutions that followed were milder, yet long-lasting, apart from the one under Julian the Apostate. The great Paul was persecuted for thirty-five years and died daily; and have you grown weary in five years? Clement, the champion of many contests, bore witness for twenty-eight years; and do you lose heart [?] in a short time? Where would I find time to tell of the other martyrs? Have you not heard of the patience of Job? Was he not tormented by a malignant sore for fifteen years or more, on top of the other tragedies brought upon him? And this although he was conscious of having done nothing on the left hand, but rather things very much on the right. But what was the divine answer to him? "That you may be shown to be righteous," it says. So now too Providence is, as it were, sifting those who are here, so that the tares may yet be thrown out and the wheat remain pure.

"…if they kept my word, they will keep yours also. But they will do all these things to you on account of my name, because they do not know him who sent me." For truly they do not know that God the Father sent his only-begotten Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law and to win the world for his own Father. Otherwise they would not deny that he can be depicted; for no one born of a woman cannot be portrayed, not even if he were a stillborn child. So then, brothers, let us prepare ourselves. And so let us be comforted by the words of our Saviour Jesus Christ as we await the reward [?]. But you know what sort of man Leontius is: of the race of eunuchs, not only dishonourable, as one of the God-bearing fathers said, but also a denier of Christ; and not content even with this, he also savagely punishes our brothers. Once a disciple, now a denier who Judaizes; once prominent among the brothers, now set against the brothers more than all the judges; he who would not say simply "icon" but "holy icon," whether of Christ, of the Mother of God, or of the saints, now burns, tears down, and blasphemes like a raging beast. That is why he is loved by the ruler and placed over our monasteries, and the wretch does everything to insult Christ. But woe is me! His shameful farces are mine. Still, he is like the man who begot him in the flesh, since that man too, in times past, was a first fruit of impiety, as also of Hermias [?]. For both are possessed, and God does not mix crow and dove, but like goes with like. So much for them. May the Lord grant them knowledge of the truth, since they have been taken captive by the devil to do his will. But as for you, together with those whom the apostate punishes, may Christ strengthen, empower and fortify you to endure still: hungry, thirsty, naked, buffeted, homeless, toiling, reviled, persecuted, slandered, as the refuse of the world, the scum of all things, in the words of the great Paul. May your portion be with him. Brothers, pray for us sinners, that we may be saved, counted worthy of the lowest rank among all who stand firm. Brother Nicholas, who is with me, greets you. The grace of God be with all of you. Amen. [?] Theodore to the brotherhoods scattered everywhere. [?] Rejoice, my beloved brothers and fathers, for I bring good news of joy. Once again we unworthy ones have been counted worthy to confess the good confession; once again we have both been tortured for the name of the Lord. For brother Nicholas too contended most nobly and faithfully. We lowly ones saw blood poured out from our flesh onto the ground; we beheld welts, oozing wounds, and all that goes with them. Are these not things of joy? Are they not things of spiritual gladness? But who am I,

wretch that I am, to be ranked with you, Christ's worthy confessors, when I am the most useless of all people? Here is the cause of what happened. The ruler got hold of the earlier catechesis and sent it to the commander, ordering the count of the cortis to come to us. He came with officials and soldiers at an unseasonable hour, and suddenly surrounded with shouting the little house where we were, as if he had found some game to hunt. With picks they quickly broke down the barricade; then he brought us out, interrogated us, and showed us the catechesis. We confessed that we had written it, as God willed. He asked one thing only: that we submit to the emperor's will. We said what the truth required: "God forbid! We do not reject our God," and whatever else had to be answered to our hearers. At this he beat us severely. After his immediate confinement and the recording of his deposition, the brother suffered nothing so dreadful in the way of pain. But I, lowly and frail, was seized by violent fevers and unbearable pains, and almost despaired of life itself. Yet the good God, little by little, had mercy on me, the brother also helping with what was needed, though the wounds still remain, not yet fully healed. So much for that. I have told you of the suffering, knowing that you wish to learn of it so as to share in the pain. What then, since things are like this? The threat is more terrible and the guard stricter. For beatings have been ordered for the guards and for the under-guard, to keep us from uttering a sound, let alone writing to anyone. Shall we then cower and fall silent, obeying men out of fear rather than God? Not at all! As long as the Lord opens a door to us, we will not stop doing our duty as far as we can, fearing and trembling at the judgment that hangs over silence. "If he shrinks back," it says, "my soul has no pleasure in him." And again the Apostle: "But we are not of those who shrink back to destruction, but of those who have faith to the saving of the soul." That is why this present letter of mine goes to all the scattered brothers who are enduring the persecution in affliction, but especially to you, the [?] of Christ. My beloved brothers, let us endure, growing still stronger and not cowering in our sufferings. It is only flesh [?]. Let us not spare it; when we are tortured for Christ, let us rejoice. Let him who abounds in toils rejoice the more, since he gains more in rewards. Let him who is afraid of the whip and cannot bear pain shake off his fear for this very reason, thinking of the eternal torments. For compared with those, their blows are a dream, children's arrows. Yes, I beg you, I implore you: let us find sweetness in pains suffered for Christ, even if they are very painful to the flesh. Let us fix our eyes on what is to come and lasts, not on what is present and passes away. Let us long to mingle our blood with the blood of the martyrs and our portion with the portion of the confessors, so that we may dance

with them for ever. Who is prudent? Who is wise? Who is a good merchant, to give blood and receive the Spirit, to despise the flesh and gain the kingdom of God? "He who loves his life will lose it," said the Lord, "and he who hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life." Let us listen to his words; let us follow him. "Where I am," he says, "there my servant will be also." Where is he? On the cross. And we lowly ones too, as those eager to be his disciples, must be there. I urge you to bear with this word of exhortation, for the letter is brief. Know that we sinners are rejoicing, not losing heart, as long as you only stand firm in the Lord. Nicholas, my fellow prisoner, fellow labourer and fellow soldier, and your truest brother, greets you. Greet one another with a holy kiss: the champions their fellow champions, the persecuted the persecuted, all of you all who love you in faith. If anyone does not confess that our Lord Jesus Christ is circumscribed in the body, let him be anathema from the Trinity. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. Amen. [?] To Athanasius, my son. [?] Among other things, this too is a good thing for us in these days, as we contend for the truth of God: that we hear each other's voices more often through letters and share the feelings of our hearts. For you see, beloved brother, how letters are like daily journals, joining us in closer friendship. See how many good things persecution for Christ has brought us, and may it bring still more, if it finds us more fervent for what lies ahead, not cowering before anything human but eager to bear the sufferings that imitate God, for which you yourself also contend, driven from place to place. But it will go well with those who help you and share your struggles; I have rightly spoken in their defence before, and will do so again. I turn now to your question, leaving aside any rebuttal of the gifts for which you praise me, so that I may not seem to agree with the praise. For I am bare of every good. Where the great Basil, the light of the world, has given his ruling, who that has any sense at all would dare to contradict him? This is found in the question in the Ascetica, as you pointed out: "Whether one ought to lie for the sake of a useful accommodation." To this he says: "The pronouncement of our Lord Jesus Christ does not permit this, for he said once for all that falsehood is from the devil, and indicated no distinction between kinds of lie. And the Apostle also testifies, writing that 'even if someone competes, he is not crowned unless he competes according to the rules.'" So much from the Father. You said that a scholion was added to the chapter, saying that the question concerns what is useful, not what is necessary, for the two are not the same. And again

that in another chapter the same luminary says that one must lay down one's life for one's friends, even to death, whether the friend is a sinner or righteous. So you are perplexed by this: how not to lie at all when circumstances arise that bring a brother to the point of death, and yet also to lay down one's life for him. "For if I do not lie," you say, "my friend dies; and if I lie, I do not compete according to the rules, and I fall away from God." This point is perplexing to me too, and I think to many. Nevertheless I will try, as far as I can, to give an answer to your love, if God is pleased. That, as the scholion says, the useful and the necessary are not the same is true. The one is contingent. For example, it is useful for me to speak with so-and-so about such a matter; yet even if I do not speak with him, it is possible to obtain what I seek. Or again, it is useful to turn away from so-and-so; but even if I do not turn away from him today, I can turn away from him tomorrow. That is what the useful, or contingent, is like.
