The necessary, on the other hand, is unavoidable; it admits of no alternative at all. For example, if I am unbaptized, it is not possible for me to be saved without being baptized. Or again, if I say, "I can live without breathing," that is false, for breathing is necessary, and without it one cannot live. Now the commandments of God were pronounced by the mouth that cannot lie as necessary, and must of necessity be kept. They do not shift so that in one way they may be kept and in another not, by one person yes and by another no, at one time yes and at another no. They must be kept always, by every person and at every time. It was in this sense that the great Basil said, "indicated no distinction between kinds of lie": because the ruling concerns what is necessary, even though the question was put forward as concerning the contingent. For, as I said, the useful and the contingent are the same. Then what will happen, as you put it, in a case where a brother dies because I do not choose to lie? This is not [?], I think. Let me apply something like this to myself. A girl came to me, pursued by a man who meant to violate her, and asked me not to reveal to him, when he asked, that I was hiding her, since he would certainly violate her. So when the violator came and asked, "Did a girl come here to you?", I say, "No." I am not lying. I do not mean that I do not have the girl; I am speaking according to the unspoken sense, that he will not do this evil thing near me. Here is another case. Someone entrusted a sword to me, meaning to kill himself with it; then he comes and asks me for it. If I say, "I do not know, and I did not receive it," I am not speaking falsely. For I mean, "I do not know, and I did not receive it, so as to hand you the sword for your death." Because if I say yes, the girl is violated and the one who gave me the sword has killed himself, and that is evil. And evil does not come from good but from falsehood, for the father of falsehood is the inventor of wickedness. But that the girl should not be violated

and that the man who gave me the sword should not kill himself is good; and the good is the truth, for God is both good and truth. So what seemed a lie has been found to be acknowledged truth. In what only seemed to be a lie, I laid down my life for my friend, and the commandment is upheld on both counts, fulfilled not in a lie but in truth. One must not, however, do this for one's own sake, to avoid dying, for in that case it is a lie. Nor must one swear an oath at all, either for one's own safety or for another's, for the transgression is obvious. That is how it seems to me. After all, Sarah too said to Abimelech, "I am Abraham's sister." And the prophet Jeremiah, when the officials asked him, "What did the king say to you?", gave one answer in place of another, as the king had instructed him, for fear of death, both the king's and his own [?]. And something of this kind is recorded in the Sayings of the Fathers. If you find anything yourself, whether of your own or from someone else, do not hesitate to make it known to us, for the knowledge of the truth and the enlightenment of our dim mind. I greet the one who shares your hardships. The one with me greets you. [?] To Naucratius, my son. [?] You always make the opening of your letters long, heaping many praises on us unworthy ones; they are not true, but they are signs of your friendly affection. I, however, will be brief. What do I wish? That you may be well in the Lord, my brother, growing ever more fervent in the love of Christ to endure what is suffered for his sake, and never slackening from sloth. May you be kindled still more, so that you may sing with holy David: "As the deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God." One would truly sing this if one's heart were purified, or being purified. "For where there is purification," as the Theologian says, "there is illumination." How blessed is the soul that longs intensely to suffer all things for Christ and regards every work of the flesh as an abomination! Pray, brother, that I, who reek of the passions, may catch the scent of this fragrance. That is the first point. The second concerns Anatolius. How grievous to me is his fall! Yet I approved of your treatment of him. Continue, then, to care for him with brotherly affection. The third concerns the questions you put to me. 1. If an Orthodox person, accused of not being in communion, makes the sign of the cross and swears, "I am in communion," without being questioned further by the heretics, while secretly [?] holding in his mind, "I am in communion from the Orthodox side," this is not accommodation but betrayal of the truth. The penance is half that of one who has entered fully into communion with the heresy. How much that is, since I have already been asked and have answered, it would be superfluous to go over the same ground twice.

2. If someone, to satisfy [?] the impious, exposes to their view a priest who is in hiding because of the doctrine of orthodoxy and who does not commemorate a heretic, and he had himself received the sacraments from that priest, then he too is a betrayer of the truth. Let his penance be one year's abstention from the sacraments. 3. If someone swore not to venerate a holy icon and not to receive an orthodox monk, and after taking the oath recognizes his fault, repents and venerates in secret, his fall is grave, for he has already denied Christ, the Mother of God and the saints. Let him be kept from the sacraments for three years, with much clemency. 4. If someone, out of fear, daubs over an icon of Christ or of one of the saints, let him be kept from communion for one year. 5. Suppose a priest commemorates the heretic in public, but in private, when an orthodox person invites him into an oratory, he refrains from commemorating the heretic. Should someone who keeps the faith strictly pray in such an oratory? By no means. 6. Can someone reasonably take on something extra beyond his own penance in order to lighten it? Where communion is concerned, by no means; where the other parts are concerned, it is not to be rejected. Nor could he cut anything out of what was prescribed on his own authority by giving alms. For the one who imposes the penance certainly knows how to weigh the person, the time and the outward circumstances when deciding to relax it. I see that with canons laid down conditionally it is not possible to cover such cases, as the great Basil himself said. In giving the bishop authority to increase and reduce, he laid down the canon not as binding, that is, inflexible, but as conditional, so that the one who gives it must consider how he gives it. And I, the humble one, answer the questions put to me, whether by you or by anyone else, not definitively but by way of concession, that is, as advice, as I have often said. For the rest, pray for my lowliness, and help as far as you can those who are contending at the Studios, and indeed wherever you have strength in the Lord. Brother Nicholas greets you. 41. To Theophilus of Ephesus. [317] I received your holy letter as a book written by God, and I accepted your gift as well, as something that kindles longing. And who am I, wretch that I am, to be praised in such terms by your holy mouth, I who am not worthy even to untie the strap of your sandal? See the marks of a humility that imitates God! You, most blessed forefather, are great and much spoken of, magnified and praised in East and West. You have worthily adorned the throne of the greatest apostle, evangelist and theologian through the contests you have fought and are still fighting, making your life radiant with the blood of your holy flesh, and confessing that Christ is depicted

as embodied, and not denying it as the impious do when they refuse to accept him portrayed in an image. For what cannot be portrayed in an image is not embodied either. I pass over the point that even an angel, though bodiless, is shown by tradition from the theologians to be depicted in sensible images. Yet they deny that the embodied Master, the bodiless servant, and moreover the Mother of God with all the servants of the Lord may be depicted, and so through the images they plainly deny the prototypes as well. They do not even reflect that they hold their power by the acceptance of their own portrait, and that if it were removed or dishonoured, their power too would plainly be removed and dishonoured. But still they do not wish to understand so as to do good. For them it is kicking against the goads. As for you, may the mighty hand guard you for the glory of his Church, as a pillar, as a foundation, as a champion. And may we humble ones see you either returning from there to the land of Asia, as those of old saw John [?] of the Gospel return from his prison on Patmos, or glorified as a hierarch in heaven over ten cities. 42. To his child Thalelaeus. [323] I have understood what you set out in your letter, child, and this is my answer to you. The holy Apostle commands us to keep away from every brother who walks in a disorderly way. How then can Gregory of the Adelphia say that you shun him without reason, when he was not merely disorderly but was carried off entirely with the iconoclasts, signing up to the heresy and eating, drinking and keeping company with them? If he says he has repented and is keeping a penance, let him show it by a written confession, anathematizing the heretics together with the heresy and having nothing at all to do with them. Until he does this, let him be shunned by you who fear the Lord. For he is deceitful, pretending to have converted, drawing you away and sowing pestilent words, supposedly as if they came from the mouth of the opposing side. That is why you, being less mature, got caught up in his arguments and were left perplexed about this and that. But since you asked for the answer, receive it with understanding. Chrysostom's saying, 'Our Christ is not circumscribed by walls,' spoken in praise of Saint Romanus, must not be taken at face value. One must know whom he was addressing when he said it, since in discourses one must pay attention to time, person and manner. Time, because the same laws were not given to those of old as to those under grace. Person, because a heretic is one thing and an orthodox believer another. Manner, because speaking dogmatically is not the same as putting one's words more simply. To whom, then, was Chrysostom speaking? To an orthodox believer who rejected [?] the icon of Christ? By no means. He was speaking to a pagan, who depicts the cause that transcends all things in the lowest of beings, as the divine Dionysius says, and who holds that it is in no way higher than the godless and many-shaped figures

that he fashions. So the Father spoke well and quite fittingly when he said, 'Our Christ is not circumscribed by walls.' The words 'with respect to the nature of the Godhead' must be understood, since that man's gods were set up in walls and confined there, and there was nothing more to them to be grasped beyond what those who looked at them could see. 'They have eyes, and do not see; ears, and do not hear; hands, and do not feel; feet, and do not walk; noses, and do not smell,' as they are accused in the words of the prophet. But our Christ is not only man properly and truly, according to what is seen, since he became like us in all things: embodied, endowed with breath, growing in age, and having everything else that belongs to human nature, except sin alone. He is also God by nature and in truth, and the same one is both. What I mean is what Chrysostom himself says somewhere: 'Below he grows weary, and above he holds the elements together; below he hungers, and from above he supplies the rains; below he is afraid, and above he thunders; below he stands before a court, and from above he beholds all things.' It was in this sense, then, that he said to the pagan, 'Our Christ is not circumscribed by walls.' He did not think it necessary to word the statement precisely with the heresy now raging in view. It is clear that the saint knew for certain that the one who grew weary and hungered, who was afraid and stood before a court, is circumscribed in the form of a body, whether in colours on a wall or on a panel. And where things were obvious he had no reason to spell them out. For if he said that he saw the bodiless angel in an image, does he not see the embodied Christ portrayed? It is foolish to suppose any such thing of the saint. If, then, they take him as a witness for their wicked doctrine, why do they reject that same man, refusing to accept that an angel or any of the God-bearers may be portrayed, when Chrysostom says somewhere: 'What you did with names, you did with his image too,' that is, the image of Saint Meletius, 'for many engraved that holy image on the bezels of rings, on cups and bowls, on bedroom walls, and everywhere'? Yet they cannot bear even to hear him. As for the story of Saint Pancratius, that it does not show who wrote it: what of it? Nearly all the accounts of the martyrs are anonymous, yet they are reliable, and from them teachers take their material for composing encomia of the martyrs. Saint Pancratius is honoured in Sicily in a very large church, in which they say miracles have also taken place. So whoever does not accept the story has plainly rejected the martyr along with it. This much, then, in brief. But you, child, be well

and be saved, and keep far from Gregory [?], so that he does not destroy you through your carelessness. 43. To a recluse. [325] I have read your devout letter. But what is this praise you have given us, who are strangers to every good? And why ask for a word of teaching from us, who have nothing to make our own, let alone to water others with? Nevertheless, since it is written, 'Give to everyone who asks you,' accept a few words from our poverty. Those who live in the common life of the world cannot have the eye of the mind so purified that they gaze without hindrance on the beauty of God's glory, since their attachment to the flesh dims their sight like a blight. But for us, who must renounce everything and are commanded to take up only the cross of Christ, the vision of God comes easily. That is, we are to have and to think of nothing else than how we may please the Lord, and to serve him with a pure heart, breaking off every fleshly attachment. So let the enclosure of your seclusion be a city of God adorned with golden achievements, a locking up not of the body only but of the spirit too. It is fitting, then, for you to flee the sight of men, ties with your blood relations and friendships with the whole world, and to live among yourselves alone, having one soul and one heart in imitation of those who believed at the beginning, in the time of the apostles. Let the abbess lead as one who bears the image of Christ, doing first and only then teaching, and leaving nothing that is commanded without showing it in practice. Let the one under obedience obey and yield as one rendering obedience to Christ himself. Where these things are, there is the fruit of every good work. Where they are not, there you will surely find their opposites: cliques, quarrels, whisperings, private possessions, conceit, and attachments, both to one another and to outsiders, whether through kinship or through friendship.

So much, then, in brief, by way of a reminder on this matter. And I, the humble one, urge you to keep your faith as resplendent as your life, and in no way to enter into communion with the heresy that fights against Christ. It differs in nothing from Judaism, for by destroying the venerable icons of Christ himself, of the Mother of God and of all the saints, it denies Christ's saving dispensation. The image is one with its prototype in honour and veneration, as is the case with the life-giving [cross] itself and its figure. So do not deny Christ, you who bear Christ through your holy habit. Do not throw away the many labours you endure in living out the virgin life in enclosure, and so become part of the opposing faction, which God forbid we should even think or say. Rather, knowing that neither life without right faith nor faith without godly deeds can save, may you be

distinguished [?] in both, to the glory of God, to the renown of the Church, and to the attainment of the eternal goods that are promised. And pray also for us sinners, that we may be saved. 44. To his child Symeon. [327] Late, but all the same, I received your letters, child, and I gave thanks to the Lord for your defence, for your understanding and for your safekeeping, since you are also keeping so many brothers safe with you from the hunt of the heretics. They tear apart not flesh but souls, though bodies too, through the blows and deaths they inflict. Be well, my beloved son. Excel, lead your brothers, encourage them, show them the things of the truth, sharpen them for bearing witness. For such is the time, even if you are lawfully in hiding. As for throwing oneself into temptation, which you asked to learn about, it means this: someone acting on his own initiative and revealing himself to the murderers. As for Saint Gordius and some other martyrs, who came forward of their own accord, the circumstances demanded it, since no one at all was speaking out boldly and godlessness was blazing more fiercely. Besides, they had beheld God as in a mirror with a pure heart and had been spurred on by him. The great Forerunner too, at the risk of his life, rebuked Herod. But now many are resisting and bearing witness by the grace of God, and throwing oneself forward is not lawful. I rejoiced greatly that other Fathers too are of one spirit with you; their names are in the book of life. I greet them through you, and I beg their holy prayers to help me toward salvation. It was a benefit that you found something good from brother Hypatius. 'Let brothers be useful in times of need,' Scripture commands. From my lowliness there is no benefit, even if you boast of us out of love. Since you also asked for the catechesis I gave to all the brothers, I have just sent it to you as well. Pray unceasingly for my salvation. I received the wooden cup; let it serve to keep you more vividly in my memory. I greet the nine, my brothers and children, and earnestly ask for their prayers. Brother Nicholas, who is shut in here with me, greets you and all the others. Grace be with you.

45. To Basil the abbot. [?] I read your little letter with pleasure, holy paternity, as something offered from a pure heart. I did not, however, take pleasure in the praises, being a stranger to what was said. But rather, if you will, pray that I may come close enough to touch your portion and your station. So much for that. May it be, as you say, that brother Hypatius and any other of those contending prove useful to God, so that through them we humble ones may also find the Divine favourable. The question about those who have become entangled in falls, whether according to nature or against nature,

has this answer. True repentance, shown by its fruits, which are abstention from the sacraments according to the canons together with the accompanying self-restraint, obtains forgiveness of sins, even without scourges and martyrdom. For until he shuts the door against us, as it is written, and that shutting is death, even if true repentance comes on the last day of life, it saves the one who has turned from sin. This is what God decreed through Ezekiel, who spoke of God. Such is the loving God we have: he received the thief into his house in a single hour, he justified both the first and the last, and the tax collector likewise. And if, as has just happened, the sinner gives himself up even to receive blows on his back, and something more besides, who could doubt that he has been forgiven his sin? For even to die in confession of Christ makes one in the proper sense a martyr of the Lord. But perhaps the question concerns the penance. If he is subjected to tortures but does not die, then let the one who imposed the penance decide how much to remove on account of his sufferings, perhaps half of the whole. For it is not possible for us to lay this down. Such is the word of our lowliness. But if it should be otherwise, teach us, Father, and enlighten us who are uninitiated. My brother, the lord Procopius, [I greet] most warmly

46. To Arcadius the monk. [337] This is now the second time I have written to you, beloved, since you were seized by the Judaizers. You did not receive the first letter; I pray that this one at least may reach your hands. In the first place, I consider myself a debtor under the common law of love, since those who are joined together in the mind of confessing Christ must encourage one another; so I am bound to write to you. In the second place, because of our special bond, whose nature and depth from the beginning you know, I write with great urgency. But thanks be to God, my most honoured brother, that in this bitter winter of unbelief you have appeared as a flower blooming with orthodoxy, or rather as a confessor of Christ. Once you were brought before the eyes of those in power, you did not cower. You confessed the good confession. You were scourged severely, exiled, and confined somewhere in a hidden place. Again you were delivered into the hands of torturers, and you did not lose heart. You did not deny the faith. You were torn by blows once more, and you have remained unconquered, not fearing those who kill the body, but only the Lord, God and King, as he himself commanded. Blessed are you, and it will be well with you, for you are noble, nobler than all the people of the East. And if they counted you among the weavers as an imperial servant, do not

be surprised. Such things happen to the saints. Besides, even against their will they truly showed the world that you are a servant of the King of heaven, a proof of witness to God and a refutation of impiety. Stand firm, then, noble soldier of Christ. Excel to the end. Endure hardship, do the work of an evangelist, fulfil your confession. You have God as your unseen helper, and the angel who guards your life encircles you, tends you, rejoices greatly, and carries your prayers up to God as a fragrant offering. In them remember us too, sinners though we are, who long for you greatly. 47. To an abbot. [348] Since I learned that you were arrested and beaten for Christ, thrice-beloved one, I rejoice, and I rejoice with you. For this is joy and gladness, not the joy of the world, which is joyless, seeming to be joy but not being so, since it flows away and does not stay, and in the end brings about death, but the joy that is according to God. This alone is delight, and it remains always the same, and its end is eternal life. Rightly, then, I am glad, and glad with you, most honoured Father. And that, as they say, the hail of blows numbered a hundred, and you were severely flogged besides, behold, my joy increases still further. I did not hear the report without feeling, even from far away. Yet glory to God who has glorified you. Struck down on your back by the impious, your glory is unquenchable, your suffering holy. You are a support for your fellow confessors, a spur to eagerness for the orthodox, a blow that shatters the heretics, a building up of God's Church. 'Holy stones roll upon the earth,' as the prophet says. What does this mean? They roll to make the way of piety level, to build up the Church. You too, then, are one of them all, fitted and joined together by the Holy Spirit to the cornerstone. But remember us sinners too in your prayers, most holy one, that we may not fall away from the building, but may be found somewhere in it, if only as a pebble, by the grace and love of our good God. 48. Theodore to the brotherhoods scattered everywhere, together with those contending in the confession of Christ: greetings. [?] Count it all joy, my brothers, in the present afflictions. For it is for Christ's sake that the persecuted suffer persecution and the imprisoned their prisons; I might add, the scourged their scourges too. So I will not cease to address you all in common and each of you individually, to exhort you and to remind you, even though I know that you are firmly established in the faith and have within yourselves the means to encourage and admonish. Nevertheless, I, the sinner, am a debtor

and to add something of my own, especially since longing compels me. For I am jealous for you with a godly jealousy; I, who have nothing to boast of, take pride in your virtues as confessors. You are my joy and crown, my support and unconquerable stronghold. Yes, I ask and exhort you all to remain unshaken in all good cheer and eagerness. “Rejoice always,” says the divine Apostle; “pray without ceasing; in everything give thanks.” And how are these things not joy and gladness, since “if we suffer with him, we shall also be glorified with him; if we die, we shall also live with him; if we endure, we shall also reign with him,” as it is written? How great a promise, beloved! For even if we are thrown into fire, let us bear it; even if we are handed over to wild beasts, let us endure it. For so did those who have carried off the prize from the beginning bear it, men and women alike, looking ahead to the things of that world, lightening present pain with their hopes, counting painful things a delight, and longing for more sufferings rather than loathing them, like those who snatch the larger share of the money from their partners; as you yourselves know, having tasted the immortal sweetness. O deceitful world! What seems sweet in you is bitter and deadly, in every pleasure and every joy. And O longing for Christ! To you belong blessing, and joy, and lordship, and to those whom you possess. See with what words I, the worthless one, exhort you: not words of any of those worthy of praise, but at least friendly ones. Those who think the Lord's visitation slow should consider this: the goodness of God leads the persecutors to repentance, and the sufferers to testing. Let them not lose heart, nor scrutinize the judgments of the Lord. It is not for grateful servants to say, “How long?” The celebrated Job did not say it, nor Peter, nor Paul, those men of countless contests, nor any of the martyrs. The sleepless Eye knows what is sufficient for both. Do you not pity such a man, because “he is storing up wrath for himself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the righteous judgment of God,” a man for whom there is no end of punishment, nor any release by confession [?] from the unbearable torments in unquenchable fire? So we must exhort you to forbearance, as far as it lies with us, unless it be for the sake of those who are perishing and have fallen away from endurance. Whoever is eager to see the death of the sinner cannot have peace with God, and nothing is worse than that. For he is always in turmoil of soul, desiring what God abhors and willing what he does not will. From this come listlessness, slackness, blasphemies, and the other offshoots of wickedness. Let us say from the heart, brothers, “Your will be done. I became like a beast before you, yet I am always with you.” And so the soul at peace will have boldness before God, choosing to spend a hundred years in sufferings for his sake. For if we pray for it, the end will not come any sooner; and if we pray against it, it will not be delayed; but it will come at the time

which God, who fixed it before the foundation of the world, knows to be expedient and a just judgment. Pray for us sinners, I beg you, that we may be saved. Your brother and mine, Nicholas, greets you all. Grace be with you. Amen.

49. — To my holy Fathers, who have gone into exile spiritually for the Lord's sake: Theodore, least of presbyters and abbot of the Studites, greetings in the Lord. [353.]

To receive a letter even from a single orthodox person in these hard days, let alone from many gathered together, is something strange for the times, like a many-petalled rose in winter. And to my humility it was delightful indeed, so that at the very greeting my spirit leapt and I gave the Lord fitting thanks, who in the present persecution of Ahab has kept for himself so many who have not bent the knee to Baal. For I think those who refuse to bend now are equal in number to those of that time, counting not only those who, for their confession, stand openly exposed, but also those who have been preserved here and there in deserts, and mountains, and caves, and the holes of the earth, to speak with the Apostle; just as the three-peaked mountain, bearing renown as thrice-blessed, is adorned by your company. Thanks, then, be to God, who makes you rich together with all who call upon his name. I praise your holy flight; I hymn your life together on the mountain; for though it is full of hardship, it makes one godlike. Moses conversed with God on Mount Sinai. Elijah on Mount Horeb was found worthy to see God, as far as that is possible. Jesus himself, the supreme Source of divinity, goes up the mountain to pray as a man. What does this mean? To me it seems a symbol and figure of the soul's ascent. For as the mountain rises above the plain at its foot and above the hollow, by just so much does the mind of the one who prays rise up to God by means of the lofty place. See, thrice-beloved, what sort of dwelling yours is, and how great. Remember from there us sinners too, who live on the ground, so that we may be joined to you, the Lord's high-flying eagles. But let this suffice, even though longing urges me to say more. Why have you come to such a measure of humility as to learn from me, an unlearned man, the answers to the questions you have put forward? By the grace of Christ you yourselves know what is needed; and if not, you could learn it from those preeminent in rank and learning. For there are very many, as your letter showed, who need to be instructed. So, that I may not seem to grieve you, and at the same time fearing disobedience, I submit myself to the command. But first I have this to say: this heresy, even if it seemed otherwise to those before us, or may seem to some now only moderately evil and not very grave, seems to me at least, dim-sighted as I am, nothing other than a denial of Christ. For if the archetype is manifested in the image, as the all-wise Dionysius says, and if the honor paid to the image

passes over to the prototype, as the great Basil says, and if the image of Christ is now set at nought, denied and trampled underfoot by the fighters against Christ, then in his image and through his image Christ has been denied, dishonored and rejected, as the Jews rejected him; and there is no other way to escape this conclusion. That is why this is a time for laments and mourning; that is why so many resist, not only men but women too, since Christ is being denied both in word and in deed, something not seen in the heresies of old. In word, because the impious say that Christ cannot be depicted in the form of a body; in deed, because they take down every holy image of Christ, of the Mother of God, of the angels, of every holy man and holy woman, from every church and from every sacred offering, handing them over to the fire, jeering and laughing at the great mystery of godliness, and calling Christ depicted with his Mother and his servants an abomination. To think, say and do this belongs to Jews and pagans. For the Arabs and Scythians, out of reverence, have not been seen to do any such thing. How then is all this not a denial of Christ's dispensation?

But now let us turn to the questions you put. Some submitted of their own choice, without anyone compelling them; others after blows; others under threat alone; others without threats or tortures, from fear only; others so as not to lose their possessions; and some also through ignorance. How should these be received when they turn back? Clearly, all of them must show fruits worthy of repentance. What are these? Abstention from the holy things, with weeping and laborious supplication: for the first group, lasting three years; for the second, two years; for the third, fourth and fifth, the same as for the first; for the sixth, one year. After this is completed, what should their standing be? If a man is of the priestly order and did not sign, and no longer takes part in the impious communion, let him be as he was ranked in the clergy. But if he also signed, let him be barred from the sacred ministry until an orthodox synod, though he may still receive the holy things.

Is it permitted, under the compulsion of fear, or because of famine, or even without necessity, to eat with those who are altogether impious, or with those who under force communicate with others but confess themselves orthodox? By no means whatever; except perhaps with the latter, and not indiscriminately, but out of some necessary circumstance, once or twice. May one eat the leftovers of their food, under necessity or even without it, since the cross has been marked on it beforehand? If it was from a priest, by no means; if not, it may be partaken of under compulsion. May one enter their house of prayer for the sake of prayer? And should one celebrate the holy anaphora in it with one's own altar table? By no means, in either case. Should one greet them and embrace them? By no means; as the great Basil says, the Lord forbade the common greeting. So this may be done as a matter of convention, but as a sign of love and friendship it is to be avoided, so that this may be fulfilled: “There is no greeting for the impious.” There are some of the monasteries which joined them neither in word nor in deed, by flight

securing their salvation, and then returning again after the impious had withdrawn. That would be well. But if the church was also used by the impious for the liturgy: if only once, let them enter and perform only prayers in it; if often, let them keep far away from it. There are some lay people, or monks too, who vehemently loathe the impiety or even lament it, yet because of the threats of the godless come to their communion, thinking it to be poison, and they ask us to pray for them. May they be given the divine mysteries? It is permitted to pray, but not to give them communion, whatever they may say or do. If they set up crosses along the highways, should one venerate them? This is not to be forbidden. Should one bring up the offerings of such people? By no means.

These things, then, as the Lord brought them to mind, we have spoken, not as legislating, since we are not of those who hold hierarchical office, for it is theirs to lay down rules canonically, but as giving counsel, since we are of the same rank as you, and since, for lack of those whose hierarchical duty it is to lay down rules, we have been compelled by you to come to this. But you, most holy Fathers, forgive me if anything in what has been said displeases you. Only, the physician should take into account the condition of soul and body and the character of the person, the particular nature of the time, the habit and the passion, the strength and the weakness, and so prescribe and heal, using reductions and additions, things which cannot be comprehended canonically in a summary, as our holy Fathers themselves have laid down.

50. — To his son Lucian. [?]

Our good God, knowing how prone to slip human nature is, and that even one who seems to walk uprightly is tripped up without knowing it if he grows a little careless, in his love for mankind has granted repentance, which calls man back from his fall and restores him to health. Since, then, you too, my brother, have suffered what you suffered, and have completed the time of a worthy repentance with much hardship and very many tears, as I have heard, as one who has made his peace with God, and now seek release, as was made known to me through the steward and the assistant steward: may it be granted you by the Lord. And from now on may you be in health, my son, rejoicing in Christ and prospering in him, giving pledges to the Master never to fall again, but to die for him, as he too suffered for you. Before, I, the unworthy one, cried out to you tearfully by letter, “Adam, where are you?” echoing the divine voice, because
you had fallen from a lofty life, as it were a life of paradise. But now I, wretched as I am, must make bold to say: Peace to you; arise, Christ commands; live

51. — To Albeneca, wife of a protospatharios. [?]

Your nobility's letter astonished me not a little: it was dictated from so God-loving a heart, and composed in so contrite and humbled a spirit, that after reading it through twice I said, “Who is this soul, of what kind and how great, that speaks such things to me, the wretched one?” And when the letter-bearer also reported to me what you had charged him to say by word of mouth, I admired it still more, and glorified our good God, who inspired you with such a resolve, and you eager to put it into action. Great, then, is the work you have longed for, lady, and one of those hardest to accomplish: not only because of the lofty and heavenly nature of that life (for renunciation is nothing other than a promise of cross and death, for one who truly becomes a monastic), but also because you are bound to a husband, from whom you may not be separated lightly, since it was God who joined you to him. Who then could separate you, when you are eager to advance to a higher way of life, except the One who joined you? So it is necessary, as the rule of St Basil prescribes, first to set matters right with your spouse. What does this mean? To lay bare to him the reasoning behind your desire; to show him how vain and dreamlike the world is; that nothing in it is lasting, but passes away like shadows, whether it be joyful, or pleasant, or prosperous, or delightful, or kingship itself. For all things fly away like the flower of the field. And not only this, but also the inexorable judgment awaiting those who have lived in the present age with passionate attachment and not according to the commandments of Christ, which are laborious to fulfill in ordinary life. Speak of these things, exhort him, win him over gently, so that you may persuade him to share with you the aim of renunciation: “For how do you know, wife,” it says, “whether you will save your husband?” And do this for a good length of time. If you come to agreement, that would be well; but if not, then, if the longing for God so inflames you, you may do what seems right to you even against your spouse's will. But, as I said before, the thing is hard to accomplish, especially in days of persecution, and since you are no ordinary woman, but one of the most eminent, indeed of the [?] in the imperial city. And so it is something to marvel at that amid the great glory of life here below you loathe it and long to put on the humility of Christ. Blessed be the Lord who persuades you so; for truly, compared with the glory of God, the glories of this vain life are an abomination. Hold fast, then, to your most excellent way of life. For I hear what good works you do, and how, leaving aside the pastimes of the court, you devote yourself to your own soul and to good things. For it is possible to be saved even in

the world, and with a husband. So from now on, as the Lord may prosper you, live in this way, not grieving your spouse, but rather winning him over by your godly conduct. About the sister: I have let her know what seems right to me. About the steward and beloved son: I thank you very much for your compassionate zeal on his behalf. May you find mercy from the Lord.

52. — To Maria, a nun.

I have read your precious letter and recognized your devout resolve: that, in keeping with the same disposition as that blessed Father, you are ready to suffer for Christ. And rightly so, so that it may be shown that the one flesh is governed by one mind as well, and is not unequally yoked in matters of faith. Thanks be to God, then, who for the sake of fear and love of him has thus separated you from one another in body with the sword of the Gospel, and again joined you in soul by one spirit and one mind. Strive, then, my lady, to be found worthy of an equal portion with him, and to meet him there and be with him forever, choosing him as he chose you. For with great love he took great care for your salvation, as I too know, since he shared his affairs with my humility as with a son. As to your outward pretense of wearing worldly clothes under the necessity of the persecution: for a short time and in a certain manner, this is found among the saints in some necessary circumstance; but permanently, by no means. Beyond that I do not know what to say. If I permit you to throw off the pretense, you might say you cannot bear martyrdom, for you will be brought even to tortures. If, on the other hand, I let things stay as they are, I have no testimony from Scripture. So, with two evils set before us, it is better to be a secret nun than, being unable to bear the blows, to communicate with the heresy that denies Christ and to fall away from him, for which there will forever be

[?] The present time is such as compels us to care for one another, because of the dignity of being of one soul and one faith; since God has called together, as one Church, or rather one community, all who hold fast to the truth and confess it. Just as it is not without danger for one in the same monastery not to care for his fellow disciples, or for the superior not likewise to care for his disciples, so it is for all of us, since, as has been said, we are one Church living in community. I visit you by this letter and ask how you are in the Lord, my spiritual sister: whether you remain in the good confession of Christ; whether you keep the deposit of faith safe through the Holy Spirit; whether you stand strong in God, not frightened by the

Well done, well done! May you be strengthened still more, so much that you sing with holy David, “I will not fear when the earth is shaken and the mountains are moved into the heart of the seas.” For one who is truly firm in faith is utterly immovable from the love of Christ, from which neither affliction, nor distress, nor famine, nor persecution, nor danger, nor sword can separate us. In this confidence all the saints were perfected; may your honor be perfected in the same. For you are not of lower birth than Thecla, Febronia, and the blessed choir around them: a daughter of God, a bride of Christ, as they were, so are you too. For his sake the witness is borne now as it was then. Let us endure, then, I beg you, not only in the afflictions we are in, but even if all the things mentioned above should come upon us. God shows no partiality, loving us with the same love with which he loved those of old. This I write briefly, knowing that your reverence has encouragement both from within your household and from others; yet you have it from us too, so that you may know that we share your sufferings as we ought, and that you may pray for us sinners to be strengthened.

54. — To Basil the patrician. [?]

It was the work of your God-imitating condescension not only to bring our brother in the spirit into your holy presence and to speak with him about what you had decided so gently and modestly, but also to bring the lady patrician, whom I too revere, together with your most noble offspring, and to direct them to bow before him not the head but the knee. O your very great humility! O your God-loving understanding! O your surpassing faith in sinners! You will not miss the reward for your kind welcome. For all these things, and still more for the sake of virtue, rightly, my lord, you have become beloved in blood and in spirit by all who know and see you. Witnesses to this are your high ranks, which have been the prize of virtue; and besides, having formed sons and daughters with your spouse according to the law of nature, you have displayed in them truly vivid images of your piety, who are recognized most unmistakably by the likeness to you that appears in them. But enough on this subject. What word of consolation shall I, the humble one, find for the suffering of your most beautiful offspring who bears the Forerunner's name, to soften a little the grief of your precious souls? For the brother himself reported to me what the pain was like; what warm tears dripped from your eyes; the cries, the laments and the groans; so that, hearing each of the child's excellent qualities, I very nearly suffered as you did. O how we have become like David, who sang a mournful psalm over his son! And if he grieved so over a reckless son who rose up against him and paid the just penalty for attacking his father, what must one say here? And how great

…to make a [?] contribution of words? A boy has departed in the very prime of his life. He was well brought up in manners and in speech, graceful in character and in voice, and his very appearance drew anyone who saw him to affection. Greater still, he was pure in body and white in soul. He was pure in body through virginity, which is admirable: he was not caught like the reckless [?], but leapt over passion. He was white in soul because he took no part in the heresy now raging like the Corybants. These two things came together wonderfully in one person: incorruption of soul and incorruption of body. How praiseworthy are the parents who were called the fathers of such a child! They bore a most well-grown shoot, not only in body but also in spirit. How blessed is the offspring! He took after his father, and he also made himself an image of Christ. Christ honoured virginity by his virgin birth, and he has taken your son as his follower, as a son of light. What then? Is this an occasion for weeping or for joy? For gladness, clearly, even if his parting has brought you grief. He now rejoices with joy in heaven, where he has been made an intercessor. So from now on we must rejoice with the one who rejoices, and not grieve him by grieving. Let my letter end here, and let it carry with it my thanks for the gift you sent and my apology.

55. To Gregoras, a layman. [?]

Hail, confessor of Christ! I was right to call you a man of God long ago. See how my humble word has not proved false, but has been shown to be lofty in you. How [?]? I hear that you even bear iron, which presses your flesh within. [?] the thing. But may you be strengthened in the Lord as you contend in holiness and as a martyr. O brother, O, how you have shone forth! How high you have been raised! Of all the laymen (I mean those under this authority), you alone have been shown to angels and to men as confessing God. Do you see where the persecutors are holding you? In the palace, like a pearl, like a king over the passions, even if they do not see it that way. Do not be afraid, friend, and do not fear the scourges that are coming. May you endure them. Christ is the one who lightens your load and helps you, since he fights alongside you and is beaten with you. Suppose you were held by one of the officials, and you had the emperor defending you and, in his sympathy, being flayed with you while you were flayed. If you loved the world, would you not rejoice to suffer, so that by suffering you might reap the money, the honours and the [?] that you longed for? How much more should we think this way here! We must love this of necessity, so that we may receive the eternal, true and unspeakable goods rather than these vain dreams, and escape the eternal punishments that await those who sign their names to the denial of Christ. May we be delivered from them as we pray for one another.

56. To Leo, Patrician and Sakellarios. [382]

If you love to learn about our humble

life, as you have said out of your good and friendly disposition, how eager would I, the humble one, be to write to your unsurpassed eminence! In doing so I learn of your health, for which I pray, and I seem to see your beloved face and hear your sweetest voice through your gracious conversation with the letter-bearer and your [?] regard for him. For the sake of God you receive people most kindly, and you are easy to approach in conversation even for an ordinary person. He also told me how gloomy you are over what has already been dared because of our sins, and how you groan and are pained at heart at each thing that happens. And rightly so. For you are a man of God, with a sacred mind, a Christ-loving soul, a knowledge perfected by God, a harmonious understanding and a sincere faith. So you writhe at what is happening, unable to help matters as you used to, and seeing the Church in such danger, the Church which the Lord acquired with his own blood. O master, what dreadful things we have come to, and what great evils we have seen! These are the repayment for our earlier sins. We did not see fit to keep God in our knowledge by keeping his commandments. We broke not one but many of them, both privately and publicly, and split the Gospel of Christ. You are wise, and you know what I mean. So God handed us over to what we now suffer, so that we might not be condemned along with the world, even those of us who seem to be something. So let the impious not exalt themselves as if they were pious, but let them know well that they deny Christ by rejecting his venerable icon. He still puts off unleashing his vengeance, sparing them in his mercy and love for mankind and waiting for repentance, but in the end he knows how to punish those who do not turn back. So pray, as one dear to God, that these hardships may come to an end. But do not leave it to us, for we are not even able to appease the good God for our own sins. Even so, we too make this request.

57. To Anastasius, protospatharios. [383]

How good friendship is, for many reasons, and not least because it is used to doing good to those it loves when absent as much as when present! Such has been your illustrious love and piety toward me, wretched as I am, from long ago until now. You have shown it both when we were face to face and when separated by so vast a distance. You did me good from Sicily when I was in Byzantium, and again when I was banished from Byzantium to one place and another, as I am now. Why do you treat a sinful man so, one unworthy of your nobility? The only reason is that I love you greatly for your virtue in all things and your love of God. Not only Sicily sings of these, and this or that region, but the imperial city itself. That is why you are dear to emperors and to those in office, and why your honours come to you because of your virtue. Since you love God in this way, you are loved both by him and by his

people. But I am at once unloved and orphaned. My father has left me and gone to the Lord, as you surely know. So too has Kalogeros. My brother the archbishop is the only one left to me, and even he has been torn far away from me by the troubles that have now overtaken us. I am hemmed in on every side, yet for Christ's sake these straits are very sweet and very broad. But what is this compared with the storm of unbelief, which has brought shipwreck on the whole world, at least as far as the realm under our authority reaches? See, master, what evils we have been kept for! We differ little or nothing from Judaism, now that the icon of Christ, of the holy Mother of God and of every saint is rejected, despised and insulted. For it is Christ himself, with his mother and his servants, who suffers these things, even if those who deny him do not think so. But may the Lord keep you unsprinkled in right belief, even if the waves of heresy splash you from outside, since you cannot escape them completely while you move in their midst. And may he give you many times over the reward for your care for my lowliness, both here and in the age to come.

58. To the brothers at the Stoudios. [406]

Rejoice in the Lord, brothers and fathers! Rejoice, soldiers of Christ! Rejoice, trinity of brothers, made rich with the grace of the Holy Trinity! You are truly worthy of such greetings, because for Christ's sake you nobly bear the harshest imprisonment, punished by Leo, that avenging demon. O the apostasy of that Jewish-minded man! Had he been a wild beast, he would have had his fill after so many years of draining you with ill-treatment and drinking your blood. But this possessed man remains an insatiable drinker of blood and grows ever more savage. He has no feeling of mercy and no compassion for you, the lambs of Christ. Instead he crushes you and schemes in every way with Satan to swallow you up, so that the dragon may boast, and so that through you he may terrify all the rest of us too. But it will never happen. For God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation he will also provide the way out, so that you can endure it. Remember the saints of all ages: none of them pleased God without trials and many afflictions. One was sawn in two, another was stoned, another was burned in the fire, another was beaten to death. Where would I find the time to count the cloud of witnesses that surrounds us? You too share their lot and their contest. So rejoice, my brothers, with unspeakable joy, as you reign over heresy and over the passions. You, my Karterios, steadfast of soul as your name says; you, Aphthonios, most bountiful, richly endowed with endurance; you, Agapios, most truly named, made strong in divine love! The gloom of the prison wins you the eternal and unapproachable light; starvation wins you the delights of paradise; nakedness wins you the

garment of immortality; solitude wins you life with God; your uncut hair wins you the comely form of God, so that with unveiled face you may behold the glory of the Lord as in a mirror. Is this not joy? Is this not a gladness that surpasses all gladness? Perhaps we should even be sorry that our feet are not also in the stocks and a chain not hung around us. For the more the sufferings abound, the more abounds the consolation of God's glory. I have exhorted you in these few words, dearest ones, knowing that you already have endurance of your own. In return, may you and the one who is with me [?] give me your sacred prayers for our salvation.

59. To nuns. [420]

If I, the humble one, owe any debt, it is this: to encourage you with words and anoint you with counsel. You are truly the Lord's sisters and mothers, as the Truth himself said. For Christ's sake you endure the loss of your spiritual mother, separation from one another, the taking away of your holy monastery and even imprisonment, and you have already been scourged for confessing the truth. But what can I say that would do justice to the praise you deserve? Rulers and ruled alike have turned aside in our time, thrusting away the Lord's word for fear of death, and so have monks and nuns, though a very few have been left. Yet the whole sisterhood of one monastery, thirty in number, has been of one soul and has bound on the crown of the contest for Christ. This must be compared with the times of old. It is the likeness of the holy Forty, or the image of some other of the blessed victors. How blessed you are! Each of you outdoes the other in burning zeal, and all of you together have sharpened one another for the arena of confession. It is a sight worthy of an angelic choir, a gathering of martyrs lovely to God, for whose sake the sufferings are borne. Come then, daughters of the Jerusalem above, branches of the true vine, true disciples of the Word: let us exult as befits God. Let us give thanks to Christ, who strengthened you to endure what has passed, and then let us prepare for what is to come. And what is that? Even if scourges come again, or chains, or fire, or the sword, do not shrink back at all, but be ready to bear everything with Christ. For we shall be strong, since he has said: "All things are possible for the one who believes." Do you see what praises these are? And what remains? The rewards to come: the kingdom of heaven and joy beyond words. So let none of you fall to Satan, and let none of the thirty love her life, as one of the Forty did. They were an image of fasting; you are a figure of the Holy Trinity, the three multiplied by ten. Such is my poor exhortation. In return, O thrice-blessed mothers, give me your prayers as provision for salvation.

60. To canonesses. [425]

Even from earlier occasions we had enough proof of your devout disposition toward our lowliness, but now we have far more. We were truly amazed to see your gifts, how many and how great they were. Then the letter-bearer, who had seen it for himself, told us how much consideration and care you have for us. You are eager to show mercy and compassion, to feed us, give us drink and clothe us, and to do for our poor self whatever else is needed for life, and you seek to learn what is needed so as to provide it. Is it not right, then, that I should thank God for this, since I have found spiritual mothers and sisters? Is it not owed and fitting that I should offer hymns to you, who seek God with your whole heart? Rejoice, mothers and daughters in the Lord! Rejoice, diligent workers of the Gospel commandments! Rejoice, lilies of the spiritual field! You are set among thorns in place, but in your way of life you run far from the thorns of heresy. Rejoice, fair pair, who hold fast to one another and are bound together to God through one another! How great is your godly harmony, your loving bond, your monastic life! Rejoice, you who are the lady of the lady, the mother of the mother, the superior of the superior, at once ruling and ruled! How fine is your work and your practice! You gather the reward of obedience, and you are a safeguard to the one who presides. Rejoice, you who are both superior and subject: superior to the many, subject to the one! Blessed is your understanding, which steers and is steered and is guided into the harbour of salvation. These praises are brief, but from a few things many are understood. May the Lord repay you the reward for what you have done for us, for the steward and for anyone else who has been treated well. I beg you, keep yourselves still from the soul-destroying heresy, for communion with it is estrangement from Christ. At the same time make your way of life more radiant, a golden chain not entangled [?] with the many, so that, adorned with both, you may come with bright lamps to the bridal chamber of the Lord and enjoy the eternal goods.

61. To Naucratius, my son. [?]

You have found such a faithful letter-bearer that I, the humble one, thought it a provision of our good God that I should write to you, holy child. Just to learn that you are well, together with all the confessors and your brothers — how could that not be a joy to us sinners? And all the more since you are the foremost [?], and since you deal with everyone in a godly way, with words of love and care. Then, since brother Adrian has arrived safely where you are, we have been relieved of our worry and have given thanks

to the Lord. Still, we are always anxious about brother Epiphanius, as you told us beforehand, and we are ready for trials, since we suspect, as is likely, what is coming. But let these things be and go as God pleases. "For those who love God all things work together for good," as the sacred word says. Pray, brother, that we may become such people, even though we are far from God because of our sins. Then we shall not fear what man can do to us. We have endured nothing like what you sang of when you crowned us with praises. And if there is anything good in us, that too is because of you and from you, for your prayers have strengthened us and made us worthy. May the mercy of the Lord be upon us, unworthy as we are, from now on as well. I was glad that you kept company with the patrician lady in the Lord, and that you did so for our sake. She herself told me this very thing, and she has been moved to do even more good. You live for us, brother, and we also live for you. Do not be surprised that the persecutors of Christ rage like Corybants, or that Christ bears with them. All things must be fulfilled, so that those who are approved may shine out more clearly, and the lawless may pay in full the wages of what they have done. I have sent you a little book and fourteen quires, which contain discourses and lives of the brothers in verse [?]. Read them yourself, with some of the faithful brothers, and then hide them securely. I am doing nothing worth mentioning, brother. But since I have the time, and since I am prodded as if by my holy Father, and since I hear the divine Paul saying again to holy Timothy, "Do not neglect the gift that is in you," I do what I do, unworthy as I am, with fear and trembling. Greet brother Athanasius and the assistant steward. Though I wrote that brother Adrian had arrived, I said it without knowing; I learned later that he had not yet arrived when you wrote. Brother Nicholas sends you many greetings and holds your words in reverence. The Lord be with your spirit, my brother and father.

62. Catechesis. [436]

Until recently my letters were read to you from the Anatolikon; now I appear from the Thrakesion. For the rulers of this age have moved us to Smyrna, into a prison more secure and more trying than the former one. But the word of God is not bound, nor does longing rest, nor does the commandment keep silent. So the humble one speaks again: Rejoice in the Lord, fathers and brothers! Rejoice, you who are persecuted for righteousness' sake! Rejoice, you who live in mountains and caves, and also you who hide in cities and in more deserted places! The Apostle has instructed us that we must always rejoice. How much more, then, must we rejoice now, when we suffer for Christ, who is painted on a panel, who appears in his own icon, who

is honoured through it. For these words are not mine, wretched as I am [?], but those of Dionysius the all-wise and Basil the Great. And this letter is not yet the place to bring in the citations of the other God-bearing Fathers. Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth! Moab has rebelled — that is, Byzantium. She has shaken off the yoke of the Gospel and, like a heifer stung to frenzy, she has thrown off the rein. "I do not wish to know your ways," she has declared, in deed and in word. She raves like a Corybant, she is mad, she drinks blood like a lioness. Like an asp she stops her ears, and when she is reproved she shakes off [?]

A voice came to her as if from heaven to remind her, from the most preeminent see, the throne of Rome, crying: "What have you done? You have denied Christ by rejecting the icon of Christ, of the Mother of God and of all the saints. Open an obedient ear; listen to the words of the Gospels, the Apostles, the Prophets and the Fathers." But she did not accept it and would not receive it. Instead she has torn herself away from the five-headed body of the Church, though the holy Nicephorus is still alive. She stiffens her neck against God Almighty, insulting Christ and trampling on holy things. These are her deeds, O thrice-beloved. But God is with us, and so are East, West, North and the sea. In this lies our joy, and if there is also lament, it is for those who are perishing. Come now, stand with me, noble and thankful ones, and seize the sufferings for Christ as treasures. What a good season this is for those who contend! It breathes sweetly, and its martyrs' contests are fragrant beyond all spices. Martyrs' blood flows upon the Church and waters it more richly than Eden was watered from its spring of four rivers. New members are joining the choirs of the martyrs of all ages, and the deeds of the confessors, which were called blessed long ago, are now seen before our eyes. Will not the one who hears this hasten to the contest, chafing at life in the mountains, or in the desert, or in hiding of any kind? Yet stay where you are, for you too have a great blessing. Pray, and praise those who are more blessed. Strike down the invisible dragon for me; rout for me the civil war of the flesh. Let the spirit conquer and the body be enslaved, so that the soul, the lady and mistress, may be free and have peace with God. If you do this, it is a martyrdom every day, and crowns woven by God. Do not be grieved about us sinners, even if you have heard that we have been scourged again. Through your prayers we bore it thankfully and with great joy, even though the sting lasted only a little while. Only do not stop stretching out your holy hands. For we believe that by this, weak as we are, Amalek will be put to flight. Your brother Nicholas sends many greetings. Greet one another with a holy kiss, community greeting community, the small greeting the great, and also the Fathers who live near you. When this letter has been read among you, do not refuse to have it read among them too, if only it is worthy, since all are of one soul and one body, though different members. The Lord Jesus Christ be with you and with us sinners. Amen.

63. To his son Naucratius. [431]

How my ear is filled with the sound of your words! For what you report is necessary and urgent. Now that I have heard it, fair child, I, the humble one, have sung thanksgivings that the Lord has not wholly abandoned his Church, but has shown that it still has its strength. He has stirred up our brothers in the West, to refute the drunken outrage of those here and to bring light to those who fight in the night of heresy. The obdurate may have shaken it off; they may not have opened the eyes of their hearts. But I now bear witness before God and men: they have broken themselves off from the body of Christ, from the supreme throne, on which Christ placed the keys of the faith. Against that faith the gates of hell, that is, the mouths of the heretics, have not prevailed from the beginning, and they will not prevail until the end, according to the promise of him who does not lie. Let the most blessed and apostolic Paschal, rightly named, rejoice, for he has fulfilled the work of Peter. Let the whole company of the orthodox leap for joy, for it has seen Christ's visitation with its own eyes, as our holy Fathers did of old. As for everything else, let it go however God pleases. Let the blood of martyrs water the Church; let the choir of confessors grow. This is God's good pleasure, this is joy and gladness, even if it is most pitiable for the sake of those who are perishing. What will our opponents say? They do not have the East; they have been deprived of the West; they have been torn away from the five-headed body of the Church (for the holy Nicephorus is still alive). They are therefore estranged from Christ; they are therefore dead; they therefore walk in darkness. And if they rule over a desolate heresy, so do robbers, since robbers also kill, as these men do, shedding blood, so to speak, every day. Let that be enough on this. But how greatly shall I sing over the change in Leontius! O the greatest of God's wonders! You, my good friend, have reshaped this man, so hard to win for Christ, from one thing into another. I supposed that he was playing the part of Cyprian in the affair: rebuffed by the emperor, he ran ahead to those who contend and struggle for the prize, as Cyprian did with the celebrated Justina. May the Lord grant that both things be fully shown in both of them. That your prison has become more confined grieves me, because of your weakness. But be strong and take courage, confessor of Christ, as we told you before. And so that you may know still more clearly, I add this too: the commandant still keeps us under close guard. Why, and how? Since one must use economy in necessary matters, when we were brought face to face with the heresiarch of [?] (for that is where we were first taken by those who removed us from the Anatolikon), we bent the knee, and he knelt along with us, and we embraced him. And since he allowed me and the lord Athanasius to come together, we also drank with him once or twice. We did not, however, eat with him, though the serpent begged us earnestly and whispered deceitful things. This same measure

we used after we were brought from there to the dragon in whose hands we now are. He had learned of our course beforehand and pressed us no further, since he could not persuade us. Still, when he saw us he stirred up talk about the matter: 'It is nothing,' he said, 'and the point in dispute is trivial.' I replied: 'On the contrary, it is among the very greatest. If you wish, speak, and hear a reply.' 'But let us leave it for now,' he said, and so it was. The rest would take long to tell, but my account is aimed at something further, which is why I began. The clever fellow thought he could draw us in little by little, not by engaging in argument about images, but perhaps by doing us favours, conversing with us in a friendly way, confiding the business of his command to us (for he has been placed over the five themes), and also by extolling the ruler's doings. He came and started such conversations; and, something he had not done even once in the prison, he offered us a drink. I was caught off guard: I drank, after sealing it with the sign of the cross three times, for I feared the ploy. Woe! Little by little, without your noticing, he drags you down. I began a discussion about the truth, and he too was roused. We shot proof-texts at each other, he trying to silence me with mockery, while I spoke in some matters with restraint, because our words would be reported to the emperor, and so that we would not part from each other in turmoil. Then I put a proposition to him, and he was at a loss. I said: 'Is this not blasphemy? Did the Father and the Spirit share in what Christ did as a man, yes or no?' He nodded, and insisted it was so. That is why I eased off, and why we parted as though in battle. He went out and said: 'I thought he knew something, but he knows nothing at all; in fact I silenced him.' For my part, I recognized him as utterly irrational as well as impious. One thing I aimed at: to lay aside my pretence and show another face, as one must toward a ringleader of impiety, since it is not right to cast pearls before swine. Hence the strict security, and the order that we see no one, though God arranges things otherwise. Even if this has been rather a digression, it had to be said, so that you may pray fervently that we be delivered from the ambush of the impious man. Your brother greets you.

64. Theodore, the sinful monk, to my spiritual Fathers and brothers who have confessed and are contending in prisons, whose names are in the book of life. [?]

Having heard, O thrice-beloved, the testimony of your good confession for Christ, I hymned and glorified God, who called you from a foreign land to the queen of cities like rational lambs, to shed your blood as a fragrant offering to him, a light for those in the darkness of the heretics' night-battle. Then I, the humble one, longed with all my heart to see you, the athletes, and to

embrace you one by one, drawn by a burning desire. But since this is bodily impossible, I am carried off through this letter and stand in your midst. I kiss your holy footsteps, and kiss your sacred faces with a holy kiss. O good soldiers of Christ, called as though by a heavenly enlistment! O bright stars shining in the night of impiety, [?] more precious than gold, more brilliant than emerald and pearl! I wish to crown you worthily with many titles, but the limits of a letter constrain me and do not allow it. Gathering the whole into one word, I would say this: your martyrdom is equal to the martyrdoms of old. For whoever confesses that he accepts the image of Christ plainly confesses Christ, and the same holds for denial. For the honour paid to the image passes over to the prototype, as Basil the Great said; and the archetype is manifested in the image, as the all-wise Dionysius said in turn. And since Christ is perfect man, lacking nothing that is seen in human beings, he can be depicted like any man, just as he cannot be circumscribed, insofar as the same one is also perfect God. If he could not be portrayed in a bodily form, he would surely not be man. For the first and truest sign that someone is a man is that he can be depicted. And I say nothing yet about the Mistress of all, the Theotokos, and about all the saints together, who are rejected when their venerable images are destroyed. But whoever understands, understands; and whoever rejects, rejects to his own ruin, contradicting the oracles of God. Authority always acts as authority does, and God's people are few, even if all are his creatures [?]. In the end the gates of hell have battered [?] the rock called by God, from above and from the beginning, but have by no means prevailed against it, nor will they prevail, according to the promise of him who does not lie. Therefore, my Fathers and brothers, stand firm in the faith, be courageous, be strong in the Lord. The choirs of the martyrs are calling you to themselves [?], and likewise those of the confessors. These things in brief. We, the least, join ourselves to you in spirit, though absent, so that you may know that you have a last member confined somewhere here for the same confession, [?] asking you to include us in your holy prayers, so that we may follow after your precious footsteps.

65. To his son Naucratius. [439]

I learned from the letter-carrier, good brother, that quarrels have sprung up among you. I mean this: one says, 'I venerate the image of Christ as Christ himself,' and another refuses. I did not receive this without grief, knowing that these squabbles are secretly sown by the devil and usually cut

[Notes: 78 [?] 16:18 [?]; 75 1 Cor. 13:15 [?]]

into the healthy part of Orthodoxy itself. That is a joy to our opponents, who use our ailments to confirm that their own impiety is sound. Yet I did not think it right to suppress in silence what I had heard, but rather to find some healing remedy of my own, God willing. The point, then, is this. In the divinely inspired Scripture the word 'as' (hōs) is sometimes used to express likeness, sometimes affirmation. The first: 'I became as a sparrow alone on a housetop,' and, 'I am as a fruitful olive tree.' The second, where the same word means 'how': 'How good is the God of Israel!' and, 'How lovely are your dwellings, Lord of hosts!' For here the word expresses not likeness but affirmation. If, then, someone says that he venerates the image of Christ 'as' Christ himself in the first sense, his thinking is sound; but if he means it in the affirmative sense, by no means. For image and archetype are not the same in nature, but the same in likeness. Though the two are identified in likeness, they differ entirely in essence; I mean, of course, images made by art. How, then, could anyone venerate the image as Christ himself in the affirmative sense, when Christ is not in it by nature but relationally, that is, by likeness? Otherwise this saying would be false: 'The archetype is manifested in the image, and Christ is venerated in the image.' To say 'in the image' indicates one thing in another; one thing is venerated through another. Chrysostom saw an angel in an image, but Cornelius saw the angel himself. We see Christ in an image, but the apostles saw Christ himself: 'We have seen the Lord,' it says. We venerate him in his own image, but they venerated him in person: 'And when they saw him,' it says, 'they worshipped him.' So Christ is venerated in an image by likeness, or relationally, or homonymously, for these all come to the same thing; but not by direct sight. He is therefore also venerated without an image, in the mind, since he is not always and in every case seen in a sensible image. But if someone should say, 'Since I can venerate in the mind, venerating in an image is superfluous,' let him know that he has denied even venerating Christ in the mind. For unless the mind pictures him as in a mirror, in the likeness of a man seated at the right hand of God the Father, it will not offer him veneration, unless perhaps it rejects that the Word became flesh. His image is a faithful witness that he was made like a man; and in the acceptance and veneration of the image, Christ is accepted and venerated, just as, conversely, he is rejected when it is rejected. Abgar, when he received the faith, venerated Christ in his mind; but he venerated him more manifestly in the image not made by hands that Christ himself sent him. So in that image Christ was venerated both by likeness and in the mind. That is how it is now; but in the age to come it will be by direct sight, when, as the all-wise Dionysius says, his visible theophany fills us in all-pure contemplations

and shines around us, as it did the disciples at that most divine Transfiguration, and when we partake of his intelligible gift of light with a mind free of passion and matter. This, whether inadequately or sufficiently, is what I have to say. I urge you to make your inquiries in discussions about God reverently and attentively, and to find the truth either by yourselves or from others, putting quarrelling far away. And if anything is lacking in what has been said, let it be corrected, since I am a person of little understanding and a sinner.

66. Catechesis. [445]

I am sending this letter to all of you together and not to each individually, but not out of contempt or neglect—far from it! How could I despise my own heart, the confessors of Christ? I would rather shed my blood instead of ink and offer my flesh instead of paper, to write to you and address you every day, if that were possible. Nor is it because you are not firmly established by yourselves; for I know and am persuaded how great is the power you have from God. Rather, I write to satisfy my own longing and to discharge the debt the commandment lays on me. The reason is my prison, which is now more securely guarded, since we have just been transferred, as you have already heard, from the Anatolikon to the Thrakesion, to Smyrna; and also because we have not received any replies for some time; and besides, because the same letter may well suffice for contestants on an equal footing. Come then, my brothers, let us sing thanksgivings now too, that we have been counted worthy to serve the living and true God, and not only that, but also to suffer for him, which is more glorious than any glory and more delightful than any joy. For what is your suffering for? Is it not for Christ? For you confess that Christ, having become man, is truly circumscribed in the flesh, that is, can be depicted, and that the acceptance of his image is the assurance of his incarnation. When the image is abolished and rejected, the incarnation is clearly abolished and rejected with it. But since the god of this age has blinded the minds of the Iconoclasts, so that the light of his image should not shine on them, they walk in darkness and deny Christ by denying his image. And they strive to have everyone blinded along with them, persecuting, torturing, imprisoning, and, one might say, constantly killing. But they will not drag away those who are confirmed and established in the unchanging truth. Nor indeed have they escaped being refuted by the chief throne of the Church, as has happened, as you know. We had certainty and purity even before the Westerners came; but it has been increased all the more

by this, so that we may know that God visits our generation too, just as he did the generations before, and has brought into view the testimony that those who deny the image are estranged from him. For if they are broken off from the chief throne and from the other three patriarchs, they are clearly broken off from Christ too, who is the head of those just mentioned.
