So it is for them to mourn and be downcast over themselves, and for us to rejoice greatly and beyond measure. Let us therefore bear the afflictions of the prison from now on, beloved, and what is still to be expected—the trial itself: dying daily, bearing witness, contending, until the time of peace comes, which the Lord has judged sufficient as a test for those who confess and as a recompense for those who disobey. Let each day carry you through to the next with patience and eagerness. Let the hand work at whatever work it may; let the mouth sing psalms; let the body be kept in subjection; let the mind attend to itself, so as not to open the door to the passions; so that the prison may be spacious, pleasant, sweet, a palace of Christ. For the opposite is obvious. Those outside, men and women, nuns and lay people alike, show you their faith and devotion. And rightly so, since by the grace of Christ you are the light of Byzantium, not to say of the whole world. But let us watch out for the devil, who sows tares among the wheat. Let us use the sieve of discernment to let faith through but shake off attachments, so that the field of the soul is not ruined. The great Paul too had women he loved: Apphia and Persis; and he exhorts Euodia and exhorts Syntyche to be of the same mind in the Lord, as women who laboured, contended and served alongside him. It is certainly necessary to have such women, but to have them as he had them. For he says of Priscilla and Aquila: 'who risked their own necks for my life.' Do you see the warmth of his love, and the apostle's welcome? In the same way, my brothers, let both us and you have and embrace the women who are placed in such a position for us, so that God may be glorified and we may give light, and not be muddied and confused. I have heard about you three, that you were reunited through the repentance of the humble [Reg. cod.: pitiable] Leontius; and I, the sinner, glorified God both for his change of heart—if indeed it lasts—and for your contest, because, like the three holy youths from the furnace of fire, you too have come out of the dreadful prisons unharmed, astounding the tyrant. But keep up the contest, my noble ones, and prepare yourselves to be tested even to the point of blood. For such is the law of martyrdom. May your trainers be blessed, both those inside and those outside. We wretched ones have been flogged again, but we accepted it with thanksgiving, and we are content even more. So do not be grieved at our humiliation, but rather rejoice, and pray that we may still be strong in all things, to bear what is inflicted by those in power and to endure what is

planned by the enemy [Reg. cod.: by war], together with our brother Nicholas, who greets you most warmly. Remember my groans. Grace be with you. Amen.

67. To his son Naucratius. [447]

It was beyond hope, yet still in hope, that I received your letter, precious child: first because of the tightening of the prison on the emperor's orders; and second because of the boundless goodness of God, the lover of mankind, who for the sake of you saints sets right even the affairs of us sinners, even though men try to bring us to an impasse. What shall I say, wretch that I am, or what shall I think? Only this: 'All my bones shall say, Lord, Lord, who is like you? You deliver the poor from the hand of those stronger than he.' This is the first cry of my pitiful self, though it is taken from David's song. Second, I was also relieved of my anxiety when I read your letter, since I found that your confinement was as you described it; for I had only heard beforehand that you had been moved to another prison. Take heart, brother, and rejoice, because as the sufferings of Christ abound in you and in those who share your mind and your way of life, so too do the consolation, the reward and the glory. And how could the vessels of election have come into the open if there were no scandals? God permits them, showing those who cause them for what they are, tares kept for burning in eternal fire, and proving those who endure trials, who will shine like the sun in the kingdom of heaven. So do not be surprised at what happens every day: that one man has been seized and another bound, one woman beaten and another exiled, and whatever else happens in this way or some other. A little later the time of recompense will come. I read what you sent (and having taken note of it and given thanks to the Lord, I sent it back again) about brother [?] Ignatius. Alas that he was caught! For the man is a particular friend of mine. But you did well to give the penitent his treatment. What you have imposed, child, is sufficient, and I, wretch that I am, pray that he may return to the contest; I have also received his offerings. I, the humble one, feel compassion for brother Anatolius, since you too love your brother. So I venture to say: let him be spared another year, so that when the two years are completed he may share in the holy things. May the brothers who have fallen asleep, sons of light perfected in the persecution for the sake of the light, pray for us. Those who have died otherwise are to be pitied for their departure, because of my sins, as you said. Such too is Severian. Yet even from perverse things there comes some good turn for the careful; and let the argument be put to the test whenever it comes up, even from opponents, so that in the testing, as when stones are struck together, the fire of truth may leap out. And indeed now too such a

…your proposition. In certain histories, you say, images are found inscribed "Divinity," "Lordship," "Kingship." Clearly you would be saying this of the image of Christ. And how can that be? Such terms are understood of the Trinity in common, not of one person distinctly. For although each person may be called both God and Lord, he is not simply called Godhead and Lordship. For example, he says, "I am the God of your father," not "the Godhead"; "I am he who is," not "Being"; and "The Lord rained fire from the Lord," not "Lordship from Lordship." If this is so in theology, then all the more in the economy there is no reason to inscribe the image of Christ "Divinity" or "Lordship." He may indeed be called God and Lord, or something equivalent to these, though even this by homonymy; but not Godhead or Lordship. In the same way, to take an example, a painted man may be called a man, but not humanity; and a king of those on earth, but not kingship. So the inscription is mistaken, in my view, for it circumscribes the Father and the Spirit along with him, which is absurd. So much, in brief. For your part, pray more fervently for my lowliness, and also for the brother, who sends you his most heartfelt greetings. I have received the cloak; how long will you go on clothing us, beloved? May the Lord warm you in return in the Spirit. The letter-bearer will report what is lacking. Farewell in all things. 68. To Irene the patrician. [?]

Earlier, when the fall took place, my letter to your honour was a painful one; but now it is full of joy, because of your rising again and the scourges laid on your honourable flesh for the confession of Christ. Well done, well done, bravest among women! You have made your return to the contest more glorious than your defeat, gladdening God and the angels and the most devout of men. You are truly noble, sprung from the rising of the sun; you love God and love virtue; you slay the passions and are an enemy of the world. How praiseworthy is your name, and how widely spoken of is your witness! Why do I say this? You took up the sword of the gospel as a soldier of Christ; in ecstasy you cut through the ties of the body; you were cut off from the bowed head of your daughter, your only offspring; you bade farewell to the imperial city, to an illustrious family, to eminent friends, to a most splendid house, to the most exalted rank, to a multitude of servants on your estates, to every kind of possession, and to other things which it is not easy for me to tell. And taking up the cross-bearing life, you have been banished somewhere far away, as I have learned, on an island. Blessed are you, and blessed is the fruit of your witness. And where does all this good come to you from, this great renown, this highest praise, if not from the achievements that went before it,

from your constant intercession and prayer, from your surpassing love of doing good and your heart that loves monks? The fruits have not perished, even if for a little while they were shaken; the serpent, the adversary, did not break your tower of virtue, even if he bit. The envy of the mockers has been repulsed; the drivel of the scoffers has fallen; Christ has conquered in you and through you, O noblest of women, O lover of martyrs, and, for the third time, O my mother. For I call you this in the Spirit, as a fellow athlete, closer to me than those known to be one's own flesh and blood. For this is how the Spirit knows how to unite those who are brought to birth by him. I know your labours; I know the [?] of your soul, and all that you will endure, having torn yourself away from the world. But take heart: great is your reward in heaven. You are called a bride of Christ, though you came from a husband; a fellow citizen of the righteous and the saints, provided we remain in the divine confessions to the end. Now I beg and urge you to bear patiently your exile and your deprivation of everything, contemplating the things of heaven and knowing that what is on earth is a plaything, quick to pass away. With you is the angel who guards your life; Christ himself is with you, who said, "I and the Father will come and make our dwelling with him." One thing I remind you of: look after yourself, and adopt a more comforting diet. For now is not so much a time for abstinence as before. And finally, pray for me, the sinner, that I may bring my life into harmony with my words. 69. To Euphemia the recluse. [?] Even if we fail to write to your honour more often, we have not forgotten to remember you in the Lord, because of the purpose we share and the generosity of your choice. For, as I learn, from your earliest youth you chose the cross-bearing life, and moreover a life of enclosure. How great is your praise, bride of Christ! But I remind you, cherishing you spiritually as a sister: make haste, lady, to serve your Bridegroom still more. A woman who has been betrothed withdraws herself from every attachment, and turns her whole heart, her soul and her whole mind in love toward her own bridegroom. If this holds for one who is corruptible and transient, how much more for one who is incorruptible and immortal? We too ought (the word applies to all) to be so disposed toward the Lord and Master, never to have our fill of longing for him, and in this to stand apart from every corrupting pleasure. For he too is held by love toward us, and, as it were, goes out of himself in a love beyond the infinite. Was it not for your sake that he, being God, took the form of a servant, which the iconoclasts now dishonour? Did he not become poor, though he was rich? Did he not endure every affliction: insults, spitting, blows, scourges, the cross and death? So each soul ought to be disposed as though he had suffered for it alone, though he suffered for all; and to cherish and love him, and to long to have suffered

in return. And if perhaps one is not permitted to undergo these things, the intention too is accepted as the deed, so generous is the good God. I say this not as though these things were not already ringing in your ears, but as one sharing your feelings in

70. To Theophilus of Ephesus. [?] Having lent you a letter, I was eagerly waiting to receive back the debt of love; but since I have not received it, I am glad to lend again. For the loan is very sweet to me, I mean conversing with your sacred head, which has suffered for Christ, or rather has been crowned and adorned as a confessor. For the mind that sees God and divine things does not look with the same eyes with which the world sees. The world thinks that things that perish and pass away belong among the goods, knowing badly and in error; but the mind judges that alone to be blessed which does not set the limit of its enjoyment here, but is stored up for the age to come, for endless gladness of heart. So, wretch that I am, when I see the things of your holiness, I rejoice and rejoice with you, thrice-longed-for one. You despised earthly glory; you chose with Christ what is lowly and despised, or rather affliction and distress, blows and exiles. How blessed are your deeds! How praiseworthy your sufferings! They are proclaimed in East and West, recorded in heaven; they gladden angels, delight confessors and martyrs, and brand with shame the demons and the iconoclasts who share their mind and their ways. Rightly then do I exult with you, first father. But I ask you to pray for me too, wretched in every way, that I may not fall away from standing in your footsteps. 71. To Naucratius, his son. [?] We have been slow to write to you, beloved son; but the reason is that here too persecution is seething, with blows, chains and prisons. Such is the rage and threat breathed by the man who holds us, who arrests and punishes the devout found here and there. Indeed, when he left for the city (for he is staying there now), he did not hesitate to say: "I will ask the emperor to send an imperial officer with me, so as to behead him outright, or else cut out his tongue." I do not know whether his word will come to pass. In view of this we have already made our farewells, guessing in any case, from the man's malice and from the concurrence of the bishops there (for, as they say, they are present), that something of the kind would be carried out. And the attendant, who had become fearful and trembling, since he too had been sharply threatened beforehand by that chief of the impious that if he were found guilty of even a small thing he would not live, was too afraid altogether to give us paper and ink. Hence the delay. Then a report also came to stand in our way: that you yourself had been taken

out of prison, and also that the bishop of Sardis (which one was not specified) had been beheaded for some impiety. So the delay came from both causes. Nevertheless, since we lowly ones have been granted to make our voice heard in your ears once more, we let you know that we are well in body, and, if it may be said, in spirit too, through your holy prayers, together with those of my blessed father. As for what you told me, what shall I say, what shall I speak, except that bitter persecution follows the harshness of the heresy? For what do you expect to see, when Christ is denied through insult to his holy image? Is it not blood poured out and flesh cut? Is it not affliction and distress? Is it not chains and prisons, and every other kind of maltreatment? Is it not vessels of wrath fitted for destruction, of whom the one you mentioned is one? And there will be worse things still, if the heresy lasts long. But blessed are those who endure, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Already the choirs of the confessors and the martyrs exult and rejoice, welcoming some through a happy death, and anointing others invisibly with their visitations. And why do I speak of martyrs? Christ himself, to whom they bear witness, rejoices and contends together with each one of those who confess. For if it were not so, those who bear the present trials would not bear them nobly; women would not show manly courage like the holy women of old; laymen and senators would not strip for the contests; young girls would not despise the sight of impious men; public prisons would not be seen everywhere, and deserts, mountains, glens and caves would not be filled with those driven into flight for the Lord's sake; in a word, the whole world under heaven would not be ringing with it. So it is plainly believed that Christ is being persecuted; and so we must hope, and be eager, that everyone who believes in truth will bear any punishment whatever with Christ and together with Christ. Such is our news. Let the meek hear it and be glad. Let East and West hear what is happening in Byzantium, and give praise. Where sin abounded, grace has overflowed all the more. Here is an athlete's resistance; here blood flows, watering the Church of Christ more abundantly than the watering of the paradise in Eden. "As I live, says the Lord, those who glorify me I will glorify, and he who despises me shall be dishonoured." You too, whoever you may be who are zealous for the Lord, write down these new, or rather divinely wrought, martyrdoms, so that those who come after may know that God is truly among us, that the seed of the righteous lives, and that the golden race of martyrs bears Christ, against which the gates of Hades have not prevailed and will not prevail, as he who cannot lie has promised. "It is hard for you," he says, "to kick against the goads," and it cannot be otherwise. Wretch that I am, I address these words to you. But you, holy child, give me your prayers in return. Greet by name your fellow confessors and fellow disciples; and not only these, but, if you reach them, all the other elect of God too, those chosen out of tens of thousands, those who are

lights in the world, vessels of mercy, useful to God, longed for by the Trinity; by whose prayers may we too, the unworthy, be saved. The one who is with me greets you along with everyone. 72. To Nicholas, his son. [?] Since you are eager to learn, brother Nicholas, on what four grounds the truth about the venerable image of Christ is established, know that it rests on natural doctrine, on ancient history, on the words of the saints, and on synodal pronouncement. How on natural doctrine? Because the very nature of a body is subject to touch and colour; and what is subject to touch and colour is circumscribable, that is, can be depicted. Such is the body of Christ, just like ours: tangible and coloured. Indeed it is written: "And all who touched him were saved." And elsewhere: "And the appearance of his face became different." Therefore he is depicted according to the form of his body, without anything happening to the uncircumscribability of his divinity. For neither am I, who am circumscribed in body, necessarily circumscribed as well in my invisible soul; nor, because my body is circumscribable and my soul uncircumscribable, is the one person cut in two. So much the more, then, Christ undergoes no cutting or division by being depicted in bodily form. How on ancient history? Because the whole world under heaven, from the time of Christ's ascension itself, shows his venerable image painted in the holy churches. What could be clearer proof of the truth than this? For a deed is surer than a word, and the eye a more trustworthy witness than the ear. How on the words of the saints? Because in one place Peter, the chief of the apostles, says: "Bring out the image of our Lord Jesus Christ and set it up in the little tower, so that the peoples may see what form the Son of God took"; and in another the great Basil declares: "Let Christ too, the judge of the contests, be painted on the panel." And clearly all the saints agree with them. How on synodal pronouncement? Because the synod assembled after the sixth ecumenical council says this: "We decree therefore that from now on, in place of the ancient lamb, the image of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ be set up." And if the iconoclasts should say that they establish their own doctrine on the same four grounds, let them show how, for instance on the first head. Do they say that his body was such as the truth has shown, or not? If it was such, they will admit, even against their will, that Christ is depicted. But if it was not

such, the only thing left for them is to say that it was altogether intangible and colourless; for there is no middle ground between these, just as there is none between material and immaterial, visible and invisible. But to say that Christ took such a body belongs to the Manichaeans, who babble that Christ's saving economy took place in appearance and fantasy. On the second: even if they themselves keep silent about the truth, the stones will cry out that the world under the sun is radiant all around with the image of Christ. On the third: those who set themselves against Peter the chief and the great Basil are complete strangers to the fold of Christ. On the fourth: the synod against the image of Christ which they call that of Blachernae is much later than the one assembled after the sixth in support of the image of Christ. The latter was accepted by the five patriarchs; the former was anathematized by four of them as fighting against Christ. Then too, the second synod at Nicaea, being of one mind with the synod after the sixth, is acceptable to the five; while the one assembled now to confirm the synod of Blachernae against the image of Christ is to be spat upon like that one. This, then, is a concise account of the truth and a refutation of its opponents. 73. To Naucratius, his son. [?] The sacred Scripture says: "A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children, and she would not be comforted." But I, wretch that I am, adapting the saying, might fittingly say this: Glad tidings of joy have been heard by us from your honour, at which not this city or that, but almost, one might say, the whole world under heaven should leap for joy. For the Lord has brought down, not Sihon king of the Amorites, nor Og king of Bashan, petty kings oppressing a small part of the world, but the newly appeared great dragon, who plundered much of the world; the crooked serpent hissing blasphemies; the abomination of desolation; the vessel of wrath; the son of Tabeel, not to say of Caballinus; the offspring of Ahab; the copy of Julian; the full measure of the evil one; the insulter of Christ; the enemy of the Theotokos; the adversary of all the saints. For he proved himself the utter enemy and persecutor of those whose venerable features he persecuted and destroyed. Let the heavens be glad and the earth rejoice; let the mountains drip sweetness and the hills righteousness. The enemy has fallen; the one who struck us has been crushed. The mouth that spoke unjust things has been stopped; the hand of Absalom has been held back; hard-hearted Pharaoh is gone. And this is not yet the time or place for me to tell what is worth hearing about that most wicked dragon. But I would add this to what has been said: that it was fitting for the apostate, in just the way you have written, to [?]

end his life. It was fitting that the son of darkness should meet death at night; fitting that he who laid waste the divine churches should see swords bared against him in the church of the Lord; fitting that he who abolished the divine altar should not be saved by fleeing to it; that the hand stretched out against the holy things should be cut off; that a sword should be driven into the throat that belched out godless words; that a mortal wound should pierce the shoulder that was brandished to insult Christ; that for the shedding of righteous blood unrighteous blood should be shed; that in return for the cutting and scraping of limbs and backs his limbs should be cut off by God's hand; that in return for holy deaths an unholy death should be displayed; and that instead of purple his accursed [?] seed should be clothed in rags. And it is not out of gloating over the fall of the impious man that I describe the manner of his death, for I am groaning and weeping; but because the wicked man has perished wickedly, [?] … shall perish, as the sentence of him who cannot lie declares; and everyone who rages against God will perish, even here, in a manner matching what he has done. I do not yet speak of the fire to come at the last, by which every impious and lawless man will be tested. What then is to be said to this? There is need of a new Josiah, or, if you like, of a Jovian or someone else of that kind, who, being zealous for the Lord, would hasten to restore what has been broken down, to join together what has been separated, to render to God what is God's, as the saying goes, and to set up again the image of Christ, and of the Theotokos, and of each of the saints. Not that the image of Christ ever fell, far from it, but that we who fell through impiety may be raised up. Such a man we sinners pray may appear and become emperor, most devout and chosen by God. If it is so, that is best, and to be celebrated for ever. But if, because of my sins, it is not so, let us at least remain firm in the confession of Christ, not departing from his holy guard, not cowering at all, nor fearing anything before God: God himself is our surety. Show these things to your fellow confessors, and greet them from us too, along with any whom you judge to be friends and devout. May we be granted also to come and converse face to face. But if this is not God's will, make use of the letter, my brother, seeing and being seen through it. Your brother Nicholas greets you warmly. 74. To Michael, autocrat and emperor. [?] It is right, now above all, that praise should be brought to perfection from the mouths of all who have been persecuted: first to Christ the King of all, and then to your God-chosen Majesty, through whom we who were fettered have obtained release, we who were imprisoned relief, we who were afflicted comfort, we who were wounded health, we who were condemned [cod.: "in hiding"] freedom of speech, we who were exiled our return. And indeed I think I am right to suppose that the suffering of your Majesty came first as a figure of Christ, so that, having done like for like, it might now say

and she too, with Christ and after Christ, [says] to those in bonds, “Come out,” and to those in darkness, “Show yourselves.” And: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has raised up a horn of salvation for us”: the new David, the second Josiah, the emperor who brings peace, who will surely do what pleases God, who may raise up what has fallen and bind together what has been cut apart, who will dress the wounds and heal them, and, to speak in the words of the prophet, raise us up on the third day. But, Christ-imitating emperor, those who died in the heresy before this have gone off to the portion of perdition, for by denying his image they denied Christ, even if they are called Christians. For to believe in Christ is nothing other than to believe that the Son of God the Father, having become perfect man, is portrayed in an image in our likeness, so that he is nothing other than what we are, while remaining the same, uncircumscribed with the Father and the Spirit, inasmuch as he is true God. In this way, then, let him be understood as mediator between God and men: as having what belongs to both, and lacking nothing whatever in either, as the whole choir of the God-bearing fathers proclaims. And just as in the case of your Majesty the acceptance of your stamped image is a confession that you reign, and the reverse holds likewise, so too it is possible to take the same in the case of Christ, the King of all the earth, and much more so, since of his kingdom there shall be no end. If, then, it has been shown in all truth that by denying the image of Christ one has denied Christ himself, clearly by rejecting the veneration of the image Christ himself has been refused veneration. And for this reason the whole world under heaven, from the time of the apostolic preaching itself, carries and venerates, both in the divine churches and on the sacred vessels, the holy image of Christ, of the Theotokos, of the angels (since these too are depicted in bodily form by God's command, although they are bodiless), and of the saints of every age. Sight bears witness to this through pictures, and hearing through written accounts. Our Church, however, has lately been torn away from the four patriarchs and has acted lawlessly to no purpose. But now is the acceptable time, most Christ-loving lord; now is the day of salvation, for us to be reconciled to Christ through the mediation and goodwill of your peace-bringing reign, and to be united to Rome, the head of the churches of God, and through her to the three patriarchs, so that with one accord and with one mouth we may glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, together with the Son and the Holy Spirit, and magnify also your most pious reign, for which so many have prayed.

75. To Stephen the Asecretis. [?]

Long ago, my dear friend, you sent us a greeting through the voice of the man who guards us. May we both be rescued from his madness! For he breathes out threats and fury against the pious beyond all measure, binding and imprisoning, tormenting and ravaging the churches of God with every kind of blasphemy and drunken violence, in a way I doubt any other of those who have been

condemned for impiety has ever done. But I praise your love of wisdom, and very rightly. For it was the act of a philosopher to break into speech before the Majesty you know of, as were your other words and efforts to bring back our fallen Church. And truly a wise man, one known for his piety, ought to do this, both for his own good and for the good of the whole body of Christ, which the great dragon cut apart: the apostate, the crooked serpent, the forerunner of the Antichrist, the foul and blasphemous tongue, the one who exalts himself above every temple of God, the Assyrian mind, the barbarian abortion, the hand like Rabshakeh's, the God-accursed heart, the servant of Satan in his whole body. I do not know what satire I could compose worthy of that wretch, given the many names of the abominable man's impiety. But going through all that is for another time. Now tell me this, thrice-beloved: how is it that, though the winter has passed, there is no full spring, but only a spell of fair weather and a gleam of good sailing? The fire has been put out; why is something smoky still left? Bestir yourself still more, my beloved; contend the harder, member of Christ. Do you not see the burner of the pious, how he has fallen, a portent spoken of and heard of everywhere? “If this man's ruin does not bring us to our senses,” says the Golden-mouthed, “who will have mercy on us any longer?” Shall we not sober up? Shall we not consider that, had Christ not been denied when his holy image was set aside, he would not have destroyed its abuser in this way? Hear this, all you nations; give ear, all who inhabit the world, to what has happened among the Greeks. Before the Antichrist, an Antichrist: the sign of the kingdom of Christ has been taken away from us. For if this, which is the likeness of his bodily features, is not displayed among us, while [they] carry the figure of the cross [?], and the one is cast out while the other is taken up, then Christ has been divided. Or rather, the King who slew the devil is spat upon, while the spear by which he slew the enemy has had its power crowned with a diadem, as though by an equal victory it had subjected the one who was slain, as an enemy, to the one who slew him [?]. Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth! What is this bewilderment that has come over the people of God? Hear, East and West, how Byzantium has been blinded, how she has been deafened, not hearing your voice of reproof, not looking to your testimony that shows the way, but [following] Jannes and Jambres, the opponents of Christ, that destructive pair, which I know well the Trinity will soon destroy, so that this pair too may be carried off together with the two impious men who perished before them: the four-headed chariot of the devil. Come then, come, brother; enter the contest still; the Lord commands it. Speak good things into the honored ears of our pious emperor. Let him imitate the celebrated Josiah. Let him become a new David, spurning the deeds of the abominable Leo as those of a Saul or an Amon, and thereby winning the favor of God

and securing the invincible power of his reign with the crown of peace.

76. To Stephen the Magister. [?]

I know, my lord, how to hold back before those of high rank, and especially before yours, which none surpasses. Yet your approachability and the modesty of your mind gave us the boldness to write to you once long ago and to do the same now, since the time calls for it and we sinners have been released from the imprisonment we suffered for the Lord's sake upon the end of the persecutor. When the news of that end was heard, it made both ears of every man ring, not simply because he was removed, but because it happened in such a way. This, then, is the occasion of the letter. But before the subject that moved me to write, I want to say this: I did not receive the news of the death of your good and ever-memorable wife unmoved or without groaning, thinking how great a wound your honored soul received in that separation. For she was a blessed woman, one of those truly worthy of praise, so far as one hears from outside. I too, lowly as I am, had some slight experience of her, and my blessed father much more; but you, my lord, know everything in every respect. May her memory be with the righteous. For I gather that, along with her other virtue, she was also very orthodox. Why I write is plain to your great-hearted authority. The choir of the persecuted seeks you; the word of truth calls upon you, the former because you love piety and love monks, the latter because you are its outspoken lover. Not that you have failed until now to stir yourself as the champion of both, since we have heard what you have done and said under God's prompting, but so that you may do so in what follows as well. Do you see, my lord, how great the evil of the heresy is? For if it were not so great, the sufferers would not be so many, nor the tortures and afflictions that have spread to the ends of the earth. You also see the death of the persecutor. Take courage, you who are quick to be encouraged; be moved, you who are quick to be moved. Stretch out a hand to our Church lying on the ground, as far as you can; as far as your strength allows, speak still more good things into the ears of our pious emperor. Your contest is for Christ, for the Theotokos, for all the saints. For if someone who holds fast to the emperor's image says or does something, he does his favor to none other than the emperor. And if the matter concerned only a single saint, your prize would be very great. But where the action is about Christ and for Christ, is it not a joy to you, glory and exultation, to give your whole self with great eagerness? Yes, my ever-beloved lord, I too, wretched as I am, implore you. Besides, we do ourselves good by caring for the common good, since we share in the sickness: even if not with a perverse mind, we are still stained by communion with the heretics. This is our humble

petition, this our reminder. Moreover, no small rewards are laid up for you even for a simple good word, let alone for one who has given himself to such great toil, as we have heard. May the mighty hand of God keep you safe, you who are truly admirable and foremost [?] of the senate.

77. To the holy confessors, fathers and brothers. [?]

Now is the time to cry out with David and say: “Rejoice in the Lord, you righteous; praise befits the upright. Sing to him, and make music to him,” because the Lord has heard your earnest supplication, together with that of all who share your glory. And what has happened? The impious man has perished; the one who struck us has been crushed. You have conquered the son of wickedness; you have cast down the beast of wrath, that crooked mind. O thrice-beloved, how powerful your blood is! It struck down that avenging scourge; it poured out the defiled blood of the murderer, since the One who does not lie promised to hear those who cry to him night and day, as the Scriptures say. Learn, enemy of Christ, how much the cry of those whose flesh you tore availed. Know, leader of defilement, what a result your war against Christ has brought you: since you were kicking against the goads, you fell headlong and burst open. There was poured out, if not your entrails, yet your defiled blood, through three wounds, as befits one who offended against the Trinity by outraging the holy image of Christ. Go off with Judas, you Jewish-minded one. Join your father, Uralyphius [?] Caballonymus. [?] this first, as the prophet says, and the sharper [?] upon

O his madness against Christ, and your confession! You are Christ-bearing men, nurslings of piety, fragrances of immortality, the public indictment of the enemy. You are the sinews of the Church, the foundation of the faith, the glory of the world under the sun. Your memory is a blessed one, and the time to come will receive it too. Yours is a heavenly crown, fittingly woven with the flowers of hymns. What remains? We must praise God and give thanks to the pious emperor for releasing you, for the present, from prisons and pains; and we must hope that God, who granted a favorable beginning, will bring the end along with the beginning, and make the horn of peace-bringing orthodoxy rise up. Only I beg you to remember me more fervently in your prayers, and always to take heed to yourselves. For as long as we breathe, the tempter is at hand. Your brother Nicholas greets you according to the

my lowliness; but I did not receive it because of some mishap. Yet as though I had received it, I write you this paltry little letter of mine, which brings a greeting and says, “Rejoice.” Why? Because the one who struck us has been crushed, or rather cut down; because the Lord has shown before the eyes of all that the one who rejects his holy image is one who denies him. For as a ray is not separated from the sun, so neither is an image separated from its prototype, except only in the difference of substance; I am speaking, of course, of things made by art. Yet even though the truth has flashed out in this way, no one looks, no one anywhere comes to his senses. And who would not groan, who would not weep? Not for those who have won the prize — let no one suppose that, for how could those blessed by God be wept over? — but for those who do not see and who persist in the same gloom of impiety. I, wretched as I am, think this way and weep this way. But you, sacred head and friend of my nothingness, do not cease praying that reconciliation may come from above to the people of God, and then that we too, unworthy as we are, may be saved, following behind you saints. The brother with me greets you. I greet my brothers who are with your holiness, and especially the holy Arsenius.

79. To Nicephorus, the most holy patriarch. [506]

I, wretched as I am, wrote long ago, not looking for a letter in return, since masters owe none even to their servants, but longing to show my own disposition, as my longing and our separation compelled me to, not unreasonably. But you, divine summit and chief of sacred heads, not only deigned to write back to the unworthy, acting plainly in imitation of God, but even in the very address showed us such a divine height of humility that our pitiable mind was struck with amazement. What a wonder! If one so great and so lofty in rank, whose virtue shines forth equal to it, as the facts themselves bear witness, called himself the son of a weak man, what should the worthless and obscure man call himself? And if the lamp of holiness signs himself a sinner, what answer will the sinner and the destitute give? Even if nothing else had been written in the letter, this alone would have been enough to astonish the mind of the one who received it and to proclaim the unsurpassed virtue of the one who sent it. But when we lowly ones also read through the whole texture of the sacred document, we were even more delighted, finding the whole body of the discourse fitted in perfect harmony with its heading. You know, holy one of God, what you uttered under the Spirit's prompting: how you strengthened our weak mind with the medicines of praise, how you rooted us firmly in endurance, so as not to lose heart in afflictions, and all the other things you indicated, adorned with divine wisdom. But blessed be God, who in such an earthquake of impiety has given to his

Church so great a champion and helmsman, unshaken, unwavering, holding fast the word of life and kindling the light of confession for the world under the sun. And if the winter has not yet passed, even though some small patch of clear sky has gleamed out, we must not lose heart, thrice-blessed one. For the Lord who gave the little spark of peace is able, swayed by your prayers that bow before God, to spread out the whole spring of orthodoxy as well; and that will surely be when the cloud of wrath has been completely transformed and the longing of those who love God has been proved more brilliantly. This much I have now dared to growl, like a little dog, to my truly good chief shepherd, having received your venerable letter with overflowing joy.

80. To John the Logothete. [507]

The time has opened a door of boldness for us to speak to good men who are also friends. And among such, who could be greater than your piety? For precisely because of your piety you endured no few afflictions and ill-treatments from the man who offended God, ruined the world with impiety, and had his life broken off in a manner equal to his apostasy — not in a holy place, even if the saying frightens some. For a church profaned by heretics is not a holy temple of God but a common house, as the great Basil says, since the angel set over it, as over every church, has withdrawn because of the impiety. That is why the sacrifice performed in it is not acceptable to God either. Hear him saying: “The impious man who sacrifices a calf to me is like one who kills a dog.” But if you take it that the impious man died as though in a church, this way of seeing it would fit too. For it was necessary, truly necessary, that the one who had acted against the churches of God should see swords drawn against him in a church; that the one who did away with the divine altar should be done away with at the altar; that the hand stretched out to outrage Christ should be cut; that a sword should be driven through the head that had moved to such destruction; that a mortal blow should fall on the shoulder raised to torture the pious; that the one who dishonored the holy image of Christ, of the Theotokos, and of any of the saints should be sent out of the imperial halls in dishonor. Why, my lord, have I described the abominable man's death to you so dramatically? Because from this not only the pious emperor but every person must recognize the outcome that fits the impiety of the impious. And I very much wonder how our good sovereign, knowing this, does not expose publicly the impiety of that murderer, and grant to himself and to his subjects the atonement of orthodoxy, as an emperor of peace in imitation of Christ. For this reason I, lowly as I am, ask and implore you, most pious one, to press on, as indeed I have heard that you are [?], and to give yourself wholly to the restoration of the faith, in which lies the salvation both of the Majesty and of the subjects.

81. To Pantaleon the Logothete [?]. [508]

The virtue of others we have come to know by hearsay; but yours, my highly honored lord, we knew first by sight, and now by a report that has reached even the remote place where we are. And what is the report? That your Spirit-moved mouth spoke out boldly the wisdom of God, words of truth, for the benefit and salvation of your own soul and of our whole Church. Blessed are you, and blessed is your name; may all the pious who heard you praise you. May a crown of graces be upon your honored head, and a golden chain upon your sacred neck, son of obedience, child of light, nursling of piety. Thus says the Lord: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it,” because you obeyed my voice. For it is a commandment of the Lord not to keep silent when the faith is in danger. “Speak,” it says, “and do not be silent.” And: “If he shrinks back, my soul has no pleasure in him.” And: “If these keep silent, the stones will cry out.” So when the faith is at issue, no one can say, “Who am I? A priest? Not at all. A ruler? Not that either. A soldier? How so? A farmer? Not that either. A poor man, earning only my daily bread; I have no concern or care for the matter at hand.” Alas! The stones will cry out, and you remain silent and senseless? Insensible nature has obeyed God, and are you [?]? What has no soul, and has never been called to account in a court, utters a voice as though fearing the command; and you, who are going to be called to account by God at the time of examination, and must give an account even of an idle word, even if you are a beggar, say thoughtlessly, “What concern is this of mine?” “These things, brothers,” says Paul, “I have applied to myself and Apollos for your sake, so that you may learn through us not to go beyond what is written.” So even the poor man is deprived of every defense on the day of judgment if he does not speak now, knowing he will be judged for this alone — let alone those who follow him in rank, up to the very one who wears the diadem, whose judgment is beyond compare. “For the mighty will be mightily examined,” it says; and: “Severe judgment falls on those in high places.” Speak, then, my lord, speak. That is why I too, wretched as I am, speak, for I fear the judgment seat. Speak out to the divinely resounding ears of our pious emperor, since you are among those in high places, and tell him that no heresy that has sprung up from the Church is more terrible than this heresy of the iconoclasts. It has denied Christ; it strikes him in the face, raging in deed and in word. On the one hand, it babbles that Christ is not circumscribed in the form of his body, which does away with the Word's becoming flesh. For if he is flesh, he must surely also be circumscribed; otherwise what the gospel proclaims is a phantom, by Manichaean thinking. On the other hand, it [?] breaks, demolishes, and burns down every divine church, every sacred

…[?] offering bearing the image of Christ, of the Theotokos, or of any of the saints. We Christians are perishing. Let us come before the face of Christ with confession; let us embrace Christ, whom we deny by rejecting his holy icon.

82. — To Demochares, the General Logothete. [?]

Meeting good men gives boldness even to those who do not know them to [?] approach them, and not only to those who know them and have experienced their kindness. That is why we humble ones have taken courage and are writing to your extraordinary and most pious Greatness. We praise it, as is fitting, because it is the good shoot of a noble root, the holy fruit of sound judgement, and the much-prized ornament of a varied education. That is why it is welcome to emperors and spoken of by all. And so, passing from one office to the next, it has risen to the very highest of those in authority. Well done, and quite rightly so. Because of that same virtue it is also dear to us lowly ones, but given our worthlessness that is nothing much to admire. Still, the occasion may suggest that even lowly people should bring you a request. The request is that you stretch out a hand to the Church among us, which has fallen through the fall into impiety. Indeed, we have heard that you have already done this. We prayed for you, sinners though we are, and blessed you from a heart worn with toil, because you justly rebuked John, the ringleader of impiety, and said to him as much as the foul man deserved to hear. These things, I think, have already been made known to us and to many others. For there is nothing hidden that will not be known, as the Scriptures say. Besides, the leaders of impiety have been shown, quite rightly, to be guilty of such deeds. So do not give up your noble struggle, my lord. Bring help that matches your very great eminence, since God has called you to this out of the need of the time. In this way you will win more glory with God, who was pleased with you, with the emperor, who has made a start in piety, and with all who uphold the right word of truth. You will also give yourself a protective remedy against the defilement of communion with the heretics.

83. — To my holy Fathers and confessors of Christ, John, Michael and Basil. [515]

Now too I thought it right to write to my Fathers, and to write to you together, since you have been found worthy of the same virtue and concord, or rather of the same witness for Christ. Our good God has been pleased to release even us sinners from prison through the mediation of the good emperor. So I offer you this letter as a kind of wedding gift, rejoicing and sharing in the joy

of your Paternity and of your victory, so to speak, in Christ. For you have conquered the evil one, wonderful men. Within, you conquered him by wrestling with your thoughts; without, by godly endurance. You did not bend the knee to the dragon's servant. Leo was clearly the dragon's minister, his utterly wicked servant, the man who insulted the image of Christ and murdered the saints. The two were in full agreement, and both made a pact to do away with the name of Christ by removing his divine and venerable [?] image. The time of the second divine appearing has not yet arrived, so that Christ might be openly denied. But blessed be God! He destroyed the persecutor by a notorious death worthy of his apostasy, for it was right that the man who cut up the Lord's body should have his life broken off, cut down by the sword. And by showing you to be crowned victors he has won glory for his Church: you are trainers in virtue, props of the faith, foundations of the truth, and examples of endurance. You are guides in very deed, truly monks, and likenesses of those blessed saints of old who stood firm in similar trials and were adorned with the unfading crown of righteousness, dancing for ever. That is what you are, and your praise is beyond my worthless tongue. It sings only enough to pay what the occasion requires, to satisfy my longing, and to rekindle the spirit to pray without ceasing that God, when we call on him, may make the blessing of peace dawn on us in full. For you see, venerable ones, how affairs are still unsettled. But he who made the beginning is able also to bring the end to a good outcome. Please pray for my lowliness, ever-venerable ones.

84. — To Theodore the monk. [529?]

I begged your Godliness to stop praising me and instead to pray that I may not be wholly cut off from God. Yet you, carried away by I know not what, have broken out into even greater words of praise. Not so, Father, by no means! Do you not know that I, wretch that I am, am the greatest sinner of all men? I do not know how, but by God's mercy I have been found worthy to remain in prison for his sake. That is why I am afraid that when he comes to the confessors' wedding now being celebrated, he may find me without a wedding garment, that is, the garment of purity, and say to his servants the angels: 'Bind his hands and feet, cast him out, and throw him into the outer darkness, for he joined himself unworthily to my confessors.' Knowing this, Father, weep for me instead, and pray that this does not happen to me. So much for that.

Now, about the 'through' and the 'up' used by Basil the Great, that is, the prepositions in the passage about the image. I do not think the saint wrote it both ways. The mistake comes from

copying. Still, both bring the meaning to the same thing. Take this, for example: 'The honour paid to the image passes up to the archetype.' This is true of a natural image and of an artificial one. In the case of artificial images, 'passing up' means only that the honour is the same despite the difference of essence. In the case of natural images, it also means that the essence of both is the same. Indeed, the Truth himself said: 'Whoever rejects you rejects me, and whoever rejects me rejects the one who sent me.' So the Son is the natural image of God the Father, and we are an artificial image of the Son [?], that is, a made image, for God may be called the maker and craftsman of all things. Saint Basil applied the word 'artificial' to images on panels. We may take the term to cover both ourselves, who have come to be after the image of God, and the image we have crafted on a panel. And the identity is closer in the matter of likeness between our portrait and ourselves, as between Christ's portrait and Christ himself, than between us and God. For the gap between God and human beings is infinite. He is uncreated, incomprehensible, uncircumscribable, and everything else in that series, while human beings are creature, body, circumscription, and everything in that order. A man and the image of a man, however, are both creatures, even if the one differs from the other in the kind of creation and in essence.

Your addition was excellent. From the very words spoken by God it showed us that when the image is rejected, he himself is rejected, and that when Christ himself is rejected, the Father who sent him is rejected. So the Iconoclasts turn out to be not only deniers of Christ but threefold deniers.

As for 'passes through', passing through comes to the same thing as passing up. The Lord said: 'I am ascending to my Father.' And Moses said: 'I will cross over and see.' The two movements look alike. Neither is circular compared with the other, nor spiral. If they differ, it is in position, not in relation. For it is said that there are seven kinds of movement. Ascent, to draw it, is this: | . Crossing is this: — . So, as has been said, both look equal, for in philosophical terms each is a line [?]. Up stands in relation to down exactly as right stands to left. So 'passing up' and 'passing through' come to the same thing. If the argument succeeds, thanks be to God the Word. If not, my excellent friend, teach me in my ignorance.

85. — To Athanasius, his son. [542]

You ask how the icon of Christ is not given worship, while Christ is venerated in it, since there is one veneration for both. It is because the veneration offered to Christ himself is worship. When I venerate him, I venerate the Father and the Holy Spirit together with him.

That is our Trinitarian veneration and worship. The veneration offered to the icon is the same (how could it not be? Where there is one power and one glory, there is clearly one reverence and one veneration), but it is relative, that is, homonymous. For when I venerate the icon, I do not venerate others together with him; I venerate Christ himself. He is not divided in hypostasis, but he differs in the principle of essence. This veneration is relative, not worship. Even if it is the same veneration, there it is understood and named as Trinitarian, that is, natural; here it is the reverse, relative, that is, hypostatic. For if you were to call it worship, you would be implying that the Father and the Spirit had become incarnate like the Son, which is absurd. So when I venerate the icon of Christ, I am not venerating the Godhead, as some say, for that term refers to the Trinity, and the Trinity did not become incarnate. Far from it! It is Christ himself I venerate [?] in it, for he alone is God the Word made flesh. And when I venerate Christ himself, I clearly venerate the Father and the Spirit together with him. So veneration of the icon is to be understood and called [relative veneration], while veneration of Christ himself is worship, because the Father and the Spirit are understood and venerated together with him.

86. — A letter from all [?] the abbots to the emperor Michael. [548]

We, the least of bishops and abbots, who have gathered at the command of your God-revering Majesty, speak these first words before your God-appointed might, words of thanksgiving and praise: we who had been driven out have been called back, we who were in distress have been shown mercy, we who had fainted have been revived. We have passed from winter to spring, from storm to calm, from despondency to good cheer, and have seen strange and wonderful things. For such is your righteous reign: joyful, gladdening, much prayed for, a bringer of peace, a lover of justice, and worthy of many other titles. In imitation of Christ our true God, it joins together what was divided, heals what was sick, and turns grief into joy. It is an exceptional reign, equal to the blessed reigns of old, and no human tongue could easily extol it as it deserves. Since this is so, we unworthy ones beg and entreat to be granted the sight of your sacred person and to hear the sweetest voice from your all-honoured and God-wise mouth. Then, seeing with our eyes what we hear with our ears, we may leap for joy in spirit and exchange our dejection, like a mourning garment, for the exultation of gladness.

Our second matter concerns the pure and blameless faith of us Christians, and on this we venture to say the following with all respect. If the question were a human matter, under the authority of our most holy high priest or of us unworthy ones, we would be bound to yield not just a little but everything, as the commandment directs.

But the question concerns God and is directed to God, to whom all things are subject. Not this person or that, not even Peter and Paul, not even one of the angels, would dare to change the smallest detail, since that would overturn the whole Gospel. Nor is it right, under the apostolic injunction, to enter into debate with the heterodox and argue against them, except for the purpose of admonition. That is why we, the unworthy servants of your pious might, do not dare even to mutter. But if your divine magnanimity doubts or distrusts that any point has been piously settled by the high priest, let your great and God-supported hand, out of zeal for divine things and for the good of all, command that a clarification be obtained from elder Rome, as has been the ancestral tradition from of old and from the beginning

Having just heard news of your Blessedness, thrice-beloved Fathers, I, the lowly one, rejoiced greatly and glorified our good God. But I was deeply grieved that I was not found worthy to see you and enjoy the gifts that are in you. For I would have seen men of God, hierarchs of the Lord, blessed men, lights of the world, pillars of the faith, and whatever else is good, all of which you both are and are called. What a loss! What a misfortune! Yet our many sins are the cause of what has happened. We are not surprised at our bad luck. Instead we put forward a request. What is it? That you console us in your absence with letters, admonishing, enlightening and strengthening us, and showing us whatever is true, whatever is honourable, whatever is just, whatever is steadfast, whatever is worthy of the contest. If there is any virtue and any praise for confession, write about these things. Write too about how Christ depicted in an image is to be venerated, homonymously or synonymously, since the one is orthodoxy and the other heterodoxy. And since veneration is understood to be directed to Christ and to his icon, tell us whether it is one veneration or two, since the first is our view and the second is the Iconoclasts'. For where there is one hypostatic likeness, there is also one and the same veneration, while the essence of the icon

is in no way venerated. This little word of ours is a reminder, not a lesson. Your words are certainly more perfect, as far as the anointing you have received surpasses ours. In that anointing may you finish the course set before you in all holiness and courage, as men who are to receive the crown of righteousness.

88. — To Ammoun, his son. [569]

Alas! From the very first line of this letter I send up a groan from the depths of my heart and mingle tears with the ink over what I have heard about you, brother. They say you have thrown off the holy habit of a monk, that you are living among laypeople, and that you have taken a woman about with you. What a pitiful thing to hear! What a misfortune for me! For your sin, my child, is mine, as a father shares the suffering of his child. Where is the light of your mind? Where is the wing of hope? Where is your love for God? Where is the shield of faith? Where is the judgement of reason? Where is your flight from the world? Where is your renunciation of everything on earth? Where is your post in the monastery? Where is the reception, so full of compunction, that welcomed you in? Where is your training in the common life? Where is the confession that brought you light? Where are your good tears? Where is your reverent [?] bearing? Where is the testimony of the whole brotherhood? Where is the confession made at the holy sanctuary? Where are the promises made with God and the angels as witnesses? Where is the radiant brightness of the habit? Where is the marriage understood in the spirit? Where is the Lamb of God sacrificed for you? Where is the joy of the Gospel and of the brothers? Where is the most holy kiss from everyone? Where is your standing at the divine altar? Where is your divine partaking of the body and blood of Christ? Where is that whole bright rite that gladdens the angels? Where is the shining lamp? Where is the true vine? Where is the fruitful planting of the Spirit? Where is my son, wretch that I am, who advanced further and further in goodness and proved useful to the brotherhood, the child of God, the dancer in the light, the citizen of the kingdom of heaven, the chosen vessel? How has he turned back? How has the beloved kicked against us? How has the enlightened one been darkened? How has he cast off the armour of chastity? How has he become the devil's prey, taken captive by him to do his will, and denied [?] the fair Bridegroom, the Lord of glory, the ruler of all? Who will not groan from the depths? Who would not pity the one who has been deceived? Be astonished at this, O heaven! Cry out at this calamity, O earth! What has happened, brother? Were you not ashamed even before those who see you? Did you not blush before the very air? Did you not loathe the stench of that utterly accursed sin? Do you have a mind? Are you still alive [?]? Do you look at the sun? Do you see the moon? Do you behold the stars? It cannot be said, it cannot be said, how great the sin is, how deep the darkness, how great the folly. If only the matter ended there, the wretchedness would have some limit. But there is judgement, alas, inexorable

[?], eternal fire, outer darkness without light, gnashing of teeth, and all the other punishments that call for an accounting, and the accounting itself without end for ever. And I have not yet spoken of the loss of good things that you have brought on yourself. What are these [?]? To be with God: joy beyond words, life without blemish, eternal gladness, the delight of paradise, the illumination of the Holy Trinity, and every other blessedness that can be spoken of or imagined.

Come then, come, child! Come to your senses, be called back, be renewed. Throw off the cords of sin that the enemy has twisted around you. Cut yourself off from Eve. Come to Jesus, who bears no grudges and loves mankind beyond measure. He cries out plainly: 'Come, all you who labour and are burdened' with sins. He comes to meet you, embraces you, takes you into his house. He makes no charge about the past; he holds a feast once more; he saves the prodigal. Yes, I beg you, child: listen, be set on fire, wound the one who wounded you. Come, then, come quickly to us sinners. I lay down my life for you. I am the guarantor of your salvation. I will heal you with gentle remedies. With God's help I, wretch that I am, will embrace you even more than before. Only run to us, only do not stand still any longer. Leave Eve to play on her own. Or, if she is willing to listen in a godly way, put her in a convent. But you will give yourself to God and to us. I solemnly charge you, then, before God and the elect angels: when you hear these words, change your ways and hurry to us before the end comes, before the inexorable sentence shuts you out.

89. — To Theophilus, abbot. [579]

I heard a good deal about your Reverence, and it grieved me greatly. But those reports have been cleared away by your honoured letter. Indeed, I dare say the Lord has given you repentance and a defence for your return to the monastery, though that return was not seemly at a time when Christ was being persecuted. But now that the persecution has eased, what reason is there for returning, rather than for struggling? 'Watch me,' it says, 'and do the same.' That is what you ought to have said to the disciples who were calling you to hurry back home. You should not have obeyed them and become a pattern of defeat, and after a fall at that. Or do you not know that the communion you and those led away with you entered into so godlessly rested on the denial of Christ? Then, after you had chosen repentance by withdrawing (for that is the heart of repentance, and without it a fall goes unrepented), why did you turn back again to wrongdoing? Forgive me, Father. Since you have entrusted yourself to my lowliness, I am compelled to tell you what is fitting, as if from the mouth of the Lord. Why did you not either urge everyone to be persecuted alongside you in the same way, or, if they were unwilling, let them go as haters of Christ, lovers of the flesh, disobedient and no true sons? That way you would have nobly retrieved your defeat and become a good pattern

for those in your charge, and the Church of Christ would have seen you building it up instead of tearing it down as before. That is what our most God-loving brother, the abbot of Medikion, did. So did our most holy Father of Laodicea, and others too. It must be one of two things: if they acted lawfully, then you acted unlawfully, as did anyone who has done the same as you. But I learn that there are some of the fallen party, whose names I will gladly pass over, who say that they have nothing at all to repent of in this, that they need not ask for so much as a single word of pardon, and that they did well. Because of it, they say, the brothers were saved and the churches were left unharmed. What hardness of heart! What fighting against God! Christ was denied when his holy icon was rejected, and so were the Theotokos and every one of the saints. This is why archbishops were persecuted, bishops exiled, abbots made to suffer the same, along with monks and nuns, laymen and laywomen. Some were beaten, others imprisoned; some starved to death, others had their flesh torn; some were cast into the sea, others put to death; some went into hiding, others fled. The deserts and caves were full of them; the mountains and the glens were full of them. Flesh was cut and blood flowed. Our world rang with the persecution, and the whole earth under heaven, so to speak, groaned and lamented. And you, thrice-wretched man, caught in that soul-destroying communion and staying in that place of ruin (for that is what I would call it, not a monastery), say that all is well. You mock the Christ-bearers as the Jews did, or rather you mock Christ himself, for whose sake the suffering is endured. What church did you preserve, when you defiled yourself, the temple of God? What brothers did you protect, when they were corrupted by your godless communion, even if only at meals? You are a scandal to the world, a model of denial, an incitement to perdition, flesh and not spirit, one who brings darkness and not light. This is what truth itself cries out to those who act so impiously. Unless they repent of saying such godless things, they are not to be counted as Christians.

You have heard the verdict, Father. You sinned by going back and breaking your promise. But the good God will forgive you. Stay in the monastery for now, since things have turned out otherwise. Keep confessing to everyone, 'I have sinned', so that God may be gracious to you and bring you back to your former light. That was when the lamp of your way of life shone, when even emperors held you in reverence, and when you did not make light of even the slightest lapse. As for the future, we will speak as the Lord arranges the affairs of the Church, and so too we will die together with you, out of love and in love. Pray for us sinners, and do not think that we have written to you out of arrogance. We know that we are an abomination among holy men. We wrote for the sake of the truth and of your salvation. And if [?] others also, let the one who has suffered confess to God the

[?]. To my beloved spiritual children and brothers, Laurence, Symeon, Dionysius, Poemen, Litoius [?], and the rest scattered here and there: Theodore, a sinful monk, sends greetings in the Lord. [583.] Those who live according to God can rejoice at all times, even when they meet with things contrary to joy. For one work of true gladness is hope in God, and living for him and through him, and moving, and doing anything else whatever. That you are such people the facts themselves bear witness. For what other reason were you scattered, toiled and were shaken, if not for our good God himself? And [?] now by his providence the persecution has eased with the accession of the good sovereign, and a door of free speech has been opened to the persecuted, who enjoy a measure of release and peace in every city and region. For this, Fathers, we owe the Lord thanksgiving, and intercession for a richer peace and for the strengthening of our God-appointed emperors. This, then, is the first point. The second is that neither we nor you should take this release as a loosening of virtue. Rather, wherever each of us is, let us be of the same mind and walk by the same rule, giving offence in nothing, so that the ministry may not be blamed, but in everything commending ourselves, as it is written, as ministers of God, in patience, in afflictions, in distresses, and in the other things to which life in these present days is subject. In this way we may keep what we have already achieved so that it cannot be taken from us, bear lightly what now befalls us, and meet what is to come in a way worthy of God. We are here, living outside the city with the emperor's knowledge, seeing and being seen by our brothers and Fathers who come to visit us, and enjoying the freedom granted by the good emperor. As for what comes next, the Lord will prosper it as he will: whether the sovereign orders us to stay here or to move and withdraw elsewhere, that is where we shall be taken. Only, as you keep to your own work, keep also to praying for my lowliness, that we may give no offence to these people or to those, or to the Church of God. The all-good God has been pleased, in many ways, to unite to us the brothers who had earlier broken away [?], with the proper explanation given. And we unworthy ones rejoiced with great joy, because we have seen with our own eyes what we did not hope for: the torn limbs have healed together, we keep a feast to the Lord as each one comes back, we give thanks to the Lord, and we are grateful [?] to those in power. For if nothing else, so far as we are concerned the gift is a great one; and again, we could not otherwise have had a fitting reconciliation unless in this way

we had been released [?] from the prisons and settled in such a residence. Everything has worked together for our good, and will, I well know, continue to work together through your holy prayers. And since the subject is recall: the letter-bearer, our beloved son Clement, the most pious hegumen, has been recalled and united to us along with the others, and even more fully than the others. He gladly accepted everything that needed to be said to him and made the proper defence on every point. We were pleased at this and embraced him warmly, hoping that through him we sinners also have this very thing as a saving boast. I beg you, too, to receive the brother as brothers, the member as members, the like-minded as those of like mind. For in this way you will find him, by the grace of Christ, sound in all things and seeking God.

[?]. To the Abbess of Nicaea. [585.]

Even before, the good reports about your Reverence moved us to write to you. And now, relying on the same praises, we write again and greet your Venerableness, approving you and calling you blessed, because for the Lord's sake you chose to undergo afflictions and distresses, persecution from your monastery, exile and removal, and whatever other hardship serves to show confession. These things deserve praise and thanksgiving; these are the prizes and contests of a Bride of Christ. And what is still more admirable is the holiness of the sisters under your hand. Some of them chose to strip for the contest of confession with you; they acted with courage, were scourged and confined, and glorified God in their body and in their spirit. O [?], O fine training! As the ruler, so the ruled; as the teacher, so are the pupils. You may well say, "Here am I, and the children whom God has given me": prizewinners, courageous, lovers of Christ rather than lovers of the flesh, counting all things as rubbish so that they may gain Christ, offering all their members to Christ so that they may serve their Lover. You have been ranked with the confessors and crowned with the martyrs, so far as concerns what has already happened. But, mother, no one is crowned unless he competes according to the rules, and the rule is to excel to the end in both faith and life. So I exhort and remind you that we should walk worthily of the calling to which we were called, with all humility and meekness, and with care for what lies ahead: neither to be caught by the Christ-denying heresy that still raves like the Corybants, nor to turn aside in anything from the ascetic life by which we ought to be ruled, but to do everything to the glory of God and to shine in every way with the light of the commandments. This, I believe, you are doing, to the praise of Christ's glory and to your eternal boast, and, if it may be said, ours too, sinners though we are. For if we are of one Father, we are all called brothers of one another, and not unreasonably we all count the efforts of all as our boast.

Pray for us. Our greeting in the Spirit. The Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen. I have heard that you practise great abstinence, and I was glad. But since moderation is best in all things, I remind you to moderate yourself in this too, so that the body may be brought into subjection and yet not grow too weak to serve the commandments.

12. To the bishops exiled for Christ's sake in Cherson. [586.]

It is the work of true love and the proof of unfeigned faith that your fatherly holiness, from so great a distance, has sent one of the brothers persecuted with you, Agapetus, the most venerable monk, or rather the most blessed, according to what the Lord sings of those persecuted for righteousness' sake, to visit first the divine and most preeminent head, and then us, the least among your brothers and spiritual sons. O fine good counsel! O sincere love! And of whom else could this be, if not of those who for Christ's sake chose to leave even their own people and to flee into a foreign land, cut off by so great a stretch of sea, and to endure there all that is likely to befall them? This has proved the clearest evidence. Blessed, then, is the Lord God, who moved you so deeply towards our insignificance, and who gave strength and grace to the messenger to make known to us everything you have accomplished and are still bearing, thrice-blessed Fathers, for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Hearing this, we rejoiced, we praised, we gave thanks, and we said that God is truly among you, well pleased and served by your confession on behalf of the truth. It seems to me that the providence that saves all things arranged your exile not only for your own sake but also for the salvation of the people there. For when you arrived you appeared as lights to those in the darkness and error of life, guides of the blind, teachers of virtue, heralds of piety, and instructors about the fearful outrages committed here against Christ. So both there and everywhere on land and sea the Lord made the confessors shine, as a demonstration of the truth and for the turning away of [?], just as in former times. And his name was magnified, the chosen people of Christ was proved, and the Christ-hating band was rejected. And finally the great dragon, the Assyrian mind, met an end of life worthy of the outrage he committed against God. How things stand here now it would be superfluous to say, since the letter-bearer is able, by the grace of Christ, to explain everything properly. With him, along with the letter, we have also sent a small distribution; please deign to accept it, and grant us your precious prayers for the strengthening of our souls.

[?]. To the Abbess of the Gordina convent. [?] Our beloved brother Antony asked us for this present note, saying that I had promised long ago to write it. So for this very reason, and because of the gifts you have sent, see, I address and greet you as mothers and as sisters in the Lord. I remember your meeting with us and the labour of love that you showed for his name, when you fled communion with the heretics and kept yourselves unstained by the world. Look to what lies ahead as well, holy ones, since there is at hand the ...

[?]. To Eudocia, a virgin.

... we were imprisoned there, I and brother Nicholas, when guards stood before the opening of the prison and, by order of the impious, let no one come near the guardhouse. Then, to pass over the earlier things, though they were considerable, you spoke boldly out of your trust in God: you sent us things, you nursed us, as it were, fed us, gave us drink, comforted us, anointed us, giving yourself up recklessly to death. And you would very nearly have met it in fact, had the hand of God not reached you first. You know the accusations of the neighbours and the interrogations by the officials: that you had received gifts from the condemned man, that you were obeying his instructions, this and that. And yet, O great faith! Even when these things were stirred up you did not give up at all. As if nothing new had happened, you held to your service again, winning over the guards with gifts and, as the saying goes, serving God through us sinners. From this came our rescue from dangers and our unhoped-for deliverance. How is this second to Priscilla and the famous Phoebe, or to those who supported [?] them, in the service for which they were called blessed by the divine Apostle? In no way, as it seems to me, except that it was done for the unworthy. But this makes it all the more praiseworthy. For there the greatness of the person might perhaps have moved even senseless stones to do good; here, on the contrary, the contemptibleness of those in need might have persuaded even feeling minds to grow numb. But since this is so, and you were seen to act in the opposite way, let the praise fall silent. We have received, then, beautiful virgin, your mercy, and we rightly praise you, and we also acknowledge and join in praising your other noble qualities: your self-control, your unkempt hair, your neglected clothing, your almsgiving, and above all your love of purity, in which you have never been found at fault by anyone at all. O your good work! O aged head, beloved of God! [?] Like a rose among thorns, you have given off fragrance in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, like an upright lily. What remains? That you continue from now on without stumbling, safe, and cherishing every other commandment of the Lord, so that you neither swear by the name of the Lord at all nor
