overlook any other of the commandments. I say this not as one who has caught you out in order to accuse you, but because I long for you to be complete in all things and so to attain the good things of the promises. Brother Nicholas greets you, and I greet the lord your nephew.

[?]. To Basil, hegumen. [600.]

In what your Reverence wrote, brother, you showed yourself content with the penances and eager for better things. This was explained not only by the letter-bearer but before him also by our most honoured brother Peter, who is dear to you too. At this I, the lowly one, was glad and gave thanks. For what we suffered, my friend, in having communicated with the denial of Christ's image, is no small or contemptible thing; it is something quite outrageous and plainly a denial of the faith. For the denial of the image passes up to the prototype, and all who communicated in any way at all have communicated in this denial of Christ. And since you further confessed that out of fear of the persecutor you also allowed icons to be destroyed, the transgression is graver; and since you said you also signed, the sin and the denial are complete. What, then, should be done, since you seek the medicine of healing yet say you cannot bear its application little by little, pleading weakness and choosing rather to accept this or that [?]? I am hemmed in on both sides: in letting it pass, out of brotherly love, and in lessening the remedy, given the greatness of the sin. Nevertheless, constrained rather by love, I determine the following with fear and trembling. Abstain, brother, from the holy things for one more year for both offences, I mean the destruction of the holy icons and the impious signature; for it counts as a signature even if you were only caught marking a cross. Perform the same prayers and genuflections, unless prevented by illness. And since the penance is very light, contribute a counterweight to balance it by giving generous alms. How much, [?] will make clear ...

[?]. To Nicetas the curator.

... firmly; and so one would have to say, "God was not manifested in the flesh." What could be more Jewish than that? These things have been said within the limits of a letter. But if [?] God grants that we see each other some day, then you will be told so many doctrines of truth concerning both the painting and the veneration of the holy icons that not even your honoured ear will be able to take them all in.

[?]. To Basil [?], spiritual son.

We wished, together with lord Gregory, to see you

here as well, beloved child. But since this did not happen, we console ourselves for your absence by letter, letting you know that we always hold you in our lowly heart and love your salvation and that of the brothers and children with you. For a son's good repute is his father's glory, and a son's honour is a sacred boast. I exhort you, then, in the Lord, to hold fast not only to your own steadiness but also to the care of the brothers, desired and desiring, loved and loving. For where there is spiritual love, there Christ is in the midst, as he promised. As a good guide, lead the lambs of Christ, sparing them with compassion and doing them good as your own members. You know who you are: free from passionate attachment and accommodating, yet also exacting about the commandments of God. Let all have one soul by having all things in common. Let there be confession, since everything that is brought into the open is light, and the reverse as well. Let there be obedience, under which the robber finds no way in for deceit. Let there be humility, clothed in which God became man, and thereby makes men gods. Good Basil, guard the deposit: turn away from what is evil, embrace what is divine, and be set before the whole brotherhood as a model of good works. In this way whoever rejects you rejects God, and whoever yields to you yields to God. Remember my lowliness, together with the brothers.

[?]. To the beloved brothers Gregory, Ezekiel, Erastus, Theophanes, Aninas, and the rest in Greece.

There is a time to speak and a time to keep silent. In the days just past, the second was called for, and I may say in the present ones too. That is why only now, and with difficulty, having left the city by God's good pleasure, we speak to you, fathers and brothers; and we speak in the words of the Apostle: Rejoice in the Lord always; again I will say, rejoice. Not with the joy of this world, which is not joy at all but sheer affliction, since its subjects are disorderly [?]. Rather, rejoice according to the Spirit of holiness, because you have been redeemed from slavery to the enemy, from a futile way of life, from flesh and blood, and serve the living and true God. From this came both your earlier blessedness in the persecution and your present life as strangers, scattered here and there, until the Lord grants peace, presiding over his Church, and gathers us back together. For the present, I beg you, brothers, to walk worthily of the calling to which we were called, with all care and attentiveness, with all humility and obedience towards one another. Let the one who leads hold the place of authority not for demonic self-exaltation but as a model of virtue for those who follow; and let those who yield and obey do so as to me, unworthy as I am, or rather as to Christ, for whose sake is the whole of our

life and our daily, freely chosen death, children, after the mystery of salvation. Watch how you conduct yourselves: not as people ruled by passion but as people free of it, not as lovers of the flesh but as lovers of God. Do not cast your eyes on the sight of women, and do not be overly familiar even among yourselves, for familiarity is a fire that burns up the soul. Meditate on death always, so that you may be ready to depart with joy. Keep the traditions; carry out what has been laid down, in psalmody and prayer and anything else. Do not store up gold for yourselves in order to give it to relatives and friends at the time of our reassembling, as though the monastery will look after our needs [?]. That is not the way of children of God but of the carnally minded. What then? Let what is needed be done, and let whatever has come in be handed over to the brotherhood, so that the common life may be built up from many people [?]. I say this because it has been reported that some are already making arrangements from here: "This animal," one says, "and this garment, or something else, I want to leave to so-and-so." O wretchedness! O folly! Such a man, then, is neither a child nor a brother, but a stranger, indeed a sacrilegious robber, whose portion is with Gehazi the thief ...

[?]. To Abramius, the hospice-master.

... is overshadowed by fear of acting so. For nothing is greater than the fear of God, and nothing more necessary than the salvation of the soul. "For what will it profit a man," it says, "if he gains the whole world and forfeits his soul?" A physician must be sought in emergencies, and a helmsman in a storm. Do you not see that there is a great storm and a blow of God's wrath? Heal, master, steer, so that you may save yourself, heal [?] the guilty, and restore them to stability, putting up with the threat, since you yourself are also in the body and liable to stumble. For in this way you will also win God's mercy, and with God protecting you, who will harm you? Remember, my lord, that you too are flesh; and as you fear blows, spare others blows. For the measure we give will be the measure we get back. Remember, good brother, that we are here today, and we do not know what tomorrow will bring, so that we may not be found mocked and cursed both in this age and in the age to come. Remember that fearful and inescapable sentence by which the merciless will be sent away into unquenchable fire. Remember that the people we treated well and those who suffered at our hands will stand before us. And what good will it do us then to have been thought capable here? No, I beg you, let us not drive the sword into ourselves in this way. I speak as a friend who cares greatly, master; this is the end of what I have to say. From now on may I hear good reports, and of humane discipline, about my lord, so that I may sing [?], so that I may know that I shall be heeded in future too by my

…of a friend. For those who live near us here are already afraid and trembling at what they hear, even though they have done nothing wrong. The one who is coming is a tyrant; he brings a sword. A poor man does not [?] the threat, and not so as to resist it; he accepts it even against his will, and for this he is not to blame. For I myself, if I were caught in the same way, could not act otherwise. But if the cause goes beyond this, well and good. Even so, let it be handled with compassion, as in the sight of the Lord. In this way the subject people will also be more stable, won over by goodwill to the victorious emperors.

100. To Hypatus, his child. [?]

We humble ones too were not unmoved, my child, when we received news of the holy falling-asleep of James, the confessor of Christ and our most lovable brother. Yet we did not receive it without great joy either. We were moved first because of our spiritual affection. For what was he to me but a son, and such a son, one whose child I, because of my sins, am not even worthy to be called? We rejoiced because of the hope, or rather because of the gain, which is not ours alone (for he was naturally set among us as a member, a holy adornment) but belongs to the whole Church of God. For what should one call the man? Is he not a confessor? Is he not a martyr? Is he not a saint? From his youth he contended as an ascetic. He submitted himself as the rule requires, fought manfully against the passions, and kept his body virgin, through the bruising and subduing of self-control. He ate whatever came to hand and slept in the same way, even while still in health, so that those who saw him were astonished. For the most part he withdrew as far as he could and turned inward on himself, and from there he gave himself wings toward the heavenly love. Let no one think that I am inventing words to please my hearers. God is my witness, and so is his tutor, the holy Lucian, though he is hard to rouse [?]; it was from him that I learned what was not generally known. Let these things stand as a kind of rough sketch of his asceticism. And at his confession, how great a spectacle it was, and for both angels and men! O cheerful and God-loving heart! He entered the arena as a soldier of Christ, fearless and unshaken. On this side and on that, the servants of darkness tore his back, chest and arms with blows. They shed his blood, cut away his flesh, and left the saint lying flung on the ground. Yet he let slip not a single wrong word, but made his testimony perfect in God. And he did these things for Christ, the Son of God and our God. For to contend for His holy icon is to bear witness for Him Himself. Let the meek hear and be glad; let the lovers of martyrs dance and rejoice; let the devil be put to shame; let the horde of iconoclasts fall. Recognize both sides from the works of both, as God has ordained [?]. For they treated not only him but many others in the same way: many of ours, and some not ours, though ours all the same,

since all are one body in Christ Jesus, who is the head of all. They tortured them, killed them, starved them, and did whatever else goes with such things. As for him, those most grievous blows left him paralyzed and his joints dislocated, and his body was operated on amid sharp pains. From then until the end he remained broken by it, living on as one who dies daily, yet in thanksgiving and in humility. If, as you say, he also foretold his death, this too follows from his contests. You also mention that a great crowd gathered for his funeral, and that it included eminent people from both sides. This is further evidence for what I say. For such a gathering would not have taken place around a man who was obscure according to the flesh, unless God had willed it. He, then, has passed to heaven and been added to his fellow contestants, and the chorus of confessors and martyrs from all ages has grown. Over this there is joy and gladness in heaven. Through his prayers may we be saved, brothers, and may he find a reward worthy of his holy service. Blessed too are those who gathered, truly pious and truly lovers of martyrs. May their portion be with the one whom they carried out to burial. As for his precious relic, I will do as I wrote concerning the canon, if the Lord is pleased. Greet one another with a holy kiss. This letter is to be read to all the brothers. The lord Archbishop greets you, as do the protopresbyter, the steward and the other brothers. The Lord be with you. Amen.

101. To Peter of Nicaea. [614?]

This is our counsel in answer to the lord abbot's question. Until the feast of the holy Apostles, let all be released from their penance and partake of the holy gifts. However, the priests are not to exercise their priesthood until an Orthodox synod comes, which will bring complete release and complete joy. Meanwhile let all of them alike, as ordinary monks, whether ordained or not, bless and be blessed, pray and receive prayers. But since the divine liturgy must also be celebrated, let a presbyter and a deacon be ordained to fill the place of those who are barred. Let these be met not with envy but with gratitude, since we have been commanded by the Apostle to bear one another's burdens. This must first be agreed by all: if God, according to the unsearchable judgments of His righteousness, should permit persecution to be kindled again, they are to choose to suffer everything, even death, rather than betray the truth. This is what we humble ones think, since this is how we answer everyone. But whatever seems good to your fatherly holiness will certainly be the sounder judgment.

102. To Euarestus, his child. [?]

…brother, for I have heard that you have died the death of sin. They say that you have cast away the profession of virginity, the garment of the Gospel, the way of life revered by angels and men, and have adulterously taken a woman, or, to put it more properly, an Eve. For she has cast you out of the paradise of the holy life and has made you a grief to me, your sinful father, a shame to your angelic brotherhood, and a cause of pride and boasting for the devil. O, what have you become, alas! How did the dragon overpower you? Into what a pit of stench has he flung you! The light has become darkness; the fragrance of Christ [?]; the holy one has become defiled; the honored one, dishonored; the glorious one, without glory; the one who was unfettered, bound hand and foot by the demon; the beloved one, hated; the sheep of Jesus, the prey of wild beasts. I will add still greater things. The one persecuted for righteousness' sake has been seized by sin; the confessor has become a denier; the one who wore the beatitude on his head like a diadem has been stripped of the wonderful name of…

Woe is me! Who could hear this and not groan? Who could ponder it and not shudder? You have shamed the monastic order. You have frightened those who stand firm and shaken those who are faltering. You have drunk the cup of lawlessness, and, as far as it lay with you, you have drawn those who share your way of life to taste death. O, and again I say: what has happened to you, wretched one? How has the Morning Star been darkened? How has the useful vessel been shattered? Are you not ashamed at least of your name, that though you are called Euarestus, 'well-pleasing,' you have become Dysarestus, 'ill-pleasing'? Did you not come to me last year, and to the lord archbishop as well, wholly sound, cheerful and eager, to plead for another brother of yours and help set him right? How did you fall away so suddenly? How were you blinded? How did you forget both God and us, and the ascetic labors and sweat you had already accomplished? For you were one of the useful ones, one of those assigned to the higher ministries. And then one small assault of the enemy, a desire that seemed sweet but was wrapped around a two-edged sword, whose bitterness is more galling than anything, seized you. It brought you down from your lofty way of life as if from heaven, and now it shows you like a wounded man sleeping in a tomb. For what else is it to be in sin than to be in corruption? There is no spiritual light anywhere, no hope, no sweetness of soul, no holy thought. There is only deep night, the closing of the mind, the gnawing of the heart, fear of any chance thing, and rolling in the mire every day like some wriggling beast. What has the demon done? What has that all-accursed desire made of you? Through it, from the beginning of the world, those who were deceived have not even gained the things of this life; they have lost the heavenly things as well, and inherited only one thing, the eternal fire. But come, my son, be called back. I call you from the depths of my heart, from bowels that burn within me; for your glory is mine, and so, in turn, is your shame. Come, rise up. The Lord has commanded it: 'I will not remember your iniquities,' He says. And: 'Does not

the one who falls rise again?' And: 'I have seen that you go about gloomy.' And: 'I will heal your fracture.' See how good God is; see how merciful the physician is. Yes, I beg you, child, for you are my child even though you have died. Do not linger in sin. Break quickly, break apart the ropes that the devil has woven around you. Rise as if from a pit, and leap across into the wonderful light of your former way of life. I will receive you with open arms, not reproaching you but pitying you. I will not make the remedies of repentance heavy, but gentle, lightening them as far as I can. Yes, hurry, hurry, before the stern angel comes suddenly, pitiably separates you from the body and carries you off to eternal judgment.

103. To Gregory the abbot. [626?]

We have already written to you, as promised, as to our son, telling you to shepherd the flock there with understanding according to the Lord's command, overlooking nothing that serves the good of the brothers. Consider the one entrusted with irrational sheep. He does not sleep but keeps watch. He is not careless, but struggles night and day so that none is taken by wild beasts and none is [?]. He watches out for thieves and robbers, drives off wild beasts and talks to his flock. Going before them, he provides their food, leading them to the water of rest and to shady places, and he does whatever else can be done with the shepherd's staff. How much more, then, and how greatly, is this required of one who has been allotted the charge of souls! If their blood is in any way [?], it will be required at his hands, as it is written. So take charge from now on, my child, and keep watch over the flock. Heal the sick, turn back those who have strayed, exhort, admonish. Remind those who walk in holiness of the promised kingdom, and remind those who live by their passions of the endless judgment, so that in this way you may save both yourself and those who hear you. One who loves disciplines with care; one who hates lets those who follow him [?]. And you too, brothers and children in the Lord, be as sheep. Love to do His commandments, and live as monks, not as worldlings. Let there be one will among you all, one heart, one soul. Let there be no 'mine' and 'yours'; let all things be held in common and all be made pure through confession. If it is not so, you have lost the worldly life as well, and since you are not true monks, you will be liable to a just condemnation. We have reminded you of this out of love. May you fare well and please God. Pray also for us sinners, that we may practise what we teach, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory.

…we thought it a good time to write you, our sisters in the Lord, a short note. And so we ask: how is your holy pair, and how are all the sisters? You see how we ask after you and converse with you, and not with other sisters, since we are bound to you according to God. And this is fitting, for where there is faith there is also longing, drawing and being drawn in turn through the Holy Spirit; and where these are, there is also care for the body. That is why we write, unworthy as we are, exhorting you on Christ's behalf that we hold fast to the good confession which we all made before God and the elect angels. That confession is to live in the Lord, putting off the mind of the flesh. This means breaking the bonds of attachment to this present age and being with God, whom we have loved, to whom we have been betrothed, and with whom we shall be forever. Let us love Him, the true love, the unapproachable longing, the only Master of heaven and earth, whose love for humankind is so great that He took the form of a servant in order to call us back from corruption and make us gods. How great is the promise! How wonderful the meeting in heaven! There the righteous will shine like the sun. There those who have clothed themselves in virginity will be joined to the incorruptible Bridegroom. There those who have practised submission and obedience will dance forever as rulers [?] of Christ. But those of the opposite kind will, of course, suffer the opposite. So, sisters, bearers of the cross, let us not unwittingly store up for ourselves punishment and eternal fire instead of life and boundless joy, through negligence and corruption of the flesh, disobedience and a life ruled by passion. Virtue is from God and [?]; vice is from Satan, and is Satan. Those who choose the first become gods and belong to God; those who choose the second become demons and belong to Satan. With these words we greet you now as well. And may you not think me burdensome, as if I were saying heavy things, but rather sweet, since I exhort you on God's behalf. My words are not addressed to the ladies who lead you, for they are teachers of others too. They are addressed to the whole sisterhood. May it be preserved still further and [?] flourish, to be my boast as its advocate on the day of Christ, to whom be glory forever. Amen.

105. To Anthimus, his child. [627?]

The law of God is the fear and trembling of Him, as He says: 'I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel.' The watchman's duty to give warning has compelled me, brother, to warn you again by letter of the sword of God that is coming upon you. It is a fearful sword, a fiery sword, a sword that casts not the body but the soul into the Gehenna of fire for endless ages. I weep as I write, wretch that I am, and I groan bitterly, because these words concern my own son and disciple. But what am I to do? God has said that if I do not give warning, He will require your blood at my hands. That means nothing other than that I too would share the same sentence of punishment. O

brother, why have you [?] the eyes of your heart in this way? Why have you despised God, at whose glance the whole universe shakes and cannot stand? Long ago you leapt out of the ascetic wrestling-school and went to places the Lord does not watch over. You broke the seal of purity, corrupted soul and body, and became a slave of sin. Then, belatedly, at the beginning of the persecution, you came back to us. You confessed and accepted a penance, and you promised to return once the persecution had ceased. On this basis you were instructed by the Steward and received by brother Dionysius. You chose the good flight, moving from evil places to good places, on which the eyes of the Lord rest, while the beatitude of the persecuted circled above your head. Well done for that recall, that cleansing, that angelic help! What, then, has happened again? What has made you fall away from God and handed you over to the devil? Alas for my misery! You have gone back again to the mire of sin, corrupting and being corrupted, by a woman, or rather by women! Lord, have mercy; spare him, O God. Your guardian angel has left you, and Satan has taken hold of you. Are you alive, then, wretch? How can a man live who is being devoured by the murderer of men? Do you see the light, then? How can a man see who has been darkened by sin? Do you pray to God, then? How can a man approach the Lord who has enslaved himself to the devil? Where is your good beginning? Where is your fervor, your compunction, your submission, your tears, your prayer winged by God, your heavenly way of life? All are gone; they have perished. O the bitter groans I utter over your folly! Would that you were an irrational animal, which does not come to judgment! But you were fashioned by God, and you will rise again and be judged, and that is what is pitiable. Come, then, my lost son! Come, turn back to the Lord, for He loves humankind and receives you again, sanctifies you again [Reg. cod.: heals you again], clothes you again as a bridegroom, kills the fatted calf again, and will rejoice and call together the powers above at your finding. Do not, then, disobey, my son, my son. Be called back, return, and join yourself to your good brother Dionysius, before the sword of eternal death overtakes you.

106. To Eustratius the abbot. [630?]

I rejoiced when I received your precious letter, dearest of fathers, and learned how things stand with your holiness, in this respect and in that. Judging from what I had heard from those who reported it, trustworthy as they are, I had been grieved to hear of the hypocritical signature. Allow me, most honored one, to speak rather frankly. It is not without reason that, after you were detained by an imperial officer, you remained unharmed, that is, were set free. This is what gives rise to the rumors. For no one who has spoken out boldly is acknowledged to have escaped prison, or at least exile, or hiding as a fugitive. Those who have escaped these things [?] of the arrest, so that I may not [?] more harshly…

Or have you not noticed, most clear-sighted one, the harsh persecution of Leo, who is named after a beast? His Ahab-like hand has seized even people from another realm, and has killed and destroyed them, or at best, more humanely, imprisoned them after a bitter scourging, not to mention those who are under his hand. But if you yourself suffered nothing of the kind after your arrest, forgive me, holy one: you have been robbed. And do not tell me that your churches are being kept safe, that the sacred images remain intact, and that our most holy patriarch is still commemorated. Others who were taken away also make such fine speeches. These things cannot be preserved except by betraying true resistance. What good is it if we, who both are and are called the temple of God, have become useless, and have preserved lifeless houses? The image of Christ, or of the Mother of God, or of any saint, does not perish, for it remains in them as in its prototypes. Those who imagine they are destroying the images are the ones who fall. And so are those who, to spare the images, have given up their boldness of speech and the suffering it brings. Alas! Some are dying, others are exiled, some are scourged, others imprisoned. The mountains and deserts, the rocks and caves, hold those who are blessedly persecuted. And are we to stay at home and think we can remain unharmed? By no means. Let all the world's stuff of seeming goods perish; let that be preferred to the manifest harm to the soul that every maker of excuses has suffered. I have said these things out of love and by way of reminder. I have also said them because we deserve to come under penance, and because in a time of Orthodoxy nothing will be left unexamined. And it is better to walk the way of humility and heal what has grown sick than to heap greater charges on ourselves through self-justification.

107 (1). To the brothers in the city. [63?]

Now that brother Leo is going in to you, I thought it a good time to write to all of you together, blessed brothers and fathers, to remind you once more of the things that lead to salvation. For even in this absence and exile I am fearful and trembling, carrying my own burden of sins, and also because of the care and protection over you that falls to me. I fear and dread that you who are living in the city may be swayed too easily and fall into some lapse. Then, through being off our guard for a short while, we would utterly lose the good works that we gathered with many labors and contests before the persecution and during it. I hear of instability and moving about. I hear of one who goes from brother to brother and from place to place. Worse still, one is living alone, and another has his cell in a house where there are women. Another, again, is living permanently in a women's monastery. Yet another hangs about houses here and there where there are girls, where the fire burns not grass but the house of the soul. Others again, forgetting the life of the rule, have bought slaves to live with them; and

(1) In the Reg. codex: 111.

…at any rate, to buy other fields. O my wretched soul! How can I not groan at these things? How can I not be afraid if I fail to proclaim the ordinance of God? Why have you lost your senses, elect ones? Why have you, servants of the Lord, become slaves of the passions? Why do you, who are under the law, put up with lawlessness? Why do you, ministers of Christ, behave as rebellious sons and not turn back from this wicked straying? Why do you not settle in places free from scandal? Why do you not live together two by two, or even more, as the apostles did? Woe to the one who lives alone! Woe to the one who is unsettled! Woe to the one who keeps company with women! Woe to the slave of slaves! Woe to Gehazi, who bought fields and vineyards and inherited the leprosy of Naaman! Are these not divine words [?]? Am I saying anything of my own [?]? When the persecution was raging, a person had the excuse of necessity for falling into some of the things I have listed, and the necessity imposed for the sake of the faith saved whoever was found in them. But now there is no one persecuting us, and no one to stop us from settling properly and living with at least two others. For those of you who live badly stand condemned by those among you who live according to the rule. Or is not the present [?] a sign beforehand of your failure to come together in time of peace? Come to your senses, I beg you, my holy brothers, partakers of a heavenly calling. If you do not correct yourselves, you will not be called such, but the opposite, which God forbid. I solemnly declare this before God and the elect angels: if anyone persists beyond the appointed time [?] and does not correct himself, he is barred from receiving the things sanctified by God, by the authority that the Lord has given me among you. This word is for building up and not for tearing down. But you, my brothers, as sons of obedience, do well, so that you may both serve God and rescue me, the wretched one, from the death of sin, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Amen.

108 (5). To John of Sardis. [635.]

For some time we have heard that your fatherly holiness was ill, and now that you had almost been given up for lost. We in our lowliness were so troubled and so painfully moved that we were eager to hurry to you there and see the dreaded report with our own eyes. But present circumstances did not allow it. So we have been compelled to fly to you, as it were, by letter, as if in body, and to see you, the good father, the true friend, the noble witness to the truth. For on its behalf you were both exiled and kept in chains under guard, and even before this you became, to use the apostle's words, a spectacle both to angels and to men, on the day when the impious threw your sacred head to the ground in the presence of that council of Caiaphas. O, what is happening [?]? Why is the pillar of the Church in a hurry to depart from this world? Stay with us, stay a while longer; share in suffering for the

Gospel like a good soldier. Do you see how the war is upon us? How we are struck and strike back for the sake of the word? Yes, we beg you, remain. Ask the Christ whom you confessed, and whom you confess must be venerated when he is depicted in human form, and he will hear your prayer. But if you are to depart in any case, because Providence so commands, you yourself will go, we know well, carrying off the prize of confession, and you will make the good God gracious [?] to us by your intercessions, and more than that, make him hasten to visit his own Church.

109 (6). To Elias, his spiritual child. [637.]

Who has compelled me to write to you, man? God, clearly, who appointed me shepherd and lawgiver over you, and to whom I shall give account for you as for all your brothers. You renounced the world of your own free choice; you submitted in obedience. Then Satan sifted you and tore you away from the divine union. Again, by God's mercy, you were joined to us, and again, by the working of a demon, you leaped away. Afterwards you came back once more and confessed, promising to stand firm in the future. Yet when the return from exile came under Nicephorus, you did not come together with the rest, but remained on your own, lured by the serpent, and so it has been up to the present emperor, the fourth after Nicephorus. How long, man [?], will you wallow in the mire of sin? How long will you not stop behaving shamefully before God and [?]? Is there no death? Is there no judgment? Will you not pay an eternal penalty, the mere thought of which subdues the soul and turns it to repentance? Come to your senses, man; be called back, I beg you. Stop building houses in worldly fashion, you who have torn down the house of your soul. Stop working as a builder like a layman, you who are being dragged along by Satan. Do not make excuses of this and that: no one will rescue you from the hand of the Lord. Do not say, having sinned, 'I will not bear the penances.' You will bear them, my child, for I in my lowliness call you that in hope of your return. As a father I will impose them [?] sparingly, with sympathy and with affection. Only be willing, only stir yourself, break the bonds of death that hold you. God's help is near, and the angel who guards your life will go before you. There will be joy in heaven; the devil will lament; I, wretched as I am, will leap for joy at finding my lost sheep, and so will your brotherhood. But if not, you will be prey for the devil, an heir of the 'woe'. May you be delivered from it by obeying, and come back together with your brother Silas.

110 (7). To the wife of Democharis. [638.]

From the day the death of the blessed general was announced to us until now, though we tried many times, we have not managed to write to your honor. And even now that we are writing, we can do you no good, nor lighten [?] the weight of your grieving heart

in any way. For what word could be found to heal so great a pain? Yet we write to make it plain that we too have shared in the sorrow: not only over him who has departed to the Lord, because a good and pious man, a champion of orthodoxy and a fighter for peace, has left us (O, what a calamity!), but also over you, who are left bereft of your husband's support, all the more because you loved your husband dearly. So the very telling has shown your suffering to be beyond consolation. But since you are not untaught in the divine decree, 'You are earth, and to earth you shall return'; and again, 'That you may not grieve over those who have fallen asleep, as the rest do who have no hope', since they will be brought with Jesus by God in the resurrection, we urge and entreat you to pour out the greater part of your sorrow, to accept a little comfort, to come to yourself, and to brighten your soul. For you also have children [?], and you have a large household; and unless your mind rises above the grip of this suffering, it will never be able to manage and direct it rightly. Above all, what we are urging will benefit that blessed man too, and what could be more worth striving for than that? What then remains, my lady? Give glory to the good God; speak the words of Job: 'The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it seemed good to the Lord, so it has come to pass.' May you gain truly the greatest renown from this, and be seen to have been the wife of so learned a man. For he was knowledgeable and wise, and a teacher of the uninstructed. As he was a fine example to men, so be you too to women, turning away from a love of mourning and showing that God is your protector, who brought you from nothing into being, brought you to the prime of life, joined you to such a man, and, having parted you, will unite you again through the resurrection. So regard what has happened as a journey abroad. Would you not bear the loss if an earthly emperor had ordered it? Bear this one too, my lady, which the only true King of all has commanded. Yes, we beseech you; and indeed we trust that you will receive him back on that day, if you keep your widowhood in the Lord and raise your fine offspring excellently. We greet them too, and likewise urge them to bear the loss of their father and to let their mother's guidance shape them toward all uprightness.

111 (7). To the monks of Myele. [643.]

The falling asleep of our beloved brother Dionysius has now reached its appointed end, by the counsel of God determined before the foundation of the world. But may the Lord reward you, brothers, for receiving him when he fell ill on his journey, in the monastery that belongs to you, and keeping him until he laid down his tent on earth and flew away to heaven. That the brother was worthy of the journey there, there are many testimonies. First, his proven obedience from youth until old

age. Then [?] he once travelled to the West as an apostle on behalf of our Church. He was blessed by an apostolic mouth, [?] the Church of the Romans. He is attested by many of his brotherhood [?] to have been mighty in deed and word, a doer of God's commandments, a pillar and bulwark of his own community. He showed many marks of virtue, and now too, in this very persecution, he went about cities and countries, in want and affliction, ministering the word of truth, until he breathed his last and departed to the Lord. Such a servant of the Lord you [?] have escorted on his way, and so great a holy relic has been entrusted to you to be laid up as a treasure. For this reason we have been drawn all the more to your godly love, and we pray that you may have [?] the Jerusalem above, in return for receiving the holy Dionysius with a true heart. May his memory be with the saints of his rank.

112 (8). A catechesis to his own disciples. [644.]

Brothers and Fathers: others announce the deaths of their own people with sorrow, but I do so with great joy. Why? Because our brothers who have departed this life are holy, partakers of a heavenly calling: Anthus, rightly named 'Flower', who blossomed with the virtues, and Dionysius, who excelled in holiness as befits the name of Dionysius. It is right to tell what kind of death each of them had. The one had just come back from his place of exile, and indeed had taken leave of us for the last time; on the way back he fell ill and fell asleep in holiness in the monastery of Myele. The other fell into sickness and endured, if it is not rash to say so, the sufferings of the renowned Job. For he saw his flesh shriveling and his bones cleaving to his flesh: unbearable pains, the blows of wounds, an unchecked flux of the bowels, only his breath remaining. In the midst of all this he too went to the Lord giving thanks. See how the blessed ones are martyrs too: Dionysius, God's approved workman, and Anthus, the lamb of Christ. Dionysius completed the contest of obedience [?] right up to old age; Anthus was sanctified from childhood to middle age through obedience. Both were vessels useful to God the Master, not only in the things for which they were praised earlier and later, but also because they put on the crowns of imprisonment for the sake of righteousness. What could be more glorious than that? And one of them has a further boast: that he served the lord brother and archbishop, a service that was long, and not only long but also highly praised. So on both counts the brother is worthy of admiration.

What then shall we say to these things, brothers? That all of us human beings are certainly passing from here, and that the passage is from sojourning to true rest, from darkness to light, from turmoil to calm, from war to peace, where there is no biting serpent, where there is no fear of change, where each will receive what he has done in the body, whether good or evil. Therefore let us too hasten, my brothers, to end our lives in holiness, so that we may escape eternal judgment and be counted worthy of the kingdom of heaven. It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God. Our God is a consuming fire. Let us fear, beloved children, let us tremble, let us rise up against the dragon, the devil, both those of us who seem to stand and those who have been tripped up. For to the first, a little slackness brings a fall into death; to the second, a small upward glance brings healing to the wounds of the soul. Does the one who falls not get up? Does the one who turns away not turn back? Yes, my brothers: the door is not yet shut, the festival not yet over. Let us take care of ourselves. Let us consider how we spend our time in the city, where we settle, what sort of people we talk with, how much we eat, and our quiet, our sleep, our conversation, our psalmody, that all of it may be pleasing to God and all of it beneficial to our neighbor. Show mercy, give help; let no one do anything unseemly. What profit is it if I gain the whole world and lose my wretched soul? What will the enjoyment of this world's pleasures add to me on the day of death? What shall I suffer when I see those of my own rank taken up into the kingdom of God, and myself carried off into the outer darkness? Truly, my brothers, the comfort of the flesh is nothing, an earthly kingdom is nothing, passing glory is nothing, wealth that flows away is nothing, luxury that drains away is nothing; there is no profit in any of the things that lovers of this life think fine and beautiful. All is vanity and a striving after wind, as says the one who made trial of all the pleasures of this age. And would that it were only vanity! But in its place eternal torments are stored up for those who wallow in it. And for us, to whom the spiritual life has been granted by the Lord, how great and how heavy a punishment will be laid up if we do not flee from it! For this reason, my brothers, I remind you, I exhort you, I beseech you, as one in your debt, your servant for the Lord's sake: let us live justly and holily from now on, so that we may inherit eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory for ever. Amen.

113 (9). To Euphrosyne, abbess. [645.]

What has happened to the blessed lady and common mother (for I do not decline to call her our mother too, because of her virtue) called for us ourselves

to come and sing the funeral hymn that befits her, and to speak words of comfort to you who are left behind, orphaned, as it were, of the companionship and harmony of your stepmother, if indeed any such remedy could be found to soothe the pain and dejection of your soul. But since that is not possible, our visit comes by letter. O, how the good amma has flown away from us: the Christ-bearing woman, the treasure of chastity, the face full of grace, the sanctuary of piety, full of days, both those that pass and those that remain [?], the sanctified temple, the olive grove of compassion, the mercy of generous giving, the living [?], God-fashioned creature, the ungrudging eye, the unenvious heart, she who even before death had departed from the things of this world for the sake of Christ, the Bridegroom she longed for, and for the indissoluble and pure life there! O, O, how much would I have to say to empty out the praise that crowds my heart! And yet I came to know the lady and the virtues in your community only late, and had no more experience of them than someone who touches honey with a fingertip. Still, a brief taste gives proof of the whole sweetness; and besides, having been taught by those of your sisters who knew her virtue better, I have sufficient knowledge of her in the Lord. From such a life as I shall describe she was led to this way of life. For I must take the story up from the beginning and dwell on it a little for the sake of consolation. It is like this. Her family was from the sunrise, both in place and in character, since it was Armenia, the source also of her virtue. And if one must inquire into blood, she came of royal stock, with generalships and leadership of peoples both in Armenia and in Greece; I mean on her husband's side, since her husband held the highest generalship here, as well as the rank of patrician. When death tore her from him, she could not bear to remain unwed, but would have a suitor. And whom did she take? Not this or that ruler or emperor, as the many desire who are given over to flesh and blood, but the only beautiful Bridegroom, the Prince of Peace (which is why the bride bears the name of peace), Christ the King of all, the Lord of glory; and him she took as her betrothed through the monastic profession. How she excelled in doing the things her Lover desired, our account has already shown in outline. Hers was the radiant prayer, the compunction, the shedding of tears, the tongue free of slander, the bearing free of forwardness, the humility that imitated Christ, the right hand that loved the commandments, the mind that spoke of God, the heart that burned with the fire of Christ's love, and finally the orthodox worship and her keeping herself from heretical communion with unflinching boldness. And it is a marvel how, in the persecution that has swept past, she kept not only herself but also you, lady, and your whole holy community free of it, with God's help. She set a fine crowning seal on her end: having received the sanctified gifts from orthodox sources, she departed from here rejoicing [?], which is a very great sign of her

attaining what she longed for: to gain Christ and to be with Christ for ever. So the blessed one lived, and so holily she departed; and so, we sinners believe, it is with her now. Next the word must turn to you. My lady, what is this? It is that, sharp as the separation is, you should nevertheless bear it with thanksgiving, as indeed we have heard you are doing, and we have praised you highly for it: not giving way to irrational wailing and hopeless lamentation, but bearing it fittingly, as a true nun and an excellent teacher, giving by your own example a pattern to the souls the Lord has entrusted to you; or rather, to put it more plainly, as befits the daughter in the Lord of that celebrated woman, one in soul and mind with her, her daughter-in-law in the flesh, her equal in virtue in your way of life. For you two were one soul in two bodies, a thing praised and glorified. So she has not been separated from you altogether, lady, lady, but only for a little while, until we too travel the same road. Besides, she is present with you spiritually even now and helps your efforts; and what is greater, having come nearer to God, she intercedes for you and yours. So do not lose heart, we beg you, as though you had no protector, nor as though you had been left alone. You have her, and before her you have God, to whom all things belong; and if you want us sinners too, as she asked both before her death and as she breathed her last, you have us, if indeed a sinful man can be of any use. This is our funeral address. But you, O blessed soul (for we must turn to her), do not ask us to pray that God be merciful to you. Rather, you yourself reconcile him to us by your intercessions, for we are confident that you have this power; and do not let the lady, your sister, mother and daughter, have [?] only us as helpers, but give yourself both to her and to us and to your whole flock in the Lord, to whom be glory for ever. Amen.

114 (10). To Julian the vestitor. [646.]

Since you greeted us through your brother, my good friend, I thought it good to greet you in return by letter, showing by this how lovingly I am disposed toward your honor, and not only that, but also how anxious I am that you be kept safe from the devil's temptations. For you know, beloved, that like a lion he is always prowling about, seeking someone to devour. So be watchful; remember the vows you made. It is written: 'Have you sinned? Do not do it again, and pray about your former sins.' And again the Lord says: 'Every branch that does not bear fruit the Father takes away, and it is thrown into the fire and burned.' Let us then fear this example; let us strive for our souls before the hour of death arrives, so that we may not be found

fruitless and barren on the good vine, which is Christ. 'For this I came,' says the Lord, 'not to judge the world, but to save it.' And again he says: 'If I had not come and spoken to them, they would have no sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin.' And again: 'The word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day.' Our good God, beloved, has already done everything for us. He was seen on earth, he took the form of a servant, he became obedient unto death, even death on a cross; and this though he was the Lord of glory, upholding all things by the word of his power. He was calling us back from the corruption that came upon us through the first-formed man; and not only that, but he also deified us through his holy flesh, so that we have been counted worthy to be called brothers, members of one body, sharers, and joint heirs. We must therefore guard ourselves with all vigilance. You walk among snares as you go through the city; see that you are not caught. Let your conduct be in the fear of the Lord, in the company of good men. Flee those who live carelessly; flee youthful games and jokes; flee carousing and ruinous drinking. Let no rotten word come out of your mouth, but only what is good for building up those who hear. Do not be anxious to be rich, for naked you came into this world, and naked you will leave it. Do not love the glory of this world, for it passes away like smoke. Love one good thing only: to keep your heart clean from the filth of sin, to gain the kingdom of heaven, and to escape eternal judgment. Keep the commandments you have received. Incline your ear to the poor; when your hand is able to help, reach out to the needy. The two mites of a poor widow surpassed all that had been cast into the treasury. Let no oath lodge in your mouth, for the one who swears will not be saved, even if he seems to keep every commandment. Visit a man in prison, so that you may be visited by the Lord. Pray continually, and [?] in your heart, so that you may receive the Holy Spirit to dwell with you. These are a few tokens of love out of many, good commandments which let us both carry out, and may we be saved in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory to the ages of ages. Amen.

115 (11). To [?], abbess. [647.]

How fine is your honor's letter, both showing your grief at the falling asleep of your holy mother and holding fast to the reminder of hope! For just as being wholly without grief and without tears at our separation from those who have fallen asleep is blamed (since it is a mark of insensibility), so, on the other hand, being crushed by grief beyond measure belongs to those who have no hope of resurrection. Come then, sister in the Lord, the

Having paid enough tribute to mourning, let us come back to ourselves. I do not mean that we should cast the image of that holy woman out of our hearts—God forbid! May she remain in us as a reminder of all consolation and guidance. I mean that we should carry on more cheerfully and finish the contest of ascetic discipline set before us. Your mother, then, did not leave you at an untimely age, ignorant of divine things or inexperienced in the affairs of life. She left you fully equipped on every side by the grace of Christ: experienced in life, full of prudence, rich in knowledge, and well fitted for administration. And since your days have been brought to maturity in human life [?], take care for your own safety. Take a helper, either from within the community, if there is one, or from outside. For it is not hard to find a woman to consult about the difficult matters that sometimes arise, which one mind alone cannot resolve

In the same way, hold fast to the governance of the sisters under your hand, leading them in the Lord with all patience, with compassion, and with insistence on what is due. Do not oppress them harshly. Instead, as a nurse cherishes her own children, repay them in kind, so as even to give up your very life for them. Nor again should you let the reins of the bridle go slack altogether, for that causes dissolution, disorder, and a lack of love for one's children. You know how you acted while your mother was with you. You know that the eyes of all of them look to you as to God, seeing your face as it mediates to them the things that concern him. If you are like this, it is clear that they too are bound to breathe nothing but what you, their teacher, love, command, and prescribe. In short, they should be to you as true children to a mother, as members each in its part to a head, as flowers to a rosebush. This is why they came together in the first place. They left the world and the things in the world, parents and brothers, relatives and friends, possessions and ties of the flesh. They loved the single life and took Christ as their bridegroom, so that by living holily and as befits virgins they might inherit the kingdom of heaven and enter with Christ into that heavenly and inviolable bridal chamber. Such is the contest and the profession, my lady, both for them and for you. To this let us attend; in this let us move and spend our lives. Let us not look here and there, saying that this monastery does things one way and that other monastery another. That is harmful. We must measure ourselves against the commandment, not against our neighbors. Comparing ourselves with others never brings anyone to walk uprightly or to go forward in a way worthy of God. The present generation is negligent and has fallen away from the strict life, and to take one's rule from it is stale and unprofitable. So let us look where the holy life is, where pleasing the Lord has shone forth. You see, sister and spiritual mother, how love according to God has compelled me to speak freely among you. I would have said nothing more if I were speaking to my own mother and my sisters according to the flesh. For we are all the body of Christ, and we call upon one Father, our good [God?]. So we are all brothers of one

another, of one body, sharers together and co-heirs. Hence comes our love for you and your salvation, which [?] the Lord loves and has commanded. Peace to you, lady mother. Peace to the sisters in Christ Jesus our Lord. Amen.

116 (12). — To John the hermit. [648]

When someone has seen a pleasant sight, he usually keeps going back over it in his mind even after he has left. So it is with us, the lowly, O man honored by God. Having once seen you and spoken with you, we have not forgotten you. We keep you pictured in our thoughts, delighting in this very thing: that we saw a man of God whose face and conversation shone with divine grace, and who urged us to glorify God. You gained this through your solitude in the desert and your approach to God in prayer, your face made radiant like that of Moses before the ineffable light. That is why we long to look upon you again and to share in the graces that are in you, through a second-hand participation in sanctification: you receiving it from God, and we from you. Do you see how greatly God has glorified you, because you glorified him? May he glorify you still more at the end of your life, as you finish your course in a worthy manner. And for us sinners, pray that we may at least begin the course of salvation, since we, the least, are far from God. That is the first purpose of this letter. What is the second? It concerns Theoctistus the hermit. You know better than we do, most honored one, how he was torn away from the body of the Church by certain heretical notions. We too, however, learned about the man from people who knew him when we were near your dwellings the year before last [?]. Moreover, we reminded him by letter and urged him to abstain from those dark and demon-inspired utterances, and to hold the orthodox faith concerning the all-holy Theotokos and in other respects. Now Nicanor, our brother, has come to us and reported that the man has come to repentance and wishes to be of one mind with the Church. He says that he never received any letter of mine, but would very much like to receive one. Since, then, holy Father, it is written, "He who brings out the worthy from the unworthy shall be as my mouth," and, "He who turns a man back from the error of his way will cover a multitude of sins," your holiness must rouse yourself and give a helping hand to the one who has gone astray. In this you will be God's fellow worker. How is this to be done? By summoning [?] Theoctistus to you with a message of yours, and saying to him and discussing with him what is fitting. If you find him yielding to the divine word, tell him also about my lowly self: that I have been moved to this very thing out of love for his salvation. And if you, Father, approve, and he wishes it, I will write to him as is fitting, so that he may be drawn from both sides and the one who is perishing may be won. For this is what God wills, and for this

he came upon the earth: to seek out the lost and turn it back. And he makes our love for our neighbor the proof of our love for him. We must be moved with all our strength, holy Father. I too was moved to this, and so I have written to you. But if after such an effort he still persists in disobedience, the lawless one will answer for it himself. As the Lord says, "Leave them; they are blind." So, as the Lord gives success, be so good, Father, as to let me know by your precious letter.

117 (13). — To Marianus the spatharius. [?]

Your piety draws us to write, finding our words beneficial, so you say—though I do not think so, since our words are as useless as our life—but you do so because you are carried along by love. For love, says the Apostle, does not reckon up evil. However that may be, I yield to and obey our admirer: the good man, the all-praised official, the nursling of piety, the offspring of orthodoxy, the man of God, the lover of monks. Many are the praises due to you, and most excellent your achievements. But see, my master, how you walk—for this is what the Apostle cries out—not as unwise but as wise, not as a lover of the flesh but as a lover of God, not as one without a care [?] but as one mindful of his departure, the common debt, the boundary none can cross. For, it says, there is no one who shall live and not see death. What, you might ask, are the marks of each kind of life? I will explain to you, my friend. The marks of the first are dances, jests, games, obscene talk, drunkenness, gluttony, frivolities, empty puffings of pride, one adornment after another, love of wealth, love affairs. The many heavier things I pass over out of respect for your authority. And indeed the Apostle declared that "those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God." Come, let me show you the strengths of the other life as well: poverty of spirit, tears of compunction, meekness, peace, almsgiving, the mind's contemplation of God, freedom from avarice, hatred of the world, contentment, self-control. And, as far as each person is able, to love the Lord who made us and who gave himself up to death for each one of us more than spouse, more than children, more than parents, more than brothers—in short, more than everyone. These things, and others like them, belong to the true Christian. Do not imagine, master, that what has been said applies only to the monk and not equally to the layman. It all applies to both, though more intensely to the monk, except for celibacy and the renunciation of possessions, in which the man of the world is not condemned. Yet even here there are times for self-control and rules of contentment. For, it says, "If we have food and clothing, with these we shall be content. But those who want to be rich fall" into the inescapable pit. And again: "Let those who have

wives be as though they had none." There, my master, you have compelled me to declare God's ordinance to you. Let us both hasten to be saved. The time of our life that is past is enough for doing the will of the flesh. "Now," says the Apostle, "is the acceptable time; now is the day of salvation." See, the good God waits for our fruit until our last breath. May he not say, "Cut it down; why should it even use up the ground?" May he not shut the door against us, with no opening again. May the devil not take us as his portion, to be punished with him eternally. May we not be snatched away suddenly. How often have we given pledges that if we were rescued from this illness, or this danger, or this affliction, we would serve God sincerely—and then forgotten our agreements? How long will he bear with us? How long will he let it go on? In a little while we must surely depart from here. Let us not, then, be found unprepared with good works, lest the "woe" be ours forever and without end. Let us be found ready, having pleased him, so that we may be counted worthy to reign with the Lord to endless ages. So be it.

118 (14). — To Euphrosyne, abbess. [653]

I think all the more highly of your honor now, after you wept for your blessed mother, when the steward came and reported that you had been comforted in the Lord. At this my lowly self was relieved too, since I care about your affairs as those of a sister in Christ. For, my lady, when we lose those dearest to us, we must show our love by mourning as nature requires, and then, resting on the doctrine of hope, be comforted in a manner worthy of God, so that we spoil what is good in neither direction. For excessive grief is as wrong as insensibility. We are guided by divine measures and rules, especially those of us who have taken up the profession of perfection. The people wept for Moses, who saw God, but for forty days. The patriarch Jacob and his children wept for the admirable Rachel, but for a few days. The renowned Joseph wept for Jacob himself, and others wept for others in both the Old and the New Testament, but within limits, and not forever. In doing and continuing to do the same, you are worthy of praise before God and men. Keep the one you long for always before your mind's eye—I strongly advise it. From this you will be easily moved to compunction, you will hate the world and love God, and you will be prepared for the same departure. What could be more conducive to salvation than this? Shepherd the flock of God entrusted to you in holiness, as a spiritual mother and not as one who rules in human fashion; as one who sets an example in herself of what the commandment requires, not as one who demands things beyond their strength; as one who divides her love equally among all, not as one who attaches herself to one more than another, as happens with ties of blood. Do you see how the truth has laid down the law for us? But

what does the great Peter say? "And when the chief shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory." What a great thing it will be for you to cry out before the Lord, "Here am I, and the children you have given me!" And I would add this too: "I have not grown weary of following you, and I have not desired the day of man, Lord." And indeed it is so. You have given everything to God; you counted all things as rubbish, so that you might gain Christ. So even if you bear afflictions, my lady—those afflictions with which people who live godly lives must live, for many are the afflictions of the righteous, as holy David cries out, kindled by the enemy both in the mind and in the senses—do not be ignorant of his designs; turn back his schemes with your prayers. Our wrestling is not against blood and flesh, as the Apostle says, but against the principalities and powers of this world, and to escape their snares truly calls for a contest. Have someone to whom you can refer what happens to you. From this comes a bridle on sin and help from God. It is just as the sisters have you as their superior: they must refer their impulses to you, and what each one is more inclined toward, and you must receive them. You must encourage one, spur on another, steady another—in short, offer each of them what is suitable. And do not grow weary in this. God fights at our side; the Lord supports us. Let us only make a beginning, and he himself teaches knowledge. "I am jealous for you," says the Apostle, "with a godly jealousy; I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ." Understand our relation to you in this way, at least as a faint echo of that likeness, even though we are sinners in other respects. And may the God of peace, who took to himself in peace and holiness your mother, whose name was the same as peace, count you worthy to live in her footsteps, shepherding you as you shepherd, and guiding you as you guide, in Christ our God himself, to whom be glory forever. Amen.

119 (15). — To James the monk. [654]

"...nothing prevents one from residing in a bishop's residence in which the occupant has committed impiety, and being fed by compromisers who are not bishops [?] does not conflict with the rule of piety." But how does this not conflict with Scripture [?], when holy David sings, "Let not the oil of a sinner anoint my head," and holy Athanasius commands that we have no communion with heretics, nor even with those who are in communion with the impious? How is it not communion, if one has to reside in such a place and be fed by such people? It cannot be otherwise. Even if someone does not reside there but is fed from there, the very giving and receiving would create communion. For the Apostle says, "You Philippians yourselves know that when I left Macedonia, no church shared with me in the matter of giving and receiving except you alone; for even in Thessalonica you sent help for my need once and again." If, then, the light of the world declared that receiving once or twice is communion, who in his right mind would not flee from constant receiving as something opposed to the light? Your holiness should present these reminders to the Father gently and humbly. If he is persuaded, we have won the Father; if not, let us not give up our own safety. As for children being baptized by these people, I have sent your honor the whole letter I wrote on the same matter to the person who reproached me about it, since I thought it superfluous to talk idly about the same thing twice. This, then, is what I in my lowliness think, and I see the saints thinking the same; but let each fare well as seems good to him. Perhaps someone [?] might say that the receiving comes from one who has returned to right belief and been placed under penance. But that is not yet the case, so long as he holds the bishopric, even if he does not celebrate the liturgy or partake of the holy gifts. True repentance consists in leaving the bishopric and going far away, as some have done. From such people it is safe to receive, and with them it is acceptable to eat together as well. I have nothing more to say, except to ask you to pray for my lowliness, that I may not only speak rightly but also walk rightly in practice.

120 (16). — To Nicetas the topoteretes. [656]

Since your right hand, which loves the commandments, has brought us gifts of this and that, master, may you also accept what comes from us humble ones. Our offerings are prayers and thanks and, if something else must be added, admonitions. And what are these? That you fear God; hold the right faith; abstain from fleshly desires, from fornication, adultery, impurity, and every other licentiousness; choose to do divine things; show mercy to the poor; spare your slaves; stretch out your hand to your neighbor; be humble-minded; be restrained, and

not let yourself be scattered through the senses, through which the death of sin comes in; hold to contentment; do not get drunk with wine, in which, to speak with the Apostle, there is debauchery; do not love money, in which lies the root of all evils; devote yourself to prayers, to readings, to psalmody, to the remembrance of death, from which come compunction of soul and tears. For the present life, Christians, is a time for tears, not laughter. Never swear, nor carry the precious name of God on your lips as an oath, for one who swears cannot be saved. Keep yourself pure of the envy of Cain, of deadly slander, of God-hated hatred, of abuse, which shuts one out of the kingdom of heaven. Honor the emperor and your parents. Love your wife as yourself, and do not know another woman in fornication, which brings the wrath of God; for God will judge fornicators and adulterers. Bring up your children in a godly way, and set yourself as an example of good sense for them; and do whatever else the word of the commandment requires for the salvation of the soul. These, master, are our return for your fine gifts. Do not despise them, even if they came from a contemptible mouth. For the commandments of God are more precious than all gold and precious stones.

121 (17). — To Thomas, Patriarch of Jerusalem.

Your supreme beatitude can easily see how greatly we lowly ones rejoiced at being deemed worthy of your all-wise greeting by letter. You stand far above us by your apostolic rank, and by lawful succession you hold the place of the Brother of the Lord. You might well have honored us, who deserve no honor, with a bare greeting, as would be fitting—to say nothing of such heights of praise. We fall so far short of these that we hardly dare to think that you said these things about us; rather, the praises belong to one of those great men [?], namely our most divine chief shepherd, to whom every kind of praise might fittingly be attached. But how else could your God-imitating and compassionate nature have been displayed, if not by being shown forth triumphantly in fatherly affection, as the rising sun is scattered abroad in rays? And how else could your oneness of soul and mind with us have been made known, if not by your setting yourselves apart from those, whoever they were, who deserted to the other side? About these matters, even if it is bold, it is nevertheless just for us to say: What does this mean? When heresy boiled up in persecution, those preeminent on the lofty thrones, as allies of the Spirit and full of apostolic precepts, ought to have been moved together in brotherly love and to have stretched out a compassionate hand to those suffering for the truth. For, it says, "If one
member suffers, all the members suffer with it; if one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it"—the head of the whole ecclesiastical body plainly being Christ, the true Lord and God [?]

What need is there to say how much good the apostolic one of the West did by acting in this way? He greatly strengthened the resolve of those standing firm [?], since even a slight push usually gives strength to someone who is struggling. And he struck down the arrogance of the impious with a refutation moved by the Spirit. What could be more conducive to salvation than that? But that it was possible to do this, and yet some did not do it but did the opposite [?]—out of respect for the messenger of your beatitude I cannot say, wretch that I am, how grave a charge that would be. But those things have come to an end, as indeed everyone has heard: the good God has removed the accursed dragon from our path, and that by a sudden death, a just reward for his apostasy. The present situation, however, is not as some had somehow supposed: that winter has passed and the longed-for spring has come [?]. Only a little clear sky has begun to glimmer, and even that is [?] because of the cloud from the east. I think it enough to leave my account at this image, since your magnanimity needs no instruction and the times do not allow me to speak more plainly. For this reason too your holy letters went undelivered. Where could they have been delivered, when we humble ones have been cast away somewhere far from the city, as other persecuted people have been elsewhere? And so the [?], as we longed, have not yet come about; except that the [?], as was indicated in the enclosed note by those who delivered it, who acknowledge that they received rather than paid out [?], who have been deemed worthy to [?] some communion in the most holy places, where the great mystery of godliness was accomplished, God being seen in our form.

O the ineffable wonder! This, which is also recorded in Scripture and handed down from the Fathers, that is, transmitted by God [?], we—or rather the whole world under heaven—confess and venerate, from the very starting point of the proclamation. For otherwise Christ would not be confessed, as you most blessed ones teach. But the ill-named Iconoclasts have denied it as the Jews did, as men driven by an evil spirit. O divine and sacred head, may you by your prayers that move God [?] overturn the heresy that deceives the people and kindle the sun of orthodoxy; and may you then also take under your care us, the least among your children, who follow our most blessed Father and high priest. So be it. I and my brother, the most God-beloved archbishop of Thessalonica, send our warmest greetings to the Fathers who serve you and to our renowned brothers. For [falling?] before your holy face, at your feet [?], we ask rather—as it is more fitting to say—that we both may be blessed, together with those who are with us.

122 (18). To Theodore the eunuch. [658.]
Here, master, is the letter you asked for; now release us from the charge. "But why not sooner?" you might say. Because we were shy of addressing your honor in the manner of admonition. But since you want it, receive it, dearest friend. The true Christian is nothing other than an imitation and imprint of Christ, and he ought to be as closely joined to him as each member is to the head and a branch to the vine. For the Lord himself said: "I am the vine, you are the branches." And again the Apostle: "You are the body of Christ, and members each in part." So let us bear the clusters of the virtues, master, and not be fruitless. For the Lord says: "Every branch that does not bear good fruit is cut off and thrown into the fire" (the fire of Gehenna, that is). Let us fear that fearful threat. Let us glorify God in our body and in our spirit, as the Apostle again commands. He is also the one who says: "Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a harlot? Never!" So let us guard ourselves. Let us love our own wives as our own bodies, and we will not lust after a licentious body. "And let the wife," he says, "see that she fears her husband." For if she blends fear with affection, she will live the best life. "Children, obey your parents," as he says again. For it is just that parents should be honored and cared for in old age by their children, since after God they are the reason their children came into the light. And: "A father's blessing establishes the houses of children, but a mother's curse uproots their foundations." And again he says: "Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord." So parents too have a task: to keep their children at peace, to teach them the rudiments, and to mold them in the stamp of piety. What else? That slaves should be subject to their masters with fear and trembling, wholeheartedly [?] and willingly; but also that masters should give up threats and look after everyone with equal care, knowing that there is one Lord of all, God. Here, slavery exists, as does marriage; but in the age to come both are abolished, and all are one, like the angels. Therefore everyone who wants to be saved must be watchful to live according to the commandment: not to swear, not to be flighty, not to laugh, not to live in luxury, not to play, not to rage, not to fornicate, not to get drunk, not to hoard gold; but rather to pray, to weep [?], to sing hymns, to keep the commandments as far as possible, to be content with little, to be humble, to love one's neighbor, not to slander a brother, not to envy, not to be angry; always to be ready to face dangers for the sake of the good; to fear no one else on earth but God, who is good; to submit to the emperor in matters where God's commandment is not violated; to honor rulers as ministers of good order; to rejoice in the Lord always; and even if distressing things should happen, to give

thanks to the Lord for whatever he arranges in one's affairs. I have reminded your blessed soul of these things briefly, to make it known that I love my namesake, a pious man and an ardent friend. If we are still alive, we will speak again, exhort again, and counsel again that everything should be counted secondary to the love of God. For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his soul? May we escape that, and find mercy on the day of judgment, and be with God in joy unspeakable forever.
123 (19). To Euphrosyne, abbess. [661.]
Having heard just now that your honor has been consoled in your grief over your blessed mother, I gave thanks to the Lord. He has shown you to be both a true daughter who loves her mother and an outstanding lover of God: the first through your loving grief, the second through your measured acceptance of consolation. These show that you loved both your mother and God. But come, lady, walk your road rejoicing and trembling: rejoicing because you have been counted worthy to be called the daughter of such a mother; trembling because the charge of governing the community now falls to you. Its struggle is no ordinary one and its reward is not to be despised; indeed, for those who have sense, both stand very high. So you, as one who is sensible and intelligent, and who was led by your mother in the Spirit, must pass through an excellent and well-ordered life, setting yourself before the sisters as a model of good works. Do not let the eye of your heart grow drowsy in guarding the commandments of God. Do not stop the ear of your soul from hearing the voice of teaching. Be taught and teach; be enlightened and enlighten; be guided and guide; be brought to God and bring others. May your name be spoken of for your good way of life, so that God may be glorified in you and in your monastery. Do not cheapen yourself by sinking to the lukewarmness of the many, but be exact in keeping the ordinance of the Spirit, in one mind, one will, one heart and soul, imitating the saints whose story is told in the Acts of the Apostles. For it says: "All had one soul and heart, and no one said that any of his possessions was his own." This is the good life, this is the Lord's portion; this is true common life. Where these things are absent, plainly the opposite is present. How great a joy and glory it is for you, most honored one, and for your children too, to live apostolically, to be guided by what the fathers handed down, and to live nobly. For this is true nobility: to live pleasing to God, to conduct yourselves as befits saints, to be called a chosen race, an honored seed. Whose seed?
