That of the famous Thecla the protomartyr, of Febronia, of Eupraxia, and of the holy and blessed company like them. For if you have left the world, if you have renounced your parents,

if you have embraced virginity, if you have been betrothed to Christ, if you have loved the kingdom of heaven, why should you not devote all your zeal and care to this? Rejoice that you have been counted worthy of so great a gift from God, an unsurpassable dignity. I do not mean in human terms (those are shadows and dreams, and pass away with the present age), but in spiritual terms, since virginity and poverty are the choicest of the greatest gifts. And if people in the world are insatiable to get a share of vain and perishing things, what and how much ought we to desire insatiably among the countless and unspeakable good things? Yes, I beg you; yes, I entreat you: win the heavenly things. May you become daughters of God, queens honored by heaven, brides of Christ, co-heirs with Christ, a light in the world, a holy byword, a praiseworthy way of life: you, lady superior, ruling in Christ, and you, the fair children, daughters of the Jerusalem above, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory forever. Amen.
124 (20). A catechesis to his own disciples. [662.]
I, the humble one, do a work in my catecheses that comes not from a habit of display nor from some strange elation of mind, but from fear and trembling, from a laboring heart and from love, brothers and fathers. For careful instruction is a sign of one who loves. "Reprove," it says, "rebuke, in season and out of season." And also exhort and admonish, and whatever else the law of God contains and commands. What, then, does my word mean to point out? Disorder. When you are invited by pious people to sing psalms, you do not gather and keep the vigil as is fitting, but with quarrels over words and contests for the first seats. "You went ahead," one says, "and didn't wait for me. You ate your own supper and didn't invite me." "I will lead the canon, not you," says another. And this in church! And this in the hearing of those who invited you! For this there is the wrath of God, though unseen, and grief and admitted harm to those who invited you. Do you have no room, if something distressing happens, to bring your complaints against one another in private and to settle what has happened through apology and due humility? Instead brother fights with brother, rages, insults, and behaves shamefully in front of everyone. O the disorder! O the unmonastic spectacle! O the contempt for the divine laws! Then the blame falls on the superior. "Such a teacher," they say, "such disciples." Have you not made me hated even by the people in the city? Is not the good name that was given to our brotherhood turned into its opposite? You fight and make war; you eat and drink, not reverently, not

quietly, but shamelessly [?], unmonastically. "Whether then [you eat or drink] [?] do everything for the glory of God." But you do not do so in good order [?], and you put the holy habit to shame; you scandalize the devout, and even the undevout. Would that each of you were spoken of like this: "What a reverent face so-and-so has! How great so-and-so's silence is! Well done for that one's reticence; for another's orderliness; for another's dignified chanting; for another's affability!" These things adorn those who have them, benefit those who see them, gladden God, and bring honor to me, the sinner. But now, because of my sins, it is the reverse. I am not accusing [?] everyone, for by the grace of God there are many such as my word is looking for; but I mean those who are held fast by carelessness. So I exhort you, or rather I command you: change your bad character and habits, your manners and your words, your bearing and your speech. For what need is there to show those who invite you wickedness instead of goodness, to grieve God, and to shame me, the wretched one? I will be heard, my brothers, when I cry to the Lord, unworthy though I am. And then I will separate myself from whoever disobeys. Perhaps I speak simply and act without discrimination, not distinguishing the holy from the unholy. Do you not fear God? Shall we not give account for every idle word? Our God is a consuming fire, brothers. Let us fear him; let us serve him in holiness from now on, so that [?], abstaining even from idle talk and holding fast to virtue, we may become heirs of eternal life, escaping the punishments threatened against the contemptuous, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory and might with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
125 (21). To the canonesses [?]. [669.]
Yesterday, when I saw you, sisters in the Lord, I was prevented from speaking with you as much as I should have, because there was urgent business on account of the illness of the most God-loving archbishop. Now I have thought it good to make up by letter for what was lacking. I saw your sisterhood, how large it is and of what quality, grown in numbers and distinguished in understanding; and I glorified our good God, who has gathered so great a multitude of you together to serve him in the cross-bearing life in holiness and righteousness. Whom then should I praise? The superior more, or you who follow and obey her? Both deserve full measure of encomia, praise and commendation. And not only for the unity of your spiritual life, but because, as I have learned, you also keep a strict life, in self-control, in serving one another yourselves, and in every kind of ministry. You are blessed in the Lord; your company is blessed; your way of life is praiseworthy.

You are all brides of Christ; each virgin, in the words of the Song, is a garden locked, a fountain sealed, a rose of God's fragrance, a lily of purity. O fair paradise! O meadow pleasing to God! Christ is in your midst, who is the tree of life. But for the trial and testing of virtue there is also the forbidden plant, which is lovely to look at, yet is not what it seems, but bitter and deadly to eat. And what is it but pleasure, by which Eve our first mother was caught? So we remind and urge you never to touch the deadly fruit, but to partake of the commandment, the all-beautiful and truly genuine fruit, tempered with obedience and humility, with love for one another and freedom from envy, with poverty and peacemaking. For if you live this way you will glorify God in your body and in your spirit, as the holy Apostle cries out; this way you will multiply all the more; this way you will be called by a name of holiness here, and in the age to come you will be glorified together with Christ. For it is written: "If we suffer with him, we shall also be glorified with him." What then is lovelier than you? What more venerable? To be called daughters of God, offerings, holy things, temples of virginity! Since this is so, rejoice, sisters in the Lord, rejoice, hating the joy of the world; hating attachment to your own kin according to the flesh; hating to have an inheritance on earth; hating everything that is desired in the world. For your citizenship is in heaven, your allotted inheritance is the kingdom of heaven, and your bridegroom is Christ himself, who has called you to follow after him, and who will bring you at your end into the heavenly bridal chamber with the wise virgins. These few words I have written so that you may know that in the Holy Spirit we count you as sisters, and that we pray for

The greeting at the head of this letter brings you joy, brothers; but the occasion for writing brings the deepest grief. For the good shepherd has left you, your Father in the Lord, the lamp [?] and luminary, who shepherded many sheep for many years and left the flock full of nurslings, numbering in fact twenty short of two hundred. He was a venerable man and a partaker of divine grace; very white of hair, and whiter still of heart; rich in love, and richer still in almsgiving; truly adorned with many virtues, so many that I would be drawing out a long speech if I counted them one by one. Alas, alas! How is this not distressing? How is it not lamentable? How is the sight of the flock not one of desolation, as far as outward things [?] go? But what then? Shall we

dwell on our mourning? Shall we be downcast in deeper despondency? Shall we give ourselves up to grief? Not at all, brothers. We know that it is God's decree that all human beings who have come into being must depart again and receive the better life that is free from pain, whose firstfruits is Christ our God, the author of life. So let us be comforted with the comfort of God; let us come to ourselves; let us say: "The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away" the good teacher, the holy leader. "For what man is there who shall live and not see death?" Why then should we find our Father's lot strange? We must give thanks that we were counted worthy of such a man; that his span of life reached old age and seniority; and that he did not leave you unprotected or desolate, but gave you his parting blessings, offered fitting prayers, and appointed one of your own number to preside over you. We urge him to gird his loins as a perfect man, and to hold fast to the ministry entrusted to him with a humility that imitates Christ, walking by the rule and in the footsteps of that blessed man, in keeping with the word of God's commandment. Likewise we urge you, the good brotherhood, to yield to your newly appointed superior in the Lord with faith and love of one mind, and to show that God is truly among you, and that your holy Father is still zealous for you and binds you all together in concord and harmony. Yes, longed-for brothers, so may you be; be firmly established in this. Every beginning may be hard, but with time it settles into a skilled habit. And do not become like those who, through love of strife [?] and love of power, are unstable and unskilled. Since the matter of the persecution stands on a razor's edge, I beg you, do not betray the faith or piety. If it comes, do not on any account be drawn into union with the heretics in any way whatsoever. Bear everything nobly, counting all things secondary: not only monasteries and everything in monasteries, however vast they may be, but even your own bodies. Choose the good exile, and be crowned with the beatitude of persecution, which is surpassingly glorious and wonderful, just as the blessed man also commanded you. And if you say that he was caught, yes, alas for that defeat! But he has been recalled; he has done penance, and has been joined with the orthodox, and is one of our brothers and Fathers, since he has also been received by our most blessed patriarch, the celebrant of the holy rites. Knowing this, brothers, take courage, keep good order, and fare well in Christ Jesus our Lord. May he give rest to that man with the righteous and make you complete in every good thing, our beloved brothers.
127 (25). To Peter of Nicaea. [671.]
Now we have the chance to write to your fatherly

holiness, now that we have returned from exile. For the Arab invasion had driven us humble ones, along with many others, from our lodging and carried us off to the island of Prinkipo, in front of the city. Why even speak of how much we suffered there from the crowd of refugees pressing on us, from the heat, and from the undrinkable water? Then, when we moved closer, to Chalcedon, there came the second of two troubles: we fell into an unbearable illness, with kidney pains chastising our wretched flesh for a whole week. In short, our journey became more painful. Yet by the grace of God we achieved three things. First, we venerated our most blessed high priest and received his holy prayers. Second, we saw various holy Fathers and brothers. Third, by the mercy of God, we cleared away the objections and counter-charges that the "makers of peace" had kindled against us, from where I do not know. They had painted us beforehand as schismatics, cut off from communion with our divine high priest, and declared that we were a law unto ourselves in the penances we imposed on those who had fallen into communion with the heretics. Other things it would be tedious to unroll in a letter. But, as I said, by your prayers we answered each point squarely, and it was shown that we are in communion with our holy patriarch. He received us with exceeding condescension, treated us kindly, and sent us on our way, without any mention being made of the intrigues. More than that, mention was made of the lord Tarasius, who is commemorated among the saints. For the would-be lovers of the Fathers said that we had separated ourselves from him too, and that we called the holy second synod at Nicaea a local one. But we made it clear that we hold him among the holy Fathers and confess that synod as ecumenical, both in writing and by word of mouth, even if somewhere, at some time, in some way, we answered some people otherwise. Such things, like the things done otherwise at that time, ought not to be sought out and scraped open again now. That causes disturbance and brings no benefit, but rather wrangling and offense to the Church of God: "this one and that one wrote and did thus and so," each thinking he held the truth. As you know, thrice-longed-for one, the much-discussed affair went on for many years and became known in East and West. What was done and written cannot be overturned by either side. Now is the time for concord; now is the time for contending side by side. As for what the writer left behind, if those who come after think it sound, it will deserve praise; if not, the opposite. Faithful is the saying, and we have nothing more we wish to say about this, neither now nor hereafter. "The day of revelation," it says, "will disclose it," and the last fire, by which our works are judged and purified. These things have been written out of necessity, both to you as a Father of one soul with us and a maker of peace, and also because speaking out one's griefs, as I know, brings relief to those in pain.

If you could be persuaded to come and see us humble ones, taking on the labor of love, you would surely make us entirely your own in everything. Those with us send your holiness many greetings. We too send many greetings to those with you, most holy one.
128 (24). To Mary, a virgin. [676.]
Since we have now received gifts from your honor once and twice, we judged it necessary to greet your dignity not merely with a bare word of greeting but by letter, and not so much because of the gifts as because of your holiness of life. For we learn that you have chosen the life of virginity and have consented to serve the Lord in holiness and righteousness. What is better than virginity? Its care is how to please the Lord, how to attain the good things to come, and how to escape the intricate schemes of the devil. But the married woman's care is the opposite: how to please her husband and how to manage the affairs of the world well. She is washed over by the salty waves of life as she cares for children and for male and female slaves, and above all for pleasing her husband. She is not yet able to rise above the twists and turns of the world and be lifted on the wing of the mind to the Lord. You then, fairest of women, are truly blessed, thrice blessed, because you have chosen the good portion, after that celebrated Mary, sitting, as it were, at the feet of Jesus and hearing his word through a quieter life. You have sanctified yourself by dedicating your life to God as a treasure. You have ennobled your blood in the Holy Spirit, setting yourself forward as a fine example. For what will those under the yoke gain, unless perhaps they too seek and grope after God as far as they can? Are not all couples unyoked by death? Do not the beauties of this life pass away like a dream? And how many are the miseries that attend marriage! Some are childless, others have bad children. There is poverty and there is wealth: the one presses hard and, as it were, fries people in the pan; the other is tossed from one hand to another as in a game of dice. Bridal chambers are raised up, but they are also torn down with lamentation; there are dirges and beating of breasts, and disasters one after another. Life is full of them, and the examples are before our eyes. But you have escaped all these things, fair virgin, living alone at home, kept in your virginity as a fragrant rose for the Lord, though you surely also have afflictions from enemies both visible and invisible. For where there is an offering to the Lord, there the robber lies in wait to steal and plunder what is holy. But take courage in the Lord, in whom you trust and for whose sake you gladly bear your labors; for he is the guardian of your life, the helper

and a helper in afflictions, who, bringing your course to its end, will make you worthy of his heavenly kingdom. We sinners have addressed these words to you so that you may know that you, the handmaid of the Lord, have in us too, who strive to serve the Lord, brothers according to the spirit, as well as fellow servants by nature, who pray for your honored self.

Letter 129 (25). To Leo the sacellarius. [?]

Since we owe a great debt of thanks and of apologies, we think we repay only a small part of it in the letters our lowliness writes to your all-praised and much-loved eminence. For now too, regarding brother Silvanus, what apology shall we make? First, that your God-loving soul received him into its presence as though he were one of your intimates, speaking with this humble man and mingling with him with a gentle manner and an approachable face. Then, that you discussed with him the affairs of us sinners, made known the weakness of the lowly body of us both, and showed the rest of your loving fellow-feeling — to the point of saying, "I am even suspected of being a Studite by some of those hostile to you," and praying that no wound might ever come to so great a bond of friendship. All this astonished us, and rooted us more and more firmly in your sincere love, so that we say the same: Never, O Master of all, grant that we forget our good benefactor, our faithful ally, our proven lover, the holy man who is in every way and in all things our patron and guardian, our lord and master. Rather, may this affection remain settled in us even after death, or better still pass over with us into the age to come, in which we believe that we shall recognize one another, and that those who have loved one another by the prompting of the Spirit shall rejoice together in God.

But from here let my discourse pass on and dwell on the two questions, as you bade me. On the first, as you, our lord, are disposed, so are we also. Let the argument first be set out thus. A murderer, if he is caught, will justly pay the law the corresponding penalty. But what we have before us now is a civil war, which, like the other visitations of God's wrath — earthquakes and famines, floods and fires — was fanned into flame by God's just judgment for our correction, and destroyed as great a number as perished. Since, then, the Lord in his compassion has stopped the slaughter, he does not wish those who are left to be destroyed. Otherwise he would surely have wrought total destruction, as at the Flood. Rather, he wishes those who were spared to be saved and to become worthy of mercy. For he says in the Gospels, "Forgive, and you will be forgiven." And through the blessed Paul: "Let no one repay anyone

evil for evil, but always pursue what is good, both for one another and for all." Yet not without penalty. For Cain too, when he had murdered his brother, fittingly received his manifold and much-sung punishment. Lamech also was penalized by himself. And Absalom, having killed his brother Amnon, was spared by his father, in accordance with the case put before him by the woman of Tekoa, [?] unslain; and David himself did not wish Absalom the parricide to be killed. Nor is it written that he ordered those who had rebelled with him to be put to death after the war had ended. So much, in brief, on this matter. For God, being merciful, wishes that through penalties — that is, exiles, imprisonments, or other measures — the chance of repentance be kept open for them throughout their lives.

As for the other question, what need is there to say anything [?], since your prudent and energetic mind knows everything? It was for this very purpose that the former Leo insisted that we engage in debate with the heterodox, intending, as he supposed, to deliver judgment between the opposing sides himself. And the present emperor too made the same demand when he spoke with us face to face three years ago — not saying that he himself would judge the dispute, but that this or that one of those supposedly of our mind would. But neither we who were present face to face nor our renowned archbishop would accept it, as unlawful and alien — which indeed it is, our much-loved master. For the matter is not about worldly and fleshly things, over which the emperor and the secular tribunal have the power to judge, but about divine and heavenly doctrines, which are entrusted to none but those to whom God the Word said [?]: "Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven." And who are those to whom this command was given? The apostles and their successors. And who are the successors? The one who now holds the first throne, that of Rome; the one who holds the second, that of Constantinople; those of Alexandria and Antioch; and the one of Jerusalem. This is the five-headed authority of the Church. With them lies judgment on divine doctrines. The part of emperors and rulers is to lend their help, to set their seal on what has been decreed, and to reconcile differences of a fleshly kind. In divine doctrines they have no other role; none has been given them by God, nor will any they assume stand. That is why, regarding the doctrine of the holy icons, what was convened in council and babbled out by imperial power and audacity under the former Constantine and Leo was rejected. At that time the Church here was cut off from the other four and fell under eternal anathemas, sealed by the Holy Spirit. Then by God's mercy a horn of orthodoxy was raised up under the renowned Irene together with her son, and under her what had been divided was joined together again, until the recent Leo, under whom the Church here was cut off once more, anathematized by the others just as before.

It is impossible, then, master, to set the divine tribunal on a level with a secular tribunal, or for the Church here to be reunited unless the five patriarchs are of one mind. If anyone should ask how this can come about: by the heterodox withdrawing from the churches of God, and by Nikephoros, the holy patriarch, recovering his own throne. Sitting in synod with those who shared his struggle (if it is not possible for representatives of the other patriarchs to be present — though it is possible, if the emperor wishes the one from the West to be present, since the authority of an ecumenical council is referred to him), he would bring to completion the prize of peace and union, namely through his own synodical letters sent to the holder of the first throne. But if the emperor will not accept this, and, as he says, Nikephoros the president has strayed from the truth along with us, then envoys should be sent from each side to the bishop of Rome, and from there let the certainty of the faith be received. For so it stands: if one of the patriarchs strays, he is to receive correction from those of equal rank, as the divine Dionysius says, and not to be judged by emperors, even if all the orthodox emperors should rise up. Our emperor ought not to neglect this point, but should above all take care for it, for in it his reign is blessed and lawful rule is granted him. We, the humble and unworthy, hold no other view, and we pray for your much-desired well-being. And if anything is lacking in this letter, its bearer, who venerates your honored footsteps, will explain.

Letter 130 (26). To the brotherhood of Kizara. [684]

The news of the falling asleep of our spiritual father and yours, beloved brothers, has troubled our soul, as is natural, and brought it to grievous sighing — not on account of the one who has fallen asleep, for he is blessed, having been brought to perfection by a blessed life. He was a proven monk, he practised asceticism excellently until old age, and, the chief thing, he departed from this world with his orthodox faith kept intact amid persecutions and hardships endured for the good, crowned, as it were, with the righteousness of confessing Christ. No, it is on account of us, or rather of you yourselves [cod. Reg.: and those] who are left behind like a flock at a loss through the departure of its good shepherd. For the memory of the superior draws us to pity and contrition of heart, as we recall the place and the manner of his guidance in the Lord: how he encouraged one who was downcast, rebuked another who grew insolent, called back another who was restive, and roused another who was sluggish, governing with gentleness and forbearance in imitation of the Master himself, who said, "Learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart"; and in short, in all that he did

he shone among you like the morning star. Besides, after long habit, separation from one's [physician?] [?] usually weighs very heavily on the soul. But what shall we do, brothers, against the law of God, which commands, "You are earth, and to earth you shall return"? Or rather, this is a journey home to the Lord, not a separation. He was bidden to depart, and he left the body. He was parted from you and was gathered to his fathers, leaving you his own life as a fine example and likeness of virtue. What, then, remains to be sought? That you come to yourselves and encourage one another in the Holy Spirit. And just as he left you the lord Antony as hegumen, so begin to live by the same rule and in the same footsteps of piety, guarding the faith and suffering for it, if need be, even to death, in the present persecution. Never betray the truth, and embrace with all your strength love for one another and obedience to the hegumen. For this leads to your salvation; this is a boast for that blessed man on the day of Christ; this is most delightful to us, your friends and brothers, as well. For if you walk thus, most excellently, you will have us following along with you, as far as we can, in the things of the Lord, most honored brothers.

Letter 131 (27). A catechetical letter to his own disciples.

Theodore, least of presbyters and so-called hegumen [?] of the Studites, to my beloved brothers and spiritual sons, scattered here and there for the Lord's sake. [685]

Grace to you and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, who has granted you persecution for his name. Though it is bitter [?] to the flesh, it brings joy to the spirit; for it is the cause of blessings spoken by God and the procurer of eternal crowns. For this reason I too, the humble one, rejoice with joy and exult with exultation, that I have been granted to see my beloved ones in such progress, at so high a degree of the good confession which we confessed before God and men: to venerate Christ depicted, that is, portrayed in an image, as did all our holy fathers. Only I exhort and remind you to live worthily of the gospel of Christ: keep your conduct good in the places where you stay and among the people with whom you live; your speech gracious, seasoned with salt; your bearing full of reverence; your food and drink held to what is sufficient; your clothing and your gait governed by good sense — so that you may be a light to the laity and not the opposite, an occasion for praising God and not the opposite. As each has received a gift, employ it among yourselves as good

stewards of God's manifold grace, as it is written: if anyone speaks, let it be as the oracles of God, not as idle talk; if anyone serves, as from strength, not out of arrogance; if anyone works with his own hands, so as not to be a burden, and not as an idler condemned even to go without eating. If anyone does all things according to the commandment, let it be as God's workman, not as a stumbling block to his neighbor; so that in all things God may be glorified, and I, wretch that I am, may hear of it and take heart and rejoice.

Beware of evil pairings; beware of ruinous freedom of speech; beware of the gluttony that breeds fornication. Let no one converse with a woman without necessity; let no one settle down to live alone; let no one love money, adding coin to coin and heaping up gold, in which sin takes root, and the portion of Judas. Let no one barter away his monastic freedom by acquiring a slave bought with silver. For the wickedness of some has gone this far: enslaved by attachment, they have lost the monastic dignity. Let no one be given to drink, but listen to the Apostle: "Use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent illnesses." For from such things fleshly desires are kindled against the soul, and the house of God, which is our inner man, is set on fire. Rather, brothers, let us be strangers and sojourners, each of you in this persecution: as dying, and behold, we live; as chastened, and not put to death; as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich in spirit; as having nothing, and yet possessing everything — to speak in the Apostle's words. My eyes are ever upon you, my beloved; my heart burns within you in the Lord; my senses are in turmoil whenever I hear a deplorable report about anyone; when I learn of some God-hated straying, my eyes shed tears. My soul is crushed whenever someone who does not love God walks contrary to the tradition, the established rule, and the guidance set out above. You went out from the monastery, fathers, into the higher light of persecution. Were we parted from one another at the Spirit's prompting so as to fall into darkness? So as to live by our passions? Does God not see? Does each one's deed, how he conducts himself, not come to be heard? You who keep slaves, hear this; you who live alone, you who keep company with women, to say no more; you lovers of money, you lovers of roaming [?]. I do not reproach you willingly — forgive me — but I accuse you in pain, since I am appointed for this. Make my joy complete, children, by being of one mind and walking by the same rule, stamping good examples and reminders on the souls of those who see you, to the glory of God, to your unfading renown, to the gladness of me the sinner, and to the praise of your brotherhood
in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory and power, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages.

Letter 132 (28). To the abbess of Igna [?]. [?]

I welcomed your piety, sister in the Lord, both in the gifts you sent and in the feelings with which you regard our affairs. But we are not such as you think: we are not even sufficient in good things for ourselves, so how could we impart good teaching to others? May it be granted you, according to your faith, to live in a manner worthy of God, completing the life of virginity blamelessly, and not only that, but also holding the office of superior without reproach. For know that the task is richly rewarded, but for those who are not watchful it is also dangerous: to govern souls made in the image of God. So, as one who governs in the Lord, lead and guide your flock, setting yourself up as a model of every good, so that you may be counted worthy to say, "Here am I, and the children whom God has given me." For God has entrusted these souls to you through their renunciation, and you must bring them to him as an acceptable offering; and in this your reward will be great in heaven. Teach them, admonish them in the saving commandments: to long for Christ alone and not for flesh and blood; to be without possessions, having nothing of their own; to be free of attachment, not fond of intimacy with their relatives; to work eagerly and not be sluggish in ascetic practice. For if they do so, Christ the Bridegroom will soon meet them as they carry their lamps, and they will meet him with great joy; he will embrace them and be embraced in holy fashion; he will open to them the heavenly bridal chamber not made by hands; he will give them the kingdom of heaven, the delight of paradise, the drink of immortality, the sweetness of everlasting life; he will clothe them in garments of light and adorn them with the ornaments of incorruption, with bridal diadems; he will fill them with boundless good things, to the ages of ages. For this, you and they, toil; strive day after day to work out your own salvation; refresh yourselves with hope; with divine love quench the fire the enemy brings into souls, and whatever else is burdensome in the ascetic life. Console yourselves by taking up divine readings and chants, guarding above all [?] your refusal of communion with the heresy, even if you must suffer something for it, even unto death, and never surrendering the faith. For nothing is more precious than the love of Christ, as virgins through the ages have shown down to the present; for even now some, being persecuted, are driven out of their convents for Christ's sake rather than partake of the heretics' bread. I have written this to you as to a sister and daughter in Christ, and to those under you, so that you may see that

the Master of us both is the same, and that we long for all to be saved, since we are of one body of Christ and through him are called brothers and sisters of one another. For in Christ Jesus there is neither male nor female, but Christ is all and in all. May he save both you and us.

Letter 133. To Ephraim, Agathon, and the rest of my children. [688]

The blessed Laurence has fallen asleep, and for him death is rest. How could it be otherwise for a good man who has passed out of life from ascetic labors, or rather has gone home to the Lord from persecution for righteousness' sake? Many are witnesses to his virtues. For you, most honored brothers, as for us humble ones too, it has brought grief, for we have lost a proven monk, an honored brother, who had been set as head to guide souls. Yet the grief has turned to joy for us both, because the one snatched from us by the command of the good God is God's chosen, in holiness and righteousness. Therefore I too, the humble one, rejoice and rejoice with you, that we have sent on to God so great a vessel. For Laurence was truly a chosen vessel: first, through his unfeigned renunciation and obedience; second, through his zeal for virtue and his progress, for which he was also counted worthy of the priesthood and received the charge of overseeing many brothers, serving the flock well by shepherding it with love; living truly to God and to the hegumen, and not to the world and its affairs. He also endured exiles for the Lord's sake and persecutions, both earlier and later. His feet too were beautiful, to speak in the words of Scripture, as he went about here and there proclaiming to the brothers the saving promises. His spiritual sweat was myrrh; his struggling course of virtue was holy dew [?]. Taken up in this very persecution, what else has he won as his crown but the Lord's beatitude? And now he dwells in heaven as a fellow citizen of those of his rank, while we still stand in the contest, exposed to the fear of turning back. For no one attains perfect blessedness until his departure, because the outcome is uncertain. Therefore I exhort you, brothers, to keep watch and be sober, to be courageous and strong in the contest before us, the persecution both spiritual and visible. For whoever lives according to God is always pursued by the invisible persecutor, who seeks to catch him in sin. Let us flee him as noble soldiers of Christ. And how can we flee? By placing ourselves under the mighty hand of God, pleasing him in everything. This will come about if you live not by your own will but in common life — that is, with brother Ephraim as your superior, as Laurence himself arranged, as we also approve, and as time and circumstance may require. Let all things be common; let "mine" and "yours" be banished; let love [?]

…let it [?] strengthen; let obedience guard. And: “If you know these things, blessed are you,” he says, “if you do them.”

134 [?]. — To Euphrosyne, abbess.

The memory of your blessed mother has moved me to address you a few words now as well, sister in the Lord, as though she were prodding me. She was your mother on both counts and mine in the spirit, and I dare say the mother of many others too, since she was a venerable lady. What are these words? That you should fight the good fight of the ascetic life to which you were called, having made the good confession before many witnesses. And how is one to fight? By having the fear of God in the heart, for where there is fear, there the commandments are kept. By meditating on death, for where there is meditation on death, there is estrangement from the passions. By being concerned about the soul's separation from the body, the angelic escort that follows, and the soul's being led up to heaven. How will it get past the ruler of this age, who tries to drag the ascending soul to himself if he sees it branded with the passions? Then where will it find its place of rest until the time of the resurrection, when its partner, the body, will be united to it by the ineffable power of God? And I do not yet speak of the coming, a little later, of Christ the Bridegroom from heaven with the angels of his power, and of the catching up of God-loving souls into the air. Nor do I speak of the gathering of all creation together before the fearful judgment seat, and then of the sentence on the two parties standing there, which calls the righteous into the kingdom of heaven and sends the sinners away into the outer fire. The soul that ponders these things with keen feeling trembles, fears, is pierced with compunction, weeps, is cleansed and is enlightened. It stands apart from its attachments to this world and is changed with the good change. It runs up to God in spiritual joy and unspeakable delight, so that it turns away even from looking at the sun and from the other pleasures of the present life, because its contemplation of the good overpowers them. This, most honored one, is how one fights the good fight. Your good mother fought this fight, clung to God and departed from here in a praiseworthy way. Let us too, then, I beg you, hasten to follow in her footsteps. And do not grow dizzy when you are called to the heights of virtue. For one thing, by the grace of God you are already being lifted up by good ascents, and I hear that you are doing well in them. For another, where the will is present, perfection is gradually added too, since God gives strength and loves the salvation of the one who chooses this way. Perhaps you will think that having charge of the sisters is an obstacle to such a purpose, and feel weighed down by the work of guiding them. But by no means, my lady. For nothing is so dear to God

as shepherding and guiding those who follow. For he says to the great Peter: “If you love me, shepherd my sheep.” And again: “He who brings forth the worthy from the unworthy shall be as my mouth.” And again: “He who turns a sinner back from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins.” If someone rushes forward and seizes the shepherd's staff out of love of power, he is hateful and abominable to God, and he neither saves others nor is saved himself. But if someone is called and accepts the charge out of obedience to God, he will prove to be a friend of God who both saves and is saved. Since you yourself have been called in this way, rejoice and tremble: rejoice because of the hope, tremble because of the struggle. Lead and prosper as you shepherd the sisterhood and carry the care of it. The rumors going around frighten you, as you say, but you have God as your helper, and your mother's prayers work with him. Cast your care upon him, and he himself will make your circumstances easier. Do you say you have no one who truly protects you? But you have the Champion himself, the Lord whom you have loved, and then the angel who guards your life and rescues you from every evil. So be of good courage and do not lose heart. Be strong and not sickly, and take care to keep your body healthy, so that you may serve God sufficiently and govern the sisters. Now let my word turn to the sisters in their turn. They should follow in a reasonable way and be shepherded in a manner worthy of God, living for you alone, recognizing you as their true mother and one another as true sisters. For where there is such unity of soul, Christ is in the midst, and the blessed life is brought to perfection. They have chosen a blessed life: they have embraced virginity and have Christ as their bridegroom, not mortal suitors. Union with such suitors is painful, and the separation that follows a little later is more grievous still. But Christ, whom they have as their bridegroom, never dies; he is the life of all, and if they keep their vow of fasting they will go in with him to the heavenly bridal chamber. Let them eat and drink and be clothed, and receive whatever else they need, from your discerning [?], since the Apostle says: “Being so affectionately desirous of you, we were pleased to share with you not only the gospel of God but also our own souls.” Only let them be of one mind and think alike, having one soul and one will, holding all things in common, with nothing privately owned and no one going her own way. Then the whole work of their salvation is accomplished, and the short and most beautiful course of the coenobitic life is completed, and they will dance for ages of ages with you, their good and godly-minded mother. For in this way the good community and the one who shepherds it well will rejoice in a common joy, and they will be with the Lord always. This is our small and worthless address. But you, my lady, have received these few seeds; add from yourself what is lacking, and

be pleased to pray for us sinners, so that we may be seen to practice the words we teach, and may be saved with you in the kingdom of heaven.

135 (26). — Catechetical.

Your honor has asked our lowliness for a word of admonition, although our word is despised and our life neglected. We are writing nonetheless, because we long for your salvation, since you are a virgin, a bride of Christ, a treasure of holiness, and because you seek our admonition with confidence. You seek it because the holy Forty Days now stand at the door. The true virgin of Christ seeks how to please her Lord and Bridegroom not only on appointed days but at all times and every day. Still, the season of fasting certainly calls for a special zeal for virtue compared with the rest of the year. So, most honored one, be eager to keep your accustomed rule of ascetic life now as well. We cannot lay down this or that for you or for those who practice the ascetic life with you, because we do not yet know your order and way of life. But there is one rule and canon common to all and owed by all, and especially by those who have taken up the monastic profession: that we do nothing that displeases God, but work out our salvation with fear and trembling. For true fasting is abstinence from every evil. Let us fast, first, by not letting evil thoughts take up residence in the heart and then flare up into vivid desires. For there is one desire and one true love: our Lord Jesus Christ, the good and beautiful Bridegroom. The soul that longs for him with its whole being hates flesh and blood and all the phantoms of corruption. Ever winged by its longing for him, it turns away, so to speak, even from seeing the sun itself, and it yearns ardently to leave the body and be with the one it longs for, which is the highest object of desire for those who share in reason. Let us fast, in the second sense, from foods, both in quantity and in quality, as far as the strength of the body can bear. For the Apostle says: “Each as he has decided in his heart, not grudgingly or under compulsion; for God loves a cheerful giver,” and what is done according to one's ability. This can properly be said of you, the superior. In the case of the sisterhood, however, it does not apply, because each of them eats and drinks and conducts the rest of her life according to the arrangement you give. So you need a discerning eye to oversee their affairs fittingly. Common to all is the duty to abstain from untimely idle talk, unseemly envy, and idleness

that meddles in others' affairs. Instead they should keep silence at the right time and speak the words that are needed, love and cherish one another in the Lord, and have all things in common, with nothing set apart as one's own… [One page is missing.]

136 (27). — To Theodore, general.

…the opposite outcome for those who are… O the calamity! What is this forced abduction? What is this compulsory partaking, which threatens bodily danger to anyone who does not choose to partake of the heterodox bread? Freely offered, O most Christian mind, is the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. For the great Apostle says of him: “Who, being in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men; and being found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross.” Since, then, it is freely offered, it is freely given to those who are willing, not to those who are unwilling. For the Lord himself in the Gospels says to the apostles, “Do you also want to go away?” He said this because some of those who seemed to be his disciples had already gone away from him. And the great Peter answered: “To whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life. And we have believed and come to know that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” And again, the great Peter says in his own epistle that one must shepherd willingly, not under compulsion. So let those who forcibly drag the unwilling into their own communion know this: they are acting in a pagan fashion. What they offer is not the body of Christ, which is a willing sacrifice. On the contrary, it bears the appearance of food sacrificed to idols, like the unwilling victim offered in their demon-loving libations. The argument is true and the proof is plain, yet no one listens. But “Spare, O Lord, spare, and do not give your inheritance over to utter reproach,” as one of the prophets said somewhere. And what of us, [?] thrice-longed-for and all-praised one? For it must be said, even if rather harshly; otherwise how could the word be a friend's? Shall we still be carried along by the times? Shall we cower before authority more than is right? And where is the voice of the Lord forbidding human fear, and declaring instead that God alone holds all authority and has the power to cast both soul and body into the Gehenna of fire? Alas for the collapse! Alas for the cowering! Before what sort of person did it happen, and one who above all bears the name of Christ? Nevertheless, come back again, friend and good lord. Let us be called back; let us repent. The Lord is near to those who seek him, and he does not want us to fall

into any sin. But when we have fallen, he longs for us to rise quickly, and when we sin, to turn back, however often this may happen through some mishap of poor judgment. Perhaps your honorable soul will say: “He who struck will also heal.” And what of the penance? No illness is incurable when it is treated, and the course of treatment will not be heavy for you.

137 (28). — To Prokopios, monk.

I am writing to your honor just now because I have found that the bearer of this letter is a friend of both of us. He even urged me to write, saying that your piety was asking for this and would like it. But greetings, man of God! Greetings, best of friends, and one of the oldest! Greetings, you who are renowned for reverence [the Royal codex reads: “who are renowned for reverence”] and famed far and wide for your knowledge! Where have you been all this time, leaving us and hiding your honored face for so many years? Second, what is the manner of this confinement at home, without ever going out or appearing in public? And third, to speak more frankly, or rather more lovingly, since it belongs to love not to hold back useful reminders from the one it loves: what is this way of life of yours? You fled the world through monastic consecration, and then returned home again. You were freed from the bonds of your former attachments, for that is what renunciation is, and then were bound again by living with the lady your wife and your God-protected children. And what is stranger still: you were tonsured with the mark of the solitary life and consecrated by the divine mystery, and now you grow your hair long again in a [?] way of life. “Let each one,” says the Apostle, “remain in the calling in which he was called.” And again elsewhere: “Give no offense to Jews or to Greeks or to the church of God.” And elsewhere again he says of himself: “I will never eat meat, so that I may not cause my brother to stumble.” Each person makes himself recognizable by his own dress: the soldier by wearing a sword, the townsman by wearing a cloak. In short, nearly everyone in public office, a craft or a profession carries the tools that belong to him. A doctor would not choose to carry a shepherd's staff, nor would a shepherd take a medical instrument in hand. If this is so, much more in spiritual matters of the highest importance ought one neither to live contrary to what belongs to one's state nor to change one's appearance. Otherwise one will incur the judgment that hangs over anyone who scandalizes the world, as the Lord said. May we escape it, thrice-longed-for one, especially we who stand above most people in knowledge and rank. For judgment is severe on those in high places, but the least is pardonable, as

it is written. And again the Lord says: “From the one to whom much has been entrusted, they will demand more.” So I beg you: we who ought to be a light to those in darkness must not become the opposite. And we who have been appointed by the Gospel to be salt must not lose our savor through carelessness. “Let all things be done decently and in order,” cries the Apostle; let everything be for our neighbor's benefit and not his harm. Even in things permitted to us, if scandal arises, the great Basil cries out the same thing, and indeed the whole Old and New Testament: each person is commanded to remain within his own bounds and ways. And do not think, master, that I have attacked you overbearingly. I have written very lovingly and with pain, taking your affairs upon myself as love blends us together, and desiring the salvation of your honorable soul as my own. If anything in my words is unreasonable, let your reply teach my lowliness and persuade me that you are acting reasonably in the things I have shown to be out of place.

138 (29). — To Theoktistos, hermit.

God's commandment requires us to love one another, even to the point of laying down our lives for one another. It has compelled me, spiritual brother, to write to you again, because I am troubled for your salvation. I hear that there is a schismatic division between you and other brothers, and no ordinary one but a very grievous one. The common people have been torn into two opposing parties, each attached to its own side and withdrawing from communion with the other. This whole thing is the work of Satan, the ancient murderer of men. It is a great scandal, and the Lord has said: “Woe to the world because of scandals.” And again: “It would be better for him to have a great millstone hung around his neck and be thrown into the sea than to cause one of these least ones to stumble.” I wonder how your honor, after practicing the ascetic life and devoting yourself to God for so many years, can be unconcerned about this danger. Unless you correct it with all your zeal and care, it will not only make all your ascetic labor empty but also put you far from God, which God forbid. That is why, brother, moved by brotherly love, I wrote to you three years ago. I had come near your area on my way back from Smyrna and had learned of the schism. I wrote you what I had heard, how you ought to think about the truth, and how to escape the danger of scandal hanging over you. You did not write back. I wrote to you again, and you did not answer me. That is clear evidence that you do not wish to serve God or walk uprightly in the truth. Forgive me, and do not be angry

with me for speaking the truth. It is written: “You shall surely reprove your neighbor, and you shall not incur sin because of him.” See, wretched as I am, though I have never seen you, I could not bear what I had heard, because you are a brother in Christ and I was afraid. I reproved you and exhorted you earnestly, to free myself from judgment and because I love your salvation. How will you, the accused and the father of the schism, bear the judgment? How will you make your defense to Christ when you are called to account for so great a people? Even if you had the works of John the Forerunner, he will send you away empty from the kingdom of God unless you first hasten to set things right. And how are things to be set right? In person, if possible. If not, then through your messenger, with a written defense concerning the charges brought against you earlier. Clear yourself by this defense, and show that your faith is orthodox and that you rightly divide the word of truth in all things. Once concord in the Lord has been reached in this way, the scandal is removed and what was divided is joined together. I do not mean concord with this person or that, but only with me, the humble one. Then the Lord is in our midst, and his name is not blasphemed because of us, I do not say among the gentiles, but among Christians. And if some still disagree after we have come to agreement with each other, they will be taught and brought together by us humble ones, since we will defend you as we would ourselves. God will be merciful, your life will be blessed, your end praiseworthy, and what you leave behind will rest in righteousness. See, this is my second humble letter. If you do what is needed, declaring yourself and making your defense on all the charges against you, you have been won back, our brother, in the proper sense of the word, and we humble ones rejoice greatly over you. But if, God forbid, you persist in the same silence and disobedience, you will bear eternal judgment. Your ascetic labor will be useless, or rather you will be ruinously splitting the people of God through your own self-will. We, for our part, will heed the Apostle, who says: “After a first and second admonition, have nothing more to do with a heretical man, knowing that such a person is perverted and sins, being self-condemned.”

139 (30). — To Stephen, hegumen.

The frequency of your letters shows how abundant your love is, honored one, and that it rests on your father's habit. For that blessed man, besides his other achievements, also produced the good fruit of love toward the brothers by this same practice. So write, thrice-longed-for one, taking after your father in this, and making us happier by hearing from you constantly. But do not praise us, and do not compare lead with gold or clay with a pearl. Rather, pray, you and the rest of that man's followers, [?] because I am useless in every way. You yourself may say that you are helped by us, useless as we are, but that is because you are carried along by

love. And if anything does help you, the credit must be given to God, who through one another and in one another arranges what is needed. So much for that. Now to those who have recovered through repentance. The question is whether those who have already escaped their fall may be accepted to make the sign of the cross over the table, or on any other occasion. This was already examined by the holy Fathers, almost in synod, and settled as right. We humble ones accept the practice, keep it, and pass it on to others. So if you too wish to hold to it, we both praise and approve. For some to reject it is the work of self-made religion, which the Apostle condemns, and it is neither lawful nor brotherly. On what do they rest their confidence, when no canon decrees it and our divine hierarch does not forbid us to accept this practice? Is it not rather destructive of repentance, and does it not drive people to despair of salvation, to say that one who is counted worthy to partake of the holy gifts, and to sign himself with the image of the cross, may not bless ordinary food, whether in private or in public? Do we not know that our good God and Lord, the only sinless one, who takes away the sin of the world, allowed a harlot to touch his spotless feet and anoint them with tears as with myrrh? Moreover, he eats with tax collectors and at their houses, and makes tax collectors his disciples. Nothing is so dear to him as turning back from sin and love for one another. This is also the mark by which he says his disciples will be known. And indeed, after his denial, he made blessed Peter the first of the other apostles. What greater proof could there be for the matter at hand? And what is more senseless than those who, out of ignorance and conceit, will not allow those already improved by repentance to bless and to pray? We humble ones, then, hold this view, as has been said, and so we advise you. Others who think differently will answer for it. As for what our brother Symeon asked, we have answered, and we humble ones hope that you, venerable ones, may be at rest in all things. We pray that you may be kept safe from harm in everything.

140 (31). — Catechetical letter to those in Cyzicus.

We were glad to see brother Symeon and those with him. Symeon has been appointed as your head. We were glad, first because he had been away for so long, and second because of your good way of life. For it is a good way of life, both for him and for us, that so many brothers live together in times of persecution. Where even two or three are gathered, it deserves praise, since Christ is in their midst according to his promise. But when there are so many that they make up a whole monastery and a large community, the praise is beyond dispute. And thanks be to the Lord, who has given us in one

…in spirit, with one soul to strive side by side for the faith of the Gospel, and in the same way to carry through the ascetic life, a life of struggle and of radiance, and to complete in it a contest crowned at every point. We also wished to see you yourselves, who are absent, face to face, and to be comforted together with you in the fellowship of the Spirit, so that we might learn the name and face and character and words of each one of you. But since this could not be, we have already seen you through your superior and those of the same rank as you. The sight of them nourished our hearts, for it bears the stamp of piety. What, then, remains to say? Only this: by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ you were gathered together, joined in spiritual harmony, and shone in concord of soul among the people there like stars in the dark night of heresy. So may you remain the same from now on: one in soul, minding the one thing, of one mind, submissive, obedient, attentive, grateful, [?], lovers of purity, self-controlled, not forward in speech, complete, equipped for every good work. Still shine, still beam, still give light, still salt, so that the Lord's words might fittingly be said of you: "You are the light of the world," and again: "You are the salt of the earth." And perhaps, since you live in the mountain country, this too might fittingly be sung over you: "A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden." That mountain is the lofty way of life. Those who have climbed it live on earth as if in heaven, people "of whom the world was not worthy," as the apostle said. See, children and brothers, how the word of truth has lifted you up. It has set you on high with its praises and shown you to be true monks, confessors of Christ, fugitives from the world, men who desire higher things, slayers of the passions of the flesh, crowned in the spirit. For now these are only bare words of recompense. But if you fully complete your contest of obedience and confession, then, when you pass from this life, you will receive the blessedness that your works have earned. May we all attain it, by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and dominion to the ages of ages.

141 (53 [?]). To an abbot. [?]
God has given a very great gift to our province, most honored brother: the most glorious curator, a man mighty in piety. He has become Christ's avenger and brought under his hand the man who was living like a robber among the Christians, even though that man had once been dedicated to God through monastic profession. I mean Ammous, once our brother, but now placed under your hand through the mediation of that admirable man and by the good pleasure of Christ himself, who rejoices at the salvation of the lost. What a marvelous deed [?] by the God-loving curator,

and worthy of his virtue! And it was worthy not of him only, but also of you, the spiritual father, who like Christ took the lost one up on your shoulders. So I, the lowly one, rejoiced and was glad that what was lost has been found and what was cast out has been brought home. Thanks be to the might and mercy of God's glory, which has shown him mercy and has also raised me, lowly as I am, out of my despondency. For many years I had been grieving over the loss of my son. Now, by God's mercy, you have become his father with the help of the good mediator. May you lead him to God from now on. For see, I hand him over into your hands as if from my own eyes. Let him be called your disciple, and he will be your disciple to the end, and you will inherit his reward forever. Read this letter to him, so that he may have assurance, just as I have also written to him directly. And so fulfill the Apostle's words: "Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ." May Christ keep you with all your God-chosen community, as you pray for better things for us sinners too.
Your brotherly honor is always accustomed to write things beyond what we deserve, dignifying our nothingness with honors and praises. But we have been taught not to go beyond our own measure, and to regard ourselves as nothing, which is what we are. Enough of that. The [?] of your honored letters has certainly not grieved us. Why should it? What would compel it? What has grieved us, since we must disclose how matters stand, is this: your stay in the city; your exchange of words, back and forth, with the emperor; and your departure under orders, while our situation remains just as it was, with the monasteries held under the control of the heterodox. We might add your being sent by the steward to the emperor himself, and your dining with them and being led off with them. All these things have grieved us, most honored one. Forgive me, but they keep us from meeting you [?], from mingling and keeping company with you, from receiving and giving, and from anything else that belongs to friendship and custom. For, as it says, "Why should my freedom be judged by another's conscience?"

[?] Grant us this freedom, and leave us to grieve over our own sins. I know that this letter is painful to your honor, as it is to us. But nothing is to be preferred to the love of God. For its sake we too, with our holy fathers, when Christ was insulted, renounced what we renounced, and we still choose what we have professed.
142 (54 [?]). To the same.
The grief our soul felt over you, most honored one, has been eased a little, if things are indeed as you have written and you are withdrawing from holding the office of abbot. For there is no fellowship, my dear friend, between the persecuted and those who are not persecuted. And these are not merely unpersecuted: they are subject to the persecutors while presiding over the monasteries they control. Unless, of course, fellowship between light and darkness has now been agreed upon. But that cannot be, as the sacred word has declared. Up to now you had given yourselves up among the captured by way of a medicinal submission. This was done on the following terms. We received pledges that in no way whatever, neither by word nor by deed, would you be made subject to the heterodox again, and that you would stand, as it were, in between holding and not holding the monasteries. In short, the confession was to remain lawful because you would draw away from the opponents and resist those who stood against us. But when the time for what was sought arrived, what had been agreed was not carried out before God and men for a more exact healing of the earlier submission. Instead there was again a being led off and again a falling away, in words and in deeds, as the facts themselves testify and as we have heard from those who know. And once again the abbots were unprepared, through their recent reception by the emperor and their dispatch. This applies to all who have acted in this way. It is laughable now to rebuke anyone; or rather, it is derangement on the part of those who rebuke, a stumbling block for the pious, and confusion and blindness about the confession of Christ. We must listen to the Apostle when he says: "Keep away from every brother who walks in a disorderly way and not according to the tradition you received from us." Or rather, we must listen to God when he cries out through the prophet: "Come out from among them and be separate, and touch nothing unclean, and I will welcome you." He means those who separate themselves in this way and do not confuse the confession of Christ. For what will they say, most honored one, the abbot of Komai and the abbot of Goulaios, along with the others recently persecuted for their resistance, if they see you holding the monasteries by betraying the truth, and us being led off with you? And what of those who endure hardship in the mountains under the pressure of persecution? Will they not mourn? Will they not lament? Will they not consider a game

the confession of Christ? And what about those who have served as abbots [?] since the founding of the monasteries and have been persecuted with us for Christ's sake? Will they not set their seal on this, as though what we suffer were a kind of play? "Do not be deceived," says the Apostle, "God is not mocked." The confession of Christ has not been made common, even if some think otherwise and say otherwise. So if you wish, beloved brother, to be ranked with us lowly ones, withdraw from holding the monastery, as you promised. This is what we beg of you, and this is what we pray for: that you may be orthodox outwardly as you are inwardly, and so save your precious soul, which nothing in the visible world can equal. The lord archbishop, who is with us, sends you many greetings, [longing] greatly for your salvation, since the rest also

144 (55). To Theodore the patrician.
This letter comes late, but that is because we learned late of the dreaded news of [?] misfortune that has befallen our master. Oh, what a lamentable report! Our [?] lady has left us. You have been cut off from your good wife, torn from the flesh that Scripture praises, of which the holy [Apostle] says: "The two shall become one flesh." And if they are admittedly one flesh, then plainly the separation inflicts on those who are parted as great a wound as a sword does when it cuts one man in two. Painful is the cut [?], and the blood seems to flow before your eyes. No salve can be applied to it, and no bandages, as far as human help goes, because the one who has departed was no ordinary wife, but truly praiseworthy and wonderful. She held the piety of the faith unbending and loved her husband as no other woman did, which the holy Apostle requires above all in marriage. So she offered petitions and prayers for her head, cries and constant attendance on God, and the blessed woman walked barefoot in the night processions, so that God might be moved to mercy by this as well. And what of her care for the home? What of her raising of the children? What of her care for the servants? What of her simple character, her graciousness toward friends, the way she bound the family together, her [?] toward women of equal rank, and her decorum and modesty in all things? These things, rather than [?] ornaments, pearl adornments and costly clothes, were what truly adorned that celebrated woman, whether she stayed at home, went out in public or was seen in the imperial halls. And yet all this is gone, and we have become, to put it with feeling, half-dead and torn apart. Or rather, in the words of the psalm, we are "like a night raven in a ruin, like a solitary sparrow on a roof," as we see the house bereft of her who presided over it, and the children before your eyes

going round and round and being gathered round, with nowhere to rest their hands and nowhere to receive a mother's caresses or the comfort of her nursing. The hearth is cold, as if the sun had left it. No one sings in your ears, or in the ears of your children and all your household, now that she is gone, she whose voice was truly lovely and who delighted all who heard her with her truly harmonious conversation and her way of greeting people. These things are truly pitiable and lamentable, whether spoken in figures or pondered in thought. But what are we to do, master? It is God's command, or rather his sentence, which we sing through the divine David: "What man is there who shall live and not see death?" So everyone, from Adam our forefather until now, who has entered the world through birth, leaves it again through dissolution for the world beyond, a world higher and more godlike. For, as it says, "It is sown in corruption, it is raised in incorruption; it is sown in dishonor, it is raised in glory; it is sown in weakness, it is raised in power; it is sown a natural body, it is raised a spiritual body." For we shall be equal to the angels and sons of the resurrection, when what is mortal has been swallowed up by life. Do you see, master? Even if our lady has left us, she has gone out from darkness into light, and from a perishable life into an immortal portion. You will see her there a little later, when you too pass over. So let us not grieve like the rest, who have no hope. Let us hope instead to be raised at the resurrection to something better, a life free from suffering. Rather, I urge you, let us come to ourselves. Let us take charge of the house and care for the children, and above all for our own precious soul, adorning ourselves with virtues after the example of that blessed woman. And let us rejoice in this: we have sent our spouse ahead of us as an intercessor with God, and she has left a model of good living to us and to all who knew her.
145 (56). To the [?] of Hellas.
If it were a matter of acquaintance, we would not have written to your honor, since we are unknown and unfamiliar to each other. But the encouragement came from a God-loving person known to us, I mean your kinswoman, the all-praised patrician lady, and her blessed daughter, the lady. Then your greeting to us lowly ones came through the letter-bearer himself, Ignatius, our spiritual son. So we felt bound to write a word of consolation to your worn-out soul, after the death that has befallen it in the war. But what remedy of consolation could be found to cure so incurable a wound? Oh, a misfortune that is lamentable even to hear of! Gone is your honored offspring, his mother's eye, the child of her heart, a fine branch, wholly the light of her who bore him,

who bore in himself his father's features, eased the loneliness of widowhood as far as possible, and was the comfort of your whole life, both in your own household and among your blood relatives. And what has happened? He has flown from his mother's eyes, cut off from the good root. And his death did not even happen before your eyes. Those who send off their own loved ones gather consolation from the funeral words and the holy burial, but now, besides everything else, we have been deprived even of this comfort, since the good sapling was cut down by the sword of war. Oh, pitiable tragedy! Oh, comfortless calamity! The mind is now unsettled as it goes over the suffering: where and how he was [?] taken, on what limb the murderous hand fell, in what place he fell and breathed his last. Was it quick? Was it from a single blow? Did he say anything? Alas for the tale! Oh, wretched hour [?]! We sent off our treasure with good hope, and reaped comfortless lamentation. What could anyone say that would be worthy of a lament, bewailing such suffering? Perhaps for you even the sun is gloomy, the air downcast, the sea unpleasant, the earth undesirable and heaven burdensome, now that it no longer holds your spiritual star. So many things, and more besides, shake your soul and grip your heart, pour out hot tears, send up wailing and make you despair even of living. But come, lady, come, revive. It is time to recover. Open your ears and listen to the divine voices: "As for man, his days are like grass; like a flower of the field, so he flourishes." "What man is there who shall live and not see death?" "If we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so too God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus." So we have not lost the son after all. A little later, when the last trumpet sounds, he will rise to meet the Lord in the air, and there we shall see him. Here he was struck a mortal blow, but there he will not taste eternal grief. For he put on Christ through baptism and held the orthodox faith, and because of his youth he had not yet had his fill of the pleasures here, but only tasted them with the tip of his finger. For this reason we believe that through such an untimely and unjust death he will also receive forgiveness for whatever he overlooked or did wrong, as human beings do. How many evils, lady, would he have had his fill of had he remained in the flesh? Does it not seem to you that life here has become a place of trial for man? There is the taking of a wife, the getting of children, an abundance of servants and of other things useful for life; I might add the advance of earthly fame. Freed from all these, he will have great freedom of soul, drawn close to God, his soul only lightly splashed by the salty tempest of life. From now on, therefore, let go, lady, put away this inconsolable grief, and set a firm limit to your suffering. Offer God a sacrifice of praise and thanksgiving.

Say with blessed Job: "The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it seemed good to the Lord, so it has come to pass." Utter David's words: "Return, my soul, to your rest." For your soul [?] is your son's departure. And as you look on your widowhood, cry out: "The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man can do to me." If you dispose yourself in this way, first you will gladden God, offering up your son of your own free will as a sacrifice, like Abraham. Then you will also give the best of gifts to your dearest child himself, as he sees you bearing this with thanksgiving. And you will set an example of good endurance for everyone else, in Christ Jesus our Lord. We pray that he may touch your heart with mercy and compassion and kindle in you a light that brings ready comfort; that he may bring your life to its close in peace; and that, once you have lived out here a life perfected in God, he may make you worthy to see your son again and to rejoice with him forever.
146 (57). To the brotherhood of Pelekete.
What has befallen your honor is painful indeed, brothers and fathers. How could it not be? You have lost your shepherd and become like a bewildered flock, and in such days as these, when savage wolves are attacking the flocks of Christ and scheming to carry off souls as plunder. Still, what has happened comes from God. It was he who took your shepherd to himself, at the time when the Lord, who governs all things in his wisdom, knew what was best for both. So we must give thanks and not be indignant. For he gave, and he also took back; and as it seemed good to the Lord, so it has come to pass. What, then, is required? That you now come to yourselves. You have chosen to elect as your shepherd the lord Sergius, our most pious brother, provided the lord Macarius, our spiritual father, has no hesitation about it. So persevere in being directed and governed by him, the spiritual father you have chosen, so that your community may be kept safe by God and you may complete a life inclined toward God. Then you will escape the storm of the heretical spirits and be brought into the harbor of salvation, and God's name will not be blasphemed because of you but rather glorified, as it has been through the holy conduct of your life until now. And you, brother Sergius, have not acted unreasonably, if things happened in this way, in coming down from the cleft of the rock to take the lead of the brothers. For our Lord Jesus Christ also condescended, and so accomplished the mystery of the dispensation for the salvation of all. Stand firm, then, in what you have decided and what the brothers have decided, until the day when our holy archbishop is appointed. Then what must be done will be done in a more lawful and canonical way. But until the time we long for comes,

lead the brothers and prosper in the Lord, as one who will give account for their souls, and also as one who will receive a reward for them. For the heavier the yoke of leadership, the greater its reward. Only have eyes to see and ears to hear, a heart that is watchful and seeks God, a shepherd's disposition, a teacher's speech, a well-ordered character, and a seemly bearing in standing and in walking. Let your speech be wholly guarded and directed by the Word. Blessed are you, carrying out an apostolic work! For the Lord showed Peter, the chief of the apostles, that the shepherd's staff is the foremost proof of love for him: "If you love me more than these, Peter," he says, "shepherd my sheep." So shepherd the Lord's sheep. Keep them safe in the fold of orthodoxy, feed them in the green pasture of his commandments, and settle them beside the restful waters of his will. Take care that neither you yourself nor any of your sheep is snatched away by the heretical beasts. What is past is enough for past times. Now let us walk safely and without stumbling, counting everything as secondary when the time calls for it, even our very bodies, let alone anything else that perishes, for the sake of the love of God. And his peace will rule your hearts and your thoughts. May he direct your way in Christ Jesus our Lord.
[?]
Now that holy Lent is approaching, I thought it a fitting time to say a few words to you, beloved children and most honored brothers. The Apostle, of course, urges me to exhort, reprove and rebuke in season and out of season. But now the season of fasting carries its own exhortation, for it knows how to bring even the hard-hearted to compunction. So welcome these joyful days gladly, brothers, each of you in the lodging where you are a guest, performing the customary observances as far as you can. Then through stillness and moderate eating we may purify the heart, give wings to the soul and trample down the passions.
