For this is what fasting is; this is what stillness is; this is what the commandment requires; this is the sum of our salvation. From it, too, our partaking of the holy things may become easy of access for us, or rather a provision for eternal life. For "whoever eats and drinks unworthily," that is, without purity, as far as our lowly nature allows, "eats and drinks judgment on himself," in the Apostle's words, "not discerning the body of the Lord." Therefore, my brothers, we must strive to keep ourselves pure from inordinate desire, from envy that devours the soul, from love of money that sinks the mind, and from listlessness that darkens the eye of the soul, always awaiting the

…departure from the body, by which the passions melt away and the soul is strengthened. Close the entrances of the passions; flee the places where people fall; flee conversation and shared living with women. For how could a heart not be inflamed, or rather set on fire, when it exchanges words with a virgin, with a woman who sings psalms, or with any woman at all? "How," as the Theologian [?] says, "will a stranger save the man whom his own woman destroyed?" For even if someone seems to keep himself safe in deed, he will still not be kept safe in his heart, according to the verdict

So persecution is meant for salvation, not destruction. Nor are we under such pressing necessity to live alongside a woman as the Fathers sometimes were, when circumstances forced the celebrated Athanasius to spend seven years in the care of a virgin, or when one saint or another was served by a woman. Now, though, both cities and countryside [?] offer freedom to receive hospitality in ways that do not involve living with women. And you, supposedly moved by confession and persecution for Christ's sake, are moving against Christ. Do you not realize what you are doing? You talk with women often. Perhaps you sing psalms with them. Perhaps you even eat with them and live with them, devouring with your eyes the face of the woman who shares your house, and being devoured by her to your ruin. Flee as from fire: men from women, and women from men. And if you must meet, let it be only as far as necessity and need require, and avoid putting a stumbling block before others. For "why," he says, "should my freedom be judged by someone else's conscience?" And: "If food makes my brother stumble, I will never eat meat again, so that I may not make my brother stumble." Live, then, my children, without causing offence and without giving cause for stumbling, to Jews, to Greeks and to the Church of God, as it is written. Keep in mind too how uncertain the hour of death is. Brother Silas has already passed away, and before him Abbot Theosostos and Brother Procopius, and no one will remain here. Blessed is the one who understands how to pass through this life without reproach. Do not forget to pray for us in our lowliness, that we may be saved.

148 (59). To Demetrius the consul. [731.]

What other consolation [?] can bodily absence find than being joined together through letters? By this means, then, best of friends, we in our lowliness now join ourselves to your love. We embrace you in spirit and want you to know that absence has not severed our love. Instead it stirs love up, so that it thirsts for affection, just as the thirsty run to springs of water. But enough by way of showing our love. How you yourself are faring in the office entrusted to you by the emperors we do not know; or rather we are

anxious, since we hear that a second office has been added to your first. You did not want it, but the ruler ordered it. We also hear that it lies farther off than the first and close to the barbarians, and so, people say, your honored soul has been afraid, since you neither wish nor are inclined to carry a sword, to wage war and have war waged against you. All this has moved us too to offer supplications and prayers that you may be kept unharmed in both offices. And indeed we trust that you are being kept safe, since you have the fear of God before your eyes and the help that is called down from there. For where God is the helper, every evil is put to flight. "The angel of the Lord," it says, "will encamp around those who fear him, and will deliver them." Be such a man yourself, then, our longed-for master, through your piety and good works, guarded by the angel who watches over your life. Keep watch in prayer and stay sober in supplication. Give just judgment, look kindly on the poor, and become a defender of the wronged. Practise moderation in food and drink, for intemperance is the mother of evils. If others play and laugh, my lord, listen to the Lord of all, who says, "Woe to you who laugh, for you will weep." If others talk obscenely, stop your ears, I beg you, for words are the road to deeds. If others fill their right hands with bribes, my God-loving friend, be content with your wages, to put it in Gospel terms, that is, with what is customarily given to those in office. If others are impious, be pious yourself, keeping away as far as you can from wicked men. For you know that this life sends off those who serve it like a dream. "And what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world but forfeits his soul?" Far be it from us to think this of your honor, for goodness is inborn in you, and you love to serve God, who brought you from nonexistence into existence and gives you life itself, movement and breath. So guard the deposit he entrusted to you through the Holy Spirit, both faith and right action, and return it to him intact at the time of your departure, so that you may hear from him: "Well done, good and faithful servant; you were faithful over a few things, I will set you over many; enter into the joy of your Lord." May it be granted to you to hear this voice, and to be saved with all your household in Christ Jesus our Lord. Amen.

149 (40). To Lykaseos the consul. [734.]

The man who brings this little letter to your honor told us of the misfortune that has befallen you, and grief for you has truly touched us. For he is your own and close kin, an old friend and a man of your age as well. And one who loves cannot help suffering with the one he loves

if he loves sincerely, just as, the other way round, he cannot help sharing his joy. But oh, what dreadful news! The lady, the consul's wife, has left us. She was, as the saying goes, a woman worthy of praise, as we have heard from others and seen with our own eyes. First, she loved her husband, which the Apostle sets down as the finest thing in marriage. She was prudent, kept to her home, was easy to approach and pleasant to speak with, loved piety and loved the poor. Greater still, she was adorned with chastity and overlaid with the silver of orthodoxy. Her fruits, the children, bear witness to the good life of you both. For just as a tree is known by its fruit, so the parents are known from their children: what sort of people they are and how great. Since I had no deep acquaintance with that blessed woman, how could I extol her qualities? Yet I met her only twice and talked with her, and I knew that God had truly given you a wife as a helper. She was not like our ancient foremother, a cause of deception, but became for you a means of salvation throughout your whole life. Oh, the misfortune! She is gone; she has flown from your eyes. She has left you half-dead, torn from your good spouse. We can no longer see with our eyes the comfort that surpassed every delight, the encouragement in [?], the consolation in misfortunes, the reminder of every duty, the helper and partner in all things. The sun of the household has set. Who will come to meet us? Who will give us joy? Who will comfort us? We have already become like one [?] who has just been shorn of her own adornment, "like a sparrow alone on a housetop," to use David's words. What then? Shall we grieve beyond measure, and wrap ourselves in mourning that admits no comfort? By no means, by no means, thrice-beloved friend. We know that the God who first gave her to us to share our life is the same God who has now taken her to himself. So let us bear [?] what has happened with thanksgiving, and imitate that blessed saying which that man uttered [?]. He spoke it not over the loss of a wife but over ten children who died together, after he had already lost all his outward possessions, and then after the further blow to his own body. Sitting on the dunghill, he who had once been a king, scraping the discharge from his flesh with potsherds, he said: "The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it seemed good to the Lord, so it has come to pass." If, then, dear friend, we take these words to heart and also speak them, we will not be far from the portion of such men. We will also make this a fine epitaph for that blessed woman. And by our own example we will shape the branches God has given us into an image of a life that pleases God, and from then on everything will turn out well for you. For if the eternal God, the Master of all, finds us receiving kindly what he does in us, how could he fail to arrange our present affairs well through the comfort of his Holy Spirit, and to prepare future joys for us in endless ages? These things I,
brief as they are, have nonetheless written as your own [?], and I have urged them on you. And you, master, please greet your honored children for us.

150 (41). To Euphrosyne, abbess. [735.]

That we care about your honor, this humble letter of ours bears witness. For it would not be holy to break the promise we made to that blessed and holy mother: to look after your reverence by visiting you with words as far as we can, whether we are far away or near. And even without that promise, your trust in us and care for us lowly ones would by themselves have persuaded us to give you our attention through letters. Be well, then, my most honored one, and lead the flock that the holy amma entrusted to you, or rather that God entrusted to you through her, in a godly and careful way. Know that the task of leadership you have undertaken is a very great one. Understand what the souls under your hand truly are: a guarded bridal chamber of the King of heaven, of Christ, the only beautiful and incorruptible Bridegroom. He has not entrusted to you one bride for the day of his wedding, through union in the Holy Spirit, but as many as you have, and you yourself are the first bride. For Jesus takes as his brides even those who, like you, have come through life [?], since he is a Bridegroom of many brides, of countless brides. He loves all souls, of men and women alike, and betroths them [?] in order to fill the bridal chamber above. In it the many mansions, like so many bedchambers, have been prepared by the Father for the souls that will be found worthy through a pure life and sincere faith. When the time of the Bridegroom's revelation comes, they will run after him, go in with him into the bridal chamber, and enjoy that boundless joy for ages of ages. See, the ministry you have received from the Lord has been shown to you. It is great, and it repays many heavenly rewards, since you will bring not only yourself but many brides [?] to the immortal Bridegroom. And for them, how great and how rich the reward! It will rank you among the foremost brides, among chosen maidens. It will give you the everlasting gifts of the Spirit as ornaments, and garments full of light, flashing with incorruption. It will crown you with the crown of righteousness. You will dance an unending dance, like the angels, with untainted exultation [another reading: unceasing]. So then, lady, watch and take heed to yourself, and guard the brides of Christ with great care. Feed them with the pure bread of orthodoxy; give them to drink from the stream of good works, so that they may be well nourished and beautiful, wholly [?] in the beauty of the soul. Christ our God desires this beauty, as holy David hints [?], for he says: "Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and

forget your people and your father's house, and the king will desire your beauty; for he is your Lord, and you shall worship him." You see that because you forgot, that is, renounced, parents, brothers and sisters, relatives, friends and everything that belongs to this life, the King desired the beauty of your soul for his bride. And the words "he is your Lord, and you shall worship him" will be fulfilled for you on the day of his appearing. Oh, oh, how wise you were to forget all things! Ah, ah, what a Bridegroom you have won! "Clap your hands, shout to God with a voice of exultation," for you have been raised above all the kingdoms on earth and made beautiful beyond every beautiful thing on earth. Angels hold you in reverence, and archangels attend you. You are queens of the first rank in heaven, above all the mothers and daughters born of the flesh. So rejoice, and rejoice with one another, and bear bravely from now on the hardships of the ascetic life, or rather of the bridal chamber. Know that "all flesh is grass, and all human glory like the flower of grass," and that all the desires of this age arise from corruption and end in corruption. Only your love and desire are boundless and incorruptible. Wait just a little longer and endure. You, for your part, must submit well and obediently to the lady, the first bride, who commands you to keep the loving ways and observances of Christ the Bridegroom. And let the lady herself, as the one who leads the brides to the Bridegroom, give even her own soul, not to mention anything else, to care for the maidens, in body as well as soul. So she will fulfil what the Apostle said: "Longing for you, we were pleased to share with you not only the gospel of God but our own souls as well," in Christ Jesus our Lord. Ask him also on our behalf for the salvation of our humble soul, so that we may ourselves be admonished by the admonitions we have given, and that we may all be saved from the Evil One.

154 (42). To Severianus, spiritual son. (45)

As much as your small letter gladdened us, child, your longer one grieved us just as much. You had never raised the propositions it contains with us before, and you had not heard from us what is right on the matter. Yet now you have been led to put these statements forward, supposedly in a fight against someone else, but really in opposition to the truth. And you ought not to be teaching at all. I say this not so much because you hold a lower rank (and do bear with me patiently), but because those who have been caught in heretical communion, and you are one of them, have no freedom to open their mouths. They must remain in fitting silence and ask for pardon for their whole

lives. Besides, you have no great skill in doctrinal precision, enough to know how to speak exactly, since you have studied neither grammar nor philosophy. Even those who are versed in these, if they live according to God, teach no doctrine of their own but follow the God-bearing Fathers. Where then, I ask, did you get the idea of saying, "The image of Christ is not venerated relatively"? Do you know what relation is? Relation belongs to the category of relatives, and relatives are the prototype and what derives from it, that is, Christ and his image. For each is contained in the other, and they are not split apart either in power or in glory. You see, you are ignorant and do not know. It is fitting to say here: "I saw an evil under the sun": a man who thought himself wise, and, worse still, was eager to teach others. And what about your second proposition? "Christ receives worship in his image, so the image too is to be worshipped." Where did you get this? From whom did you learn the doctrine you are teaching? None of the saints has ever said this. They say that Christ is venerated in his image, and that the image is to be venerated, whether we call that veneration honor or reverence, for both lead the mind to the same thing. And rightly so, since worship, like faith, is offered to the Holy Trinity alone. Other forms of respect go to others: to the Mother of God, the holy cross, the saints, the revered image of Christ and all the other holy images, in proportion as the prototypes surpass the things derived from them. If, then, as you say, Christ is worshipped in the image, then since worship belongs to the whole Trinity, the Father and the Spirit are also worshipped together with him in the image. And what follows from that? That the Father and the Spirit also became incarnate. What could be more impious than that? And since you also say, "The image of Christ is itself to be worshipped," it follows that you will turn out to be nothing other than a Tetradite, worshipping the image of Christ together with the Trinity. The same absurdity does not follow, however, for someone who venerates the Trinity because he also venerates the image. For it has been said that honor and veneration are shared even with any ordinary person, but faith and worship are not. Just as we believe in the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit alone, so too we worship them alone. Now that you have heard this, brother, I urge you to keep away from empty talk and from the Tzykalic, that is, the Kentoukladic heresy, which stands diametrically opposed to iconoclasm. But if, God forbid, you persist, know that you have no part with us, or rather with any orthodox person. It was with pain that I dictated this letter about you.

152 (44). To Theodore the [?]. [627.]

I was pleased, not stung, by your reproaches against me, most honored friend. For I am not so incorrigible as to be annoyed at [?]

loving reproofs. And if I was stung, it was not because of the reminder, but because of everyone's partisanship, which has cut the body of Christ apart and divided it into countless opinions. To tell the story, then, from the beginning [?] (for I must defend myself, since I have been accused): I was compelled from the very first day to impose penances, and that from prison, by letter, since monks and clergy also made their requests by letter. I answered that the penance came from me as advice, not as a binding decision. Why? Because I am not a bishop but a priest. With my own disciples I act by admonition [another reading: by laying down rules], but not so with others. Instead, as has been said, I referred the matter to them until a time of peace. Then they were to accept whatever the most holy patriarch decided, together with the judgment of the holy synod, whether that meant increasing the penance or reducing it. And I do not think I acted unreasonably. I stretched out a hand to the fallen out of kindness, but I did not claim authority for myself, which would have been out of place. What is the penance? It varies with the various sins [another reading: transgressions], and a letter is too short to set it all out. In summary: a priest who has been caught by signing or by heretical communion, or a deacon likewise, is to be barred entirely from performing the sacred rites, and indeed from communion as well. After he has completed the penance, he may receive the holy gifts, but he is by no means to celebrate the liturgy until a holy synod meets. He may bless and pray as an ordinary monk, not as one in holy orders, but only after the penance has been completed. He is not to enter churches held by heretics. And if a church is taken and held by an orthodox person after heretical anaphoras have been offered there, an orthodox priest is not to celebrate in it without a release from an orthodox [bishop]

Then, by God's good pleasure, we were released from prison and joined the most holy patriarch and the holy bishops, and we also referred these matters to holy abbots. No one found fault with us in anything, except for one person over the matter of blessing. We answered him: "If it deserves blame, let a ruling be issued by the head, and we will keep silent." So those who accuse us should accuse not us but the lord bishops, whom we follow in our lowliness and subordinate rank. They have pressed us urgently, and so to this day we have given penances in the order described, and we still give them when the occasion arises. But let the fault-finders consider whether, while straining out the gnat, they have failed to notice that they are swallowing the camel, and whether, while groping for specks, they do not see that they are carrying the beam. This, then, God-honored brother, is how we have conducted ourselves, as God is our witness: out of compassion and brotherly love, not from partiality or any other human motive. "But the one who troubles us," says the Apostle, "will bear the judgment, whoever

153 (45). To Laurence, my son. [632.]

We have heard, my son Laurence, of the drama the wicked demon staged in the market town of Antisara [Regius manuscript: Antizarchos], and we groaned deeply over it. We did so by the common law of human love, and also because the man who hanged himself was a blood relative of brother Athanasius, the protopresbyter, at whose prompting I am writing. O fearful tragedy! He was a man held in honour, more prominent than the natives of that place and comfortably provided for. He was a sensible man who kept steadily to prayers and supplications and was distinguished in the rest of his way of life. No misfortune had befallen him, of the kind that often turns a person a little aside from what is right. Yet in a time of calm he committed so great an evil and used a noose! O, I will say it again, what an abominable report [Regius manuscript: hearing]! Such are the devil's devices. He is a murderer from the beginning, as the Lord said. He first persuaded Ahithophel and then Judas to hang themselves, and to this very day he does not stop bringing about the same end in those who obey him. As we have learned by experience, I think he plunders a person in two ways: through inconsolable grief of heart or through irrational desire. Either way he darkens a person and turns him upside down. In murder, adultery and similar acts of licentiousness he shows darkness as light and the bitter as sweeter, since he would not get us to [?] unless he first rearranged our reasoning in this way. In the same way, in the case of hanging he [?] death, darkened the mind and brought about the hanging. [?] what the dragon is like, and with how many tricks he commits murder time after time. He kills one man in this way and another in that way, and no one will escape his snares without God's help. May that help be with the one who lives faithfully, with fear and trembling, according to his commandment.

But let us turn to the urgent matter. You have told us that everyone in the village alike shuns his household, that is, his wife and children. They will neither touch nor handle them, and will not even lend them bread. If the family of the man who hanged himself were declaring that his act of hanging was a good one, and that they would gladly do the same, then the villagers would be right to keep away. Even so, they should not do so at once. They must first teach them, enlighten them and urge them to flee destruction, for this is what Christians do and what those who love their brothers do. The Lord also knew what Judas was going to do, yet he tried to win him over with many kindnesses and with prophecies meant to correct him. He pronounced the 'woe' over him and said, 'It would have been better for that man if he had not been born,' even though the wretch did not understand. But if, as you say, they are mourning the man who died as Judas did, and pray that every Christian be kept from his portion, and are beside themselves

with unbearable affliction and seek comfort, what does your account show except that the villagers are opposing Christ? They are opening to the devil a door to destroy people who deserve comfort. Woe to those who act like this, for they are the devil's fellow workers. The lord Macarius, their spiritual father, did well to comfort these people, and he also did well to eat at that house. Let no Christian hesitate to do the same.

Since the question of a penance has been raised, I will answer it. They are not guilty, for Scripture says, 'Each shall die in his own sin, and children shall not die for their fathers,' nor fathers for their children. Nevertheless, for their consolation, they are to abstain from meat for one Lent, and of course also from receiving the holy gifts. Let them come into church and pray, staying until the dismissal of the catechumens. Let them also give the dead man's share to the poor [proposed reading; manuscript: 'to one poor man']. It is not lawful to make an offering or celebrate the liturgy for him at all, but let alms be given. Alms benefit even an unbeliever, as Chrysostom says. Moreover, the silver pieces connected with Judas's hanging were given for the burial of strangers. Let them also plant the sign of the life-giving cross on the spot where the hanging took place. The cross itself was planted at the Place of the Skull because the skull of Adam, the devil's victim, lay there, and the place was named after it. This much we can say from the Scriptures. We urge those who have suffered this loss to end their great grief and to wait upon the good God with thanksgiving and good works. We also exhort the people of the village to give up their wicked discrimination and to keep the members of that household in communion as before, in Christ Jesus our Lord.

151 (15). To the abbot [?]. [632.]

I think this letter to your fatherly holiness is not out of season. It fulfils the duty of love, and it also discloses a grief that has settled in our humble soul. If you will, please attend to what I say. After returning from our meeting with the holy Fathers at Akritas, I met our brother Athanasius and told him everything that had been discussed in the Lord. I added that the abbot of Medikion was also commending the abbot of Maximina for his excellent change of course, that is, for his defence and confession. But Athanasius shook his head. When I asked him why he disapproved, he said, 'In the Apology he wrote, which I have read myself, he says that he partook but did not communicate, and that this was an act of economy, a relaxation of strictness, not a falling away from the truth.' What does this mean, most honoured Father? Ought he not to confess, to put it in outline, 'To spare my old age

I lost my soul. I communicated in the denial of the icon of Christ, of the Mother of God and of all the saints, for that is what the Iconoclast heresy is, and in this I was swept along with the impious. Then, while our Church [Regius manuscript: the world] was being shaken, I stayed in my monastery to the end without being persecuted'? Ought he not to make his confession in this way and weep bitterly? Instead he utters those babblings. As our informant says, he even calls one of the Fathers, a certain Dianius, as a witness in his defence, claiming that Dianius did the same and that the holy Basil received him back. He cites the father of Gregory the Theologian as well. O the just indignation of our holy chief hierarch and of the whole body of confessors! If what he did was neither communion nor a fall, what was the good of all their struggles and contests, their blood and their hardships? Why was he himself cut off [Regius manuscript: put under penance]? Why did he leave his monastery? Why is he barred from celebrating the sacred rites? O, I say it again, the divine indignation! He holds the truth in unrighteousness and imagines that the Fathers went through the same thing he did.

Come, then, let us examine this senseless argument: 'I partook, but did not communicate.' The renowned theologian says somewhere, 'I partook of the image and did not keep it. He partakes of my weakness so that he may both save the image and make the flesh immortal. He enters into a second communion, far more wonderful than the first.' Here, you see, 'partook' is explained as 'communicating'. Partaking and communion are the same thing. One is named from sharing in something, the other from making those who share in it common to one another. So the divine Apostle says: 'The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a communion in the blood of the Lord? The bread that we break, is it not a communion in the body of the Lord? Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread.' Here too, you see, the light of the world has shown that sharing is communion. And no one in his right mind would refuse to call sharing partaking. When the orthodox partake of the divine bread, it makes all who share in it one body. In the same way the heretical bread makes those who partake of it sharers with one another, and so it forms a single body opposed to Christ. The empty talker talks emptily and in vain. He may claim that his mind did not agree with what was being done when he partook, but that ruins his case all the more. Although he knew he was doing something monstrous, he still sinned knowingly. He did not fear God, who destroys both soul and body by casting them into Gehenna, but feared the one who strikes the body for a time. What good are such incoherent arguments? Why does he imagine that the saints who testify against him are his advocates? For them, even a mere nod or shake of the head in matters of confession or denial is held to be the full deed. They would not even allow a pretence when it came to martyr-

dom, such as merely touching a sacrifice. They would not allow it even when the sacrifice was not idolatrous, or was simply someone's private offering, and the examples of this are countless. What else, then, did the recent persecution consist of but this? The holy patriarch was deposed, banished and confined in an out-of-the-way place. A rival was enthroned, a fighter against Christ. A synod was held by those who reject the icons. The holy synod of Nicaea was anathematized and the old anti-Christian synod was proclaimed again. Holy bishops and abbots, monks and nuns were sent into exile. Blood was shed, and there were untimely deaths, imprisonments, starvation and plundering. Most terrible of all, both to see and to hear of, the venerable icon of Christ was insulted and trampled underfoot, and so were those of the Mother of God and of all the saints. Churches and altars were laid in ruins, and holy things were profaned and given to the fire. Since this is how things stood, is not everyone who communicated, that is, everyone who partook of the venomous bread, a denier of Christ, an outcast and unholy, unless he is brought back through repentance? This is the truth. For it the martyrs were put to death, and for it those who held fast endured everything. 'And as for all who walk by this rule,' says the Apostle, 'peace be upon them, and mercy, and upon the Israel of God.' As for the case of Dianius and of the Theologian's father, and any other like it, the heretics contrived a cunning document. It was a theft from the simplicity of men who were outwitted. Those saints did not sign out of any fear, perish the thought! That is why they recovered themselves and boldly made their defence as soon as they recognized the deceit. Holy Father, if you think it proper, explain [?] these things to the man. Then, once he knows the truth, he may reject that unjust treatise and take his place among the pious, even though he is old, has been placed under penance and has therefore left his renowned monastery. If not, at least pray that we may have no communion with the man in this matter, unless he repents.

155 (?). To Theophilus of Ephesus. [670.]

I took in hand the letter that your sacred eminence sent to our brother Athanasius, and when I read it I was greatly grieved, my most honoured Father. First, I grieved because quarrels are arising and schisms are springing up among us, who rightly handle the word of truth against the Iconoclast heresy now raging. Second, I grieved because I, the least of all, am forced to argue against you. But let your greatness forgive me, for the discussion concerns the truth, and nothing should be preferred to it or held in greater reverence. What, then, does the letter contain that [?]? 'We,' it says, 'advised neither that the Manichaeans should be killed nor that they should not be killed. But even if we had permitted it, we would have

done the greatest of noble deeds.' What are you saying, you who are honoured by God? The Lord forbade this in the Gospels when he said, 'In gathering the tares you may uproot the wheat along with them. Let both grow together until the harvest.' Would you call permission to uproot the greatest of noble deeds? He called heretics tares, both those of that time and, clearly, those who came later, that is, all of them. Let us hear Chrysostom interpreting this very point. He writes: 'Why, then, does the Master forbid it, saying, "In case you uproot the wheat along with them"? He said this to prevent wars, bloodshed and slaughter. Heretics must not be put to death, since that would bring an implacable war into the world.' And a little further on: 'What else does he mean by "Do not uproot the wheat along with them" but this: if you were to take up arms and slaughter heretics, many of the saints would inevitably be cut down with them?' This is what has happened in our own times. Blood and slaughter have filled our world, and many of the saints have perished along with the rest. So the Lord's word did not fail, as many acknowledge.

But why speak of not allowing heretics to be killed? We are not even permitted to pray against them. Let us hear again what the Lord said to the holy Carpus, as the all-wise Dionysius has recorded: 'Strike at me, then. I am ready to suffer again for the salvation of human beings, and this is dear to me, provided that other people do not sin. But consider whether you really want to give up dwelling with God and with the good and loving angels in exchange for dwelling in the chasm with the serpents.' You see, divinely wise one, the divine indignation. Carpus had prayed that the heretics might be taken out of life, and if he had persisted in that frame of mind the saint would have been condemned. So, as the truth has shown, we must not pray against them at all. Rather we must pray for them, as the Lord himself showed at the time of his passion when he said to his Father, 'Father, forgive them their sin, for they do not know what they are doing.'

Your holiness says that you have these saints on your side on the question [Regius manuscript: declaration]. Forgive me, Father, but we do not understand the sayings of the saints rightly. That is how we end up fighting against the Fathers, or rather against God. In his writings against Julian, the divine Basil put forward that saying in keeping with what had been legislated of old. He was not placing the Old Testament on a par with the New, God forbid. He knew perfectly well that whatever the law says, it says to those under the law. Nor was he setting aside the Saviour's contrast, in which he says, 'It was said to those of old this; but I say to you this.' So, as Dionysius, the revealer of God, writes to a certain Demophilus: 'We will not accept your misguided impulses, even if [?], not even if you cite Phinehas and Elijah ten thousand times. For when Jesus heard such things,

he was not pleased with the disciples who had no share in that gentle and good spirit. Our most divine lawgiver of sacred things also teaches with gentleness those who oppose God's teaching. The ignorant should be taught, not punished.' You have heard, then, blessed one, what holy Paul has said, the sun of the whole world under heaven. And the God-bearing Ignatius also says: 'Those who hate God must be hated, and one must pine with grief over his enemies. Yet we must not persecute them or strike them, as the nations who do not know God do.' If we must not strike them, much less may we kill them.

You have also claimed, master, that holy Symeon of the Wonderful Mountain agrees with you. Do not imagine, holy one, that he contradicts Christ or the teachers who rank above him. What, then, did he do? He appealed to the emperor of his day about a nation that was wounding the Christian people, so that the Christians would not be ravaged by the Samaritans. He was right to do so. We make the very same appeal now: that the emperors make war on the Scythians and Arabs who are killing God's people, and not spare them. But that is one thing, and this is another. The one concerns enemies, the other concerns heretics who are under the rulers' authority.

As for the story about John the Faster, president of Constantinople, I do not think it is true that he authorized the impaling of the sorcerers. Rather, he allowed it to happen. They too were murderers, and the rulers must not be prevented from applying the Roman laws against such people. 'For they do not bear the sword in vain,' Scripture says; 'they are avengers against the one who does evil.' But permission must not be given against those whom the Lord forbade us to punish in this way. Since rulers govern bodies, they may punish those convicted of bodily offences, but not those convicted of offences of the soul. That belongs to the rulers of souls, whose punishments are excommunication and the other penances.

This, master, is what we humble people think. And, to speak in foolishness, we have said it boldly. We told our most blessed patriarch that the Church does not avenge with the sword, and he agreed. We also spoke to the emperors who carried out the slaughter. To the first we said, 'God was not pleased with such a killing.' When the second demanded that we support the killing, we told him, 'My head will be cut off before I agree to this.' These things come from us sinners. But as for you, most holy ones, if you have read another Gospel that we do not know, well and good. If not, consider what the Apostle declares.

126 (48). To the brotherhood under Patricius, our son.

Brothers and Fathers, your Father has asked me to speak to you about what leads to salvation. I am his father too, and yours through him, so I was naturally persuaded, and I, the lowly one, now speak, starting from here: Our

salvation, beloved children [another manuscript: dear children], lies in believing rightly in the Holy Trinity and in having works that are attested by God's holy commandments. For in Christ Jesus, as the Apostle says, neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, but only faith working through love. What is said about faith concerns the doctrine of orthodoxy, and what is said about love concerns the practice of right conduct.

We believe, then, in the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. They are three persons, one nature, one power and one sovereign kingship over all things. They are worshipped as one, being one in nature, will and operation, and one in might and glory. We believe that one of the Holy Trinity, the Son and Word of God the Father, emptied himself out of supreme goodness. He took the form of a servant and appeared in a form like ours. This is what the Theologian means when he says, 'And the Word became flesh,' and what the great Apostle means when he says, 'God was manifested in the flesh.' He is one and the same in two natures, perfect God and perfect man. He is perfect in each and leaves no property unassumed. Rather, as a true son, he has everything that belongs to the Father in a divine way and everything that belongs to his Mother in a human way. So, just as from the Father he is uncircumscribable, from his Mother he is circumscribable, that is, he can be depicted in an image as his Mother can.

It is because of the Iconoclasts that this doctrine has to be set out. They do not confess that he is circumscribed, and so they are surely found not to confess him as the true son of his Mother either. Where would the genuine sonship be, rather than complete estrangement, if the offspring did not resemble the one who bore it in all its natural properties? With respect to circumscription he has nothing in common with the Father, only with his Mother. Conversely, with respect to being beyond depiction he has nothing in common with his Mother, only with the one who begot him, not with the one who gave him birth. This, then, is the right doctrine of the truth, and this is the apostolic faith: to confess that Christ is circumscribable in the flesh.

So the great Basil says, 'Let Christ, the judge of the contests, also be painted on the panel.' And we must honour the painted image, since Christ is venerated in it. The golden Chrysostom exclaims that he sees an angel in an image. If one sees the bodiless angel in an image, how much more the Word who took a body? And if he sees the angel there, he clearly venerates the angel in the image, just as he venerates Christ. To be granted the sight of someone in a painting is the same as venerating him. 'For the honour paid to the image passes over to the prototype,' as the great [Regius manuscript: divine] Basil says again. Those who insult his image are therefore deniers of Christ. By rejecting the image they direct their rejection at him, even if they say they confess Christ. As Scripture says, the demons too confess God, but they deny him by their works. Great, then, brothers, is their impiety, and great is our confession. It falls in no way [?] short of that of the martyrs of old. Stand firm, therefore,

… firmly [Reg. MS: "firm"], never wavering about what has already been proved true by demonstration, but for this faith taking on the struggles even to the point of blood, if the occasion should call for it. From this there also rises the shining life, sun from sun, since the brother of God has shown that each is the witness of the other. Love God with the whole of the three powers, as the commandment bids. Love one another too, as members of Christ. "For by this," he says, "all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another." Treat your superior with faith. Let no one keep anything from him unconfessed, for such a one rears a snake. Let no one be lukewarm in faith, for such a one has no share in the fervour of the Holy Spirit. Let no one secretly own possessions, for such a one is a thief like Judas. Let no one follow his own will, for such a one is a monk outside [?] the monastery. Let no one be insolent in speech, for such a one works corruption. Let no one eat in secret, for such a one is like a slave. Let no one give offence in anything, so that the ministry may not be blamed, as the Apostle cries out, but in everything let him commend himself as a minister of God, "in much endurance, in afflictions, in hardships," and the rest that the Apostle himself listed in shaping the true Christian. And if this is what is asked of the one under obedience, what and how much would be demanded of the superior, who ought to be set before others as a good model of what he teaches? Great is the contest, but the reward is infinitely greater, the kingdom of heaven. May we be counted worthy of it, both those who rule and those who are ruled, living a godly life in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory and might, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen.

Letter 157 (49). To Antony of Dyrrhachium. [649.]

It is late in the day, yet we in our lowliness were very glad to receive the precious letter of our most holy Father, written long ago. For nothing binds love so well, or keeps it from scattering, as affection given in return. But why, master, have you so exalted the affairs of us, who have no good whatever, with the words of praise from your most wise tongue? Surely love is the cause, which steals away the truth and attaches to those it loves things that are not as though they were? Except that in this, it must be said, we too have something, unless we are deceived: we cherish and love the brothers and Fathers, and especially those like you, who by the kindness of your good ways draw even the savage [?] into friendship. This much, then, from both of us to your sacred head, as we repay your rich and abundant letter in a few brief syllables. What we have to say in defence against the charge concerning brother Erastus is as follows. We, most sacred one, worthless as we otherwise are, are not so ignorant, nor

such despisers of the divine ordinances, as to order a disciple of ours who is outside the priesthood to dare to take in hand the things of the priesthood, and so to baptize children; for that is the charge. But whether the plea of necessity demanded it in these days, when a heresy is leading the people astray, and especially during the earlier lootings, when anyone in hiding could not so much as peep out of his secret room, I cannot judge, with the little understanding I have, either this monk or anyone else, since necessity brings even a change of law. And indeed we see such things happening in ancient times: one man in the desert, when death was at hand, baptizing with a pouring of sand, and so both baptizer and baptized; and others baptized by others. Nor is the story of holy Athanasius beyond the knowledge of your perfection. Yet that childish act, when seen by the most blessed Alexander, was judged to have been accomplished by God; the one who performed it was reckoned as a priest, and those he initiated as reborn, although that occasion involved no necessity. The Sixth Council too, in its divine canons, allows that if no ordained person is present, a layman may of necessity give himself communion of the holy things, which is not lawful without some pressing circumstance. If, then, it happened in this way, we—forgive us, all-honoured one—do not dare to say anything against what was divinely laid down by the Fathers, or to censure it. Those who bear witness that the brother acted in this way, and with great anguish, are first the very man who compelled him, one of the most pious and prudent of men, and a prominent one too, Thomas the hypatos and chartoularios; then James, the most devout monk, who has no part in the heresy; and then Euthymius, another venerable monk, who has been persecuted. "On the evidence of two or three witnesses," it says, "every word shall be established." You, master, say that it is not so, and you are clearly more eminent than all of them. What then am I to do, caught in the middle between so many witnesses? If it is as you yourself say, that he did this while priests were present, out of love of rank, courting the priesthood for himself, then let him never be advanced by us to the dignity of the priesthood, along with other penances, for that is just. But if, as the witnesses and he himself relate, he was compelled, and two choices lay before him—either to let the infant die uninitiated, which had happened before with two children when he was not persuaded, or to hand over to the heretics those who were holding fast to true piety—then I, the sinner, dare impose nothing until our most blessed hierarch has examined the matter and given his judgment. Do not, dearest of Fathers, groan against my lowliness; rather pray that we may stay within our own measure and correct our erring life. As for the other faults your godliness hinted at, he confessed them to us, and we did not consider at all that he had acted unlawfully, but rather that he deserved praise, if on hearing of adulterers he did not shrink from reporting it to those able

to put a stop to the impiety [Reg. MS: licentiousness]; or, when the countess was choosing to hang herself, to see to it that the proper steps were taken. For he knows that these are the things for which he incurred blame, and nothing else. And, as I heard with my own ears, brother Erastus had already earned [?] praises with much good report from the men mentioned above. So it was not, holy one, because he had caused scandal among the people there, but because of the scandals that remained uncorrected, that I kept the brother from making a retraction, so that by this the accused might be cleared of the charges, and those who love to accuse and [?] might be at peace. And you, our most blessed Father, having heard us, will grant us your prayers that move God, and pardon to the brother as well.

Letter 158 (50). To John the Spatharios.

The good news of the salvation of my blessed master and spiritual brother, announced even before your letter came, sweetened our lowly hearts; and when the letter was read, it filled them completely with gladness and joy—and not only us sinners, but the angelic powers too, since "over one man who repents there is joy in heaven," according to the sacred oracles. Blessed be God, who did not allow your honour to be carried away to the end with the wicked heresy of the Christ-fighters, but through your good and blessed daughter turned you back to the light of truth. O the wonder of it, both of the father and of the daughter! O the sincere love of both! She, at her very last breaths, was concerned for her father's salvation; he inclined his ear as befits God and granted her request with a fine burial gift, his return to Orthodoxy. She departed with her own goodness and nobility, having a delightful gift to offer to God, her father's salvation; he remained as the pious ornament of a holy daughter, and truly a joy to all the Orthodox. "For how do you know, wife," it says, "whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?" We must change it a little: the daughter saved her father. Blessed is that holy woman, and blessed are you too, thrice-longed-for one. For I am persuaded that you will bring with you your whole household, and perhaps your whole family, to Christ the Master in the Orthodox faith, so that the gift given to you through many persons may be the cause of thanks from many on your behalf. Such is the divine offering, and most beautiful is the confession you made in your letter before God and

For this is the true faith of Christians. In the doctrine of theology, it is to believe in the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, in whom baptism also has its fulfilment: God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit; in one God, and not three,

far from it! For the Godhead is one, not divided by the three hypostases, but beheld whole and undivided in each person. And this is a paradox: to call each one God, and yet to sum up the confession in one God. In the doctrine of the economy, again, it is to believe that "the Word became flesh"; that is, that the one of the Holy Trinity was born of the all-immaculate Virgin Mary, remaining what he was, unchangeable God and coeternal with the Father, but taking on what is ours through his virgin birth in the Holy Spirit. And he is wholly God and wholly man, bearing in himself without lack, in one hypostasis, all the properties of both the natures of which he is composed, divinity, I mean, and humanity: circumscribed and uncircumscribed, the one according to the divinity, the other according to the humanity; for these are their properties. As uncircumscribed he is one of the Holy Trinity; as circumscribed he is one of us. And in this he is shown to be the mediator between God and men, joining the extremes in himself, and through himself making us partakers of the divine nature and sons of God—a wonder beyond all praise, whether in thought or in word. So whoever says that he is not circumscribed in the flesh in our likeness denies, my blessed brother, that God appeared in the flesh, sets himself against the gospel of Christ, and is on a level with the Jews. For how will it be true that he became like us in all things, if he could not be depicted as we are? And what becomes of "Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have"? And what of "Why do you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth that I heard from the Father?" Whoever is not circumscribed is plainly not like us, nor can he be touched, nor indeed killed. But he was killed, and he was touched after the resurrection; therefore he is also circumscribed, depicted as we are. But the Iconoclasts "became futile in their reasonings, and their senseless heart was darkened." By denying the icon of Christ, together with those of the Mother of God and of all the saints, they deny the saving economy; they confess Christ as the demons do, but deny him by their deeds. For Christ is not Christ unless he is circumscribed; nor is he worshipped unless he is believed to be worshipped in his icon. This then, man of God, is the truth, and this is how it has been taught by apostles and prophets and God-bearing Fathers—even if not in these very words, then at least through a true reflection on what they said. For all the doctrinal truths have been sown, like seeds, in the meanings of the divine oracles; and against the heresies that spring up from time to time, the teachings of true piety are brought forth in opposition, cultivated from there under the movement of the Spirit

and [?] the tares of impiety. Believe this yourself, and farewell in the Lord, venerating Christ and venerating his icon too; the Mother of God and her icon; the saints and their icons. For in the icons the prototypes are venerated, and "the honour paid to the image passes over to the prototype," as Basil the Great says.

Letter 159 (51). To Thomas the Chartoularios. [655.]

When I read your honour's letter and learned that your lady and wife had departed this life, I grieved with you, master, knowing how painful such suffering is. For the separation of husband and wife causes the same pain as a cutting sword; here too they are one flesh, according to the word of the Lord. Yet it has happened, and we have undergone the penalty common to all, separation. A little later we too shall travel the same road, as you know; and such is life: not being, we come into being, and having come into being, we are dissolved. We praised your piety, which chose upon this separation to become a monk and to devote yourself [?] wholly to the Lord. For this is what your letter made plain, and also that a certain brother monk was with you to guide you in so great a life. Him you then rejected as unsuitable, through a message from George, your good man and your own notary, asking rather that we give you another who is able to steer souls and keep a whole monastery safe. The praise, then, we have rightly given already. But first you must learn what the monastic profession is, and how high is this way of life, so that we may not enter it inexperienced and run into danger on the voyage. Renunciation is nothing other than a promise of cross and death. What does this mean? According to the word of the Lord, whoever wishes must renounce all that he has and, taking up the cross, follow after him. And since every true hegumen stands in the place of Christ, to follow Christ is [?] to follow him through that hegumen. In this way the admirable precept of the commandment will be kept. But the one who does not choose this, but builds a monastery on his own property and calls in a superior, so that he may be a monk on his own estate and be saved and guided, does not know that he labours in vain and to no purpose, and that he will not find what he seeks, but the very opposite and things out of place. For such a renunciation is not according to the Lord's commandment, that one ought to be stripped of all material things, go far away from one's own, find the best guide, and so cross the great sea of this present life without danger. Here none of these things happens; there is only the building of a monastery, the putting on of the grey habit, and the appearance of having a hegumen, who is really more of a steward, both hobbling and hobbled, neither saving nor being saved. "Go out," he says, "from your land

and from your kindred." Take the cross upon your shoulders; be spat upon, be struck, drink vinegar, be scourged, go up onto the cross, pour out your blood, whether spiritually or bodily. If you cannot bear these things, stay in your house, and strive hard to be saved by the humbler life. For there too salvation does not come without toil, but through many afflictions. Do not bring me present-day examples. Everything that is not according to the commandment is unapproved, stale, and scandalous, the work of the one who renounced in that way, not of the divine command. But if you long to found a new monastery, that is not unreasonable; but once you hand it over to a man as hegumen, no longer lay your hand on it, as is done with existing ones. Then the thing is pleasing to God, and it will meet you as eternal hospitality. For anyone who chooses this way, we provide the brother whom the person asking may choose, along with nine other brothers willing to place themselves under the superior. There, good friend, I have told you the rule of the monk and the manner of founding the monastery; the choice is yours. For the rest, may the Lord be your consolation, giving you understanding in all things as you need

What was said in the former letter about the most holy metropolitan of Chalcedon, our father, was said only in passing; now it will be set out more fully. Tell him, in a manner of speech fitting for a father, that certainly, according to the declaration of the Apostle, "the fire will test what sort of work each one has done. If anyone's work that he has built on it remains, he will receive a reward. If anyone's work is burned up, he will suffer loss; he himself will be saved, but only as through fire." I ask, then: does "will be burned up" mean complete annihilation, or not? If it admittedly means the former—as Gregory the Theologian, following Paul, also says somewhere, "and that last fire," by which all that is ours is either condemned or purified—what is it that unsettles the hearer's mind? That holy Maximus was wrong to say that there are three restorations which the Church recognizes? The first is that of each individual according to the principle of virtue, in which a person is restored once he has fulfilled in himself the principle of virtue. The second is that of the whole of nature at the resurrection, the restoration to incorruption and immortality. The third, which Gregory of Nyssa among the saints made particular use of in his writings, is this: the restoration of the powers of the soul that fell under sin back to that for which they were created. For just as the whole of nature must at the resurrection receive in time the hoped-for incorruption of the flesh, so also the perverted powers of the soul must, in the long course of the ages, cast off [?] the memories of evil lodged in them; and having passed through all the ages and finding no resting place, come

to God, who has no limit; and so the powers enjoy the good things by knowing them, not by sharing in them, and are restored to their original state, and the Creator is not shown to be the cause of sin. The third restoration, then, is nothing other—for about the other two there is no dispute—than what was taught by the Apostle: that the sinful work is burned up and the one who did it is saved without being burned, yet in such a way that he does not share in the good things, but knows that he is deprived of sharing in them. And the Father very fittingly said, "and the Creator is not shown to be the cause of sin." For what is from God, namely our nature, brought from non-being [?] into being, cannot be consumed by that fire. But what is not from God, namely sin, fashioned by the free choice of the one who committed it, since it is not one of the things that exist but has only a parasitic existence, will vanish, having no place among the things that are. So then, even if neither Gregory of Nyssa nor Maximus the Father said it, the great Apostle at any rate declared that sin undergoes a passing through fire [?]; and the meaning is that of a restoration as the Father stated it, not an Origenist one—far from it! For there is no fellowship between light and darkness, nor agreement between saints and heresiarchs. Against these, who appropriate the sacred teachings of the most divine Gregory for their own evil purposes, stand both the uncorrupted text and the exposure of their theft—but not so as to overturn what has been said above, as it seems to us. If the most holy metropolitan finds something deeper, we will listen again. For our most sacred patriarch too, having heard what holy Maximus said, at the time found [?] nothing inconsistent in it.

Letter 164 (53). To Nicetas the Spatharios.

Your good brother has informed me that one of our hierarchs slandered me before the honoured person of your love, claiming that I deify the icon of Christ, and that this is found in my letter to brother Athanasius. At this slander I, the humble one, groaned, reflecting how those who have been told that they will give account even for an idle word on the day of judgment speak so simply and carelessly about matters of the greatest importance—for what is greater than the faith?—wounding the blameless with the arrow of accusation, instead of lovingly pointing it out, if there really was some error, according to what is written: "You shall surely reprove your neighbour, and you will not incur sin because of him." To slander in this way not only abolishes the commandment, but also shows that one deserves to be called by the name of the devil, the slanderer; and what could be worse than that among men? But let us turn to the charge. "He deifies," he says, "the

…the image of Christ. I said no such thing in my letter, my much-loved friend. What I said was that the image of Christ is not to be given the worship of adoration (latreia), for that is the mindset of idolatry; such worship belongs to the holy Trinity alone. I said that Christ, who is venerated in the holy icon [Reg. MS: "his own icon"], is adored together with the Father and the Spirit. The image of Christ, however, is to be venerated with relative veneration, and in venerating it we venerate Christ. He is not divided in hypostasis from his image; the two differ only in the principle of essence. And this is true. For the archetype is shown forth in the image, and each is in the other, allowing for the difference of essence, as the all-wise Dionysius says. Since my letter says this, why does my opponent slander me [?] and show himself opposed to the saints? And what is he saying [?]: that those who venerate the image of Christ admit to venerating another [?]? What an absurdity! That would be dividing the indivisible, and it cannot be allowed. For "neither is the power split nor the glory divided," as the great Basil says in another place. Therefore, when the image is venerated, Christ is venerated, whose likeness it is. The material that has received the likeness is not venerated, as the figure of the cross also shows. Anyone who thinks he is venerating the material is a child, without reason. So neither the material that bears the image is venerated, nor some hypostasis other than that of the one depicted. A deviation in either direction is equally impious. This is why the figure of the cross is called a cross, and the image of Christ is called Christ [?]. These names are used not in their proper sense but by extension. If this persuades us not to call the figure of the cross a cross, then let it also persuade us not to call the image of Christ Christ. And if in the first case it persuades us that we do not venerate the cross when we venerate its figure, then let it persuade us in the second case that we do not venerate Christ when we venerate the image of Christ. But the first is true: the cross's own figure is both called a cross and venerated as one. Therefore the second is also true: Christ's own image is both called Christ and venerated as him. Anyone who thinks or says something novel against this is babbling in vain. I have written this partly to clear myself of blame and partly to spare your loving eminence, so that you may hold fast to the orthodox faith and not be swept away by the words of false teaching.

162 (54). — To Theodore [?].

I received your honour's letter with its title: "Encyclical letter, or, Therapeutic." Right from the starting line I was astonished, brother. As I went on to what followed, I very nearly lost my wits. I did not know what to think or what answer to give my beloved friend. Bear with me patiently [?], even if what I am about to say is rather harsh, since I have no way [?]…

…of holding back, as one would expect, the things that have struck my humble heart, and I have to speak. Did someone, beloved, put on your mask and become so puffed up with pride that he could conceive things above the clouds and do things that come crashing down? Or did we ourselves go out of our minds at some point and decide to play a childish game, putting our names to ventures that are no game at all but very grievous? What are you saying, my good man? We have no portion in the priesthood and are counted merely among the monks. Are we permitted to seize priestly rank and draw up an encyclical letter without putting the truth in danger? Are we permitted to use it to rise up against hierarchs and priests, monks and abbots? Are we even permitted to issue private laws from a heart that judges for itself? And are we permitted to heap insults and reproaches, condemnations and excommunications, on the whole body of the confessing brotherhood? For these, as you say, though not all of them, are the shield-bearers of the truth. Yet they play-act at piety [?], just as those of the opposing party falsely put on the name of piety. With dreadful words they launch most grievous attacks on the truth and on repentance [?], and they bring in a heap of wretched reasonings. They stir up dissensions and wrong the blameless faith. They dishonour the charioteer, overseer and creator of all. They quarrel with one another, and, overcome by gain, they devise ways of making a profit. To win favour with the allies of those who acted impiously, they offend those who confessed the faith and put themselves in danger for the truth. They prefer and put first those who did the truth the greatest wrong and persecuted it. By what they do they are harsh toward the truth, and they count suffering for Christ as nothing. They know evil, and they have cruelly and improperly forgotten the cause for which they themselves were endangered. Is that what you say? Heaven was astonished at this, and I, wretch that I am, shuddered still more. Had I not heard your own words, I would not have believed the person who first told me that your honour had composed a letter against the Church of God. For it is an attack on her to denounce with such babblings these famous men who confessed the faith. They "went about" in all kinds of trials, "destitute, afflicted, ill-treated," persecuted, "wandering in deserts and mountains and the holes of the earth, of whom the world was not worthy," to use the apostle's words. And I have not yet set out the more accusing and more inhuman parts. Tell me: would anyone enrolled among the soldiers dare to act on his own authority, issue an imperial decree announcing this and that, and insult those in high office as disorderly and reckless? If he were caught doing this, he would be seized at once and led away as one condemned to death. What then will a simple monk not suffer from the Church's tribunal if he has dared something like it? Do we not have a high priest who is able to sympathize with our weaknesses, as it is written, and able to deal gently…

…with the ignorant and the erring? To him belongs the encyclical letter, by the authority given him by the Spirit. If he knew of anything unlawful or harmful in what was being done, he would certainly have said what was fitting. But he sees the heresy prevailing and straits pressing on every side, and so he has allowed all who are eager to heal the diseases that have befallen us to do so, each as far as his power reaches. In this the most divine man does well. What is being done is not legislation, and yet no soul for whom Christ died is left unhealed. Clearly this holds until an orthodox synod meets. Then what has been well begun will be approved, and whatever is otherwise will be rejected. And this is most pleasing to God, who wants all to be saved, and above all those who run to the medicine of repentance. He helps the one who stretches out a hand in brotherly love, and he raises up the sick together with the one who lifts them. For his is the voice that says: "Comfort, comfort my people, O priests; speak into the ears of Jerusalem." And what else could comfort be but keeping safe those who have stood firm, and setting right through repentance those who have turned aside? Then to those who have sinned he says: "When you turn back and groan, then you will be saved, and you will know where you were." And again: "While you are still speaking the words of your prayer, he will say: Here I am." He is the helper of those who turn from the evil way. He lifts the stray sheep onto his shoulders, and as long as it is called "today" he applies the medicines of repentance. He counted the thief worthy of paradise in a single moment. He accepted the great Peter after his denial because of his bitter weeping. And he gave David the gift of prophecy once more, as though he had not sinned at all. But why should I bring out many examples and drag out the discourse [?]? He is kind toward those who are kind to their fellow servants, and severe toward the unsympathetic. That is why the healings [?] being carried out at the present time are not what your honour has mocked them as (away with the blasphemy!). Nor are these acts causes of scandal. They are proofs of true love. For the Lord says: "No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends." So the healers lay down their lives for those they heal, in the true sense of the word. They do not traffic in the dispensation ordained by God, like those who make a trade of Christ. And the people of God is purified day by day. "The house of Saul" grows weaker and has dwindled, "while the house of David" is magnified and has grown, as each one who has recovered [Reg. MS] passes from the one to the other. But what do you want, my admirable friend? The heresy has prevailed for so many years and God's creature is perishing. Should no physician appear? Should there be no methods of healing? Should the blind not be led by the hand, and the sick [?] not be made well…

[?] Should the wounded not have their wounds dressed? Should the lame not walk straight? Should the broken not be bound up? Should the wanderer not be turned back? Should whoever chooses to do so not fight against every disease, as far as he can? Yet among the physicians of bodies we see great diligence and many places of healing. One has undertaken to treat this ailment and another that. Not even the man appointed to the rank [Reg. MS: "station"] of assistant is prevented from laying hands on the sick, according to the medical knowledge each possesses, whether superior or inferior [Reg. MS: "lesser"]. Every day the patients crowd in, and the hostels that receive them are full. No one finds fault with this care, or blames anyone for being zealous about healing. Leaders and chief physicians, those in the middle and those at the bottom, all carry out this work of love for humankind. If it is so there, surely all this is seen and ought to happen much more in matters of the soul, by analogy. Whoever prevents it will be counted a destroyer and a common enemy of the human race, a fellow-worker with the one who was a murderer from the beginning. "Ours is not like that," he says, "but here is what I want to know. Repentance turns aside from the strictness of justice toward the good. Now the Lord did not dare to grant it before he had himself laid down all the just punishment owed to the scales and balances of justice. Who then is so daring and arrogant as to allow himself to cleanse by repentance those who denied the sufferings our Saviour Christ endured for us, without their first paying the whole penalty to the inviolable severity of justice?" Alas for this daring and senseless proposition! When [?] was Christ seen preaching repentance? When did he say to the paralytic: "Take heart, child, your sins are forgiven"? When was forgiveness granted to the prostitute who wet his divine feet with her tears, while he rebuked Simon his host? When was it said to the man who had lain sick for thirty-eight years: "See, you have been made well; sin no more, so that nothing worse happens to you," since the sickness had clearly struck him because of sin? But it is not the right time to set out these and other things while unrolling the record of his miracles. Did they happen before the Passion or after it? Everyone knows and agrees that they happened before the Passion. In the same way, when he sent out his disciples he gave them authority "to heal every disease and every infirmity," and that healing he granted through the repentance and prostration of those who prayed [Reg. MS: "approached"]. So what [?] daring tongue says that Christ did not dare to do this before he had himself laid down all the just punishment owed to the scales and balances of justice? And what tongue on that basis rebukes those who have taken up the dispensation of repentance, calling them daring and arrogant for not first exacting the full severity of justice? Is it not clear…

…that the rebuke comes from a Pharisaic mind, and the prohibition from Novatianist inhumanity? See then, my man, how you were lifted high and then thrown down headlong. You stepped outside your proper limits and did not keep the rank you had. Have you not read that everyone who meddles in another's office is to be expelled? And: "I did not send them," he says, "yet they prophesied." And: "No one takes this honour upon himself, but only one who is called by God. So also Christ did not glorify himself to become high priest," as it is written, "but was appointed by the one who said to him: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek." But who called you, brother? Who made you a lawgiver over the Church of God, when you have perhaps not even learned to be ruled? And since you have been seen to rule no one, you ought to receive laws rather than give them, to be led rather than to lead, to be enlightened rather than to enlighten, to be taught rather than to teach. Only by experience of the first should you rise to the second. Such is the divine law, and it is the best of laws for divine and human ranks alike. For let us not imagine, friend, that knowing how to say something drawn from the wisdom that has been made foolish, or how to slip in a crafty argument, is what makes lawgivers. Even the Moabites and Ammonites may not approach the altar. Lawgivers are those whom Christ-like obedience has proven, long endurance has borne witness to, and the word of the Gospel has perfected. If secular learning is present too, it is not unwelcome, provided it is adorned with humility and governed by the Gospel. But it must not pride itself on its own distinctions. Those who pride themselves on such things are like men leaning on a staff of reed, and they are rightly wounded and thrown into confusion. "But," he says, "I have been very zealous for the Lord, and what I see is unbearable." And where is our gift of prophecy, my excellent friend? Where is Mount Carmel? Where are the heavenly keys? Where is the mantle that divided the Jordan and came upon Elisha with a double gift? Even if we have some gift, to whom should we leave it, since we do not even have a disciple? So let us take care now not to reach for what is beyond our power and so fail even in modest things. Let us not strain out the gnat and swallow the camel. Let us not presume to remove the speck from our brothers' eyes while we ourselves carry the beam in our own eyes without noticing it, and so stand condemned, as the saying goes, by those we live and eat with here and there. "So-and-so," he says, "made a false confession and hid his shameful sin. Another hid his impiety and recounted one thing in place of another. So how can the so-called healer claim that these people have been healed?" Are they not to be believed [?], my good man? Rather, such a charge is very much to be condemned. For no one who comes of his own free will to be healed will choose to leave his own sickness uncovered. And even if it is true in some case, the judgement is not ours but belongs to God, who watches over all. For it says: "The things revealed belong to God and to us, but the hidden things to the Lord your…

[Notes:] 88 2 Kings 2:8. 82 Matthew [23]:24.

…God." "But why do you judge your brother?" Or why do you despise the physician? "For we shall all stand before the judgement seat of Christ," "who will bring to light the things hidden in darkness and disclose the purposes of the heart; and then each will receive praise from God." "Everyone," he says, "stretches his foot beyond his measure, dares what has not been permitted, and reaches for higher things." You have been caught by your own feathers, as one of the pagan writers put it somewhere, and that is where your proposition comes from. You were appointed to be a foot, but in your presumption you raised yourself to be the head. You have been run through on your other two propositions, my noble friend, and now comes yet another charge: "Everyone entrusts himself with things beyond his power and thinks others are inferior. They rush to loose and bind without restraint and without being called. They compete to drag everyone to their own feet. They want no one else to be, or to be thought, the one who looses, and they envy those who do such things. They receive only those whom they have loosed themselves. Those who have received a penance from others they turn away from and accuse, because they did not run to them and ask forgiveness from them." These accusations are fabrications of a demonic mind, and these propositions come from an envious heart. One might reasonably laugh at them as games, nonsense and toys. Or rather, to tell the truth, since no one comes to us for a penance out of distrust, it is we who are raving against those who heal because of the trust of those who come to them. We would be suffering some demonic passion, insulting modest men just as the Iconoclasts do. "What," he says, "is the difference between this policy and Manichaeism? Did we not fight against the Manichaean heresy in word and deed? The written treatises of those who fought against it show this. In them they proved it with unerring syllogisms and irrefutable demonstrations, even if now they forget themselves and their own writings." You seem, my friend, to be reasoning without reason, and leaning on your own reasonings to set the truth aside. You do not know that when likenesses are compared with prototypes, they are not those very archetypes. They are the same as one another only so far as they share a name, and in everything else they differ. Some things are named properly and others not properly. Some are said by extension and others in truth. Take, for example, the image of Christ and Christ himself. The one is and is called Christ in truth; the other is called Christ by extension, that is, by sharing the name. So too the holy apostle Paul called greed a second idolatry. He did so by way of cause, referring by likeness to idolatry in the true sense. It does not follow from this that the greedy are to be punished as idolaters, since then we would have to leave the world. As it is, many greedy people are…
