…overlooked and go entirely unpunished. So what is out of tune here, if the Iconoclast heresy is compared with the Manichaean, so far as the principle of image and prototype is concerned? In the same way the holy and ecumenical second synod at Nicaea did not prosecute and treat those caught in that heresy as Manichaeans. And those who drew up works about that synod, and who fought against the heresy in word and deed, have by no means forgotten them. It is you who have truly failed to know yourself, and that is a charge carrying heavy blame and stupidity. I would have liked to add to what I have already said other propositions from your many-branched and repetitive document, and to show that they are refuted at every point by right reason. But some I threw far away as useless and incoherent, some as refuting themselves, and some as obscure and contrary [Reg. MS: "heterodox"] to the truth, as if into the fire of Hephaestus. At the end of my discourse I add only this. If we ask forgiveness for the rash way we provoked God, dishonoured the saints, [?] the confession of faith and slandered the Church, it would be well. If not, we humble men will at least lay a hand on our mouths and not provoke your holiness to a second written address.

163 (55). — To Theodore the Patrician.

From your honoured letter we came to see your most praiseworthy eminence, and from hearing what it conveyed we came to know your good soul. To address such respectful words to us sinners, to desire to see our lowly face, and then to hear a saving word, is truly the mark of a man inspired by God and of a soul that longs for God. How wonderful are the works of the great and only God of us Christians! He called you out of an unholy nation to the holy knowledge of his truth, and in so remarkable a way. It seemed to be against your will, but it was in fact entirely your own choice, together with the high priests [Reg. MS: "kinsmen"] who came out with you, since divine providence did not see fit to snatch you from godlessness in any other way. O wonderful calling! O praiseworthy redemption! You were brought out of darkness into his marvellous light. You stripped off the old man, together with his absurd and pagan thoughts and deeds, and you put on Christ. You are called a Christian instead of a pagan, a son of light and of day instead of a son of darkness and of the night of impiety. You worship one God, adored in Father, Son and Holy Spirit. You have fled the impiety of polytheism and Bulgarian idolatry. And you confess that one of the holy Trinity, the Son himself and Word of…

…that God, out of his surpassing mercy toward our race, became a man like us in every respect, while remaining the same perfect God. For the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God: one God, not three gods (perish the thought!). He is one because of the single Godhead and three because of the three persons. This is the true faith of Christians, and it overthrows every error and heresy. Christ is twofold, since he is perfect God and perfect man. As God he was begotten of the Father before the ages, like radiance from the sun. As man he was born of his mother in the last times, as we are born, or rather in a way beyond us, since she who bore him was a virgin before, during and after giving birth. For this reason she is truly understood to be, and is called, the Theotokos. Therefore, just as he cannot be circumscribed in respect of his Father, so in respect of his mother he is circumscribed on a panel. His circumscription, that is, his icon, is to be venerated and revered. In it we Christians see what form he took on, and he is glorified as having become like us in all things except sin. He abolished every idolatrous likeness, which the human race had worshiped to its ruin from the days of old. So whoever refuses to allow that he be depicted, my good friend, denies by his very deeds that the Son of God became man, even if he agrees in words. And whoever does not venerate his holy icon is shown not to venerate him, even if he professes to venerate him. For the honor paid to his icon passes over to the prototype, just as the denial of the icon sends the denial back up to him. I learn that you yourself hold this conviction and for that reason keep away from communion with the Iconoclasts. I rejoice and rejoice with you, and I give thanks and give thanks together with you, that you see the truth, even though you learned it late and are a newborn son of God. And do not be surprised that error creeps in even among Christians. Where salvation is, there the dragon, the devil, runs to work destruction, and he does it through one man, the one who holds power. This error has only recently been brought in among Christians, since the icon of Christ, and of the Theotokos and of his saints, has existed from of old. Most honored lord, I have said these things to you to confirm your faith, as one moved by God, sinner though I am, since you are our brother and not a stranger, as you said. If you are a stranger to the world, though, that would be well. We humble ones are in the same state, and for this reason we have been cast out [?] for the sake of the word of God. Blessed are you, who believe rightly in Christ and count all things secondary for his sake. It is difficult for us to see one another because of those in authority, unless God should command it in whatever way he will arrange. But we will not cease to remember you and to love you as our brother. Once we did not know you through flesh and blood, but now through the Holy Spirit we hold you as a kinsman, since we were both born of the mother of adoption, the font

of baptism. Peace to you, my friend, brother and lord. Peace also to your house and to all who belong to you, from the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit.

164 (56). To the archimandrite of Gothia. [708]

We give thanks to the holy God that we were counted worthy to receive the loving letter of your holiness. There is no need to apologize for the delay. For who are we, worthless as we are? Why should you refer to our nothingness at all the pressing matters that trouble you? Yet you are humble-minded and know how to stoop even to the least, so you rightly wrote to us. We have learned not only what the letter contains, but also what the most reverend brothers and fathers who brought it told us. In all these things our God is your defender, and he will reconcile you against the charges thoughtlessly brought. We humble ones too will contribute our part, if ever there is occasion, [?] among those who are quick to slander, not to curry favor with you but to pay what is owed to love. For this reason we were compelled to write also to the most God-beloved father and high priest, the lord Philaret, in the hope that the appeal of us humble ones may be accepted. It seeks to bind things together for peace, and nothing is more profitable than peace; by it those who are called disciples of Christ after him ought to be marked. That, in summary, concerns the urgent matters. As for the rest, why were we asked to answer at all? You who are taught by God have the whole divinely inscribed book of the great Basil, which teaches what is saving and beneficial in the monastic, that is, the cenobitic, life. Without it no one can guide in a manner worthy of God or be guided to any profit, whether he rules or is ruled. Basil was asked about every matter and occasion of the sacred life in a cenobitic community, and he answered through the Holy Spirit. Whoever keeps in step with him has kept in step with the Holy Spirit, and whoever disobeys him has disobeyed Christ, who spoke in him. So the faults that the brothers fall into through carelessness may not be judged before lay persons. The holy Apostle himself cries out: "When one of you has a dispute with another, does he dare to go to law before the unrighteous and not before the saints?" And further on: "Is there not one wise man among you who can decide between his brothers? But brother goes to law against brother, and that before unbelievers." Having the affairs of monks examined before laypeople is the same as having them examined before unbelievers. It opens a door to those for whom it is unlawful to pry into our affairs. This is entirely out of keeping with the Church and harmful to it.

Since renunciation and tonsure were also raised, here is our answer. It is not without danger to turn someone away, for he says, "Whoever comes to me I will never cast out." Nor is it holy to admit someone carelessly and haphazardly, or to tonsure him without understanding. For if "no one serving as a soldier entangles himself in the affairs of life, so that he may please the one who enlisted him," as it is written, how much more does this hold for this army chosen by God? Whoever is truly to follow Christ must renounce all things, be stripped of all things and be torn away from everything: attachments, household, friends and relatives. In his disposition he must become a stranger to the whole world. Then he must be instructed [?] and formed in the monastic way of life, which God teaches and God forms. He must give proof and be tested in virtue, and only then, on the testimony of many, be brought into monastic consecration and become one of Christ's sheep. To be tonsured uninitiated and untaught, as we have been told is happening, is dangerous and utterly ruinous, both for the one tonsured and for the one who tonsures him. Moreover, to strip a monk of his habit is the same as to unbaptize him. That anyone should dare such a thing at all is horrifying even to hear. But suppose someone has been properly tonsured and some then slide back toward what is worse. If they persist in wickedness and do not heal themselves of their sicknesses of soul, they must be cut off from the brotherhood like rotten limbs, so that the healthy part is not harmed by contact with them. For the Lord says, "It is better for you that one of your members be cut off than that your whole body be thrown into the Gehenna of fire." If another is able to receive the one cut off, out of kindness, that is not unreasonable, provided he is found more skilled at healing and does not simply go along with those who are perishing. But those who otherwise leap out of the cenobitic community in utter frivolity are not to be received by other brotherhoods. In this way all may stand together and agree in everything, and not undo one another's labors. Of such undoing Christ is not the head, he who binds all things together in peace, but one whom it is abominable even to name. To keep a slave as a monk in a monastery is as foreign as to have a wife, for both are inventions of the disobedience. Those who long to return to the original state through the monastic way of life, and strive to imitate the harmless life of paradise, must reject [?] the things just mentioned. We have not said these things on our own authority. We gathered them, by way of reminder, from what the God-bearing Fathers have said. We ask you, most holy ones, to pray that we may not only say what is good but also do it in the Lord.

165 (57). To Gregory, his child. [203]

I rejoiced at your letter, beloved child: the road of you town-dwellers has been a pleasant one, and you have regained your health

together with brother Zosimas through bloodletting, and everything else turned out for you as you intended. As for the propositions of the Guestmaster, why did you still ask us for clarification? You answered him judiciously, according to the teaching of the God-bearing Fathers, and we have nothing more to say than your rebuttals. It seems the questioners are talking idly and are not eager to learn. Nevertheless, since it is written, "Always be ready to make a defense to anyone who asks you for an account of the hope that is in you," we too will answer as follows. The habit of monks is a profession of virginity, and it is a mystery, the mystery of monastic consecration, according to the word of the divine and all-wise Dionysius. Some say, "Where was it handed down that one should renounce the world and become a monk?" That is no different from saying, "Where was it handed down that one should become a Christian?" For he who established the one by apostolic tradition also handed down the other. He set out six mysteries: first, illumination; second, the synaxis, that is, communion; third, the rite of chrism; fourth, priestly consecrations; fifth, monastic consecration; sixth, those who have fallen asleep in holiness. What then follows from this? Whoever disputes one of these clearly doubts the others too, whether they come from divine tradition. If one is abolished, the rest are necessarily abolished with it. There would be no priestly consecration, and no rite for those who have fallen asleep in holiness, if monastic consecration did not exist. We would then think like pagans, being without God in the world and having no hope. That is the kind of man who raises the question of where the practice of a person becoming a monk was received. I have not yet mentioned that all the most eminent of the God-bearing Fathers became monks and extol the monastic life as angelic. They also wrote the treatises that lay down the rules of the sacred life. And anyone with sense will surely find that the divine Dionysius himself, in correspondence with the angelic orders and the priestly ranks, assigned an equal number of orders [?] to those outside the priesthood as well. The first and introductory order is of those still being brought to birth, that is, the catechumens; the second is of the illuminated; and the third is of those being consecrated as monks. To fight against what is evident belongs to those without perception, or to the unbaptized [?]. [1 Pet. 3:15]

He himself also laid down, for those who receive people who come from their earliest years, the rule of governing them. The book shows this, and quoting it word for word here would not be practical. In short, he ordained that after they reach the age of reason, that is, from sixteen years upward, the age at which honors and punishments also apply, as he himself says, they must be examined and joined to the brotherhoods through monastic consecration. If any afterward go over to secular life out of wicked perversity, he commanded that not even a door be opened to them, according to the bare tradition [Cod. Reg.: "period"], to the place they had left. But within the year mentioned, if they do not choose the life of virginity, or choose it but are unwilling to be trained for the monastic life, they are to be separated and sent away to secular life, so that no reproach may attach to the sacred life [Cod. Reg.: "so that no reproach may attach to the sacred life through their failures"]. But some do not do these things at all as commanded. They tonsure people from infancy, or at the lawful age but not lawfully and without proper training. That is why everything is upside down, and "priest and prophet have gone astray," as it is written. There is a tradition of countless opinions and self-made legislation, not out of love but out of love of money, not for salvation but for love of gain. To this I, wretch that I am, have no answer but to groan, to be downcast and to weep for our own sins. But may you be saved, beloved child.

166 (58). To Theoctistus the hermit. [?]

I received the letter of your honor and read it aloud in the hearing of the most God-beloved archbishop, my brother, together with the brothers who are with us. Then I, in my lowliness, gave thanks to the Lord, who inclined your heart to write out the creed of the faith correctly. To profess that one accepts the Old and New Testaments and all that the holy Fathers have handed down to the Church of God is, in sum, orthodoxy of faith. But heretics can also say these things without being found, by their words, to rightly handle the word of truth. So we inquired precisely of the brothers who were sent, and especially of Abba Sosipater, as you yourself asked in your letter, since a letter cannot report everything. By the grace of Christ we found that they reported in an orthodox way what you had set before them. What were these things? They must be noted in summary. First, concerning the holy Theotokos: they say that you hold that the Virgin existed before the ages. You deny that you either say or think this, and you confess that she was born of a man and a woman, Joachim and Anne; that is well. Second, concerning the Lord, that he was not crucified. You confess

that he was crucified according to the Scriptures; that is well. Third, concerning angels and demons: that after the judgment there will again be a restoration, and there will be one flock and one shepherd. You deny this and confess that both the judgment and the kingdom of heaven are eternal; that is well. Fourth, concerning a single monk: that he can rescue a hundred and fifty of those being judged from punishment. You deny this and say that there is no repentance after death, and that no one can rescue anyone from the punishment God has allotted to each; that is well. Fifth, concerning the book called "of Antony": that you say it is acceptable, though it contains many blasphemies, as we ourselves learned by reading it. You confess that you reject it as foreign to the Church of God, and that neither you nor those with you will keep it or read it any longer; that is well. Blessed [?] be God, who has cleansed you of these stumbling blocks. And blessed be the name of his glory, which persuaded you to call yourself rustic and unlearned, and to yield in everything and obey the word of my lowliness. I will advise or prescribe nothing beyond what has been divinely revealed to the holy apostles, prophets and Fathers, but only this, as you have written. You are to believe in the holy Trinity, undivided in essence but distinguished by its distinctive characteristics: in Father and Son and Holy Spirit, one God, one Lord, just as there is also one faith. The Father is God, the Son is God and the Spirit is God, yet there are not three Gods (God forbid!) but one God, as there is also one Lord. This is the doctrine of theology. Concerning the economy, you are to believe that the one of the Trinity became flesh from the holy Theotokos, by the good pleasure of the Father and the cooperation of the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit first came upon her, and so the power of the Most High overshadowed her, according to the Gospel. From her he was born as man, being perfect man and at the same time perfect God, one in hypostasis and twofold in nature, as the God-bearing Fathers and the seven holy ecumenical councils have set forth. You are to confess the Virgin as Theotokos, higher and more honored than all, and able to intercede as a mother with her Son and Lord on behalf of the whole world. And you are to confess

…[anathematizing] those anathematized by the councils, and proclaiming all the orthodox whom they praise. This is the true [Cod. Reg.: "sincere"] faith of Christians; this is the testimony of the confession of Christ. Whoever thinks otherwise, let him be anathema from the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. As the apostle Paul says: "Even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be anathema. As we have said before, so now I say again: if anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to the one you received, let him be anathema." You yourself set these things out in detail in your letter, so you must confess that you think this way. How is this to be done? By signing at the end of this letter, following the enclosed note. And the peace of God [?], which surpasses all understanding, will guard us and you and direct us in one spirit and one heart. Then we may believe in and worship the holy Trinity for the salvation of our own souls and of the people that has been divided into two parts, in the presence of the lord Ioannicius, our spiritual

Father, and of you, our honored father and brother.

167 (59). To Diogenes, imperial secretary.

The question has a twofold answer, that is, a twofold designation, for what is named in it is spoken of both properly and improperly. The image of Christ is properly called his image. It is spoken of improperly when it is called Christ, by an extension of usage, as is customary. The same principle applies to the life-giving cross and its figure. The same is true of veneration: veneration is like the figure of the cross. For it is relative, since the prototype and the image are things that stand in relation to each other, according to the word of the great Basil: "The honor of the image passes up to the prototype." There is one veneration of both, not split or divided. It is present essentially in the prototype and relatively in what derives from it. The same holds for the form of a shape, which is present naturally in the one and by participation in the other. So whoever venerates the image of anyone at all venerates in it the one whose image it is. This holds whether it is the image of Christ, of the Theotokos or of a saint, or simply of an emperor, a ruler or a person of lower rank. Whoever venerates in this way does not err. He stands firm in orthodoxy and rightly repels those who oppose the truth on either side. Who are they? Those who refuse to venerate the holy icons, and those who say that in this veneration they venerate the prototypes themselves

by nature. The blasphemy of the two is equal. The first abolish the mystery of the economy. The second deify, that is, give the status of essence to, things far removed in nature from the prototypes. Therefore the image of Christ is to be venerated (for here is the culmination of the argument) relatively, but it is not to be worshiped. Worship belongs by nature to Christ himself, since there is one worship of the Trinity. Not even the Theotokos herself is to be worshiped, nor the life-giving cross itself. So too the image of Christ is not to be worshiped but venerated. All venerations are referred, through their respective prototypes, to the one and only veneration that is worship, the worship of the holy Trinity. The others are not worship but are all venerations, differing according to whether the person is lower or higher.

168 (60). To John the Grammarian. [?]

Your honor has shown how unfeigned your sincere love is in your corrective notes on the treatise that we, unlearned as we are, composed. Those points may be judged in the treatise one way or another. But you were at a loss as to how we understood "subject," and you indicated that the treatise takes it in another sense [Cod. Reg.: "that it takes it in another sense"]. So we too were at a loss, that a man wise in all things should be at a loss. For, my admirable friend, the blessed Leontius, whose scholia are superb, says that "subject" is essence with hypostasis. The great Basil too speaks of "not in the subject" with reference to the holy Trinity. Moreover, the all-wise Dionysius says somewhere: "Many in the accidents, one in the subject." But accidents are observed not in the universal essence but in the hypostasis, as you know. So when he said, "Many in the accidents, one in the subject," he took "subject" to mean essence with hypostasis. And it is not unreasonable, I think, that the term stands this way in the treatise. Otherwise, how could "not in the subject" fail to lead to the Trinity being spoken of as three in both names and realities? So the subject is nothing other than essence with hypostasis. But if your holiness can put forward [Cod. Reg.: "find"] anything more precise [?], do not decline to teach it. It is a gift that you take pride in [Cod. Reg.: "for which you are praised"].

169 (61). To Theodore [?] of Eustratius the abbot. [?]

My good sir, I will pass over the rest of your little phrases before and after it as unclear and ungrammatical. The problem you raise, which you think does you credit, reads word for word as follows: "Christ our true God has two natures, two wills and two operations, but one person of the two natures. Whose person shall I depict?" Since you asked which person, listen attentively. The one that took on form, since the formless stamp of the Father's hypostasis took on form

[?] …what is ours. The temporal: because the eternal has taken on temporal extension [Cod. Reg.: "has received"]. That which has eyes, ears, nose, mouth and cheeks: because the one without form was found in form as a man. That which was kissed: because the uncontainable, having been contained, was kissed by the traitor. That which was struck: because the untouchable, having become touchable, was struck [?] by the servant. That which was seen stretched crosswise on the cross: because the immortal bowed his head and gave up the spirit. And this does not point to two persons (away with such impiety!). It shows one person, who is from two natures and exists in two natures, without division and without confusion. That is why the holy [apostle] says: "Concerning his Son, who was born of the seed of David according to the flesh, and declared to be Son of God in power according to the spirit of holiness." So by saying "according to the flesh" he has shown you that the same Jesus Christ is circumscribed, that is, can be depicted in an image. By saying "according to the spirit of holiness" he has shown that the same Jesus Christ is uncircumscribed. All the God-bearing Fathers took this from him, and they declare most clearly that he is circumscribed and uncircumscribed, visible and invisible, temporal and eternal. If you do not accept this, your premise is Jewish. And how can you say that Christ is of two natures and yet call him uncircumscribed only? That term signifies only one of his natures. To speak of the two natures is, consistently, to say both circumscribed and uncircumscribed. So you contradict yourself. If he seems to you uncircumscribed only, that suits the Manichaean, who strips the Word of humanity. Whoever is bare of humanity is uncircumscribed and cannot be depicted, for the two go together [?]. And again, how do you partake of the body and blood of Christ? According to you he is uncircumscribed, yet the things you partake of are circumscribed. Either do not partake, my good man, or, if you partake, confess that the circumscribed body and blood you receive belong to the circumscribed Christ. Otherwise you follow Paul [of Samosata] by partaking of a mere man and not of God incarnate. So it has been concluded, truly and firmly, that whoever circumscribes Christ is not a worshipper of a man, as Nestorius was, nor a worshipper of a creature, as Arius was, as you babbled in your ignorance. He is in every respect an orthodox and most genuine Christian. Whoever refuses to circumscribe him, as you do, is at once a Manichaean and a Paulianist. With the word "uncircumscribed" he brings in a bare God who became man only in appearance. And with the same word "uncircumscribed" he partakes of the body and blood as of a mere man, in the manner of Paul, and not of God truly made man.

170 [?] (64 [?]). To Theodore the deacon. [?]
At the request of your love I come to answer the heretical problems. And if well [?] … [?]

[?] A heretic's problem: "You confess one incarnate nature of God the Word, and so you say that Christ is a whole, that is, one totality made of parts, namely of divinity and humanity. We ask, then: what do you count together with the Holy Trinity, the whole or the part? If the whole, the Holy Trinity will not be consubstantial. If the part, then if you count the divinity, you plainly leave the humanity outside the Holy Trinity. If you count the humanity, you will be caught saying that the divinity is [outside?] the Trinity [?]."

The solution to this: When we confess one incarnate nature of the Word, we do not confess Christ simply as some whole. We confess him as made of two wholes brought together, divinity and humanity. These wholes were taken as parts for the composition. According to them he is wholly God, joined by nature with the Father and the Spirit, and he is wholly man, ranked in essence with his mother and with us. In his single personal character he binds the two extremes to himself, and in the union he keeps the boundaries of the extremes unharmed and unconfused. So the Trinity remains a Trinity and admits no addition foreign to its nature. The humanity remains humanity and is never divided from the divinity united to it. Your problem is therefore irrational, and it springs from the confusing heresy of the Acephali.

Another problem from the same heretic: "Is this Christ whom we confess counted together with the Holy Trinity or not? If he is counted with the Holy Trinity, how then will the Trinity be consubstantial? If he is not counted, then he will not be God either, but only a mere man. The arguments you use to solve this difficulty while keeping the doctrine of one Christ intact will serve us too in answering it."

The solution to this: The truthful arguments with which this Christ whom we confess struck down the first proposition can also be used to strike down the present one, since it is equally impious. But the Christ you champion, one natural totality made of parts, divinity and humanity, would not be consubstantial with the Father, since the Father is God only and not also man. Nor would he be consubstantial with his mother, since the mother is human only and not also God. It is time for you to look for other Christs with whom this one might be consubstantial, since a nature belonging to a single person cannot be recognized. And if you cannot find any, you are caught

by your own problems, and your empty fabrication would leave you believing that there is no Christ at all.

We have read the book that your holiness sent us through the most God-beloved metropolitan. Its author is not orthodox on the doctrine of the venerable icons. He says: "The ineffable and incomprehensible love of God for us, and the holy contests of the saints, we prescribe to be praised in the Holy Scriptures, and so far as it rests with us we take no pleasure in sculpture or painting at all [Cod. Reg.: "once for all"]. We allow those of moderate capacity to learn such things by way of introduction." What, then, must be said about this? First, he divides our faith, which is one and complete and admits neither addition nor subtraction. To himself he assigns the portrayal given through the Holy Scriptures, while to those who are supposedly simpler and less perfect he leaves the story told in sculpture and painting. Next, he claims the perfection of grace for himself and throws Jewish childishness onto the others, as though they needed an elevation suited to their nature [?]. On his view, then, the holy Apostle lies when he says: "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus." But if the Apostle speaks the truth, as he certainly does, and there is "one Lord, one faith, one baptism," what is this empty division into two unequal sections? You split up the holy nation, the royal priesthood, and assign one part to the more perfect lot and the other to the lower one. Further, everyone of sound mind strives for perfection and will regard what is imperfect as blameworthy. So by this reasoning the doctrine of the pictured story is necessarily superfluous. He also flatly contradicts the great Basil and does not agree with what Basil equally taught: "What the word of the story presents through hearing, painting shows silently through imitation." So this fine fellow sets himself against the holy Oracles, as well as against the leading Father. He thinks he is correcting someone else on this very doctrine, but he himself is caught in folly. For this reason we strike out such babblings entirely. We also remind your grace to walk by the same rule of orthodoxy. You know that every perfect person, even one enrolled in apostolic rank, needs the book of the Gospel, and in the same way needs the painted story that corresponds to it, since both deserve equal honor and veneration.

St Theodore the Studite

172 (64). To Hesychius the protonotary. [?]
The letter of your most excellent honor is a fine one. It was spoken from the good treasure of the heart, and it shines with the beauty of love. But the words of praise with which it extolled us unlettered people do not fit. When did I become, as you say, "a burning and shining lamp," in whose light my master rejoiced? Or a spring flowing crystal clear, from which your friendship drew a saving word? On the contrary, has not our appearance grown "darker than soot," to use the prophet's words, because of the uselessness of our life? And has not our word grown weak, lacking the power that comes from deeds to establish the hearer? I do not say this to find fault with my imprisonment at Smyrna. God forbid! It is venerable, the guardian of my venerable confession. I blame myself for not having lived worthily in it. But I will leave these things aside, since they are tokens of love, and turn my discourse to the urgent matter.

Your goodness has informed us, to put it briefly, that you have two daughters given by God. Before her birth you promised the first to God by dedicating her to the monastic life, while the second was left undecided. Now, because of some pressing circumstance, you have changed your mind and wish to exchange them. You would give the promised daughter to the world, that is, marry her to a man who is good in every way and of the girl's age. The undecided one, who is still very young and not of a matching age, you would dedicate to God. Yet you hesitate over this and are uneasy, in case it should displease God.

Most honored lord, you ought to have consulted others about this affair and received the solution from them, since they surpass our nothingness in knowledge. You should not have turned for an answer to us, who live so far away. Nevertheless, since you have decided to trust us, we have considered the matter together with our most God-beloved archbishop and brother. We judge it contrary to what is right, contrary to the true faith [Cod. Reg.: "judgment"], and contrary to the examples of all ages. Long ago Hannah of blessed memory promised Samuel before his birth. She did not substitute another for the one she had promised, though she had other children, but brought him to God. Blessed Nonna likewise promised Gregory the Theologian and paid her vow to God. Saint Euthymius, too, was given to God by his parents before his birth and was not exchanged after it. These men were seen as a marvel by the world, and their parents were called blessed because of them. How then, most admirable one [Cod. Reg.: "most wise"], could we act against these examples and escape blame? Would not the blessed Peter rather rebuke us, saying something like this:

"While it remained unsold, did it not remain yours? And after it was sold, was it not in your power? Why have you contrived this deed in your heart?" I pass over the ill-omened words that follow, since I am speaking to one who knows them. Once anything has been set apart for God by an auspicious vow, it is not without danger to transfer it to common use, and married life is common use. Someone who has promised to become a monk and is committed to it is condemned if he turns back and marries. In the same way, whoever has chosen to offer a son or daughter to God and then changes his mind would incur the same condemnation. This is what we think. Forgive us. We do desire your relief, and we want the vow you made concerning yourself to be fulfilled. But one commandment must not be broken for the sake of another, nor should harm be done to one person for the sake of another's salvation [Cod. Reg.: "be transacted"], as the God-bearing Fathers have declared. So much on this point.

The third point of your letter is this. There are certain monks who seem to hold the right faith and have endured many persecutions for the truth. Nevertheless they associate with heretics, eat with them and make concessions to them, thinking the matter indifferent. They claim that some Father laid down that only three things must be avoided: being blessed by those who hold heresy, chanting with them when they lead the singing, and sharing in their bread. What they say is contrary to what the holy Fathers have ordained. The Fathers do not permit associating with heretics, eating with them, chanting with them, or having any communion with them at all. They even pronounce woe on those who share with them so much as food, drink or friendship. So whoever teaches those things, whoever he may be among men, is to be cast out as a teacher of alien doctrine.

17[?]. To Gregory the consul. [?]
Until now your honor deprived us by not writing, though you write well, as your letter itself shows. We praised in it not only your aptitude for learning but also your continuing love of learning, since you long to share in a higher education. We do have the volume you asked for, but not here. If our deputy steward happens to come to your parts, he will take it from the place where it is kept and give it to you. Education is a fine thing, my lord, so long as it works together with the true education and does not rave like a Corybant and so show that those who share in it are uneducated.

The meaning of the Apostle's saying, "For in him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily," seems to me to be this. In the flesh that the Word took from the Virgin, that is, in the temple he built for himself, all the fullness of the Godhead dwells. He says "all the fullness," not some part, as it appears [?] to those who divide the indivisible Godhead. "Bodily" means "essentially," for so it has been understood

by the Fathers, against those who babble that the indwelling is merely relational [?]. The saying "The Word became flesh and dwelt among us" is of the same kind. To prevent anyone from thinking that the Word had been changed into flesh, he added "and dwelt among us." Clearly the one who dwells is one thing, and the dwelling in which he dwells is another. So the two, divinity and humanity, are together in the one person of Christ. If you see the matter differently, do not deprive us, who have little learning, of a clearer and truer view. I might add that we are careless too, even if you yourself have exalted us otherwise with friendly praise.

The letter of your honor [?] is welcome both to God and to any pious person. At this present time of heretical battle in the dark and storm of unbelief, it has told us that you shine like a star in your region. You have not been darkened by heretical communion, nor sunk beneath the [?] of unbelief. Blessed be the Lord, who even in the [military?] rank [?] has people who cling to his law amid the present confusion and overthrow of orthodoxy! Blessed are you, most honored brother, and your name truly suits you, for you have both loved God and guarded the deposit of the faith. You reported in your letter that you were guided in such and such a way by those blessed Fathers who departed to the Lord with a good end, whose names are in the book of life. That is well, and it too is a mark of your ardent zeal. Since their departure [?] left you orphaned, you have asked to be attached to our humility in their place. We are paltry and worthless. Yet since it is written, "[Bear with?] one another in love" [?], we have agreed for the sake of this love in the Lord, and we accept your dedication, which is truly good and praiseworthy.

You have striven to abstain entirely from heretical communion, and by the grace of Christ you have abstained, as you say. Abstain still. In this way you would show yourself dear to your God and in communion with him, for communion with his enemies separates one from Christ. But the general compels you to chant with the heretics and to eat the food [offered?] [?], since otherwise you could not avoid the lord general without danger. [It is said?] [?] that we cannot easily answer this, because strictness forbids the orthodox person to share anything at all with the heterodox, or to meet with them in eating, drinking or friendship. Knowing this, let your goodness hold fast to its good

zeal, building the golden structures of strictness on the good foundation, and praying also for our humility.

175 (67). To Irene the patrician. [732]
Since you greeted us lowly ones, lady, through the most reverend presbyter, we return your greeting by letter. We welcome your good faith and warm confidence, and we have learned from them that you are a good woman, a lover of God and of monks. So it is fitting to quote the scriptural saying: "Blessed is the husband of a good wife." You see, lady, that because of your goodness Scripture calls blessed the lord patrician, the husband God gave you. So strive eagerly to make him still more blessed. How might that be done? By becoming still better yourself, that is, by reminding him, exhorting and imploring him. Urge him to exercise his high military command in a God-pleasing way, as indeed he does, and to visit orphans and widows in their affliction. Urge him to keep himself unstained by injustice and to be a lover of monks and of the poor, tempered by gentleness, since his authority itself is enough to strike awe into those under his hand. Urge him also to hold back from threats, and when he strikes, to strike for correction, scourging humanely and with measure. Complete license does not bring salvation, and excessive punishment is not acceptable either. Above all, urge him to be orthodox in faith. Outwardly it may be said that he cannot keep this, because of what has already happened. Even that is no adequate defense before God, for nothing should be preferred to love for him. Yet at least in the inner man it is possible to preserve it, and so he can become the savior of many, monks and laypeople, rulers and ruled. Moved by spiritual love toward you, we have made bold to remind you of these things, knowing that you hold to the good even without reminders.

176 (68). To Bryenes the general. [740]
The death of your blessed mother has been announced to us. Need we even say how much we groaned? We did not grieve for her, who has fallen asleep in holiness. Far from it! Her departure was gain to her, since she has escaped this life so full of sin. We grieved when we thought of your excellence, now completely orphaned and without any consolation in life. And this has come upon you in so grim a situation. You could not even attend her holy funeral, which can bring some small comfort: a farewell word and last utterance, an embrace of the honored remains, and a look at the very tomb in which she is laid. You seem to have suffered the fate of Tantalus, if the

comparison is not too mythical: wasting away with thirst in the midst of springs, since you received the news of your mother's falling asleep with your ears alone and not with your eyes. What then shall we do? Shall we groan beyond what is fitting? Shed tears without end? Complain without restraint? Then where is the knowledge, where the wisdom, where the understanding with which your nobility has been adorned, beyond many who are now seen in office? By no means, beloved, by no means! Let us groan and weep in moderation, enough to pay the funeral honors due to a mother and to show what nature demands. Then, if you will, let us return to ourselves and look on the things of this world with lofty contemplation. They are a dream and a shadow, and this game on earth, as one of the theologians says somewhere, is "not existing, to come into being, and having come into being, to be dissolved." We too shall travel the same road our fathers have already traveled, and the same lodging awaits all alike. Perhaps one person's end is more tragic than another's. One may happen to be buried in peace, while another is not. One becomes a casualty of war, another is swallowed by the sea, and another dies in some other way, as we see in the various pitiful forms of sudden death. Your blessed mother rose above all these, departing from this world in holiness and in a cross-bearing life.

It remains for us, then, to repeat that celebrated saying of blessed Job: "The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it seemed good to the Lord, so it has come to pass." I would add that this saying helps us too in our present afflictions and perplexities. For that celebrated man, as you know, gave thanks to God amid countless sufferings. Let us not lose heart, then, dearest, nor despair even of life, knowing that the Lord will not let us be tempted beyond what we can bear. Who knows what the coming day will bring forth? And "who will announce to Abraham that Sarah is nursing a child?" The saying is symbolic. We pray that the Lord of glory himself will touch your heart and kindle in it the light of unfailing consolation, so that it may draw the sources of comfort from within and need no other voice.

We have also seen our beloved brother and spiritual son, the lord John, your excellence's [?] brother, [?] who visited us sinners, as was fitting. We comforted him with a few words in his grief for his mother. We also urged him to bear, with brotherly fellow-feeling, what befits godliness [?]

177 (69). To Euphrosyne the abbess. [741]
Now too we visit your honor by letter, longing to learn whether you continue in good health, bearing reverently the spiritual [?]

Notes

[?] life. Doing this is a duty we owe, just as you yourself have devoted yourself to our humility, ever since the time of your blessed mother. Her memory is in the book of the living. She lived well and left her own life as a pattern of piety, not only for you, holy and godly-minded as you are, and for the women in your charge, but also for everyone else who longs to imitate what is good. Since, then, you have the example of virtue from your mother, add to it what is your own as well, lady, we beg you. From that most excellent image, become yourself an image of a godly life to those who see you, as indeed may you become. For we hear again and again of the good things you are doing. On the one hand there is your guidance of the sisters: you hold them all together lovingly as one soul, and keep watch over the things of God in prayers, in psalmody and in readings. On the other hand you divide yourself in many ways in sisterly hospitality, with your cares and your gifts. As I see it, your monastery is to Byzantium what an eye is to the body. Through it God is glorified, and the blessed mother rejoices beyond words, since the saints are granted to see what their own disciples achieve. Rejoice, then, good teacher and true mother of children according to God. Let others have earthly glories and splendors, diadems and crowns that pass away. For you the cross of Christ will suffice: the God-possessed life, the virgins' house beloved of Christ, and, if you will, the words of God, more precious than gold and precious stone, the grey habit and the following of Christ. These are greater than all earthly things, and [?] of the kingdom of heaven. So let the eye of your mind never grow drowsy, nor the hearing of your heart [?], nor your divine love ever cease. Rather, may you always grow by adding virtues, pricking the soul and moving it to compunction, and pouring out tears as if from a spring. For this water is excellent above all. It cleanses the soul when it is sometimes defiled by thoughts. It quenches the fire of fleshly desire kindled through inattention. It calms a troubled disposition and the effects of a hostile assault. It truly bends God to mercy, and it restores the lover to his former genuineness. You are wise; understand what I am saying. For the Lord gives you grace, and may he give you still more, to love him and be loved in return, to long for him and be longed for in return, so that you too may be able to say with the Apostle, 'I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me.' For whoever loves God wholly goes out of himself, living and moving and having his being in the one he loves. Such is the bride of Christ that the word looks for in you, and also in the daughters of God under you. And what follows from this? Christ the Bridegroom, the heavenly bridal chamber, and the good things of the Jerusalem above, the kingdom of heaven itself, and all the things of rest that have been promised to the saints. The blessed mother has already reached these, and she urges you to persevere in asceticism, in concord and in unity of soul; to trample the passions,

to hate flesh and blood, and to hold fast to the virtues, through which these unspeakable good things can be attained.

178 (70). To Eudocimus the spatharius. [742]

I am late in writing to your honor, and I do so now at the urging of Silvanus, our most reverend brother. When he came and spoke with us face to face, he broke our humble soul as he recounted each thing. He told us that you, our master, bear what has happened even with thanksgiving and refer your suffering to God. You set yourself apart from what was contrived through human malice, and you seek one end: how you may make your life acceptable from now on to the Master of all. Because of all this he moved us, as was fitting, to say: 'The good man brings forth good things out of the good treasure of his heart.' For you laid up in your soul, as in a storehouse, treasures of knowledge from your earlier education, both divine and human, and now you fittingly bring out spiritual riches at the time of need, managing your own salvation. See, good man, how divine learning has turned out well for you: the reading and the understanding, the study and the practice, the intercession and the prayer, the acquiring of sacred words and books. You are very rich, even if your means of livelihood have been reduced to little. You are fair-eyed, with lovely lids, even if they have unjustly robbed you of your sight. You are very illustrious and renowned, even if you have resolved to live out a life without honor or glory. This is certainly a test and a touchstone of virtue: that in the very things in which we seem to have been forsaken, we find ourselves benefited by the good God. Through things on the right and on the left, through glory and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute, and all the other things the apostolic voice set out, he knows how to order our life to our advantage. This is an ancient teaching, and it is the mark of the way of life of God-possessed men even now. Take Abel, I pray you, the righteous man attested by God's own judgment: did he not become the victim of his brother's hand? And Enoch, who pleased God: because of the corrupters of that time who were eager to destroy him, did God not snatch him from their midst and remove him to unknown places? There he remains to this day, and he will be the forerunner of Christ's second coming. Consider Abraham, who was tested by God in many ways, and the testing of whose faith was far more precious than gold. And to pass over the others, who are many and cannot be recorded within the limits of a letter, there is Job of the countless contests. If we compare our own sufferings with his, we will surely find them slight, and we will join in his famous saying, taking it up on every occasion. So then we

urge you, [?], to order your affairs, and by better reasoning and a firmly faithful mind to transform the time of misfortune and much suffering into good fortune and well-being. Nothing human will move one who is so firmly grounded and who lives in confidence in God; he stands higher than everything that usually causes grief. If you say that you fall asleep while listening to the reader, it is no wonder, for the loss of sight naturally has this effect. If you say that you have no work in hand because your nature is idle, do not let it trouble you. The Apostle says: 'You have a psalm, you have a teaching, you have a tongue, you have a revelation; let everything be done for edification.' Eat, drink, sleep. Only keep hold of thankfulness, and read whatever you have within you and whatever is stored up in the natural book of the mind. A little while later you will see again, and you will behold the unapproachable light: Jesus the Son of God coming from heaven with glory and his power in flaming fire, judging some as deserving judgment and glorifying others as sharers in glory. May you also be among these, my dearest and most honored friend, flashing like a ray of the sun. As for your earlier [?] about making the suburban estate into a monastery, whatever was decided, one way or another, was well decided. God has accepted it all as already done, provided you bear the loss of everything with thanksgiving. Pray for us sinners. For now not only we sinners but even any of the holy ones would ask for your prayer, since you are laboring under sufferings. Our most God-loving brother the archbishop sends you his warmest greetings.

179 (71). To Sergius the hegumen. [?]

Thanks be to the Lord that your honor is well; the letter reported this, and so did the two brothers. We also welcomed your intention and desire to come to us, though you were prevented by the pressure of the civil wars and the dangers of the road. May the Lord our God quickly scatter these evils, bringing his subject people back to peace and delivering them from any further raids by the Hagarenes. For we have also been told about the sword in your region, what it was like and how great it was there. All these things are punishments from God for our unrepentant wickedness. Yet you, good man and most honored brother, stand firm and be courageous in leading the brotherhood. Do not give way to [?], even if the difficulties are many, and do not grow weary in your straits, even if your [?] is being spent. First of all, and this is the question of first importance, guard the faith so that it stays safe and unshaken, and flee communion with the heterodox in every way. For know that persecution is at hand, and it is no mark of perfection for you to sit at home and remain unpersecuted while the zealots for piety have suffered much and some have been crowned with the diadem of martyrdom.

So you need an exact life, one that makes up for the deficiency of the [?] [Reg. MS: 'of the lapse'; [?]] into which your former superior fell, and through him all of us, by our acceptance of him. For as the head is, so is the whole body. I say this not so that you will be dissolved, but so that you will be strictly preserved and strengthened by having no part in the heresy. Second, be sober, be sober; be watchful, be watchful. For many fight against us from on high; many are the snares of the devil; and like a roaring lion he seeks someone to devour. One he tries to swallow up through the pleasure of the flesh. Another he tries to tear away from fellowship with the brothers through the disease of [?]. Another he wounds with the arrows of envy, wanting to show him to be a Cain. Another he throws down with the fall of avarice, eager to make him known as a second Judas. In short, his work night and day is our destruction. Take care: guard the sheep of Christ by your conduct and your words, and your reward from God will be great. For he himself said to the chief of the apostles, 'Simon son of Jonah, do you love me more than these? Feed my sheep.' So the proof of love for him is the pastoral staff rightly used.

Abba Anthimus has also arrived, good Stephen, my beloved son. When I saw you, I duly asked you how you were living, since the duty of oversight requires this, and I did the same with your brother Anthimus. I perceived that you have love for one another, but not the kind of love that truth requires between brothers who are genuine in the Lord. What is this? You do not hold everything in common: you keep your own gold, and he keeps his own gold, and this divides love. How can there be one soul and one heart where there is 'mine' and 'yours'? From this come suspicions, and from this come slanders. And third, because of this Christ is not in your midst, he who said, 'Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in their midst.' Instead the enemy of our souls is there, who cuts apart the members of Christ. For it is clear that where there is private ownership and not community, Christ is absent from that place, since it is written of the apostles: 'They had all things in common, and no one said that any of the things he possessed was his own.' Forgive me, but are we not ashamed now that the two of you do not hold your belongings in common, when among the apostles, so great a multitude, there was community? That is why Christ was there. But he is not among you at all, harsh as the word may be. Otherwise you would be of one soul, of one mind and one heart, bearing with one another and caring for one another, self-sufficient, obedient, gentle, cheerful, content with what you have, and living a sweet life even with nothing but bread and water, such as

the saints lived. But as it is, things are the opposite, as described above. That is why you are distracted, so that one more silver coin or one more gold coin may be added to the money you have already accumulated. This is the passion of avarice, and its outcome is Judas-like. I ask you, and you answer me: do you have bread and wine and a little oil, along with the other things needed to nourish the body, for one or two months? If you nod yes, thanks be to the Lord. If not, buy them with the coin I have just given you, and there will be no distraction and no disturbance. I know it will suffice for your needs even for four months. And when you run short again, whether from here or from elsewhere, and I might add from the work of your hands, he who feeds all things will feed you too. This life is the best. In this way you will have Christ in your midst, sometimes working and sometimes praying, now keeping stillness and now reading. A sweet light will dawn for you, those who see you will find you lovely, and God will be glorified in you; may he glorify you in return, both now and in the age to come. You will be the boast of us sinners and the glory of the whole brotherhood. I have said this not as though you had gold stored up; may you never have it, lest you hear: 'Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.' For a monk, it counts as treasure if he keeps more than three nomismata for himself, as is written in the Fathers, and even that with the poor in mind. The strict monk, who masters the world through non-possession, does not own even one silver coin, and he cries out with holy Paul: 'As poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, yet possessing everything.' For God opens a door on every side to such a man, whether he is keeping stillness, being persecuted, imprisoned, or suffering anything else. Such a man is a Christ-bearer and a true Christian, an angel on earth, a man who imitates God, an heir of God and a co-heir with Christ. [?] To sum up the matter, then, brothers: if each of you has three nomismata, you are not to be rejected among monks, according to the example of the Fathers. But if you have more than ten, as I hear, or even more, know that you have fallen from the monastic state, and that you are servants not of Christ but of the adversary, and children not of me, the humble one, but of the lover of gold. You might say, 'But you have money, yes, since Christ also had it, through the purse that he carried, and so does every superior and head of the churches.' But that is for the stewardship of the brotherhood. For in the Gospel the Lord says to Judas, 'What you are doing, do quickly.' None of those at table knew why he said this to him. Some thought that, since Judas had the purse,

he was telling him, 'Buy what we need for the feast,' or that he should give something to the poor. So, in imitation of Christ, all true superiors certainly have the purse, and for no other reason; perish the thought, for that is most hateful to God. If, then, you too are superiors, and some people give to you from their means as they did to Christ himself (as it is written of the women who followed him), and as various men and women have likewise done for the saints, that would be well. Then you may have not merely ten nomismata but even ten thousand, for nothing is yours; it is Christ's, and you are stewards through Christ. So it was with Paul, who possessed all things yet had nothing, and so it is with everyone else to this day who holds oversight in a God-bearing way. But if you are not superiors and stewards of souls, I beg and implore you, quickly distribute whatever exceeds the fixed measure. Otherwise you may be caught by the devil in the passion of avarice and fall away from discipleship to Christ. I have said this not to you alone but through you to all the brothers, and not out of hatred, perish the thought, but out of great love. I do not wish to confine you, but rather to give you great breadth. For breadth is found in narrowness, and the exultation of the spirit is found in affliction for Christ's sake. Listen to me, children: I am a sinner, but I counsel you well and command you lawfully. So may we please Christ in everything and in every way, and become heirs of the eternal good things.

181 ([?]). To the Empress Mary. [?]

What sort of people are we, and who are we, insignificant as we are, that we should be thought worthy of an explanation about the painful events, and should, moreover, be honored with excessive praise by your most honored ladyship? Yet the truth of the matter will show that we have welcomed your piety's condescension. It is indeed necessary, for you will free the many from the false suspicion that tends to creep into such matters, and no wonder. For as a report flows along, it scatters among many people and does not keep the truth fully in each case. But what words can we use as we try to heal the pain of your heart, which has suffered so much? Or with what gentler touches could we soothe the roughness of your soul? To let our account begin from the beginning: you bore an unjust separation from your husband, and were thrust out of power along with it, a thing at which the world was shaken [?]. A pitiable sight! The adulteress wears the purple, and the empress is dressed in black; the slave girl rules, and the mistress serves. To pass over the rest, since you who suffered it know it better than we, who are strangers to it: you bore exile for the truth, cut off from your own child. Here too the toil was great, and great is the praise you have both from God and from all the pious. The third blow

is the present one, about which we have been asked to show what is right. Others will say that a mother should follow her daughter, since they say this happens even among wild beasts by natural attraction, as anyone can see. But we, insignificant as we are, cite the Master's words: 'Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?' And again: 'If anyone comes to me and does not hate his daughter, he is not worthy of me.' What is the conclusion? That your godliness should remain at home, while the Augusta keeps the palace. In this the sword of the Gospel has been shown, bringing division. Forgive these words, lady. We have written them [?] with great attention and anguish of heart, as though speaking into your ear, on behalf of you both, and we pray for what is better and leads to salvation, both now and for

182 (75). To Basil [?] the monk. [?]

We do not refuse to write our humble word whenever your honor reasonably asks for it, if indeed it is profitable to you. We indicated this very thing in our previous letter. So now too we send it, at once consoling and admonishing. What is the consolation? You say that the abbess, together with ten of the sisterhood, has departed in the Lord. The event is not without pain; indeed it is deeply staggering. For when the head is gone the whole body is dead, and when the most precious members have been cut off, what remains is unsightly. That is what has happened as far as the flesh is concerned. But since spiritual things are compared with spiritual things, the event is at once grievous and joyful: grievous because of the loss, joyful because of the hope. As you relate, you have sent ahead a most holy abbess and venerable sisters. This is a cause for joy. Those who have been taken up are preparing a place of rest for you by their intercession, like people who go ahead on the road to secure lodgings. And for us who remain, that is, for you sisters who remain, men and women alike, it is a cause for joy too: we are eager to lay hold beforehand of the good life and the holy way of life, and we always look toward the place where, a little later, we will meet our mother in God and the sisters. See, such is your suffering: full of hope and joy, and not like the grief for those who are dead according to the flesh. Those who mourn them are struck down with senseless laments and wailing, like the gentiles who have no hope, and they are filled with grief. That is why departure from this life is not even desirable to them, but something to be fled from with all their might. But for us, to whom to live is Christ and to die is gain, the falling asleep of spiritual fathers is an occasion for joy, since they are alive in the Lord, and in a way more lofty and immortal than the life here

[?] grief and ignoble tears, in accordance with what he established by the grace of Christ: the one over the direction of the men's monastery, the other over the leadership of the convent of virgins. Be sober, keep watch, act like men, be strong; let all that you do be done in love, all in keeping the commandments, according to the precepts of holy Basil. And between you, the two monasteries, let there be [?], so that, men and women alike, living a life without offence and without reproach, you may glorify God in your body and in your spirit, each monastery being supported and sustained by the other in a manner worthy of God. That is to say, you, brother Basil, who have also written to us and are in agreement, are to be present with both houses and help each of them as far as you can. This is not because you are not answerable as superior, but because your wish has been fulfilled by the acceptance of the one who was put forward; so rather throw yourself in alongside and help with whatever is needed. You have, then, good examples for advancing in virtue: the sisters and the brothers who have departed. You have the lives of the saints and the legislation of the Fathers. You have, greater than these, God the maker of all things in your midst, according to his unfailing promise. You have the holy Mother of God as your helper and all the saints as your intercessors. You have also our nothingness, eager to help you in what is good. So do everything well, and carry everything through in peace. "Rejoice always; pray without ceasing; in everything give thanks," cries the great Apostle. By his intercessions may both we and you be saved.

183 (76). To Elias the priest. [?]

Your kiss, O holy man of God, is most venerable, and it keeps the mark of our oneness of soul. But your question, I do not know how to put it, is unfitting and does not agree with our humility. For never yet, even to this day, have we heard of children being tonsured by their father under compulsion and not of their own will. If they are mere infants, or under age, the will is not theirs, for they cannot yet tell good from evil; the matter must instead be referred to the choice of those who begot them..... [lacuna] (77) the matter must be referred [to him?], from whom comes salvation of soul and body for both us and you. Enough about these things, since I have no time to speak at length, being occupied with other matters that are not easily settled. But concerning the bishop of Chios, why have you written this and that? When the man came here, we did not bring him into our presence, so as to avoid suspicion, nor did we leave him altogether unreceived[?], since it is not [Editorial note: ? "To Elias the priest," and letter 187, "To Auxentius."]

right to send away even an ordinary person, let alone one who has been allotted the name of bishop. We were glad, then, that he at last withdrew from his bishopric and chose to be cast aside somewhere here. We also put him under a fitting penance, as we have done with others who acted as he did. And God is the God of those who repent. This is the clear example of repentance that we and others charged with healing have required: the fallen man's withdrawal from his bishopric and his abstaining from sacred ministry, with penance until a time of peace. If, then, the man has agreed to these things, who were we to drive off one who came to us and to be obstinate [?] about it? Do not, admirable man, take offence at him, even if what you say he did should prove true. We have not heard of it up to now, and even if we had, we do not judge him in these matters. For it is written: "Does our law judge a man unless it first hears from him and knows what he is doing?" And again the Apostle says: "Do not accept an accusation against a presbyter except on the evidence of two or three witnesses." Besides, the question here is not about these things or about any authority to judge, but about receiving the fallen when they repent. What your honour has said is kept in store, either here, at the proper time, for those who preside over the Church, or in the age to come, for the Judge of all. I therefore advise your goodness to let those words go, and for now to give thanks to the Lord for the man's repentance, so that we may be fellow workers with God, who wants every man to be saved, and so that in this we may have peace with him through our Lord Jesus Christ. In the end, when you find the opportunity, if indeed you are looking for one, you may judge with uprightness. For now, pray for us, that we may be saved in soul and body, for we confess that we are more sinful than all men. The lord archbishop sends you many greetings, as he has been greeted by your voice, and so do all the brothers with us. Farewell in the Lord.

184 (78). To Auxentius, abbot. [754]

We have gone through your honour's letter as well as we could, putting far from us the praises of ourselves, since we are not worthy of any show of praise at all, but rather of reproachful mockery. For who are we, useless men, not even worthy of the name we bear[?]? As for the scriptural chapters you asked about, we were greatly astonished that an interpretation should be sought even from us unlearned men, and that about such figurative expressions,

which it belongs to the God-bearers alone to make clear. The explanation has indeed been given by them, and above all, word by word, by the great and divine Basil. So take his commentary on Isaiah and you will learn what you are looking for. Besides, deciding such matters goes beyond the measure of a letter and would need a whole treatise. As for there being a dispute with the Jews: let the fighters against Christ, O best of [?], rage against themselves. They have spurned the teachings of Christ himself, our true God, thrust aside the precepts of the apostles, and, in short, loathed the lofty words of all the God-bearers. It would hardly be fitting for them to be guided by us, or for us to join in argument with them. "Leave them," said the Lord; "they are blind." And the Prophet says: "There is no rejoicing for the wicked, says the Lord." For besides gaining nothing from the exchange of words, we would also harm ourselves with their venomous words, like people poisoned by a snake. "God will break their teeth in their mouth"; "the Lord has crushed the jaws of the lions." Let this be enough for you.

What, then, is required of us of necessity, so that we may please the Lord? How shall we escape the snares of the devil? Plainly, by becoming winged in spirit, seeking the things above and setting our minds on the things above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. From there he will come with the angels of his power in flaming fire, inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God and on those who do not obey his Gospel, that is, the Jews and any who think as the Jews do, whether by distorting the faith or by crookedness of life. Meditate on these things, my good friend, and be wholly in them, so that your progress may be evident to all. Paul, the great herald of the truth, urges you: "Avoid foolish questions and genealogies and quarrels and Jewish fights."

To answer briefly what you put to us: the whole burden of the prophecy concerns the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, at which the people that had been cast off is also saved from the four wings, that is, the ends of the earth. The walls of the new Jerusalem painted on the hands signify the mystery[?] of the cross. For when he was pierced with nails in his holy hands, he drew humanity free of the nails of its passion-ridden state of sin and adorned it with the archetypal beauty of deification. After this, a little later, through the resurrection on the third day and night, comes: "Lift up your eyes round about and see all your sons; behold, they have gathered and come to you. As I live, says the Lord." What follows in the prophecy are gifts and festive things, full of delight. The grateful man will understand them and join in saying what is fitting, but the ungrateful Jew will twist his heart, and will listen soundly to neither the Old nor the New Testament. From him may we be delivered by the prayers of the saints, sanctified Fa-

ther, and may we be saved in the kingdom of heaven, in Christ Jesus our Lord. Amen.

185 (79). To Eudocimus the spatharius. [755]

Even on our own we sensed how great was the pain and suffering that has befallen your honour. But now that we have heard from you, and heard your words full of lament describing each of the painful things that have happened, we feel it all the more and share your pain, as is only right. Even so, however you may handle these things that have come upon you by God's just requital, you do well in this too, taking the blows as having been sent to purge vice rather than to test virtue. For our part, we shall not stop setting our reply before you in a clear and easily understood way.

You have been deprived of sight. It is painful (how could it not be?) to have lost the lamp of the body. But again it is a cause for thanks that we no longer see the vanities of the world, by which every mind is naturally and unhappily carried away. You have been shut out from the processions and assemblies of the city and the palace. But you have been set free from the "assembly of evildoers" and the company of lawbreakers; you know what I mean. You have been stripped of your possessions? This too is very hard to bear. But now you can travel light and sail above the troubles and dealings of life. Where, admirable man, could you ever have found such a place as you have now, in which you can be at leisure for God and know him as far as possible? Where could you have found such a time for prayer, sighing, compunction and outstretched hands as you can now enjoy because of the injury done to you? Do you not see that things have turned out for your good, men's wickedness having been turned to your salvation? One thing above all must be recognized: in your former way of life it was difficult to take up the saving profession, since many, as you know, opposed that pious aim. But now there has been opened to you not only the door of repentance but also the entrance into the kingdom of heaven. Every right-minded person will count you among those who are being saved, which is what every earnest person strives for, and nothing in the world is worth more than attaining it.

If only there were some way to exchange our senses with one another! It would be the fulfilment of my prayer, along with the loss of sight, to lose also the goads of sin that come through sight. But these things I say in the manner of friendship. May our good God comfort you with great comfort, so that you bear all things with thanksgiving, in imitation of blessed Job. And may he grant that we someday come to speak face to face, so that what now escapes our letters we may make up with the living voice, and so that we may then know each other better, having so far tasted only a little of your sweet love.

186 (80). To Nicetas the spatharius. [757]

In bitter sufferings, whoever chooses to console the afflicted can easily find words of comfort. But for a suffering as great as the one that has gripped your God-beloved self, what word of comfort could be found? Who could undertake to heal such pain and do so with skill? O dreadful news! Your lady and wife has been torn from you, as we have just heard. The only consolation in the circumstances of your shared life has been taken away. The blessed home has lost its ornament. The branches droop, now that the good root has been cut. The menservants and maidservants wander here and there, without their mistress's face shining on the house. Everything is full of gloom; perhaps even the air seems changed to you, as your mind has been changed. Where is she who welcomed you joyfully when you came home from your duties at the palace? Where is she who received relatives so graciously? She who, to put it briefly, arranged this and that and everything, and [?], managing and keeping the house, all the household affairs, and everything that concerned others, both kin and guests. All of it is gone and lost, and we are left as in a desert, robbed of all the good things we had. Such and so great is the suffering of your honoured soul, my lord, and no consolation from men is enough to soothe your inflamed heart, but only that from God, who comforts the humble of heart by restoring good thoughts.

That blessed woman, for blessed she is, since she held a firm faith in God and lived a chaste life (of this there are many signs, some of which we too have been granted to share), at the last, tested like gold in the fire by a long and grievous illness, flew away from this world. So let this be enough consolation for us: that you have sent such a wife on to God, and that she has left us her own life as an example of the finest way of living. And besides, since you yourself are educated in divine things, you ought not to be so overwhelmed by what has happened. For you know that, since we have come into being by God's good pleasure, our departure is always yoked to our birth. No man is immortal, and no marriage is never parted. Let us look back, if you will, at those from Adam to the present day, and we shall find one generation succeeding another, coming down for as long as this world stands. Where are your parents, my lord, and those who begot them? Going backwards, you will find nothing else in human affairs but flowing and ebbing away. What, then, is called for now? That we come back to ourselves, and perform the fitting funeral rites for her of ever-blessed memory. We humble ones also prayed for her not a little, though, as sinners, we were not heard,

that she might remain in this life. And let us settle the children's affairs well, and prepare our own departure in advance, living our life in a manner worthy of God, so that when we pass from here, whenever providence allows, we may find our good wife there, rejoicing with us through endless ages as we share in the ineffable good things. Even if these words do very little to console, they do show our love for you. And may your Love be granted to us cheerful and readily comforted, by entrusting everything to God.

187 (81). To Leo the sakellarios. [758]
