We are not permitted to keep silent while we enjoy the benefactions of your most great and longed-for Eminence, yet we cannot respond as they deserve, for we lack fitting words. If your God-beloved soul does not see it so, that is no wonder. For love, it says, keeps no account of evil. Indeed, it has long been your habit to look on us in friendship and to honour us, worthless as we are, freely; and, as they say, you cannot even rank one above another[?]. But these, as has been said, are the tokens of holy affection. You yourself, all-praised one, seem to be set like a citadel in the queen of cities, or, to put it more truly, like a spacious harbour, a rest for the afflicted, an ample comfort for those who thirst for a well-tuned word. Every day, so to speak, you receive and heal, tend and care for these and those, great and small, priests and high priests, those of full rank and those of lower. How magnificent is your divine dignity, and your God-beloved office[?]! The words of famous Job also suit you: "I was a father to the orphans and a foot to the lame," "my door was open to every man," and what follows. You are the remnant of piety; you are the treasure of orthodoxy. My letter passes over much, lest it seem to speak for favour and to make what is said to your face sound like flattery. Yet, adding one word, it will stop: [?] your one consolation, your only son, who loves his father, and for the queen city, your noble and renowned leadership.

188 (82). To the wife of Flavian the spatharius. [759]

The dreadful news of what has befallen your son of ever-blessed memory has reached even our humility. Just as those whose ears have been struck by thunder cower in utter terror, so the report has left us completely at a loss, unable to say anything worthy of the grief. Oh, what has happened so suddenly? How has a wonderful man departed, at the very [?] age of life? How tall he was! How handsome in face! How noble in

blood! How glorious in renown! How he, left alone, was a consolation to his blessed[?] mother, a support to his father's house, an ornament to his family; I might add, a rare sight even in the imperial courts. While administering the emperor's affairs in a foreign land, he flew away, leaving behind his renowned mother, and leaving too his illustrious wife with their noble young children, a splendid household, a famous lineage, a wealthy estate, capable servants, loyal attendants, this and that, everything together, so that my words need not chop them up one by one. Then he came back home from abroad, a pitiful burden, a grim sight for the queen city and for his admirable household. O surpassing calamity! The very walls of the city would groan, not to mention the magistrates and his peers. The emperors themselves would groan, having lost so admired a scion. Perhaps even the common crowd of the city would weep, and the whole family would rightly be in mourning. If this is so, who could tell the tragedy of your suffering, my lady? Who that of his wife? Who that of his sister? Who that of the servants? Not even the streams of the rivers, turned into tears, would be enough to serve you in your lament. And the air? Has it not changed before your eyes? And has the sun not failed to rise, now that you have lost the sun of your household? These things, and others like them, grief prompts us to lament.

But since our words are addressed to a woman long educated in divine things, who shows her own life as a whole lesson in virtue, as almost every ear and eye bears witness, there is no need for much reminding: you have the remedies of consolation at home. You have taken many sacred books into your hands; you have read through many writings of the Fathers. Night and day you devote yourself to prayer, and persevere in all-night supplications, that is, in psalms and hymns by night and by day. From this come your self-control and your subduing of the body; your generosity to the needy and your care for priests and monks; and the many other ways of piety for which you are praised and celebrated. From your own resources, then, and from yourself, you are well able to sing to your soul what is fitting. And not only to yourself, but also to your daughter-in-law, to your daughter, and to all your household, which is like Abraham's, as a common teacher and an example of virtue, as one who has long stored up the divine sayings and is able to give each one their measure of grain in due season.

Remember, noble lady, wonderful among women, that what has happened is nothing strange or unexpected. Look back at those from Adam to this day, enter into the deep judgments of God, and see that "man is like grass; his days pass by like shadows." Since our forefather became mortal through sin, his offspring too is mortal, coming in succession down to this day. Yet since Christ came, death is no longer death, but the beginning of a rebirth into immortality. A pious and orthodox son,

who loved monks and loved the good, you both bore and have sent on ahead. Let this be enough consolation for you and a cause for thanksgiving. We urge you, comforted by God and wise in all things: be here too, as in everything else, an example of greatness of soul. Give your most beautiful son a fine funeral gift: as one who longs for him with all her soul, offer to God the portion that belongs to him. Perhaps this is why God has kept you as the last of those who went before, so that, having arranged everything in a manner worthy of God, you might depart from here as you pray to, and inherit eternal life with them. Our brother the most God-beloved archbishop joins us in saying these things, most honoured lady.

189 (85). To Pantoleon the logothete. [761]

We know that freedom of speech is liable to blame, and we also know that the times call for restraint on our part. Nevertheless, the surpassing and indescribable goodwill you show to us humble ones has compelled us to be rather bold in this little letter too. For it is truly bold not only to report our own affairs but also to make requests on behalf of others. Yet, as has been said, your great kindness and twofold piety have given us courage to dare. What, then, is our request? It concerns Theodotus the protospatharius. Your unsurpassed Eminence surely knows what distress he is in because of the steward of the Church who sailed with him to the West. Who else could be found to help the man? Who could see what is needed more wisely than your magnanimity? Who has readier access to the sovereign than your loyal presence? Give to the one in need the mercy you have received from God, my lord, greatly longed for. We fall down at your honoured feet. Your counsel is like the counsel of an angel; your voice is like a flashing thunderbolt, both in the brilliance of its frankness and in the splendour of its love. If your suppliant is found worthy to share in it, he will surely be out of reach of the accusing darts of his adversary, which, as you know, lofty-minded one, come in various forms. And we humble ones will offer you many thanksgivings and prayers for the health of you both, a truly fine and admirable couple. And perhaps this God-given gift, the goodwill supplied by the Lord for the salvation of the souls and bodies of you both, my much-longed-for and most auspicious pair, will not be less precious to you than the gifts of those who offer gold.

190 (84). To Theophanes the monk. [?]

If a letter from us lowly ones is dear to you, [Patrologia Graeca 99.]

Please accept this too, my thrice-beloved. As you kindly say, it has nothing elegant or eloquent about it, but it is at least, and quite undeniably, a token of love. The more letters are exchanged, the more the bond of love grows, and what could matter more than that? But let this rest here for now; the letter must move on to what comes next. What is this novelty now introduced in your parts, and who are these newly appeared dragons who, like Charybdis, swallow down souls not grounded in the word of truth? You yourself did not make it plain [?]. But even before your letter told us, we groaned deeply over a heretic, or rather a man who truly blasphemes against God, who has obtained from the ruling power the right to serve as high priest [?] in your parts. We said then that ruin had already overtaken renowned Sicily. This calamity was not devised through any experience in doctrine, for the little mannikin has none; it sprang from an impious mind and, to put it more truly, was trained in impiety from his father's house, together with two others of his blood. But the Trinity, I know, will strike these men down through the inspired mouths of you and of those here who fight for the truth. Do not let the heresy that still rages strike you, or anyone like you, as strange. The evil has not yet been worn away. The love of God in the faithful has not yet been tested enough. And third, we are not able to enter into the abyss of God's judgments, by whose ways he still allows his people to be tossed by the surge of unbelief. Still, the conclusion of the matter is this: "that those who are approved may be made manifest," as Paul, the steward of wisdom, has said. So we urge and implore you not to lose heart but to refute the opponents. Bring out the divine teachings from the hidden storerooms of your heart, and show plainly from them that Christ is not Christ unless he is circumscribed in a form like ours. If he became flesh, then as flesh he is certainly circumscribed. What is not circumscribed is not within humanity but plainly outside both place and time: God alone, spoken of and conceived in his incomprehensibility and boundlessness. This conclusion is compelled by natural consequence as firm and undeniable proof of the truth: Christ is circumscribed, even when he is venerated in the icon. "For in it the archetype is shown forth," as Dionysius, the revealer of God, says somewhere; and elsewhere: "Each is in the other, apart from the difference of essence." So whoever refuses to let Christ be depicted has denied that he became man. Whoever does not venerate his icon does not venerate him at all, even if he thinks he does, since the sacred word says: "The unbelieving profess to know God, but deny him by their deeds." I have pointed this out to your honor not as to one who did not know it, but as to one who shares my mind. I have drawn up only a drop, so to speak, from an ocean of doctrines; for beyond this there is an endless swarm of patristic testimonies, along with the ancient historical record from the very [?]

beginning of the preaching, in support of the blameless faith of us Christians.

185 (85). — To Philotheos, founder. [?]

Your honor counts it a great gain, you say, to receive our letters and to be remembered by us. But that is praise of your own godly mind and its deep humility, not of us, who are lowly [cod. Reg.: worthless] and worth no account. Even so, your honor will receive a reward that matches its trust, from the just judgment of our good God, who repays each person's faith with heavenly rewards and, as Christ taught, counts what is done to one's neighbor as done to himself. For our part, we truly rejoice to have come to know so great a man as a friend. Your virtue rings out, your praise is entirely deserved, and your way of life is set before many in this present generation who wish to live piously, as an example placed on a mountain lookout of virtues. You have truly shone forth as a lover of God, true to your name Philotheos, since for love of God you chose the untroubled and quiet life, keeping the divine commandments and attaining the eternal goods. In appearance you were worthy of imperial rule, and by birth your blood is most illustrious. Yet divine longing quenched all these things and showed them to be nothing, as indeed they are. It lifted the eyes of your mind to the more-than-luminous radiance of divine beauty, so that you might look there, picture things there, and move your citizenship there, where joy is unspeakable, where life is undefiled [cod. Reg.: unending], where the blessed and sovereign Trinity shines forth. Wonderful man, so longed for by us, may your virtue increase more and more, and your treasure of good works with it, so that like a great merchant you may set sail from here to share in the things that are eternal. So much for greetings. Since you asked again about the presbyter, and pointed to his unconfessed offense, we say this: the canon does not allow a presbyter even to feast at the wedding of someone marrying a second time. How much less may he crown such a person? The crown is placed on one who has conquered incontinence and kept the glory of virginity safe. One who marries a second time is not only unworthy to be crowned but is also subject to canonical penances. How then was he not afraid to crown those who lie under the canons on second marriage? Forgive me, but even if there were no other charge, we do not permit him to celebrate the liturgy at all. I know of nothing else, except perhaps that by way of economy he might give you communion from the holy gifts consecrated by a presbyter who has remained sound. As for the reader who came back after being put under penance, it is right that he not read the Apostle until a synod meets. A presbyter under penance is barred from the liturgy, a deacon from his diaconal service, and a reader from

reading. This is what we think and prescribe. [?] But let your piety act as it sees fit.

186 (86). — To Irene, patrician. [?]

My most honored lady, it is a token of your good trust that you greeted us lowly ones through our beloved brother, the lord Peter, your kinsman. Through him we return your greeting as we ought, praising your piety and your zeal for what is good. We know this of ourselves, and the brother often tells us so too. We also know that for the love of God you hold him in honor, as befits the virtue in you and the man's way of life. You asked about the monastery called "the Lions": should it be made a men's monastery? You lean toward transforming what was formerly called a women's monastery and functioned as one. Our answer is this. If you were only now beginning to consecrate the place, you could do whatever you choose. But it was consecrated long ago, through your daughter of blessed memory, who died there as abbess after governing it for a considerable time with a company of virgins. It is true that the sisterhood there was moved away because of the earlier civil war, and that the abbess herself lies here in holy tombs, together with other souls of the same rank who went before her. Even so, my lady, I do not think it lawful for you to make a change, especially since the dedicated [?] sisters, the children of the former abbess, choose to serve God there, where their abbess lies. The word of the Apostle is: "Let each one remain in that in which he was called." The monastery was called a women's house; what reason is there to change it and give it a men's name? Besides, no men are actually seen there, and the sisters who were driven out will not rest until they live there again. It is true that changes have often been made in some monasteries, but those came about through persecution, unholy seizure and unlawful authority. Those who have right faith and a life that does not contradict it should speak and act lawfully and in keeping with the canons. Therefore,

if you do not act this way, the affair will never come to rest, once it has been moved from what is proper to what is against nature. And we would not escape ridicule, nor, I would add, the fault of condemnation.

187 (87). — To Eudokimos, spatharios. [772]

We have been slow to reply to your honor, so slow that we have almost lost the force of what you wrote. The reason is that no trustworthy letter-carrier was at hand. Now that we have had to send the steward of our monastery to your parts, it is fitting that we make up what was lacking. Let me say first that we are not able to doctor a grieving soul worn down by many sufferings. Still, we must try to find a cure in the divinely inspired Scriptures. What then does the greatest steward of these say? "Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in everything." If we are commanded to rejoice, give thanks and pray at every time, in every matter and without ceasing, then no stretch of time, not even the briefest, should pass in which the true Christian is not established [?] in rejoicing and giving thanks. Are present things, then, any longer a source of affliction, however crushing the misfortune they bring? I have not said this as though your good soul did not know it, but as a reminder, since a soul in distress sometimes lacks the strength to rise to the heights of contemplation. My second point is this. The authorities may have stripped you of much of what you owned, but they could in no way rob you of your more precious possession. Do you not see, and give thanks for, the knowledge God has stored up in you, and the gift of speech he has given you? From it, as from the hidden treasuries of the heart, you bring out words and thoughts as freely as can be. This is the most excellent thing of all, more valuable than all money and of more substance than any estate. Anyone with sense would prefer the man who has it to the very rich, even if he is dressed in nothing but rags. The whole choir of the righteous has shown this, and among outside figures so did Odysseus, who was seen naked after his shipwreck by the princess. But we must turn now to your question. Although you know of yourself what is right, you like to ask and be taught by us unlearned folk. You say that at times a thought urges you to pray, and at times it holds you back, on the grounds that God knows what we want to ask [cod. Reg.: to be asking], so that praying would be superfluous. You add that since you are a sinner, prayer does you no good [cod. Reg.: is of no benefit]. There may have been other things in your letter, but I did not have it at hand. What, then, is to be said to this? That

this way of thinking implies chance and fate and, in short, does away with free will. We, who are sensible and have been enriched with the glory [cod. Reg.: knowledge] of God, must not lean on such an opinion. As for the second problem, be assured that God hears even sinners who practice true repentance. If, as the sacred Scriptures say, he rejoices over those who repent, how could he not also listen to their prayers? The first problem must be met in this way: divine foreknowledge does not abolish free will. We do not do what we do because he foreknows it; he foreknows it because we are going to do it. This keeps both the definition of foreknowledge and the principle of free will intact. In matters that are not up to us, God's determination comes first, as to time, place and manner. In matters that are up to us, where free will operates, God's foreknowledge follows, so to speak, in both virtue and vice. So we must love and pray for what is better, so that God may follow upon us accordingly, and not the opposite. For he will follow us in opposite ways: in the one case punishing and chastising, in the other crowning us and granting us the kingdom of heaven.

188 (88). — To John the grammarian. [776]

I had fallen into a conversation about the venerable icons, and our Plato was there taking part. He said that your learned self had long ago received a letter of mine on that same subject and had been puzzled by it, as if its doctrine were not clearly stated, or might even lead the reader away from the truth. If the one who threw this dart had been just anyone, I would not have troubled myself quickly about it, knowing that I must put up with the darts of envy and the criticisms of the ignorant. But since the objection comes from a friend, and a very wise one, I thought it necessary to set the letter itself before you. I have examined it as well as I can, and I send it to your friendship, either to free you from your difficulty or to be corrected by your sharp mind. For the critic, in his turn, must set out his own view against the opinion he has found fault with. Here is the letter.

"Theodore to Athanasius. You ask how it can be that the icon of Christ is not worshipped with latreia, while Christ, who is venerated in it, is, given that there is one veneration for both. The answer is that the veneration of Christ himself is latreutic worship, for in venerating him I co-venerate the Father and the Holy Spirit, and this is the veneration and worship of the Trinity together. The veneration given to the icon is the same (how could it not be? For those whose might is one and whose glory is one clearly have one reverence and one veneration). Yet it is relative, that is, homonymous. For in venerating the icon I did not co-venerate; I venerated Christ, not divided

by hypostasis but differing in the principle of essence. This veneration is relative, not latreutic, even though it is the same veneration. In the first case it is understood and named as Trinitarian, that is, natural; in the second, the other way round, as relative, that is, hypostatic. If you were to call it latreutic, you would be implying that the Father and the Spirit became incarnate as the Son did, which is absurd. So when I venerate the icon of Christ, I do not venerate the Godhead, as some say, since that term signifies the Trinity, and the Trinity did not become incarnate. Perish the thought! What then? I venerate Christ himself, relatively. For he alone is God the Word made flesh. And in venerating Christ himself, I have clearly co-venerated the Father and the Spirit as well. So veneration through the icon may rightly be understood and called relative, while veneration of Christ himself is latreutic, because the Father and the Spirit are understood and venerated together with him."

Now, my good friend, this reasoning seems to me sound. In the case of the blessed and adorable Trinity the preposition "with" is used. "With" points to the distinction of the hypostases and so presents their natural unity, as all Christians sing in the Creed. But in the veneration of Christ and of his icon the preposition "with" has no place. If it were used, it would logically split the one hypostasis into two hypostases [cod. Reg.: according to the account given] and lead us into the impiety of worshipping a creature. So it was reasonable to use the pronoun "himself" instead, which keeps the hypostasis single in both cases and sets apart the otherness of the natures. As the all-wise Dionysius says, "Each is in the other, apart from the difference of essence." By speaking of a difference of essence, he indicated through "each in the other" an identity of hypostasis, and relative veneration is understood in that sense. For relation, as they say, belongs to the category of relatives: relatives exist together and correspond to one another, as archetype does to icon. Neither could exist without the other being present, as the philosophers also teach about things that exist together. The letter adds "that is, homonymous," and this word carries the same meaning. For a name is the name of something named, so here too we are speaking of relatives. Philosophy [cod. Reg.: the philosophical definition] teaches us that homonyms are things that share only a name, while the account of essence that goes with the name differs: for example, Christ himself and Christ depicted. And since "hypostatic" is also added, this is expressly confessed [cod. Reg.: demonstrated]: there is no hypostasis in his icon other than Christ's. It is Christ's very hypostasis, that is, his character, shown forth in the form of his shape, that is in the icon and is venerated. To those who think soundly, the whole argument stands firm. To make it more convincing, I thought it necessary to attach three patristic testimonies to the letter, which are as follows [?]:

"When imperial portraits and images are brought into a city, the magistrates and people go out to meet them with acclamations. They are not honoring a board or a painting done in poured wax, but the image of the emperor. In the same way creation does not honor the earthly form, but reveres the heavenly image."

From the synod at Antioch under the patriarch Theodoret: "Not as another in form, but as himself the one Lord existing in one form. As such he is by nature the one character of the Father's hypostasis: before the flesh he was one and bodiless, in the flesh he is one, and in the icon he himself is one. He is not divided into two characters or split into two glories, but gathered into one." And after other things: "But just as he himself is one from two opposites and is gathered into one person, so too his icon is one and belongs to the same one Christ. We will not say that the character that appeared to us in the flesh is one thing, and the character shaped in the icon in the form of his appearance another; they are one and the same. For the character is not spoken of as a body but as something bodiless. This will be made still clearer by the divine Chrysostom, who calls the character heavenly, since the only-begotten God came down from heaven, not as a body but as bodiless, became flesh, and appeared clothed in our body." And shortly after: "Therefore, since the icon shows the character by reference to it, we venerate Christ himself, and not the matter skillfully shaped in the icon."

From the synod at Nicaea, the ninth [?]: "And whoever venerates the icon venerates in it the hypostasis of the one depicted."

189 (89). — To Eudokia, wife of a candidatus. [?]

Brother Silvanus has told me that your honor is distressed because fear and alarm come upon your soul for no reason at all. Lowly as I am, I was not unmoved when I heard it. I was grieved, and I prayed, unworthy as I am to be heard by God, that this fear might be lifted from you. And still the lord archbishop, the brothers and I are praying together that this affliction may be dashed away from your piety. This is a strange affliction, my lady, and easy to despise. You should not think of it as able to harm you in any way. You have put on Christ, and you have his cross as your weapon. When you sign yourself with it, believe that it at once drives away every

trick of the demons, whether by day or by night you happen to be alarmed. So sing to the Lord: "From fear of the enemy deliver my soul." And again: "I will not be afraid of the terror by night, of the arrow that flies by day, of the thing that walks in darkness, of mishap and the noonday demon." And: "If God is for you, who is against you?" It is his body you eat and his blood you drink, and through them we tread on serpents and scorpions and on all the power of the enemy. So do not give way or lose heart in this pointless fear, but take courage in the Lord. We remind you, too, to pray, as you are accustomed to do, night and day if you can, and to read a little. Then the peace of God will guard you and keep you unharmed in all things.

190 (90). — To Euphrosyne, abbess. [?]

I have learned from someone well informed that your honor has been touched by grief because one sister wants to cut herself off from your holy community. Your grief is not unreasonable. How could a soul not feel pain when one of its own members is being cut off? Still, such things happen through the malice of the one who lies in wait among the sons of disobedience. We must bear it patiently and show every care, as far as true reason allows, so that we may be innocent of the blood of such a person, whether the one in question is called a brother or a sister. You asked whether your honor would be blameless in releasing the sister who is determined to break away from you. How is it that you, wise and prudent as you are, do not see [?] of yourself that a separation made willfully is not without danger either for [the teacher?] or for the one taught? For why, and on what reasonable grounds, would she do it? If the disciple were mature and fully equipped to lead other sisters, and a sisterhood were already asking for her, that would be economy, as St Basil says, not separation. Far from it! For it is by being governed well that one rises to govern lawfully. From this arises a good zeal in those who share the same way of life to press on to perfection and to do likewise in a manner worthy of God. For our Lord and God, showing the chief of the apostles what proves love for him, said, "If you love me, feed my lambs," and again, "Shepherd my sheep." So whoever has gone forth to shepherd with such a purpose would be blessed, since he imitates Christ, the true and first chief shepherd. Our Fathers also recognized another kind of economy: when a difficult soul, after much and long care, chooses to move to another sisterhood, in the hope of being useful there, like trees transplanted from one place to another. If then this too

[?] ...you would do. This has some justification, namely when both parties, the one who gives and the one who receives, act together with each other, so that the apostolic command is fulfilled: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.” But the word of truth allows no other kind of separation. First, because it tears apart the covenant of the Holy Spirit that was confessed before God and men at the monastic profession. What could be more ruinous than that? The Lord’s saying fits here too: “What God has joined together, let no one separate.” If separation is forbidden there, even though the union is of the flesh, how much more in a spiritual union? Unless, perhaps, divine things are a game. But away with that! The word of the mystery is faithful, both for the forgiveness of sins and for the indissoluble bond of union. Second, how will the sisterhood she breaks away from be built up, if a nun released from her abbess is answerable to no one? Will it not instead be driven into division, cut apart by the same zeal: now this nun, next another, and soon after yet another? In this way the whole body of Christ will be gone and utterly destroyed. And the one who brings about this whole evil, having set off from the first starting line, is heir of the “woe,” as St Basil cries out. For neither your monastery nor any other that acts this way will have stability or footing. So “let the disobedient disobey, and the lawless act lawlessly,” as it is written. But as for you, save your own soul. Do not abandon the laws of God, but stand firmly on the teachings of the saints, first among whom in these matters is the great Basil, even if you end up living with only two or three virgins. For “where two or three are gathered in my name,” says the Lord, “there am I in the midst of them.” But he is not with lawbreakers, even if there are ten thousand of them.

Letter 91. To Dorotheus, his son. [?] Beloved son, I have learned, from the letter you have just written among other things, of your faithfulness and love toward us the lowly. This is a mark of true submission, even though we are sinners and of no account. May you be kept in it from now on, pleasing the Lord and shining with virtue in your brotherhood, and among many others as well. For it is not in the nature of the good to stay hidden. Even when it seems to go unnoticed, it makes its doer plain to see, so that he is called a city of God, as it is written. But enough of this. As for the matter you raised, that of commemorating a certain person, you ought to see for yourself the following. Suppose that at his death, having previously been in communion with the heresy out of human fear, he confessed it, as though rebuked by

someone, and so flew back to the Orthodox communion and departed this life in it. Then he may be ranked among the commemorations of the Orthodox, because our good God, out of his great love for mankind, receives the repentant at the very last hour and judges him by what he is here. So if this is what happened, you should not refuse to offer liturgies to God for him. But suppose none of this happened. Suppose he was in communion with the heresy and did not manage to partake of the Body and Blood of the Lord, for that bread is heretical and not the Body of Christ. Then one must not dare to speak of holding a synaxis for him, for divine things are not toys. Otherwise whoever makes the request for such a person may hear: “You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly.” I have nothing else to say, as far as I know the truth. For light has no fellowship with darkness, and a person who is not in communion with Orthodoxy will not be ranked in the portion of the Orthodox, even at the last hour. For where he is found, there he will also be judged, and he will be numbered with whatever provision he took with him for eternal life. For the rest, pray for me. The lord archbishop greets you, and so do your brothers. I greet the brothers with you as my children, and also the lady Thecla as my daughter in Christ.

Letter 92. To Abolius and John, monks. I received a greeting from you, holy ones, through Isaiah, the most God-beloved bishop and spiritual father. He not only taught me who you are, a holy and fatherly pair, but also urged me to write you this poor letter. We are lowly and sinners, yet we wish to kindle you to love, and nothing is more precious than love. Besides, we are fulfilling an obligation of obedience, and so we have set ourselves to writing. Indeed, we thank God that you too, holy fathers, stayed unshaken in the earthquake of the iconoclast heresy. You were not caught in its soul-destroying communion. Instead, by fleeing from persecution you received the thrice-blessed [cod. Reg.: God-blessed] crown. It is truly worthy of your virtue, and it makes plain the ascetic struggles you had already accomplished. For by what has already happened, everyone gives proof of his former life, whether it was good or otherwise. You who were already clothed in holiness have also put on the confession of Christ, and so have become beautiful on both sides. For the confession of Christ, fathers, is the defence of his holy icon. Conversely, whoever denies the icon rejects Christ. For, as the great Basil says, the honour paid to the image passes over [cod. Reg.: goes up] to the prototype, and each is both seen and venerated in the other. This holds even if Leo, who bears a beast’s name, the servant of Satan,

To the most God-beloved and most pious emperors, Augusti and autocrats by God’s grant: an apology and address from those scattered here and there.

All who share in reason know why God, the King of all, gave the reality and the name of earthly kingship to human nature. He did so in order that earthly things, imitating heavenly ones, might also possess peace and freedom from strife, and so offer him glorification and worship in harmony. Your Christ-imitating majesty, which received the reins of this kingship by God’s judgement, has fittingly summoned us, the least of men, to enter into discussion about the faith with those opposed to us. In this way it may learn which side upholds the truth and award that side the victory, so that there may be no schisms among us and all may think the same thing in an orthodox way. For this we praised your love of learning in matters of faith, and we praised still more the peace-loving disposition of your will, which so earnestly desires to establish its subjects in what is beneficial and saving. May this bring you a reward: ineffable splendour in exchange for splendour, and an unending kingdom in exchange for a kingdom. But, most mighty and most God-loving masters, this great and long-prayed-for achievement cannot come about simply and without toil. With the greatest undertakings, the greatest hardships also appear. What do we mean? First, those who oppose us have long been confirmed in their own opinions, and confirmed by synods, while we are forbidden by apostolic and [?patristic] precept to join in discussion about the faith with those who are held in this way. Second, judgement in this matter belongs to no one other than those alone who have received the authority from the Lord through the Spirit. You are to assist them and add your seal to theirs,

you who have been called by God primarily for this purpose. But it is necessary to set out what the sound and blameless mind of our most Christian religion is. We believe in one God, who is worshipped and glorified together in Father, Son and Holy Spirit, the much-hymned, all-working and sovereign Trinity, in accordance with the divinely inspired Creed handed down to us by the 318 holy Fathers. By that Creed every heresy has been beaten back, and on it every holy council depends, like branches from a root or rivers from a spring. From it the second council clearly set forth the title “Lord” for the Spirit. Next the third proclaimed holy Mary to be Theotokos, as the one who gave birth to the only-begotten Son of God himself. Then the fourth defined our Lord Jesus Christ as from two natures and in two natures, in a single hypostasis. Next the fifth, confirming the one before it, anathematized Origen and the Pre-existentialists who followed him. Then the sixth, consistently with the two natures, taught that there are two wills and two energies in the one Christ. Later still the seventh, following those before it, proclaimed that all the natural properties in the one Christ are twofold, and that the same Christ is uncircumscribable in respect of what is invisible and circumscribable in respect of what is seen. It holds this truth firmly established in four ways: from doctrine based on nature, from citations of the Fathers, from conciliar pronouncements, and from ancient custom.

Take first the argument from nature. The evangelist John shows it, for instance, when he says: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” If, then, the Word became flesh, it is clear that as Word he is uncircumscribable, but as flesh he is circumscribed. “And dwelt among us”: the one who dwells is one thing and the dwelling another. In one respect he may be circumscribed, and in another he is beyond circumscription. Otherwise, by what signs will it be recognized that he became man, unless he naturally possesses the property of being depicted? This is the first property of a man who has a form, and if it is taken away, the man is gone. Yet he is truly man. Therefore he who as God is uncircumscribable is also circumscribed as man. For this reason he was called mediator between God and men, as one who joins both extremes in himself, is both, and possesses in one hypostasis, without any lack, the properties of both natures from which he was composed. From the [?Father] he has, along with everything else, uncircumscribability, since he said, “All that is mine is yours, and all that is yours is mine.” From his Mother he has, along with everything else, circumscribability, since it is written: “For surely it is not angels that he takes hold of, but he takes hold of the seed of Abraham. Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect.” So if one property is taken away from either nature, all the properties that belong with it are necessarily taken away too. [Note: John 1[?]]

And when the properties are taken away, their natures are clearly taken away with them. The holy martyr Justin bears witness to this argument when he says somewhere: “For nothing that exists remains what it is if even one single thing that naturally belongs to it is lacking.” And so, under this new theory, the contents of our faith have vanished. In agreement with the evangelist, the Apostle also says: “Who, being in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.” If, then, being in the form of God, he took the form of a servant, it follows beyond dispute that insofar as he is in the form of God, he is not depicted, because the divine is beyond comprehension. But insofar as he took the form of a servant, he is depicted, because the servile form is bounded by being perceived through touch and colour [?]. For how will anyone believe that he came in the likeness of men, unless it is his nature to be depicted as men are? And how will he be said to have been found in appearance as a man, unless he is seen drawn in human shape? Do you see, most serene ones, how, since he had to be made like his brothers in every respect, and shared flesh and blood just as they do, he must necessarily be capable of being depicted just as they are? Otherwise he was not made like them, the one who declared it spoke falsely, and the nature has been altered. Indeed, God the Word himself says somewhere: “Why do you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth that I heard from God?” One who was not depicted would never call himself a man. Nor could one whose nature allows him to be killed fail to have a nature that allows him to be depicted, for each of these implies and confirms the other. This is he who was “put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit,” as blessed Peter has said. What else would this mean than that he is depicted in the flesh and [not?] depicted in the spirit? This is he who said: “And whoever eats me will also live because of me.” One who is not circumscribed would not say that he is eaten, unless he were some kind of phantom. If we were to accept that, we would fall into the mindset of the Manichaeans and discard the great mystery of godliness. For Mani says that the Son revealed [cod. Reg.: had revealed] his own essence on the mountain in what was visible and invisible, not as having two natures but one. So those who insist that Christ is not circumscribed, holding as they do to one nature, stand convicted of falling into the same mindset. For what is uncircumscribable is also incorporeal. Nor, on the other hand, is the one person of Christ split into a pair of persons by being circumscribed, as some suppose. For the nature of image and prototype cannot be divided in hypostasis; it has its difference in the principle of essence. As the all-wise Dionysius says: “Each is in the other, apart from the difference of essence.”

Take the life-giving cross as well. No one would say that the image in the shape of the cross is anything other than its prototype, except that it differs from it in natural principle. The example is close at hand, and the truth is indisputable. This, then, is the first of the ways we mentioned.

What is the second? The sayings of the saints, which declare, not by reasoning but plainly, that our Lord Jesus Christ is depicted. If we wanted to set them all down here, we would go beyond the proper length of an address. But we will pick out two or three from many, the more important ones, and through these we will vouch for the rest as well, so that here too what is written is fulfilled: “On the testimony of two or three witnesses every word shall be established.”

The saying of Peter, the chief of the apostles, recorded in the history of the holy martyr Pancratius: “Bring out the icon of our Lord Jesus Christ and set it up on the little tower, so that the people may see what form the Son of God took. Then, seeing it, they may believe all the more, as they look at the likeness of his form, and may be reminded of what we have preached to them.” How awe-inspiring this saying is! It all but cries out: Bring out the image of him whose virtue covered the heavens, and set it up on high, as it were, as a plain testimony, so that the people may see what form the Son of God took. It was not the form of an angel, nor of an archangel, nor of any other power, but our own servile form. “Then, seeing it, they may believe all the more”: as if the account given in words were not enough, but the working of sight were also needed to give fuller assurance that the Son of God became the Son of Man. “And may be reminded of what we have preached to them”: this is like saying, “This is your memorial from generation to generation.” The history also notes that the other apostles did the same in towns and villages. They adorned places with the whole history of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, from the beginning, when the angel cried “Hail” to the Virgin, until he was taken up. And they urged, it says, that these be honoured with fear. Do you see, most humane ones [cod. Reg.: most God-loving], that the apostles handed down from the beginning not only the setting up of the holy icons but also their veneration with fear? For honouring is acknowledged to be the equivalent of venerating.

The saying of Athanasius, who endured many struggles, from the address at Berytus: “Lift up the eyes of your mind and see this new spectacle.” And further on: “Then the Jews took down the icon of our Lord Jesus Christ and said: As our fathers once spat on him, so let us too spit on him. Then they began to spit in the face of the Lord’s icon, and they [?struck] it before the faces of those who had gathered from all sides, that is, the icon

of the Lord, saying: Everything our fathers did to him, let us do to his icon. And they say: They mocked him; let us do the same. So they mocked the icon of the Lord with countless mockeries, which we do not even dare to speak of. Then they say: We have heard that they nailed his hands and feet; let us do this to him too. Then they fixed the hands and feet of the Lord’s icon with nails. Again, in their madness, they say: We have heard that they gave him vinegar and gall to drink on a sponge; let us do this to him too. And they did it, putting the sponge full of vinegar to the mouth of the Lord’s icon. Again they say: We have learned that our fathers struck his head with a reed; let us do the same. And taking a reed, they struck the Master’s head. Finally they say: We learn on good authority that they pierced his side with a spear. Let us leave nothing out, but add this too. And they had a spear brought and ordered one of their number to raise it and strike the side of the Lord’s icon. When this was done, a great quantity of blood and water at once gushed out of it.” The saying is trustworthy, most wise ones [?]. This happened, on the one hand, because signs are for unbelievers, not for those who believe; and on the other, so that we too might know that an insult to the image is an insult to the prototype, just as, conversely, honour paid to the image is honour paid to the prototype.

The saying of the great Basil, from his encomium on the martyr Barlaam: “Let Christ also, the judge of the contests, be painted on the panel.” Here too, most serene ones, the case for restoring the icons is secure. For the God-bearing Father does not mean, as some idly claim, that Christ is written on the tablet of the soul. We do not have Christ written within us; we have him dwelling in our hearts through faith, as the Apostle cries out. Further, by adding the conjunction “also” he pointed back to what comes before, which is this: “Rise up for me now, you illustrious painters of athletic achievements! Magnify with your arts the general’s image that I have cut short. Light up with the colours of your skill the crowned victor whom I have painted too dimly. Let me withdraw, defeated by your painting of the martyr’s exploits. I rejoice to be beaten today by such a victory of your power. Let me see the struggle of the hand against the fire depicted more precisely by you. Let me see the wrestler painted more brilliantly in your image. Let the demons weep now too, struck down by the martyr’s exploits among us; let the hand, burning yet victorious, be shown to them again.” Surely no one would say that these things are written within us. And even if this were granted, he would not have called for the servant first and then the Master. Moreover, right at the beginning he says, “Rise up for me now, you illustrious painters of athletic achievements,”

and he clearly meant the makers of images, not writers of prose. Likewise, in his encomium on the Forty Martyrs, he himself says this: “For the brave deeds of war are often set forth both by prose writers and by painters, the former adorning them with words, the latter engraving them on panels.”

Since, then, the second way has come to its end, what is the third? The saying of the Fathers who met in council at Constantinople after the sixth council: “In some paintings of the venerable icons, a lamb is depicted, pointed out by the finger of the Forerunner. This lamb was adopted as a type of grace, foreshadowing for us through the law the true Lamb, Christ our God. While we embrace the ancient types and shadows that have been handed down to the Church as symbols and foreshadowings of the truth, we give preference to grace and truth, receiving it as the fulfilment of the law. Therefore, so that what is perfect may be set before the eyes of all even in coloured paintings, we decree that from now on the Lamb who takes away the sin of the world, Christ our God, shall be set up in his human form in icons as well, in place of the ancient lamb. Through it we grasp the height of the humility of God the Word, and we are led by the hand to remember his life in the flesh, his passion and saving death, and the redemption that came from them to the world.” Here, together with the icon of Christ, the case for the icons of all the saints is also present. First, the decree that he be set up in icons “as well,” in place of the ancient lamb, shows that he had already been depicted before, and that only this was lacking. Second, it shows that his image is not only to be embraced, in the way the symbols and foreshadowings in the law are said to be embraced, but is also to be venerated, both his and that of any saint whatsoever. For clearly what is revered one would also acknowledge to be worthy of veneration. Further, it shows that every image is called by the same name as its prototype, since it says: “A lamb is depicted, pointed out by the finger of the Forerunner.” In the same way the divine Gregory of Nyssa says somewhere: “Isaac lies before his father, beside the altar itself.”

The saying of the Fathers who met in council at Antioch: “Not as someone different in form, but as himself the one Lord existing in one form. In respect of this form he is by nature the one imprint of the [?Father’s] hypostasis. Before the flesh, when he was bodiless, he was one; in the flesh he is one; and in the image he himself is one. He is not divided into two imprints, nor split into two imprints, nor split into two glories, but gathered into one.” And further on: “But just as he himself is one from two opposites and is gathered into one person, so too his image is one and belongs to the same one Christ. We will not say that the imprint that appeared to us in the flesh is one thing, and the imprint formed in the image, in the appearance of his form, is another. Rather, it is the same one, since neither as body

...the imprint is so called, but insofar as it is incorporeal. This will be made still clearer by the divine Chrysostom, who calls the imprint heavenly, since it is indeed from heaven: not insofar as he was body, but insofar as he was incorporeal, the only-begotten God came down from heaven, became incarnate, and appeared clothed in our body.” And a little further on: “Therefore, since by reference the image shows the imprint itself, it is Christ himself whom we worship, and not the matter skilfully shaped in the image.” Here, then, is a clearer doctrinal explanation. First, there is one form in both, in Christ and in the image. Second, he himself, the imprint of the Father’s hypostasis, is in the image, through the appearance of his form, both displayed and worshipped with undivided glory. There remains the fourth mode of the ancient ordinance [Regius MS: legislation]. Lift your eyes round about, most kindly one, and see the world under heaven. From the apostolic preaching itself onward, everywhere on land and sea, in holy churches, sacred vessels and venerable offerings, it bears Christ depicted, and by these very works it cries aloud that Christ reigns over those on earth, as David sings: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession.” It cries too that “an idol is nothing in the world,” as the Apostle said, and that all things have been filled with blessed light, now that he has come who said, “I have come as light into the world.” For what sights there are to see! Here he is born in a cave and glorified by angels; there he is carried in his Mother’s arms and worshipped by magi. Then he is a boy, seen seated in the midst of the teachers. Then he is baptized by the Forerunner; then he works wonders with the apostles, goes up on the cross, breathes his last, is buried, rises, and ascends into heaven. As we gaze on all these things in images, as the apostles once did with their own eyes, we too may fittingly say: “We beheld his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth.” This, then, is the faith proclaimed from of old. This the holy synods embraced, and with this all the churches everywhere, in every place, agree, in East and West, north and south. We least ones also embrace it, and we pray, and pray earnestly, as is our duty, for your God-loving reign. Letter [?] (94). To Peter of Nicaea. [803] Your holy ears have surely heard of what befell our blessed and common Father, the metropolitan of Synada, and your holy soul has mourned for him as was fitting. You probably have not yet ceased from groaning, nor left off the pain that comes as if from being cut in two. But come, thrice-beloved, let us tell you more clearly, so that

we too may pay the debt we owe, and you, learning his story in fuller detail, may find some relief in the telling. Oh, alas! How can we bear the mournful news without tears? The Father was in good health, doing his usual works of unfeigned love and of welcoming the brothers and Fathers. For who embraced hospitality more than he did, or cared more for those in want? The constant arrival of visitors and their long stays never wore him down. What grieved him was rather their rarity and their quick departure. But why should I illustrate this for you, who know it well? Such, as I said, were his occupations. When the feast day of the Monday after Pentecost came, he rose from the meal and was seized with the pains of a catarrh descending from his head to his spine and the region of his back. At this we humble ones were roused, and we found him truly ill and explaining the causes of the attack. Then we returned home. Coming again the next day, we found him still struck by more violent pains and a burning fever. He was barely able to speak quietly to us, and he hinted that he had given up hope of living in the flesh. What came next? On the third day his tongue was completely bound, and not long after came bitter death. Let it be called bitter for us, because we are deprived of the holy man. For him it was very sweet, because he departed to be with Christ, and what could be more blessed than that? So the blessed man lay there (for it is good to describe this too, as a wondrous sight), venerable in countenance and angelic in form. His soul, gone home to the Lord, had left something like sunlike marks imprinted on the holy body with which, and in which, he had served the Holy Trinity. Suddenly a crowd gathered, monks and laypeople together, a very great one indeed. It poured round the body, gazing at it as at a holy treasure, or rather, to put it more aptly, as at something alive and able to speak. Tears were shed, silently by the more reserved, more loudly by his attendants. So, with the fitting psalmody and the bishops’ invocations, he was committed to the tomb in the place where the blessed man used to minister to the Lord. Thus the Father was added to the Fathers, the confessor to the confessors, the teacher to the teachers, the interpreter of God to the interpreters. We may add these as well: the self-controlled to the self-controlled, the chaste to the lovers of chastity, the hospitable to the hospitable, the modest to the humble-minded. He became all things to all, as far as possible, that he might win all, or as many as he could, building on the achievements of the apostles. And now we humble ones mourn like orphans for one who truly loved his fathers and his brothers. His Church, that is, his little flock, is utterly at a loss and calls out for its shepherd and Father, like nestlings....

Letter 204 (95). To Philotheus, founder. ...whose praise has spread through all Macedonia, among monks and devout laypeople, who have on their tongues the beauty and virtue of your piety. May the Lord grant you to go on doing good, to be rich in good works, generous and ready to share, storing up for yourself a good foundation for the future, so that you may attain eternal life. Most excellent lover of God, hold fast the deposit of the faith exactly [Regius MS: securely], ever shining with godly deeds. But enough of this. Now the matter concerns the priest again, since your honour asks that he be released to celebrate the liturgy. If what you asked were a human matter, all would be well. We would comply with your every request, glad to serve you, who have served us so many times. But since the question concerns God, and involves a transgression of the boundaries set by the divine canons, forgive me, dearest brother: we cannot give a judgment against God and the sacred canons. This is all the more so because in former times we staked our whole life on this very kind of issue, choosing to face dangers, exiles and deaths rather than consent to lawlessness and the undoing of the Gospel of Christ. So we do not release to celebrate either one who has joined an adulterous union or one who has joined a second marriage. For if the holy canon does not allow a priest even to dine at the wedding of someone marrying a second time, it forbids him all the more to crown such a marriage. If others judge otherwise, they will answer for what they do. “For we,” it says, “have no such custom, nor do the churches of God.” So, knowing how perilous this judgment is, do not put pressure on our humility. Every day we are drawn up to face dangers for the word of truth; how then shall we be moved to act against the truth? It is impossible, master, to do or say anything contrary to what has been divinely decided in the canons. But we believe that you too, seeking the one will of God and the salvation of your soul, will agree with what we have said. Rather, you will pray that we hold fast to the divine law and give up nothing whatever in transgression of the commandment of God and of the canon. Letter [?] (96). To Maria, wife of a spatharios. [814] Your honour knows that the Church is a refuge of salvation, and that one who is beset by hardships runs to it as into the hands of God. Even in the Old Testament it was not lawful to seize anyone who had found safety in the cities of refuge. Is it not far more unlawful in the New to drag away from the church those who flee to it? For this is an outrage

against the divine laws and against the divine altar. So let your piety consider how great an act of daring this was. What is the remedy? First, set yourself a rule never again to dare do this, even if everything is turned upside down. Then, for a whole forty days, abstain from the holy gifts. Kneel ten times each day and say fifty times: “Lord, forgive me my sin; Lord, be merciful to me, a sinner.” Say likewise: “Lord, have mercy on me freely.” Recite three psalms as well, namely the 6th, the 37th and the 50th. In this way God will forgive you your sin, my lady. And if you have the means, give forty pieces of silver to the poor. Letter [?] (97). To Irene, abbess. [811] The ways and words of my life fall far short of your praises, most honourable of women. But a faithful soul that seeks the Lord tends to bestow praise on those who have no honour, and so gathers for itself the glory of humility. That is how you have shown yourself to us, sister in the Lord. For we know our own state, and we do not judge ourselves equal even to the least of people today, still less fit to be ranked at so great a height as you have written. But let that rest there. Let us turn to the matter of the priest. Amma, we do not say one thing today and another tomorrow; we always hold to the same position. What is it? A priest caught in communion with the heretics, especially if he also signed, may not celebrate until the time of an Orthodox synod, at which such matters will be examined and decided. The only exception is that, in case of necessity, he may baptize, bury the dead, give the habit [Regius MS: put on the habit] to a monk, bless the water at Theophany, read the Gospel passages, and give communion from holy gifts already consecrated by a priest who has remained sound. And these, as I said, only out of necessity. For if a priest can be found who did not fall into that communion, he may not do even the things just mentioned.

Such, then, is our position. If others think or judge otherwise, whether of equal rank or higher, they are masters of their own authority, since the bishop has issued no definition that all would be bound to accept; and we for our part will keep silent. We urge your honour to hold to strictness in orthodoxy, as you do in good conduct, and to listen to the Apostle when he says: “Let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God.” For you know that no small persecution has been stirred up in the raging [?] down to the present

[?]. And not only that: blood has been shed as well, flesh has been torn, and martyrs have been made. Why even speak of all the sufferings in prisons and dungeons, the exiles, the arrests, the seizures, the chains, the starvation, the solitary confinement, and all the rest? To tell it would take no small history. If, then, this is how things stand, should not the priest have endured the same sufferings, so as to receive the unfading crown of glory? Instead he was caught in the communion and in the signature against Christ, against his Mother, and against all the saints, for this is what the reference through their own images to the prototypes means. How, then, can he not count it a great thing that he lives at all, and that his lawless deed is pardoned at all? He should shrink even from touching the things mentioned above, which are permitted out of kindness, let alone be released altogether to celebrate. Otherwise everything is stale, the martyrdoms are pointless, and the contests of the athletes of faith are in vain. But God forbid! The martyr is a martyr by virtue of this confession, and the one who denied has fallen by virtue of this denial. Everyone who has fallen ought to weep until death, if he would listen to me as a good counsellor. Letter [?] (98). To Theodosia Augusta and her son Basil. [817] We have learned how things stand with you from various trustworthy persons, and above all from our holy Fathers, the most God-loving bishop Isaiah and the most honourable abbot of Medikion. By the good pleasure of our supremely good God you have been changed over to the way and the word of piety and orthodoxy, bidding farewell to your former false belief, since it did not originate from God but from the opposing side. In this your godliness springs from the pious root of your father, for it must be acknowledged that he was such a man, beloved by God and adorned with every nobility. We gave thanks to the Lord, who did not allow you to remain in the darkness of heresy but filled your souls with blessed light, so that you recognize the following. Jesus Christ, the Son of God, came to be in our form out of tender compassion, to save his own creature, which had fallen into corruption. So he was depicted like us, so that none of the human properties might be lacking to him. Yet as God he himself remains uncircumscribed, since he also possesses all the properties of the Father in one person. In this way he has appeared as mediator between God and humankind, sharing in both extremes by standing between them, and through himself making us partakers of the divine nature. Being God and equal to the Father, he cannot fail to be beyond circumscription, for the divine is infinite, unbounded and incomprehensible. In the same way, being truly man and having become like us in all things, he cannot fail to remain within circumscription,

for what of him is touched by touch and seen in colour is graspable [Regius MS: comprehensible]. On this point the Iconoclasts have shown themselves deniers of Christ. They suppose that the embodied one is bodiless, and they teach that he who came to be with us is outside our nature. From this the world was shaken, and Christ was denied through his venerable image, as were [?] and every one of the saints. For in accepting the image one accepts the person depicted, and conversely in rejecting it one rejects him. From this came a blazing persecution, and the godly patriarch was cast out. Priests and hierarchs, monks and most godly laypeople were exiled and imprisoned, others were flogged and starved, and some were even killed. From this, those who prefer nothing in this world to God were driven as fugitives into mountains and caves and the holes of the earth. From this, churches were razed, holy things were profaned, divine offerings were given to the fire, and [?]. Such were the undertakings of impiety, so that the tree may be known by its fruit. But since, as was said before, divine grace has embraced you through the good confession that you made before the Fathers, a confession for which you are eager to stand firm even to the point of blood, we humble ones too, trusting in this confession, have received you, our lady and mistress, and the lord and master, together with the other glorious branches. We count you as belonging to the portion of Orthodoxy, or rather to the Church of God. Since you have come to our humility, we greet you with reverence and share communion with you. We send up thanksgiving to the good God, who does great and unsearchable things without number, who leads from darkness to light, and from the path of error

brings onto the road of piety everyone who desires with a true heart to be saved. So much for that. But the great emperor has given you the island of Chalkites as a place to live, and this grieved not a little, not only us but many of the Fathers too. A whole brotherhood, with its abbot, was driven out of the monastery that had long been its own and is now carried about from place to place. It grieved us also that we seemed to be giving tongues fresh occasion, on top of earlier slanders. Nevertheless, you explained through our spiritual son Clement, the most reverent abbot, that the matter came about in such and such a way by imperial authority, and so we were freed from our grief. But we urge you to make every possible effort to heal the pain of those who had to leave, since it is written: “Give no one occasion to curse you.” And again: “Why,” it says, “should my freedom be judged by another’s conscience?” Letter [?] (99). To Kassia [?], wife of a candidatus. [821] Your honour’s letter has come after a long time, and this one is

full of accusation. In places it humbles itself, and in places it rises up against our nothingness, as if we had accepted the slanders against you simply and without examination, and had moreover uttered rulings without judgment, and on matters of the greatest importance at that. We have grown used to bidding farewell to such things, and we declare only this: we listen to the gossip as to so much child’s play, and we speak not to please people but to please God, who tests our hearts, even though in other respects we are sinners. If Balaam the soothsayer would not bring himself to answer Balak, king of the foreigners, against the will of God, how can we, who hold the rank of the priesthood and will give account on the day of judgment for the answers we give when asked, speak in a way that turns aside from what is right? So that is how we answered those who asked us. We did not ourselves, of our own accord, order this or that to be done, as you were led to say. And what do you want? That we answer like merchants, to please each customer? Or that we rightly divide the word of truth? So do not strike out at us humble ones unseasonably, neither you, nor the lady your sister, nor anyone else who chooses to mock and disparage us. Know instead that we feel no hostility toward the ever-memorable Strategos, but great affection, as also toward his wife. But we grieve, and rightly reproach you, because you, who excel in knowledge and lay claim to piety, did not act toward him with true love at the end. Before all things and above all things you ought to have striven for the salvation of his soul, so that he might partake of the holy gifts, counting everything else as refuse, and so be found in Orthodox communion. For it is written: “Where I find you, there I will judge you.” This is what we think and say. If others think otherwise, they are masters of their own voice, and we keep silent. “The Lord knows those who are his,” and “let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity,” as it is written. Letter [?] (100 [?]). To the nun Hypakoe. [?] Those who have taken up the monastic life have thereby been crucified to the world and have already risen above ties and attachments of the flesh. It is not their nature to be bowed down by the misfortunes that befall their relatives, nor to grieve when these depart this life. But we find that even the saints were bowed down by the suffering of their kin and shed warm tears at their deaths. So we do not think it strange that we too have felt the same, especially over a brother, and a brother outstanding in wisdom and distinction, who held, as it were, a father’s place in caring for you. Truly the suffering is terrible, sister in the Lord,

and the blow struck your heart as if a knife were cutting it. What am I saying? I must uncover my face and speak plainly. My lord your brother, so they tell me, has fallen asleep. A good man is gone. The eye of the family has been put out, and your consolation has flown away. The children he fathered are orphans, and you too are orphaned, with your sisters, with nowhere to rest your faltering hand and no one to look to when troubles press around you. But why should we go on lamenting the loss? We are speaking to a woman dear to God: intelligent, sensible, experienced, full of divine knowledge, able to bring others to self-control by her own example. Bring out from the good treasury of your heart your spiritual wealth, the medicines of consolation, enough for yourself and for your sisters. For we know that their grief is [?] equal to yours, and so is the grief of the lady abbess; indeed of the whole family, and I might add, of the senate itself. Who would not groan over him? Who would not shed tears? Grief over him touched even us humble ones, though we have trained ourselves to bear such things. But we have considered that no one who has come into being fails also to depart from this world, and that this has been so from our forefather Adam until now. So we have thought nothing strange in what has happened. What would be remarkable is for your godly heart to bear it with thanksgiving, and so become a model, together with the lady abbess, your sisters and the whole family. As is your custom, arrange everything courageously and generously, and help your brother's household as far as you can, so that those who lie in wait when people meet misfortune may not overrun it as if it were deserted. Take care as far as possible for the precious soul of that good man as well, for the departed are helped by the living even after death. In short, we know that you manage everything well in every respect, and that your reason commands your despondency and distress rather than being commanded by them. For this very purpose we have sent brother Athanasius, to show how deeply we feel for the man and how much we care for your honour. We pray to receive him back soon as a good messenger of your thankful endurance. 207 (2). — To Olbianus the patrician. [824] George, a God-loving man and most glorious notary, brought us a greeting from your all-praised and renowned Excellency, and asked us to return the greeting in writing, saying that your Blessedness had commanded this. Since we have made up our minds to yield in the duties of friendship, we are writing this letter. First, we lowly ones offer you the greetings that are fitting, welcoming, and more than welcoming, this very fact:

that you are eager to hear the voice of people as wretched and sinful as we are. This is no ordinary sign of piety: that a man of lofty rank bends down to the voice of the humble, especially at the present time, when most people turn away even from their closest friends, to say nothing of the more obscure. Next, we remind you, with all diffidence, to rule and govern your subjects in a way worthy of God. For if every rule and authority is ordained by God, to speak in the apostle's words, then plainly the ruler and the one in authority ought to direct the people under his hand in a godly way. He should give impartial judgments in disputed lawsuits. He should also meet those who come to him with a kindly and peaceful face, and by receiving them accessibly give them the courage to say what they have come to say. For the poor man, it says, cannot withstand a threat. He should also bend down toward the poor and humbled, and discipline them when need requires; yet discipline them not in anger, but calmly, with correction as his aim. He should not use many lashes, for harshness is hateful to God, but should act with discernment, only so far as to check what is undisciplined and bring about correction, as a father does with a child and a physician with a patient. Blessed is the man who leads the people and commands in this way. For Moses, the servant of God, was a ruler, and Joshua the son of Nun was a general. One could name many others, not only among kings but also among judges and rulers, before the law, under the law and after grace, who held office and the highest rank and pleased the Lord by living in piety. In this way, then, we who love our all-praised and longed-for lord ask that you too govern, and so be numbered among these saved and admirable men. Do not take our reminder as presumption, but as a mark of love. We love you as one who loves God, and it is the mark of a friend to say what is profitable to the one he loves, as our poor letter has done. May our good God count us worthy to come at last to speak with you face to face and to enjoy your good qualities, so that what we cannot learn from report, seeing with our own eyes may show us, and make us more active in the bond of friendship. For we have learned from the excellent letter-bearer that your Piety is marked by no small achievements. May the Lord guard it like the apple of his eye, beyond the reach of every [?] assault, and save it for his heavenly kingdom. Your fatherly [?] has now made a fitting address,

not to us humble ones, of course, for we know ourselves and what we are, falling short in virtue even of those assigned to the lowest rank. You have addressed all the divine Fathers and confessors, like a good angel bringing greetings and binding us all together in love. [Or: "and indeed this."] This is just and fitting: that we who are scattered here and there for the word of God and the testimony of his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, should speak to one another by letters and be joined in spirit by what we write, and should in no way be counted as dead because we are silent. For we know that the blessed apostle Paul too, with his fellow apostles sent by God, called to one another from afar, came together through the word that unites, and proclaimed the gospel of the kingdom of God to the whole world. In this work the Holy Spirit has appointed us too, if it is not too bold to say so, and charges us: "Speak," it says, "and do not be silent, for I have many people here." And elsewhere: "If he shrinks back, my soul has no pleasure in him." So silence brings a fearful judgment, and [?] this wilful deafness of the heretics. Your Holiness, acting in a godly way, writes that you suffer many trials from them, since they refuse to let a holy word sound in their ears and deny the divinely painted image of Christ, of the Mother of God and of any of his servants. Remain, then, thrice-longed-for, set on the lampstand of the word by the command of the gospel, and shine on all who are in the house, so that those who open their eyes may receive the light, while those who close their senses reap the fruit of their own blindness. Pray that we too may do this, and may bring back blameless the gift of the charge entrusted to us. We want you to know that one of the lamps has flown away to the Lord: the most holy Metropolitan of Synada. Before him went the renowned brothers and Fathers Athanasius, abbot of Paulopetrion, and John, abbot of Chalkites. The heretics think that the company of those who confess Christ is being cut down. But they do not know that it is multiplied all the more, for even the band that may have lost its feathers flies up again with the zeal of those who have already finished their contest. Christ is still asleep. To some he opens a door by his indescribable goodness; others he tests in their longing so as to crown their endurance; others, like gold that has been tried, he takes to himself one after another into the diadem of the beauty of his glory. So much from us to you, blessed one. May you entreat God to bring peace to his Church, rooting out every evil from its midst, and to count us who remain worthy to meet face to face, as you too expressed in your prayer. [?] (6). — To Dionysius the monk. [826] Those who are treated by skilled physicians

have no need of visits from lesser ones, unless perhaps they pay their respects out of love to those who are true friends. So your brotherly honour would be doing something superfluous if, after being healed by our most God-beloved father, the archbishop of Dyrrachium, you did not rest content with that but still sought treatment from us lesser ones as well. But since the claims of love have now moved you to write, they have also persuaded us worthless ones to write back and to join ourselves to you in a loving disposition. For even without any need, those who have taken up the same profession, and so embrace the same mind, ought to be bound together in love. Indeed, the Lord has said that because lawlessness is multiplied, the love of many will grow cold. As for your treatment, keep it free of relapse, as the most holy archbishop has prescribed. But this we urge and remind you: do not slip back again, and do not let yourself be drawn into that ruinous fall through this or that token. What is past is enough. Over it we ought to groan and lament forever, to weep and wail. For while our brothers who wear the same habit were raised on high like eagles by their confession, we were held fast in the snare of heresy. While they were persecuted, we stayed at home. While they contended as martyrs, we denied with hand and mouth, if not with the heart. While others were imprisoned and starved, we lived in safety. How then can we not take this to heart and lament over it? "How shall I be with Job," says the great Basil, "I who have not received even an ordinary affliction with thanksgiving? And how with each of the saints, I who have not lived in their footsteps?" See, brothers, how terrible the warnings are, and how great the distances.
