"What will it profit a man," it says, "if he gains the whole world but loses his soul?" Is this not the voice of the Lord? Let us fear, then, and tremble. For what is past let us still pray for pardon, and from now on let us walk with straight feet, never tripping, nor limping on both legs, as it is written, but going straight in the commandments of God, [?] the faith [?] fig orchards and whatever belongs to this mortal and perishing life, but the good things of the promises: eternal life, the kingdom of heaven. For the opposite outcome, which follows from opposite deeds, may we not even think or speak of it. Peace to you, brothers in the Lord. Be at peace with one another. Pray for us your brothers. Take comfort.

[?] (5). — To Joseph, abbot of the Kerameis [?]. [828] Even before the good Sergius arrived, we heard of your mourning for the blessed Metropolitan, most honoured brothers. How much we groaned, and I might add, how much we wept, the one who knows secrets knows. [The Regius manuscript reads: "the Knower."] For he was a father to you and to us alike, and a faithful friend, something everyone seeks and few find. Oh, how the unshaken pillar of the Church has fallen! How the light of those in darkness has been put out, your own most particular radiance! The sweet-speaking tongue is silent; the wisest of minds is gone; the prop of the faith has been taken away, the champion of the Churches, the gentle word, the persuasive voice, everything good that is sung and known about the man. And we have become orphans upon orphanings, and I do not mean you alone, but the whole body of the Orthodox. This blessed Father went first; another followed; yet another flew away with them. Almost all the luminaries of the faithful have set, and very few are left. The sky is gloomy, wrapped in cloud, and gloomiest of all now is the Church, which has lost her stars. Yet the Sun of righteousness has taken the Fathers [The Regius manuscript reads: "the stars"], who ended their lives blessedly, and he himself promised to be with us until the end of the age. So although the present is grievous, it is also full of joy because of our hope, for we have our Fathers as defenders before God, watching over us graciously from above and moving his goodness to compassion for us. Now we must turn our words to you. You are not a flock left helpless, brothers. For your good chief shepherd, namesake of the blessed apostle Peter, has already given you form and order. While still alive he set an abbot over you and arranged everything that was needed. For a whole year, as if he were departing each day, he spoke words of farewell and equipped each one of you. It is something to pray for: that the hardship of the times may not make things turn out otherwise, but that both you and your affairs may remain as he arranged. Yet if things do turn out against you, you must not give up the truth on that account. As he directed in writing, count everything as refuse for Christ's sake, and do not betray the words of faith and truth.

This must be said to all of you, but above all to you, my lord abbot, since as the ruler is, so those he rules tend to become. Since we were once caught in heretical communion, we beg and remind you that we must not again, out of regard for visible things, NOTES.

for the sake of monasteries, vineyards, [?] and fig orchards, which a little later we too, like our fathers, will leave behind forever, betray the strictness of our profession and be defiled by communion with those of another faith, looking around at the crooked examples on every side. These things will not stand by us to help us in the time of death, in the hour of judgment, but a good conscience and a blameless life will. We urge this not because we want you to suffer anything terrible, but because we choose to help you as brothers help brothers, as the commandment bids. For we pity and feel for lord Gregory, our spiritual brother, since he is already well on in years and is the man you know, both in his bodily duties and in his spiritual achievements. Yet he too, with Christlike humility, has chosen to bear everything rather than do anything against the father's decrees. May the peace of God be given you, the peace he spoke to his holy apostles as he departed into heaven, and with it love for one another. "For by this," he says, "all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another." Take heart, my lord abbot, and you, lord Gregory, and then each one of the rest. Lift yourselves up from your grief, and make your spiritual struggle a road you travel as if it were new. And pray for us humble ones, for the better things that accompany [salvation?]

211 (6). — To Euphemius of Sardis. [?] You, blessed one, in your usual humility, never stop exalting us who deserve no honour. But we know you truly as the foundation of the word and the prop of the Church, and especially now, when this one and that one, the illustrious Fathers and the glory of the Orthodox, have left us. You go about among those in the city like almost a single beacon shining out above the lesser lights, enlightening many who are short-sighted for lack of light, and bringing still more to God through your honey-sweet teaching, which floods over them like a stream. May you be preserved for us a while longer, thrice-longed-for, and for the whole Church as well, for its support and its divine rejoicing. As for the presbyter about whom you asked us to let you know such and such, that he is [?] and has been ransomed from captivity among the barbarians, we know about it, having learned every detail from the man himself. But he does not wish, or rather will not bear, to be regulated by our rule. For you know, God-honoured one, that by the common vote both of the confessors still on earth and of those who have lately departed to the Lord, it has been decreed that priests who were once caught in heretical communion are barred from sacred ministry, until, that is, the time of [?] by providence from above. How then could we

loosen the canon and, by admitting one man, impose a precedent for all who have already been barred? In doing so we would be acting against our divine and supreme [?] leader, who will not even allow such men simply to bless ordinary food, let alone do anything more as priests. We would also scandalize the other confessors and sow discord among those who hold to strictness. Some, perhaps, have already acted on their own discretion, because the time was short and those asking pressed them hard, and have released certain presbyters after penance. But it is in no way for us to do this without the patriarch, for we must hold that the rule of exclusion stands rightly. Otherwise, where would the difference appear between those who betrayed the truth and those who did not, between those who contended nobly and those who would not choose to suffer for the good? And where would be the difference between Christ and Belial, light and darkness, if everything is mixed together, with judgment before synodal judgment, and peace before peace? This must be rejected, most excellent [?], or so it seems to us at least; but we would yield to the truth. For such a man this penalty imposed by the majority is enough, as the Apostle says, so that he may not be swallowed up by excessive grief. Yet he must not be advanced to the rank from which he was barred for his transgression until the proper time. In this way the kind of offence committed may still be punished as a warning, and the way of healing may become clear, since the penalty already imposed is sufficient. It is true that certain exceptional acts have been permitted to be performed as a priest in case of need, when no one who has kept himself safe is present, acts which your Perfection also knows, even by one who has been barred in this way. But this presbyter has in mind what he did before the barbarians [The Regius manuscript reads: "in the presence of the barbarians"], and how many he enlightened there, and he says that because of all this he ought to be released. He would not consent to be treated like those barred here. So we have left the matters concerning him to him, to act as he may judge best, neither loosing him nor binding him. Farewell in the Lord, most praised one. We and the brothers with us send you our warmest greetings. 212 (7). — To John the Grammarian. [836] I give thanks to the holy God that I have heard your dear voice, though late in the day. For I would not say that the man who earlier broke it off in an unfriendly way has found favour. [The Regius manuscript reads: "broke it off with unfriendly rashness."] But since your wise Honour, as you laid aside your grievance, also put forward in reply the argument about the venerable image of Christ, I can say this, thrice-longed-for: I found your recent letter agreeing with, not opposing, what I sent you long ago. For admittedly,

according to the short premises you have set out, every image points to something else, namely its prototype. If one must speak in the technical terms of grammar, an image would be relational, which is also called similative, demonstrative and correlative. And indeed, veneration must be offered to the image of Christ not as to matter but as to Christ himself, since the honour paid to the image passes over to the prototype. The matter is set aside by the mind's reasoning, because of the likeness formed in it. And worship, as you say, must be offered in veneration to Christ the Saviour, both before he took flesh and after the incarnation, both apart from the image and through it. No one who thinks rightly, I believe, would oppose what has been correctly defined. Nor is it unfitting to follow your examples of the sun in relation to water, and of the immaterial or mathematical triangle in relation to the material one. For suppose the sun or the triangular figure were taken to be worshipful, the one before it quivers in the water, the other before it appears in matter. Then clearly each remains worshipful after its falling into the water or its union with matter. In this way you aptly showed that our Lord Jesus Christ is to be worshipped and venerated after the incarnation just as before it. Christ, then, my good sir, is admittedly to be worshipped. But his venerable image is not to be worshipped. In the same way the sun, supposing it mingled with the water, would be worshipful, but not the image of the sun; and the triangle embodied in matter would be, but not the image of the triangle. For see: we Christians have one worship, offered to the holy and consubstantial Trinity alone by all nature, visible and invisible. It is not possible to call the venerable image of Christ worshipful. For one of two things would follow. Either its worship would be counted together with the worship of the Trinity, which is impossible, since nothing can be added to the Trinity, or it would turn out to be a tetrad. Or, if it is not counted there but is truly worshipful in its own right, we would be teaching two worships. And what else would the iconoclasts look for [?] from us [The Regius manuscript reads: "to seize"] than to prove from this that we worship with a twofold worship, worshipping the creature rather than the Creator, and are no less impious than the Arians? The image of Christ, then, is to be venerated, not worshipped; but [?] the one venerated in it [?] according to the principle of the hypostasis, not according to the principle of the essence. 21[?] (8). — To Michael, the synkellos of Jerusalem. Only now am I writing to your Honour, since by the will of God I have been fortunate enough to find a deacon

…of the letter, since we would have done this very thing even from our imprisonment, and not once only but twice, and perhaps many times. For it is not that, because you are foreigners, we are of a different kind from you. Rather, born of the one mother of adoption and shaped by the same stamp of sincere faith, we are brothers and fellow citizens, having Christ as our head. Since we make up his body, and are members in part, we are bound both to rejoice with one another in good things and to grieve in turn at painful ones. But oh, how did the current of the times force you, who had set out to travel elsewhere, to fall into the nets of those who rule here? What, then, is there to say to this [?]? Only what the sacred Scripture says: “And the driving was like the driving of Jehu.” But there it was in order to reign over Israel; here it is in order to bear witness to the truth, so that the saying might be fulfilled now as well: “Out of Zion shall go forth the word, and the law of the Lord from Jerusalem.” Here is the meaning, O most blessed one. Stand nobly, we remind you: “Glorify God in your body and in the Spirit.” Say yourself, together with the divine Paul: “I know that this will turn out for my salvation through your prayer and the supply of the Spirit of Jesus Christ, according to my eager expectation and hope that I shall be put to shame in nothing, but that with all boldness, as always, so now also Christ will be magnified in my body, whether by life or by death. For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” Behold the sweet contest, behold the blessed exchange: through brief afflictions and hardships, or rather through blows and drops of blood, to become a god and to attain the God who truly is. You have been left alone, then, as we have heard, cut off in mind from those who loved the present age; but you have been united with all who hold fast to the word of truth. Hence the choir of the martyrs wishes to receive you whole; their company stretches out a hand to take you in as a fellow member of the choir. Let us not, then, fall away from that fair choir, O revered one, nor again put to shame the hopes of all, O thrice-longed-for one. How much would you have had to toil for your name to become renowned for virtue among people both here and there? But now, having climbed as onto a mountain of virtues through your confession, you have become manifest to the world, and you shine brighter than the sun in both word and life, to the glory of our Father who is in heaven. You were led to a place [?]; you were handed over to a blasphemous tongue. How much did it not fawn on you? How much did it not lie, trying to bend you away from your lofty and divine purpose? But we know by report how great you yourself are by the grace of Christ, holding forth the word of life, pouring a stream of wisdom from your mouth, setting sound arguments against vain propositions. And we, the humble, say and make plain this: that chosen men, both of old and now, have presided over this hierarchical throne, who in the fruitfulness of their doctrines formulated

and published the teaching and the profession concerning the holy icons. And, if one may speak in the words of the Apostle, “Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more.” For here, where the Iconoclast heresy came forth as from the gates of Hades, here it has also been abolished, and will yet be abolished by the breezes of the Holy Spirit, when Christ rebukes this truly evil sea. Many are the shipwrecks of faith upon it, not so much from perversity of mind as from fear of the rulers. Yet many have escaped the surge, steered by the Holy Spirit; and many are the martyrdoms, and the writings of piety that refute every error and reveal the beauty of the truth to all faithful minds. Together with them may your blessedness also be kept safe, fighting the good fight, finishing the course, keeping the faith, until you receive the crown of righteousness. So be it.

Letter 214. — To Hypakoe, a nun. [838]

Though we are wary of writing, we are nevertheless compelled to open a thankful mouth full of praise to your honor. How long, then, will you not cease, child of a noble mother, from lending yourself to us? How long will your gifts not stop being sent to us from every side? And especially now, when many sorrows have besieged you. It was because of these that we were moved all the more to write, having learned how you acted over the remains of your blessed brother. For they say that when the coffin arrived from abroad you opened it, then embraced the remains and took them in your arms, wrapping the dead man, as it were, anew in other fresh linen. Who, then, would not have wailed at your love for your brother? Who, if present at the time, would not have shed tears, would not have lamented warmly? For even we, though far away, were touched by grief from the report alone, and it pierced our heart deeply. O bitter news! O lamentable event! What were we, and what have we become? Suddenly orphans, bereft of a brother. Perhaps even the sun groaned as it watched what happened; the moon wept at what had taken place; the stars grew gloomy as if grieving, and whatever else one might name among the elements suffered the same. Why, then, should we dwell on our sorrows, be darkened by the cloud of grief, and become like those who have lost everything? By no means, sister in the Lord. For our affairs are not without providence, nor without hope like those of the uninitiated nations; they are in the hands of God, who holds all things together. From him both we and those who begot us came into being; from him we have breath and life; and from him we have been brought to this virginal profession, the greatest of dignities. We have wept, then, as was fitting, for our brother. Now is the time for consolation, now is the day of thanksgiving. Let us therefore lay aside the garb of mourning and put on the armor of magnanimity.

We have sent ahead a brother good in appearance, in mind and in faith, just as earlier we sent ahead our kin and our parents; a little later we too shall follow. There is no one who will live and not die; no one who is born and not buried. Let us, then, prepare ourselves for our departure as well; let us make ready the provisions for our passing; let us train the sisters by our own bearing both to mourn in due season and to give thanks as is fitting. Let us show those who see us that God is glorified in us and thanked for whatever he ordains. “He gave, and he has taken away; as it seemed good to the Lord, so it has been done.” Yes, I beseech your honor as a mother and as one who bore me, or rather as a sister most dear to me: let us send forth a voice of praise; let us show a cheerful face; let us teach by our deeds that we carry the cross on our shoulders, that we have died by our own choice, and that we yield in all things to the divine commands. If you do so, how good that will be! You will gladden Christ, your immortal Bridegroom. Whereas if you grieve, you will naturally grieve him, as though you loved another more than him. Do you see where the argument has led you? To the knowledge that you are neither orphaned, nor without oversight, nor without a protector. “For if God is for us, who is against us?” If he is the one who cares for us, who is the one who opposes us? This is why I was moved now, sister, to console you. And you would do well to obey a foolish old man who has given good advice, and who truly, as he ought, makes your concerns his own.

Letter 215. — To Methodius the monk. [840]

However great your honor’s longing to see our humility, let it believe that ours for a face-to-face conversation is just as great. But since it is written, “It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy,” we must entrust our longing to him and cast our care upon him, and he will fulfil the will of those who fear him whenever he wishes. For the present, it is necessary to give fitting answers to the questions put forward by our spiritual brothers Hilarion and Eustratius through the mediation of your piety. So that what is said may be easy to follow, each question will be set out in turn, followed by its answer.

Question 1. — Concerning presbyters ordained in Rome, in Naples and in Lombardy without proclamation and without attachment to a church: whether such men should be received, and whether we should hold communion, eat and pray with them.

Answer. — In a time of heresy, not everything prescribed in time of peace is carried out entirely and without omission, because of compelling need. This is evidently what the most blessed Athanasius and the most holy

Eusebius did, both of them performing ordinations outside their own territories. And now the same thing is seen being done in the present heresy. Therefore those mentioned, if they are not openly condemned, are by no means to be shunned for having been ordained in this way, but are to be received on the four conditions [?].

Question 2. — Concerning presbyters ordained outside their territory in Sicily: whether they should be received.

Answer. — This question is like the one set out before, even if it differs in the lesser standing of the place. Clearly, then, it will have a like answer too.

Question 3. — Concerning churches defiled by priests who have entered into communion with the heresy, and which are held by them: whether one should enter them to pray and sing psalms.

Answer. — One should not enter such churches at all for the purposes mentioned, since it is written: “Behold, your house is left to you desolate.” For as soon as the heresy was brought in, the angel who watched over the place flew away, according to the saying of the great Basil, and such a church is reckoned a common house. “And I will not enter,” it says, “the church of evildoers.” And the Apostle says: “What agreement has the temple of God with idols?”

Question 4. — Concerning churches defiled by the same priests but not held by them: whether one should sing psalms and pray in such churches.

Answer. — One should indeed enter such churches to sing psalms and pray, but only if they are securely held by the Orthodox for good and are no longer being defiled. It has been laid down here that the reopening of the church be carried out by a bishop or priest who has kept himself uncompromised, with a prayer recited over it. So if this is done, celebrating the liturgy there is not out of place either. An example: when Saint Athanasius was asked by the emperor Constantius to grant this one favor, to hand over one church in Alexandria to the Arians for their assemblies, he consented, on condition that he in turn receive the same favor in Constantinople, namely that the Orthodox might assemble in one church held by the Arians.

Question 5. — Concerning saints in the body: whether one should enter their shrines, and pray there and venerate them, when the shrines are held by the defiled priests.

Answer. — The canon does not permit entering such shrines, for the reasons given above. For it is written: “Why is my liberty judged by another’s conscience?” Unless perhaps the entry is made out of necessity, solely to kiss the relic of the saint.

Question 6. — Concerning those who received the monastic

habit from the defiled priests: how they should be received.

Answer. — They are to be received if they confess that they have sinned and have done penance for some time, and then receive the seal from a presbyter who has kept himself uncompromised.

Question 7. — Concerning monks and clerics who subscribed to and entered into communion with this same heresy: how they should be received, with or without penance, if they promise no longer to exercise the priesthood; and whether it is permitted to us to give penances to such men.

Answer. — Clearly with the appropriate penances. For how could they be worthy to be joined to the Orthodox body without showing the fruits of repentance? As for whether we too may give penances to such men, this must not be refused. For it is written: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.”

Question 8. — Concerning monks who indiscriminately visit all and sundry, and pray and eat with them: whether such men should be received to common meals and psalmody.

Answer. — Since the Apostle says, “Keep away from every brother who walks in a disorderly way and not according to the tradition that you received from us,” how is it that you do not judge for yourselves what is right? If they abstain from the sinful habit and accept the fitting penance, they are to be received. But one must examine who these people are whom you call “all and sundry”: are they heretics, or people openly condemned for their way of life? For about such people the Apostle says: “If anyone who bears the name of brother is a fornicator, or greedy, or an idolater,” and so on, “do not even eat with such a one.”

Question 9. — Concerning presbyters who ate with the heretics once or twice, but did not enter into communion with them, subscribe or concelebrate: whether such men should be received to common meals and [?], without the seal or with it.

Answer. — In such cases one must observe whether the priests who ate did so with heretical priests or with laypeople, and whether these were professed heretics, or were right-thinking but in communion with the heretics. For the judgment is heavier in the case of those in holy orders. But with a worthy repentance, in either case, they are to be admitted to share with us in salt, prayers and the seal.

Question 10. — Concerning laypeople who subscribed to the heresy and are in communion with it: whether Orthodox laypeople should eat with such laypeople.

Answer. — Indifference is the cause of evils. “For between the clean and the profane,” it says, “they made no distinction.” Therefore, if the Orthodox are zealous, they must not admit such people to common

meals unless they have done penance according to Scripture and have then also withdrawn from heretical communion. But since some, fleeing dangers under the pressure of circumstances, become defiled by heretical communion, those who confess their misfortune and repent are to be received to common meals. Even this is not to be done indifferently, but by a certain accommodation to circumstances, one that brings gain to both parties and not harm to the soul.

Question 11. — Concerning those who wish to be baptized when no Orthodox or blameless priest is to be found: whether they should be baptized by the defiled priests, or by those ordained without proclamation, especially if death is pressing.

Answer. — A rule of this kind was pronounced here [?] by confessors, hierarchs and abbots. The said presbyters, though suspended from the liturgy because of their heretical communion, are permitted, when no priest who has kept himself uncompromised is to be found, to baptize and to give communion from the holy gifts consecrated beforehand by an undefiled priest. They may also give the monastic habit, say the prayer at a funeral, read the Gospel at matins, and bless the water of Theophany, as has been said, according to circumstance, so that the people may not remain altogether without hearing the Gospel and without enlightenment. If, then, this seems good to you as well, let such a rule be in force there too.

Question 12. — Concerning those who separated and are now hastening to repentance: whether it is permitted to us to give penances to such people, or to receive them.

Answer. — It has already been shown above that one should give them; and it would be superfluous to go over the same thing twice.

Question 13. — Suppose a bishop falls under an accusation and is deposed by a synod, and then after his deposition ordains a presbyter; and this same presbyter comes to a monastery, receives a penance for a time from his own abbot, and afterwards exercises the priesthood. We ask to be taught whether such a priest should be received, if he is otherwise blameless.

Answer. — Since the absurdity is obvious, you ought not even to have asked about such an offense. For Christ said: “A rotten tree cannot bear good fruit.” So not only if he did penance under his own abbot, but even if he did so under some saint, such a man is barred from celebrating the liturgy. He is not a priest, nor is the one who absolved him holy; for in this way all the canonical precepts would be overturned and would vanish.

Question 14. — Concerning presbyters ordained by the Orthodox who did not subscribe or enter into communion, but only ate with Gregory the metropolitan.

Answer. — An account of this has been given above. Whether the common meal took place with Gregory or with any heterodox person whatever, the one who shared it is released from the charge by a worthy repentance. He is restored not only to common meals with those who kept themselves safe, but also to the priesthood of which such men were deemed worthy. The measure of the penance cannot be fixed definitively, because it depends on the character both of the person and of the circumstances; so the one doing penance may be content with two or three Lents.

Question 15. — Concerning presbyters, likewise ordained by the Orthodox, who in ignorance ate with presbyters who had eaten with the same metropolitan.

Answer. — It is written: “Everything done in ignorance shall be cleansed.” So they are free from all penance.

[?] Question 16. — Concerning Orthodox presbyters, namely Hilarion, and Eustratius the monk: whether they have authority to give penances.

Answer. — It has been said above as well that they should give them. But since the question suggests whether even one who does not hold the priesthood should give penances, given the lack of presbyters and the faith of the one who comes, it is not unreasonable that even a simple monk should give penances

Question 17. — Concerning a monk who in ignorance received the holy habit from a presbyter ordained by a deposed bishop.

Answer. — It was said in another chapter that “Everything done in ignorance shall be cleansed.” And it is not permitted to shun eating with such a man; and likewise in the case of others who have made such an accommodation, it is not permitted to shun friendship with them.

These things we have set out for you, as one of like soul and a fellow laborer, as far as we were able. Pass them on with care to the brothers who asked. For not all have faith, and such matters have not been openly declared to many, not only because of the folly of those who have broken the law, but also because of the trials brought on by the rulers. In return for the many fine things the most pious brothers have sent, may they receive a worthy reward from God, and also these two small soft cloths as a token of friendship. Farewell in the Lord, most honored ones, and pray for us sinners for what is better and leads to salvation.

We have accepted the gift of your love, dear

and most true friend. As for the request you made, to know what the penance would be if you should happen to share a meal with heretics, we say this: for every sin a worthy repentance obtains forgiveness; but it is not permitted to fix penances before the sin, and so open the door to sin. For if you were to ask, “If I should happen to commit fornication, which I do not wish to do, what is the penance?”, I ought not to answer you on those terms, for that would be an encouragement to sin. Rather, this must be the answer: do not commit the sin, and do not strike your foot against a stone, whether in the spiritual or the bodily sense. But when you do stumble, then the physician gives the healing remedy to the one who entreats him and repents. I have written these things to you with great care, praying that you, beloved, may be delivered from every

Letter 217. — To Thomais, a virgin. [847]

I received your honor’s question with great joy, conveyed by the living voice of the most honored lord chief physician, since it came from a kinswoman and one who loves God. And I do not refuse to learn even from a woman, at times, what has escaped notice. Yet I do not think I have been ignorant of how the veneration of the holy icons ought to be. We, then, most honored one — to leave other matters aside for now — venerate the icon of our Lord Jesus Christ as our Lord Jesus Christ himself. But this “as” expresses likeness, not identity; otherwise it would not be an icon of Christ but Christ himself. Yet it is indeed an icon of Christ, and he is venerated in his icon, and is shown forth as one thing in another. For Chrysostom says, “I saw an angel in an image”; and again Gregory the Theologian: “And there was Polemon, peering out in an image.” Therefore Christ too is both seen and venerated in his own image. But even though this is by way of likeness, it is nonetheless he himself who is venerated and he himself who is worshiped; his icon is not an object of worship, for otherwise there would be no difference between the icon and its prototype. And yet these are two by the difference of their essence, not by the likeness of hypostasis. Moreover, if the Trinity alone is worshiped, how could the icon be worshiped as well? The Trinity would then turn out to be a tetrad, having received an addition, which is impious. And if the icon of Christ were an object of worship in its own right, then two worships would be found, and they would lead us into the worship of creatures, just like the heresy of the Arians. But away with such an impious thought! May our good God keep you unharmed and without stumbling, both in the orthodox faith and in the dignified way of life that you chose through virginity, to the pleasing of the Lord.

[?] We have already pleaded in an earlier letter that your faith, Master, and the honour and love you show us are great and beyond what we deserve. We are not what you suppose. We are sinners, of no use either to you or to anyone else. But may the reward and the mercy of the Lord be yours as you trust it will, together with the lady your wife, the consul's lady, and your noble offspring. We have received their offerings and have offered our thanks to the Lord for them. But let us turn to the urgent matter. Some people, I am told, have been upset about the phrase "second Herod," because he was orthodox and the Church commemorates him. First, it is customary to call rulers "Herod," as the Theologian says: "If you stand before Herod, keep silent." Second, let those who object consider whether the comparison is not apt. The first Herod was married to the daughter of King Aretas. He cast her out and took the wife of his brother Philip in a second marriage. Because this was against the law, the Forerunner rebuked him, and since he could not bear the rebuke, he killed the prophet. A little later he was overthrown by his own people and killed. God, the righteous judge, brought a fitting penalty on the murderer: for a holy death, a most pitiable death. Let us come to the one about whom

this question is raised. He too had a wife, Mary, lawfully joined to him from his youth. He cast her out and, in the words of the Lord, adulterously took as his wife Theodote, a lady of the bedchamber, in a second marriage. Because this was against the Gospels, Plato rebuked him to his face, and since he could not bear the rebuke, he shut the holy man away as though in a tomb. A little later he was overthrown by his subjects and blinded. God, who gives just judgment, brought a fitting penalty on the jailer: for a holy imprisonment, the loss of his eyes. So let everyone with understanding hear this: Constantine may justly be called a second Herod, since no one else from that time to this has done such a thing. He earned the name for himself by his own deeds. Let them not trouble us about this. Christ, who is the truth, cannot lie in saying that such a man is an adulterer, and whoever contradicts this is fighting against God. What the adulterer did will not cease to be spoken of until the end of the age. But because those who are upset were themselves carried away into the adultery, the reminder pains them sorely. They ought instead to confess the truth, and fall down and weep before God for having been led astray, for which they will give account on the day of judgment if they do not repent. Instead, as if to provoke God, they heap sin upon sin. Or have they forgotten

what persecution was kindled everywhere as a result, and how many committed adultery following the example set before them? The rest I keep silent about, out of respect for certain persons. Let them stop grieving with a grief that God hates, whoever they may be. For God does not show partiality to any man. And contrary to what we have received from the Gospel, if anyone preaches another gospel, even an angel, he falls under anathema, as the blessed Apostle cries out. Knowing this, let the most reverent abbot also not complain about the holy Theophanes on the ground that he was blamed in this matter. For nothing is to be honoured above the truth. Nor does he refuse to hear it, just as Peter the great apostle did not refuse to hear of his denial, nor holy David of his adultery, nor Cyprian the hieromartyr of his sorcery. As for his being commemorated in the Church as orthodox, that does not take precedence over the Gospel. Valentinian too is commemorated, not for unlawfully having two wives at once but for his right faith. So is Jovian, though not for what history records, that he was a corrupter of boys. So is Nicephorus, though not for being grasping. It would take long to speak of the others who, though discredited in other respects, received commemoration in the Church for their orthodoxy alone. Let that suffice. As for you, Master, keep this writing safe and do not make it public, since there is danger, as the bearer of the letter will tell you. The Lord be with your spirit. Amen.

219 (15). Solutions to various questions. [849.]

Question 1. Concerning a presbyter, a deacon, and a reader who held the right belief but communed with the heretics out of human fear: should an offering be made for them, or an all-night vigil?

Answer. If they remained in communion with the heretics until their death, by no means. But if at their departure they repented and confessed that they had been overcome by fear, and if, thirdly, they received the orthodox sacraments, it should be permitted that these things be done for them.

Question 2. Concerning monks and nuns who likewise died in communion with the heretics.

Answer. Let the previous answer be kept in their case too, and likewise for laypeople, men, women and children. But this has been said about the dead. If any of those mentioned is still alive and repents, from now on casting out fear and choosing to suffer for the good, then if he is a presbyter or a deacon, let him be barred from the sacred ministry until an orthodox synod is held; and after a fitting penance, let him partake of the orthodox sacraments. The

substance of the penance is abstention from the sacraments, for whatever period or periods the one imposing the penance may arrange. It is not possible to lay down a fixed rule, because people differ from one another in person, knowledge, zeal and age. If it is a monk, a reader or a nun, let divine communion be given at once when the penance has been completed; likewise for laypeople, men, women and children. Clearly among these too there is a difference according to person, rank and age, so that a single Lent may be enough penance for one who receives it. It is evident that the penance of abstaining from the sacraments also includes prayers, prostrations and abstinence from foods, according to the particular nature of the one being penanced.

Question 3. Concerning giving gifts to monasteries of men and of women.

Answer. They should be given, if the monasteries have kept themselves from communion with the heretics.

Question 4. Concerning monks or nuns taking communion of the sacraments by themselves.

Answer. It is not permitted for those outside the priesthood even to touch the divine offerings, except that under utter necessity, when no presbyter or deacon can be found, they may partake of the gift by themselves. How is this done? A holy book is set down and a clean linen cloth or a sacred veil is spread out. The gift is placed there by hand, with fear, after the hymns have been sung, and it is to be taken with the mouth. Then the one receiving rinses his mouth with wine.

Question 5. Concerning orthodox laypeople, men and women, who take communion from an orthodox priest but out of human fear mix with the heretics in everything else: how should those who are strict regard them?

Answer. With a member of the clergy, that is, a presbyter or deacon, or with a monk or nun, the strict person should refrain from eating, unless perhaps by way of economy, and even that rather rarely. With laypeople, eating together is a matter of indifference, even if such a person often happens to commune with the heresy out of fear while still holding orthodox views. But so that the sin may not go unpunished, let a small penance be imposed on those who out of fear treat the heretics with indifference. The penance is fifteen prostrations, and prayers likewise: "Lord, forgive me my sin; Lord, be merciful to me a sinner; Lord, have mercy on me," fifty or a hundred times.

Question 6. Should the orthodox give the sacraments to those who chant together with the heretics but abstain from their communion, whether presbyter, deacon, layman or woman?

Answer. As for giving them the sacraments, let him give them: to those in holy orders, by way of economy and with a penance, because they have gone along with the heretics in other matters; to laypeople, without penance. As for the reader who has kept away from heretical

communion, it is right that he partake of the sacraments, even if he goes along with them in other matters. These things are said by way of economy because of human weakness, so that, in seeking to make them entirely pure of any mixing with the heresy, we may not unwittingly cause them to give way in the essentials.

Question 7. Should one chant together with those who do not commune with the heretics but are indifferent in other matters? Or accept offerings or candles from them?

Answer. If they are in holy orders and do not bring offerings to the heterodox, what they have offered may be accepted with some penance. If they are laypeople, it should be accepted without penance. For there must be a difference, because of the dignity of the priesthood.

Question 8. Is it permitted, for those who ask us, to say a prayer, or bless oil, or light candles, or give out holy myrrh?

Answer. If they are heterodox, by no means, even if they come in faith. For light has no fellowship with darkness.

Question 9. If a monk or a nun comes to us for divine communion, what confession should be required, since their circumstances cannot be known

Answer. Whenever someone comes to receive communion and his circumstances are unknown, he should be asked whether he venerates the holy icon of Christ and of the saints, whether he does not commune with the heretics, and about any other heterodox opinion of which he may be suspected. When he has confessed on every point, and his confession is kept as a renunciation of every heresy, then the sacraments are to be given to him and shared with him.

Question 10. Is a nun permitted to give out myrrh?

Answer. When there is no priest or monk at all, let her give out myrrh, because of the urgent

Question 11. Should one enter a church held by a heretic when passing by?

Answer. Once and for all: if a church is held by a heretic, one must not enter it to pray, unless for some other reason arising from circumstances [?].

Question 12. When a brother we do not know comes to us, should we greet him with "Bless, holy one" before examining him, and ask him for a prayer?

Answer. When it is a time of heresy, before examination one should neither say "Bless, holy ones" nor ask him for a prayer. But the ordinary greeting should not be refused, according to the legislation of Saint Basil.

Question 13. Concerning a well: if it has been defiled, should the orthodox priest say a prayer over it?

Answer. The prayer should be said where there is orthodox communion. One should not go to those who commune with the heretics. For as they are defiled in soul through their bread, so they will be defiled in body too.

Question 14. Concerning baptism, since there is no church held by an orthodox priest: if someone asks us where one should seal, catechize and baptize, and what sort of people the parents and sponsors should be.

Answer. As has already been said, one must not enter a church held by a heretic, still less do these things there. But because of the lack, it is necessary for the one who is to perform the illumination to baptize in the cleanest place of a house, where the sacred rite is performed at a consecrated altar, that is, a table. Those admitted as sponsors should be people who do not commune with the heretics, and the parents likewise people who have kept themselves from it.

Question 15. There are churches with two or three apses, and one of them is unconsecrated. Should one celebrate the liturgy there or not?

Answer. If such a church is under the heretic who is commemorated, then even if one apse is not consecrated, one must not celebrate there. But if it is held by an orthodox priest, let him celebrate the liturgy in the apse that is not consecrated.

Question 16. Can someone keep hold of his church so that the liturgy is not celebrated in it by a heretic? For how long may it be kept locked, and what is he obliged to do about it?

Answer. This question has not been resolved by us, for it is for the bishop to resolve matters concerning churches.

Question 17. If there are lay men and women who are heretics, whether out of rustic ignorance or because the heresy is ingrained in them, may one eat with them or accept anything from them?

Answer. Whether they are heretics out of malice or out of ignorance, it is not permitted to eat with them or to accept what they offer, unless perhaps the ignorant have been corrected and profess to hold the orthodox faith.

Question 18. Concerning my father: is he worthy to be commemorated at the liturgy?

Answer. Whether it is a father, a mother, a brother or anyone else who remained in communion with the heresy until death, it has been said in the question above that he is not to be commemorated in the liturgy. Each person may, however, choose to pray for such people in his own mind and to give alms on their behalf. For how could someone who while still living partook of heretical communion, and was carried to his grave in that state, be included in the commemorations of the orthodox mysteries?

I have said these things not as canons, for that belongs to bishops, but as advice given out of love, for nothing is more necessary than love. If your piety judges that something should be handled otherwise, we have nothing to say about it, except to ask

for your holy prayers, since we are sinful men.

220. Letter of our holy father and confessor Theodore, abbot of the Studium, to the spatharia [wife of a spatharios] named Machara. [Cod. Vat. 655, f. 1.]

1. What a fine letter from your nobility! It was dictated in the local tongue, and to my surprise it suddenly brought your confession, like a bridal gift pleasing to God. But we are sinners, so where does such great faith and such a pious outpouring toward us come from? Or was it so that we too might learn who you are and what kind of piety you have? For you bring along with you the lord who is your head, and also draw along, like provisions from God's table, your ladies, your sisters. So the letter is worthy of God and shows the character of your piety [?]. I am not worthy to say that you have given yourselves over to my lowliness. In any case, you should give yourselves not to us but to God. We are therefore in your debt: to rejoice at your good life, to pray for holy things for you, and to give only what we have, namely to offer our [?] word, which we now offer as we put a question to you.

2. For what reason does your honour ask about divine communion, and why have you partaken of it only rarely for so many years? There must be some reason for this. For what is required is not partaking rarely, or simply every day, but partaking with a clean conscience. "For whoever eats and drinks unworthily," it says, "eats and drinks judgment on himself, not discerning the body of the Lord." If, then, you examine your own state in this way and wait for the right time out of reverence, that would be well, whether the time is shorter or longer. The rule in this matter is none other than to approach with a pure heart, as far as is possible for a human being. If someone has a fault that carries exclusion from communion, he should obviously take communion when his penance has been completed. If, again, one holds back because of heresy, this is necessary. For to take communion from a heretic, or from someone openly discredited for his way of life, estranges one from God and makes one kin to the devil. Consider then, O

So spare your precious soul, together with your sisters and your head. You told me that you are afraid to tell your presbyter not to commemorate the heresiarch.
